title: The Tyrant Invades My Dream Every Night
author: 程十七
synopsis:
Fang Jiyao is the cherished daughter of the Minister of Revenue's household — gentle, quiet, and unassuming to a fault. Yet unbeknownst to anyone, she possesses a singular gift: the ability to control her own dreams.
One night, a young man wanders into her dreamscape.
Handsome and noble in bearing, with cool, refined features — he is precisely the manner of man she finds pleasing. And so, in a moment of weakness she cannot quite bring herself to regret, she pins him down within the dream, and what follows is tender and intoxicating.

At a palace banquet, Jiyao catches sight of the Son of Heaven seated in the place of highest honor — and goes cold. It is him. Her dream lover.
The Emperor's cruelty is known to all beneath the heavens.
Jiyao's heart hammers in her chest. She does not dare make a sound, and can only console herself in silence: It was only a dream. No one knows she once defiled the Emperor within it. She is still, outwardly, a composed and virtuous young lady of good family.
What she does not notice is that the moment the Emperor's gaze falls upon her, he crushes the delicate silver cup in his hand.
The young Emperor's lips curve into the faintest smile.
Good. I've finally found you in the flesh.

chapters.title: Chapter 1
chapters.content:
In the early days of summer, after the rain, a fine mist blanketed the entire imperial city — thick with moisture, heavy with heat.

"Lady Liang Consort?"

Su Wan called out and nimbly sidestepped all in one motion. A shoe came flying out of the room, grazing the tip of her nose before hitting the ground with a heavy thud.

A candlestick followed, tumbling out after it and shattering against the floor.

Su Wan reflexively jumped back. A teacup came next — crack — it smashed right at her feet, scattering shards across the tiles.

She steadied her nerves, barely had a chance to take a step forward, and then the teapot came hurtling out, followed by plates and bowls. Freshly simmered vegetable congee splattered across the floor, still faintly steaming.

The crashing and clattering went on for a moment longer. Then, hair disheveled and barefoot, Chen Liang Consort drifted out of the room draped in white, her ashen face catching the brilliant post-rain light of the sixth month — ghastly, like something not quite human.

She wove through the wreckage on the ground and stormed up to Su Wan, shoving her aside with claw-like hands. "What kind of slop did you cook?! Even you dare walk all over me now — just you wait until I reclaim His Majesty's favour. You'll be the first one I kill!"

Having delivered this tirade, Chen Liang Consort turned on her bare heel, marched back inside, and immediately slipped, sprawling across the floor.

Su Wan lowered her eyes. She knew perfectly well this was all an act — she let out a slow breath, stepped over the rubble on the ground, went to help her up, and called out in a suitably alarmed voice, "My lady! My lady, please come to your senses!"

Chen Liang Consort lay perfectly still, eyes clamped shut.

Su Wan ground her teeth inwardly. She lifted her, set her carefully on the bed, tucked the blanket around her, and said in an even tone, "This servant will go at once to fetch an imperial physician to examine Your Ladyship."

Three fainting spells a month, every month, for a year now. Su Wan had gone from panic to habit, and now simply felt nothing at all.

She rose and left Chen Liang Consort's bedchamber. Wiping the sweat from her forehead, she took the opportunity to dishevel her own hair and rumple her clothes, drew a long breath, and set off at a jog.

In her youth, Chen Liang Consort had been a woman of exceptional beauty. Though born to a Regional Governor's concubine, she was accomplished in the four arts and well-versed in music. Within a year of entering the palace, she had caught the eye of Emperor Gao Zong and climbed step by step from the rank of Noble Lady all the way to the position of Liang Consort.

For ten years she had basked in the Emperor's favour — one step away from ascending to the position of Empress.

But in the end, she was outmaneuvered by her rival, Consort Xu, who arranged for the Emperor to catch her red-handed in an attempt on the Crown Prince's life. She was demoted and cast into the Cold Palace.

Over the past two years she had grown increasingly erratic, causing trouble without cease. The palace maids who served her had suffered punishment in her stead, one after another, until only Su Wan remained.

Su Wan had no desire to die. She would survive one more day, and then another.

Qingning Palace sat in the most remote corner of the imperial city. The walk from there to the Imperial Physicians' Court was long. Su Wan had no idea what sort of scene Chen Liang Consort was planning to make this time, and so kept to her usual unhurried pace as she ran — neither too fast, nor too slow.

Along the way, every consort's courtyard gate was shut fast, as though something of great consequence had occurred within the palace.

Su Wan frowned faintly and quickened her steps without meaning to.

When she arrived at the gates of the Imperial Physicians' Court, a guard stepped forward to block her, lips curling with undisguised impatience. "You again."

He had been on rotation this month and had already seen her twice.

"Lady Liang Consort has fainted — there's nothing this servant can do about it." Su Wan arranged her features into a polite smile. "Would the guard be so kind as to go in and ask whether any of the imperial physicians might be free?"

The guard narrowed his eyes and looked her over. The girl was dressed in a plain palace uniform, her hair slightly disheveled, a faint flush on her cheeks, brows like distant mountains, lips naturally rose-red — there was something undeniably charming about her, an artless prettiness that was difficult to name. He cleared his throat, waved her back, exchanged a word with the other guard, and went inside.

That serving girl from the Cold Palace — not bad looking at all. Better, even, than some of the consorts in favour.

Su Wan breathed a quiet sigh of relief.

The physicians and doctors of the Imperial Physicians' Court all had a gift for reading the situation and acting accordingly. Since Chen Liang Consort had been sent to the Cold Palace, the number willing to make the journey to treat her could be counted on one hand.

When she had first arrived in the Cold Palace, the Liang Consort had still had some silver to her name. Two years of her extravagances had left very little of it. Her monthly stipend was disbursed on schedule, but half of it was skimmed off before it ever reached her, leaving barely anything to spare.

After waiting roughly the time it takes to drink a cup of tea, the guard who had spoken to her came back out and gestured for her to enter.

"Thank you, sir." The smile of relief that spread across Su Wan's face lit up her features like a lotus after rain.

Getting in was the important thing. If she couldn't get in, she'd have to go back to Qingning Palace, where a half-crazed Chen Liang Consort would make her pay for it. It wasn't that she couldn't hold her own — it was that she was not permitted to fight back. If she killed Chen Liang Consort, she'd never get out of this cage of an imperial city alive.

She stepped inside. The scene of frantic activity made Su Wan uneasy, but she didn't dare ask questions — she kept her eyes down and went to find the imperial physician who usually attended to Chen Liang Consort.

"What's happening over at the Imperial Pharmacy? The medicine still hasn't arrived. His Majesty is gravely ill — if anything goes wrong, can you afford to answer for it?!"

"The medicine is here!"

"Get it to Chief Physician Wang at once!"

A light flickered briefly in Su Wan's eyes, and she quickly schooled her expression back to calm. She shuffled forward with a show of timidity to where Physician Liang stood and bobbed a curtsy. "Physician Liang, Lady Liang Consort has fainted again. Would you be so good as to come and take a look?"

Physician Liang glanced at her, considered for a moment, then rose, picked up his medicine case, and fell into step beside her. "What caused her to faint?"

Ever since Chen Liang Consort had been thrown into the Cold Palace, she had been fainting several times a month for two years running.

That lunatic is only pretending — how would I know the real reason... Su Wan thought privately. Aloud, she was perfectly cordial. "This servant doesn't know. Her Ladyship threw her dinner against the walls and then lost consciousness."

Physician Liang gave her another look and said nothing more.

The two of them made their unhurried way out of the Imperial Physicians' Court and back toward Qingning Palace. As they drew near, Su Wan's sharp eyes caught sight of two unfamiliar eunuchs entering Qingning Palace, and she quickly looked away, acting as though she had seen nothing.

So Chen Liang Consort was up to something after all.

When they entered Qingning Palace, the Liang Consort was still unconscious.

Physician Liang examined her pulse, then rose, unhurried. "Nothing serious. The summer heat has stirred an excess of liver-fire. Two doses of medicine to cool the liver, brewed into a decoction and taken orally, should do the trick."

Su Wan thanked him solemnly, paid the consultation fee, and followed him back to the Imperial Physicians' Court to collect the medicine.

The moment they left, Chen Liang Consort scrambled to her feet and padded barefoot into the side room next door. The altar had been set up in advance; the room itself appeared empty. She pulled the door shut, tamped down her racing pulse, and gave a sharp, deliberate cough.

"Your Ladyship." The eunuch Li Shun emerged from the shadows and nodded toward his companion, who removed his hat.

The companion removed his hat and outer robe, and revealed himself to be a Taoist priest.

Chen Liang Consort made no show of modesty. She reached into her sleeve, withdrew two banknotes, and held them out. "Begin."

Whether she could reclaim the Emperor's favour hinged on today.

The Taoist priest pocketed the notes and passed one to Li Shun.

Li Shun tucked it away and offered a flat reminder: "My lady, word has come from Taichu Hall — His Majesty fell gravely ill early this morning. It is feared that... his days are numbered. I understand he has already issued orders appointing the Crown Prince as Regent."

At her age, still hoping to reclaim his favour — was that not simply a dream? Pitiable, really. Ten years of extraordinary favour, then a moment of carelessness, and it came to this.

Chen Liang Consort's face went white. A flash of intense hatred crossed the depths of her eyes. She looked up at the Taoist priest. "Master — can a person's birth date be substituted with another's?"

With the Emperor gravely ill, she could use the Crown Prince to escape this wretched place. As luck would have it, the palace maid Su Wan — assigned to her by the Imperial Household Department — was quite handsome. If the Crown Prince became infatuated with her in his dreams, and she could then arrange for them to meet in person, the chance of getting out might be within reach.

Back in the day, it had been through this very Taoist priest's ritual that the Emperor had singled her out from a hall full of beauties at first sight.

"It can be done, but..." The priest's expression clouded with hesitation.

Chen Liang Consort understood his meaning. Gritting her teeth, she pushed another banknote into his hands. "For the man, use Crown Prince Zhao Heng's birth date. For the woman, use the palace maid Su Wan's."

The Taoist priest picked up his brush to draw the talisman. Li Shun shuddered, pulled the door shut, and slipped outside. This money was being earned with his life — he'd best make sure to spend it while he still had one.

"You would do well to apply yourself, Master," Chen Liang Consort murmured, her voice carrying the quiet menace of still water. Her eyes brimmed with hatred. "Whether your wife and daughters live or die depends entirely on what you choose."

She was going to get out of this wretched place. She was going to watch with her own eyes as Consort Xu was brought to ruin.

The Taoist priest gave a start — and in his moment of panic, stuck the two paper effigies bearing the birth dates on the wrong figures. His heart lurched; he covered it up and gave a solemn assurance. "Your Ladyship need not worry."

He had already bribed Li Shun. The moment they left the palace, he would collect his wife and daughters and put as much distance as possible between them and this madwoman.

Half a shichen later, the ritual was complete, and the sky had fully darkened.

Li Shun led the priest — now dressed again as a eunuch — away under cover of night.

Chen Liang Consort returned to her bedchamber and lay down. When she heard the door open and close again, she knew it was Su Wan returning, and shut her eyes with a measure of ease.

Su Wan stood for a moment outside Chen Liang Consort's room, then carried the medicine she'd collected from the Imperial Pharmacy to the back courtyard to begin brewing it. The Emperor's grave illness had thrown the entire Imperial Physicians' Court into a state of crisis, and the Pharmacy had been too overwhelmed to pay her any attention — fetching a simple prescription had taken half a shichen of waiting.

But she wasn't bothered. If anything, there was a flicker of excitement she was struggling to contain.

She had been inside this novel — The Marriage of the General — for a year now. Aside from the constant worry of keeping her head attached, life here was considerably more leisurely than her previous existence as a civil engineering worker in the real world.

In the story, the male lead was a military general serving under Crown Prince Zhao Heng — the future Great General Who Guards the Nation. The female lead was a reincarnated young woman, the sickly and neglected legitimate daughter of the Minister of Works.

The novel had very little in the way of harem intrigue. Chen Liang Consort had only been mentioned in passing, and even then it was because of her distinguished full brother.

Had it not been for that connection, a woman who had been thrown into the Cold Palace and still couldn't stop causing trouble — pretending to be mad every other day — would have had the grass over her grave growing two meters high by now.

Chen Liang Consort was extraordinarily difficult. When she had been cast into the Cold Palace, two eunuchs, ten palace maids, and a matron had been sent with her. Over the course of two years, every last one of them had died. The original Su Wan had been assigned by the Imperial Household Department and hadn't survived the first month either.

In the novel, Chen Liang Consort, too, had not met a good end. Three months after the Emperor fell gravely ill, she had been put to death by imperial decree when her full brother suffered a military defeat.

After that, the new Emperor had ascended the throne and issued a general amnesty. Palace maids who had served for over twenty-three years were, for the most part, permitted to leave.

As long as she didn't die, there was still hope of escaping this cage.

Su Wan brought the brewed medicine to Chen Liang Consort's room. The Consort was already awake, standing before the window in her inner robe, performing an operatic aria in the manner of a wandering spirit. Su Wan called her name twice without receiving so much as a glance in return, turned around, went back to her own room, ate the congee she had simmered on the side, and fell into bed.

Chen Liang Consort's madness had its own peculiar measure to it. After each episode, she would settle down for a while — there was no need to worry about another outburst.

Su Wan let the tension drain from her body. Thinking that she would soon be free of this palace, she fell asleep with a small smile on her lips.

"Your Majesty!" A man's shrill, honeyed voice poured into her ears.

Su Wan opened her eyes and found herself, without warning, standing in the Hall of Supreme Harmony. For a moment, her mind went completely blank.

What on earth was she dreaming about?

The original Su Wan had spent years inside the palace without ever setting foot in this hall. Su Wan herself could only recognize it because she had watched so many palace dramas.

"Your Majesty, the Minister of War has sent several companions for Your Majesty's selection. When would you like to receive them?" The man smiled, his voice softening somewhat.

Your Majesty? Su Wan looked down. She was wearing imperial robes. She looked around, realized she had somehow become a female emperor in her own dream, and slowly steadied her heartbeat. She turned to look at the man who had spoken. "The Minister of War is sending me companions?"

He must be her head eunuch. And these companions — they were consorts, weren't they? It was only a dream. Why was there even a plot to follow?

"Yes, Your Majesty. The Minister has sent six in total. Would you like to receive them into the imperial harem first?" The man presented a set of portrait scrolls of the young men in question. "Please have a look, Your Majesty."

The imperial harem?! Su Wan kept her excitement carefully in check. A light smile curved her lips as she took the portraits with an air of languid ease. "Show them in."

This dream had promise.

She had probably been browbeaten for so long by those consorts and palace maids who couldn't feel right without scheming against someone that her subconscious had conjured this up.

The strangest part was that she knew perfectly well she was dreaming, and her mind was sharp and clear — as though everything before her were real.

Setting down the portraits, she watched as six men dressed in white entered the hall in succession. The first few had excitement and anticipation written plainly across their faces. Only the very last one looked thoroughly reluctant, his eyes carrying a faint, icy disdain.

Su Wan's gaze swept across them. All six were beautiful in their own distinct ways, their one common trait being that each was handsome enough to make a person's knees weak.

She looked them over with detached curiosity, then let her gaze settle on the one who wore his unwillingness like an insult carved into his face — as though he had suffered some tremendous affront by being here.

"This one seems rather displeased," she said, her lips curving faintly.

"This is Zhao Heng, the young son of Vice Minister Zhao of the Ministry of Rites." The head eunuch explained pleasantly.

"Though the Minister of War arranged this, I cannot very well force a man against his will." Su Wan smiled lightly, adopting the air she had absorbed from countless palace dramas. "Take him away. Have him executed."

Zhao Heng. The name was the same as the current Crown Prince's — and on balance, it was probably better to be rid of him. After arriving in this novel, the very first time she had gone to the Imperial Physicians' Court, she had been given ten strokes of the paddle — because this man's eunuch had accused her of staring at him.

She hadn't even looked. To this day she had no idea what he actually looked like.

chapters.title: Chapter 2
chapters.content:
The words fell, and the entire Hall of Supreme Harmony went silent for a breath.

The head eunuch swallowed, leaned close to Su Wan's ear, and murmured in a low voice, "Your Majesty — they were all sent by the Minister. They cannot be killed."

Su Wan turned to look at him. The hand resting on the armrest curled slowly, fingers tapping at a measured rhythm. "Is it the Minister of War who rules this empire, or is it I?"

It's only a dream — why does it feel so vivid? If not killed, then... given a beating?

"Of course it is Your Majesty." The eunuch's smile went slightly strained, his eyes sliding sideways in an attempt to change the subject. "The border unrest has not yet been quelled..."

Su Wan raised an eyebrow, understanding.

In this dream, she was a puppet emperor with no real power. The ones who truly held authority were the Minister of War and the other court officials. Her role was to eat, drink, enjoy herself, and fill an imperial harem.

But this was her dream, wasn't it? She was quite certain she had never read a novel with this kind of plot. Something felt off, though she couldn't quite put her finger on what.

"What shall we do, Your Majesty?" The eunuch hunched lower, his face stretched into a full smile, his tone cautious and accommodating. "Keep him for now?"

Su Wan pressed her lips together and said nothing. Given the situation, a beating was technically possible, but not worth the bother.

The eunuch motioned for the guards to step back, then rose and clapped his hands together.

From outside the doors, a troupe of musicians poured in, along with several strikingly handsome male dancers.

Su Wan glanced at them and very nearly choked. Every single dancer was better-looking than the last, and they were dressed in very little — long legs and slim waists filling her field of vision, as though she had walked into a high-end men's entertainment club with a traditional costume theme.

Back in the real world, the most she'd ever done was read gossip about such establishments online. Actually going was out of the question — she couldn't afford it.

But in a dream, it was free. She could look as much as she liked, from any angle, and even take a little liberty. All in all, not bad at all.

No wonder emperors loved filling their harems. Too many beauties and the novelty wore off — one had to keep things fresh.

Su Wan said nothing. The musicians began to play, the dancers moved in graceful formations, and the Hall of Supreme Harmony became, in an instant, something resembling a dance floor lined with beautiful men.

This dream was absurd. Listening to music and watching dancing in the throne room — she couldn't think of more than a handful of genuinely dissolute emperors who had sunk to that level.

Too many palace dramas. Even her dreams had stopped making sense.

When the piece came to an end, Su Wan raised her hand, signaling the musicians and dancers to withdraw, then turned to look at her head eunuch.

"Did Your Majesty not enjoy it?" The eunuch wiped a bead of cold sweat, his smile turning awkward. "Shall I have them all executed?"

"No need to kill anyone — have them all dismissed from the palace. Make sure they receive adequate severance pay." Su Wan's expression remained pleasantly neutral. "And then find a new batch."

No point getting blood on her hands for something she'd forget once she woke up.

"Your servant obeys." The eunuch exhaled with relief.

Everyone else in the hall kept their heads bowed — unreadable.

"Would Your Majesty perhaps like to see Young Lord Zhao demonstrate some of his talents?" The eunuch glanced toward Zhao Heng and smiled his careful smile. "Something accomplished in verse, music, or chess — anything exceptional — might spare him from the death sentence?"

"Fair enough. The Minister did mean it as a gesture of goodwill — I ought to give him some face." Su Wan straightened slowly in her seat and raised her eyes to Zhao Heng. "What are you skilled in?"

Zhao Heng said nothing. Not a trace of expression crossed his face.

"You see that? Lord Zhao won't even give me the time of day." Su Wan's expression cooled. She shifted her gaze to the man standing beside Zhao Heng, her voice languid. "What's your name? What can you do?"

"Lord Zhao," the eunuch cut in before that man could answer, his tone no longer indulgent, his eyes fixed sternly on Zhao Heng. "The rest of you entered the palace willingly or not — whether any of you leaves is entirely up to Her Majesty. Lord Zhao, it might be wise to rein in that pride of yours."

Zhao Heng clasped his hands behind his back and slowly lifted his head. His dark eyes were sheeted with frost, and his bearing was such that the assembled hall might as well have been insects beneath his feet — as though he, not the figure on the throne, were the true ruler of this realm.

Su Wan found it amusing. She slumped back and propped her chin in one hand, watching him with a half-smile.

It had been a long time since she had dreamed at all, let alone a dream this entertaining. This man shared not only a name with the current Crown Prince, but something of his presence too.

By reputation, the Crown Prince was said to have a brutal temperament. Since moving into the Eastern Palace, eunuchs and palace maids had been dying there every month.

In the novel, however, all of this was revealed to be performance. Zhao Heng acted with ruthless efficiency — and though during his regency he was constantly outmaneuvered by the Minister of War and Grand Tutor Xu, he still managed to seize military power and ascend the throne.

This dream's version of him was merely the son of a Vice Minister. He could hardly compare to the actual Crown Prince.

Su Wan watched him without blinking. When she thought of her own reality — a mere palace maid who could not leave, destined to grow old and die within these imperial walls — some of the pleasure drained from her.

Dreams offered everything, but waking left nothing. She was determined to leave this palace.

"Lord Zhao!" The eunuch had run out of patience. "Don't mistake a toast for a punishment — don't make us force your hand."

At the doors, the guards moved again at his cue, flanking Zhao Heng on either side, poised to drag him out.

"Your Majesty," the man standing beside Zhao Heng said, perfectly composed. "Lord Zhao's thinking is somewhat rigid — it seems he has not yet come to terms with the fact that Your Majesty is a woman."

"Oh? And have you come to terms with it?" Su Wan's face brightened with a faint smile. "What talent do you wish to show me?"

"I have been learning a dance of late. If Your Majesty does not mind, I would be glad to perform it." The man gave a quiet smile — composed, neither servile nor presumptuous, not a trace of flattery in his manner.

"I would very much like to see it." Su Wan's eyes lit up, and a dimple appeared in her cheek. "Go ahead."

"As Your Majesty commands." The man stepped forward with a bow, and in the next instant pulled loose the ties of his outer robe, leaving only a thin white inner garment and trousers, and began to dance.

The others stepped back, wearing various expressions.

As Su Wan watched, she was suddenly reminded of the plot in the novel about the Empress's death from melancholy.

Back in the day, Consort Xu had won Emperor Gao Zong's heart with a dance exactly like this, surpassing Chen Liang Consort and claiming the greater share of his affection. The palace she was allotted sat right next to the Empress's Fengyi Palace.

After the Empress fell from favour, her health declined steadily, while the Emperor spent night after night in the palace next door. When the Empress's young son was thrown from his horse and died of his injuries, she took to her bed and was gone not long after.

Emperor Gao Zong, stricken with guilt, named his eldest son Zhao Heng as Crown Prince — a decision that had caused Consort Xu to make quite a scene. Palace rumour held that the Crown Prince's position had originally been intended for Consort Xu's son.

Su Wan's gaze drifted to Zhao Heng. His expression hadn't shifted, and his eyes were utterly unchanged — unlike the others in the dream, whose faces moved and emoted freely. He stood apart, cold and still, as though he were not a figure of the dream at all.

The man finished his dance. Without warning, Zhao Heng turned on his heel and walked out.

"Stop." Su Wan's voice was unhurried. "Someone — tie Lord Zhao up."

Zhao Heng looked back at her. His eyes were fathomless.

The guards, who had already been positioned to seize him, moved forward. Two of them took him by the arms and bound him without ceremony.

The others flinched and stepped back involuntarily, leaving a wide open space for the guards to do their work.

The eunuch wiped another bead of sweat, then smiled his broad, accommodating smile at Su Wan. "Who will Your Majesty keep for the night?"

Keep for the night? Su Wan let a brief flicker of interest cross her face, then tamped it down and raised a hand, pointing at Zhao Heng, now bound like a wrapped dumpling. "Him. I do love the bitter melon I've had to coax into sweetness."

The eunuch's smile spread even wider, though the corners of his mouth twitched a little. "Your servant will see to the arrangements at once."

"Wait." Su Wan cleared her throat, keeping her voice deliberately light. "Select one more."

It was only a dream, after all — she might as well try what it felt like to have one on each arm. She'd probably wake up in a moment anyway.

The eunuch's expression became thoroughly complicated. He leaned close and murmured low into her ear, "Your Majesty... perhaps just the one for tonight."

A puppet emperor had no freedom after all — she couldn't even choose more than one person to attend her for the night. Su Wan rolled her eyes inwardly, rose from the throne on her own, and began walking toward the exit. "Have the rest settled in quarters. I'll appreciate their talents tomorrow."

"Your servant obeys." The eunuch looked, if anything, happier.

Su Wan passed the man who had danced and paused, glancing back at him. "What is your name?"

"Xie Liting." The man dipped his head slightly.

"A fine name. The dance was fine too." Su Wan gave a light smile. Xie Liting — wasn't that the name of the brilliant military strategist in the novel who served at the male lead's side? He was the youngest son of Chancellor Xie, born of a concubine, and was on excellent terms with both the male lead and the current Crown Prince.

This dream grew stranger by the moment.

The young lord with the same name as the Crown Prince. And now this Xie Liting, who shared a name with the novel's strategist.

Yet the two men in the dream seemed to be barely acquainted.

Was she truly dreaming — or had she died in her sleep and transmigrated again? And how, while dreaming, was she able to remember the plot of the novel she had read?

Su Wan pressed her lips together, stole another glance at Xie Liting, then dismissed the thoughts that had no business being there. If he took off a couple more layers, the view would be better. A pity — though this sort of dream was ridiculous, it wasn't every night one had the good fortune of it.

Stepping out of the Hall of Supreme Harmony, Su Wan looked up and around. She found herself confronted, unmistakably, by the imperial city. She instinctively turned back to look at the hall's plaque. It read Wende Hall — the very hall where Emperor Gao Zong conducted his imperial governance.

A small jolt ran through her. That odd, unsettled feeling came creeping back.

This dream was a little too real.

Su Wan frowned and stepped into a sedan chair. Zhao Heng was shoved along by guards and fell into step behind her, his expression in the dark of the night still thoroughly cold.

The procession passed through the central gate, then the rear, continuing forward into the quiet depths of the night. The imperial city in the dark was hushed and fathomless.

Su Wan cast a sideways glance at Zhao Heng walking alongside the sedan chair and quietly calculated how to get back the ten strokes of the paddle she owed him.

Whoever he was supposed to be — this was her dream.

Not another word was exchanged. The sedan chair arrived at the imperial bedchamber before long.

Su Wan stepped off the sedan and instinctively looked up at the name plaque above the bedchamber.

The three characters of Taichu Hall shone strikingly against the red lanterns. She blinked, and tried to will herself awake.

This was Emperor Gao Zong's bedchamber! She was trapped in Qingning Palace with no way to move around, but she had read the novel — and in it, one year from now, Emperor Gao Zong died right here in this very hall!

Su Wan's heart lurched into her throat. Outwardly, she kept her composure, and walked in.

When they reached the inner courtyard, the head eunuch's face arranged itself into that particularly skin-crawling smile of his, and he clapped his hands together.

Both sides of the corridor erupted with people, who streamed into her bedchamber to arrange it.

Su Wan's expression cooled. "What is the meaning of this?"

"The Minister of War has declared that whoever Your Majesty selects this evening will be Her Royal Consort." The eunuch's smile widened. "Please, Your Majesty — the bridal matron from the Chamber of Ritual Affairs will arrive shortly to instruct Your Majesty."

Su Wan raised an eyebrow and decided to play along. "Very well."

She was an emperor, for heaven's sake — surrounded by beautiful men, and still untouched? Was it because she had been dreaming in the wrong position, or was this some projection of her subconscious? And really — was she so dull inside that she dreamed of being emperor only to end up a puppet with no real power?

No wonder the eunuch hadn't let her pick two to attend her that night... someone would have died.

But why was this dream so strange? She was trying to wake up, and she couldn't.

Su Wan pushed down the roiling questions and stepped into the bedchamber. Arranged as a wedding chamber, it had an unsettling quality to it — she felt like she was watching a horror film. Eerie and cold, with not a trace of warmth or festivity.

"Everyone out." Su Wan waved them all away and sat down on the great bed, draped in bridal red, then looked up at Zhao Heng.

This man was genuinely beautiful. A face like white jade, brows dark as ink, a nose perfectly straight, and eyes like cold stars — sharp, cold light behind them. Even bound as he was, there was a dignity to him, a gravitas, that made one reluctant to presume.

She wondered whether the actual Crown Prince was this handsome.

She had been stuck in the Cold Palace since arriving in this novel, with no opportunity to encounter anyone other than imperial physicians and guards.

When all the palace maids and eunuchs had withdrawn, Su Wan blinked, rose from the bed, and dragged Zhao Heng to a pillar not far from it. In the process, she took the opportunity to run her hands across his chest a few times.

"You are so very principled, Lord Zhao — of course I won't force you." A nice texture, at that... satisfied, she turned away, rummaged around for a moment, and tore down the red silk hanging from the bed, which she used to bind him firmly to the pillar.

Zhao Heng still wore that air of drifting just outside the boundaries of the dream — like a mannequin.

Su Wan paid it no mind. Once he was secured, she climbed back into bed and lay there staring at the canopy. What kind of dream was this? Why was it so vivid?

"Your Majesty?" A woman's voice came from outside the door. Su Wan gave a start — she knew it was the matron from the Chamber of Ritual Affairs, here to guide her through the wedding night. A warmth crept unbidden into her cheeks.

This wasn't... strictly necessary, was it?

But the eunuch paid no mind to her wishes. He opened the door and ushered the matron inside. Su Wan sat up awkwardly, doing her best to maintain the dignity befitting an emperor.

Even an emperor had to have a first time. Nothing to be ashamed of.

Su Wan lifted her head, and without warning, her gaze collided with Zhao Heng's. Those eyes were still black as ink, still still as a deep pool — cold and remote. For some reason, she thought she glimpsed something contemptuous in them.

Probably her imagination. He was the only one in the dream who didn't feel like a dream.

"Your Majesty, please first look through these illustrated guides — and afterward this servant will instruct Your Majesty in the proper conduct for the wedding night." The matron spoke suddenly, in the brisk, matter-of-fact tone of a professional fulfilling her duties.

Su Wan flushed again, picked up the guide, flipped through it without looking too closely, and said with forced composure, "That's quite enough. I know how a wedding night works."

"With the Royal Consort tied to a pillar?" The matron's voice carried the faintest hint of a smile. "Your Majesty need not be shy. I have attended two generations of emperors. You simply need to follow my guidance."

Su Wan: "..."

She needed to wake up. Right now. This instant.

chapters.title: Chapter 3
chapters.content:
Su Wan tried several times to break free of the dream — without success. She began to genuinely wonder whether she was dreaming at all.

A dream this vivid was more than a little unsettling.

"Your Majesty — shall we begin?" The matron's warm, smiling voice sounded again.

Su Wan composed herself and turned to look at her, schooling her expression into serenity. "We may."

The matron smiled and walked toward the painted screen at one side of the bedchamber. "If Your Majesty would be so kind as to come change your garments."

Su Wan stole a glance at Zhao Heng, who stood as still as a statue, and felt a wave of gloomy resignation wash over her. She knew she was dreaming. Her mind was perfectly clear. So why couldn't she wake up?

Behind the screen, the matron's smile faded. She looked at Su Wan strangely — an expression difficult to parse, faintly tinged with the grief and despair of one who has watched someone far too young face a terrible fate.

Su Wan was unnerved by that gaze. Then the matron did something unexpected: she leaned in close, breaking all proper decorum, and spoke into her ear in a voice meant only for the two of them.

"Princess, the men sent by the Minister of War and the Grand Tutor are not to be trusted. They elevated you to the throne to pave the way for the Fourth Prince, who is not yet three. When the Fourth Prince reaches three next year, you will be made to abdicate. Her Majesty the Empress truly died in vain."

As she spoke, tears rolled down the matron's face. Her aged features were ashen as cold ash. Her words were clear but carried no further than Su Wan's ear, wrapped in the peculiar stale warmth unique to old women.

Su Wan went still for a moment, then understood.

In this dream, both she and the Empress had drawn a very bitter lot. There was no one she could rely on — even the Chamber of Ritual Affairs matron had been pressed into service. She was, in the eyes of the Minister and the Grand Tutor, nothing more than a princess — a stepping stone to smooth her brother's path to power. The Empress had likely been her birth mother, who had spent her very life fighting to put her on the throne — and all for nothing.

No wonder the Minister of War had called his candidates for her harem consorts rather than anything else. She hadn't studied history very closely — most of what she knew came from costume dramas she'd watched to pass the time.

A female emperor's husband — surely that wasn't the right title? She couldn't recall what the correct term was, but it certainly wasn't that.

"I have carried this message at the Empress's request. I can die in peace having delivered it. Princess, you must grow up quickly, see those wolves for what they are, and keep yourself alive." The matron wiped her eyes again. In the next instant, her voice rose sharply, trembling with deference. "If Your Majesty does not wish to change garments, so be it — this servant has overstepped."

Su Wan opened her mouth, immediately understanding her meaning, and raised her own voice accordingly. "Get out! I am the ruler of this empire — I don't need you meddling!"

A glimmer of relief crossed the matron's eyes. She raised her hand and gave herself a sharp slap on the cheek, then retreated in tears. "Your Majesty, please rest well. This servant will remove herself at once."

Su Wan: "..."

What a consummate performer.

The matron opened the door and withdrew. Outside, voices drifted in — not loud, but audible — and the eunuch seemed, by the sound of it, quite pleased.

Once the noise outside had died away, Su Wan emerged from behind the screen and stood with her hands clasped behind her back, studying Zhao Heng where he was bound to the pillar.

She had no idea when this dream would end. Leaving him tied up for long didn't seem right. If she became trapped in this dream, and the eunuch came in the next morning, everything would be obvious.

Come to think of it, she didn't even have to wait until morning — the eunuch was right outside the door listening at the wall.

Su Wan hesitated.

Performing a wedding night as a solo act — the difficulty level was somewhat elevated.

The bedchamber went quiet. The faint sound of footsteps beyond the door grew gradually distinct. The man before her remained exactly as cold and remote as ever, as though he existed in an entirely different world — like a doll.

Su Wan bit down on her teeth, walked over, and untied the red silk. Then she grabbed Zhao Heng and dragged him toward the bed, and gave him a shove.

Zhao Heng fell backward onto the bed. A flicker passed through his ink-dark eyes — too fast for Su Wan to catch.

Su Wan lowered the bed curtains. The light dimmed at once. She turned her back, reached down, shrugged off the imperial robes, and threw them to the floor, then kicked off her shoes — deliberately loudly.

Satisfied with the preparation, Su Wan turned back around, pushed Zhao Heng further toward the wall, and lay down beside him with a flat expression. He was heavy; even after a year of doing every manner of labor in the Cold Palace, she could not move him very far.

She lay still for a moment, then glanced sideways at the bed's edge — less than a hand's width of space remaining. She lifted her foot and gave Zhao Heng a firm kick toward the wall.

Now she could lie down properly. Su Wan turned her head and found herself looking directly into a pair of ink-dark eyes, still as a deep pool, watching her without a ripple of expression.

She startled slightly, then remembered something more pressing. She looked down at what lay beneath him.

Just as she had expected... they had really prepared a white silk cloth.

Feudal society — truly the kind that devours people. Even a princess was subject to proof of her wedding night. Pitiable.

Su Wan sat up, looked down at Zhao Heng for a moment, then reached over and turned him onto his side. She picked up his left hand and bit down hard on his middle finger.

Zhao Heng's brow furrowed slightly, but his body remained utterly still — as though he felt no pain.

Su Wan didn't spare that a second thought. She pinched his finger and dripped the blood onto the cloth, then decided it wasn't enough. She padded soundlessly to the table to retrieve the long sword displayed there and opened a good-sized cut in his finger.

Zhao Heng moved at last — though still without making a sound.

Su Wan worked the white cloth until it looked like something dramatic, then smartly replaced the sword and lay back down.

Once her breathing had evened out, she nudged Zhao Heng with her foot and gritted out a low warning. "Not a word about anything you've seen or heard tonight — not a single character. Or I'll send you to the Chamber of Ritual Affairs and let you discover firsthand what it means to lose your edge."

That done, she closed her eyes, called to mind every scene she had absorbed from a lifetime of watching films, screwed up her courage, and produced a voice that was as artificially delicate and winsome as she could manage.

"My Lord Consort, you're hurting me..."

The soft, affected voice of a young girl drifted through the darkened room and made every hair on the body stand on end.

The corner of Zhao Heng's lips shifted — an almost imperceptible movement. He closed his eyes.

Su Wan called out a few more times, then rolled over to face away from him, scooting toward the far edge of the bed to put as much distance between them as she could manage, and clamped her eyes shut. This dream was too bizarre — she had dreamed herself into an emperor, then found herself constrained at every turn. There was nothing leisurely or unrestrained about it.

Sleep. Just sleep.

With any luck, she would wake up free of this dream. And if she didn't, she would have to undress Zhao Heng before the palace maids and eunuchs came in and give the appearance of a proper wedding night. What a nuisance.

Some indeterminate time passed. In a half-conscious haze, Su Wan felt a hand on her throat. She startled, snapped awake, and flung her eyes open.

Chen Liang Consort's dull, vacant eyes — black as holes — hovered just above her face. Su Wan very nearly lost consciousness from the shock. It took a long moment to collect herself, frightened and confused. "My lady — what are you doing in here?"

Good, good — she had finally escaped that strange dream. Except Chen Liang Consort looked like she might be going off again.

Could it be... had she discovered the silver Su Wan had been secretly saving? Surely not — she had been careful about that for a year, hiding every coin with great care.

Su Wan waited. Chen Liang Consort said nothing. Su Wan let her emotions settle, and the gaze she turned on her gradually grew calm. "My lady, shall I go and prepare your morning meal?"

"I have wonderful news for you." Chen Liang Consort fixed her with a stare that seemed to bore right through her, smiling and clapping her hands. "Last night I had a marvelous dream. His Majesty has promised to move me back to Yuxiu Palace very soon — I am going to rise up once more, and you shall become a First-Ranked Lady-in-Waiting. Aren't you pleased?"

Su Wan was strikingly beautiful. She had been in the palace for many years, watching wave after wave of new beauties come in. Some had caught the Emperor's eye and been granted his favour; others remained forever unseen in the depths of the palace; and still others had become lonely souls who never left these walls alive.

None of them were as lovely as Su Wan. Her looks were no worse than those of any of the women being considered as candidates for Crown Princess — only her birth fell short.

But in the inner quarters of this deep palace — were not all women the Emperor's possessions?

Were they not all his playthings?

Chen Liang Consort had long seen through it all. And yet she could not let go. Even playing mad and foolish, she was determined to drag down the Consort Xu who had ruined her, and to reclaim the position of first among the playthings.

Her gaze dimmed for a moment, though her smile only grew more brilliant. A dry, hollow laugh bubbled up from her throat. The bony knuckles of her hands went white as she slowly released the blanket she had been clutching.

"Congratulations, my lady. What joyous news." Su Wan made the perfunctory responses with no particular feeling, patted herself on the chest, and got up to turn away and smooth the bedding.

Madwoman. Coming to alarm people first thing in the morning. In three months she would be gone. Su Wan still hadn't figured out how she was going to keep herself alive when that happened — there was nothing to be flying about.

"I am tired — I must rest, lest His Majesty find my colour wanting and be displeased." Chen Liang Consort withdrew to one side and sat down, indifferent to Su Wan's lack of enthusiasm. She went on murmuring to herself, still watching with those clouded eyes, her hollow face wearing its haunting smile.

Su Wan finished tidying and left the room, heading out to fetch water to wash up.

The morning sun had already crept into the courtyard. The birds in the trees were noisy and bright. A golden dream, and it was over — thank heavens for that. The dream had been terrifyingly real.

It was a pity, though, about all those handsome men — she hadn't managed to get a proper advantage out of any of them. And she still hadn't settled the score for those ten strokes of the paddle she had suffered on the Crown Prince's account.

She cupped a handful of cold water and washed her face. Her mind cleared, and she glanced back at her own room.

Chen Liang Consort had come to her room first thing in the morning — not for money, then it was for another scheme to reclaim her favour.

Since arriving in this novel, she had treated looking after Chen Liang Consort as nothing more than a job. Qingning Palace was out of the way; no one came without a reason. The Consort's goal was to regain favour — killing more people would only cut off her own path forward, and she wasn't truly mad.

Over a year of coexistence, the two of them had arrived at a tacit understanding around the matter of performing madness.

The time hadn't yet come to be honest with this pretend madwoman. She needed to find a way out of the Cold Palace within three months, so as not to be caught up in things when Chen Liang Consort was put to death.

In the two years since she had been thrown into the Cold Palace, Chen Liang Consort had grown increasingly unstable. If Su Wan openly revealed that she knew the Consort was faking, it would only push her to become more extreme.

Su Wan wrung out her cloth and hung it up, poured a cup of water, and went back in. Chen Liang Consort was still sitting on her stool, lost in thought, smiling in a way that made the skin crawl.

She was being strange — she must have heard about the old Emperor being gravely ill. And those eunuchs who had come last night were unfamiliar faces — which palace did they serve?

Su Wan steadied herself and called softly, "My lady?"

"His Majesty is coming — I must go and make myself presentable." Chen Liang Consort touched her own face, stood up, and hurried out barefoot.

Had she not entered the dream?

Su Wan recalled that the first time she had entered someone's dream, the Consort had ended up in bed with the Emperor. The maid who attended her afterward reported that she had tossed and turned all night, pulling at her own clothes, making sounds that brought a blush to the face, her cheeks flushed red.

Su Wan had shown none of this. She had slept like the dead, and woken up pale, without the faintest trace of colour.

Could the Taoist priest have been bluffing?

Chen Liang Consort stopped in her tracks and looked back. The morning light fell on Su Wan's face as she followed behind — already striking features lit up even more, a beauty that made one envious.

Chen Liang Consort parted her lips, then thought better of asking directly whether Su Wan had had any strange dreams last night. Instead she began to calculate how she might arrange a meeting between Su Wan and Crown Prince Zhao Heng.

Today was the anniversary of the Empress's death. Li Shun had not yet sent word — she didn't know whether the Crown Prince would do as he had every year and go personally to the Imperial Household Department to select orchids for the memorial offering.

Chen Liang Consort lowered her eyes and stepped forward to block Su Wan again, breaking into one of her fits of madness. "Su Wan — how dare you try to seduce His Majesty in my presence! Last night in his dream, he set his eyes on you!"

There's no point arguing with a pretend-madwoman... Su Wan looked down and responded in a flat tone. "My lady must be mistaken. This servant did not dream of His Majesty."

"You had better not have. Otherwise I'll have you beaten to death this very moment." Chen Liang Consort shoved her aside and bolted back inside.

Could it be that Su Wan truly hadn't entered the dream?! Chen Liang Consort rushed through the covered walkway. The moment Su Wan could no longer see her, she turned and ran toward the gate.

Su Wan had been assigned by the Imperial Household Department. After Chen Liang Consort had injured her, the girl's temperament had changed — she no longer cowered, and the fear had gone from her eyes. Some other palace must have gotten to her.

Whether the dream-summoning ritual had worked, she still did not know. She would have to be careful.

Chen Liang Consort banished the tangle of thoughts and slowed her steps as she entered the front courtyard. The gate of Qingning Palace was shut tight. At the base of the courtyard wall — near the tunnel that a long-dead palace maid had dug before Chen Liang Consort drove her to it — she noticed an inconspicuous new brick. She peered at it closely, her whole demeanour lifted at once, and she broke into a quick trot.

Li Shun had sent word.

chapters.title: Chapter 4
chapters.content:
Chen Liang Consort retrieved the note tied to the brick and tucked it away quickly.

Her pulse was racing. A faint flush rose to her cheeks, and the eyes that had long been dull and vacant brightened at last.

There was hope of regaining his favour... Chen Liang Consort's eyes grew damp at the corners. She let out a slow breath, tossed the brick aside, and hurried back beneath the covered walkway, hands trembling as she unfolded the note.

Li Shun's letter said that the Crown Prince's morning had proceeded as usual — he showed no signs of having entered someone's dream — though he had killed two palace maids planted by Zhaoyang Palace the moment he woke.

Consort Xu's reach truly knew no limits! Chen Liang Consort spat under her breath, then her expression darkened, hatred blazing in her eyes.

That Su Wan might be Consort Xu's plant as well — she couldn't afford to be hasty. The Taoist priest had said that once the ritual took hold, as long as the two didn't meet in person, they would keep dreaming of each other.

Perhaps waiting a little longer would yield results. She had handed over the last of her banknotes to Li Shun and the priest; if nothing came of it, she feared she would meet her end here in the Cold Palace. Chen Liang Consort seethed inwardly, clenched the note in her fist, and marched back inside.

In the back courtyard of Qingning Palace, Su Wan stretched out her limbs and returned to her room to gather a handful of slightly damp herbs onto a tray to set out in the sun to dry. Then she went to pick some greens to cook porridge.

After arriving in this novel and finding the Cold Palace stripped of nearly everything, she had been forced to make do on her own. Over time she had quietly planted the back courtyard with all manner of vegetables.

As for leaving the palace — she had had ideas before, but with no certainty about when the old Emperor would fall gravely ill, she had only been quietly saving silver, preparing for an eventual departure without forming a real plan.

Now that the timing was clear, she needed to first find a way to leave the Cold Palace and return to the Imperial Kitchen.

Before being transferred to Qingning Palace, the original Su Wan had been a rough-labor kitchen maid. When the new Emperor ascended the throne, palace maids who had entered alongside the original Su Wan and served for ten full years were permitted to leave.

She had to move quickly and get out of the Cold Palace before Chen Liang Consort was put to death, or else she'd end up branded as one who knew the secrets of the inner palace — and that would be the end of any chance of leaving.

Su Wan finished picking the greens and straightened up, feeling considerably lighter.

She had thought about what she would do after leaving the palace. Her real-world skills were useless in this era — but she had inherited the original Su Wan's memories, and that was worth something.

The original Su Wan had come from a family that traded in fragrant herbs. When their fortunes declined and her parents died one after the other, she had sold herself into palace service to pay for her elderly grandmother's medicine and to feed her younger brother. She had known how to blend fragrances, how the properties of each herb worked, and had left behind a volume called A Compendium of Fragrant Herbs — which Su Wan had already read through once.

Once she was out of the palace, she could make a living from the art of fragrance blending. She had been quietly making the maids in various palaces her unwitting test subjects as she refined her craft.

She had also managed to save some silver for life after the palace. The monthly stipend for this period would be issued within the next day or two, and she could earn a little more then.

As for the original Su Wan's grandmother and younger brother — she would find a way to reach them, and look after them on the original's behalf once she was out. She had taken over this body, after all. Basic decency required it.

Su Wan went to wash the greens, returned to the kitchen, rinsed and set the rice to cook, and while she had a moment, went to lift the lid off a clay pot in the corner, thick with dust.

Inside, wrapped in cloth bundles, were the sachets and sorted herbs the maids from other palaces had commissioned, along with a few not yet finished.

She took out the bundles, settled herself by the stove, and methodically filled and packaged each sachet and portion of herbs.

She had finished about a dozen sachets when the pot began to bubble and gurgle. Su Wan lifted the lid, checked on it, put away the sachets, chopped the greens finely, shredded the small amount of pork she had left, and added it all in.

The Cold Palace's daily ration was two liang of meat, two of rice, and two of wheat — barely enough to keep one alive. Eating one's fill was impossible.

She wasn't fussy about food. In the real world, she had spent half the year on construction sites — takeout or instant noodles — just getting through the day was enough.

When the rice ran short, she could quietly buy more from other palaces. Meat she could trade for other things. She had grown up without money, and only money gave her a sense of security.

It was, in fact, precisely because she had been working herself to the bone to save enough to buy a car that she had dropped dead from exhaustion and ended up transmigrated into this novel.

The novel was set in a fictional kingdom called Northern Liang, a country that never existed in actual history. And yet it drew from the customs and institutions of every dynasty — all jumbled together between its pages.

For instance, the Imperial Household Department appeared to be an institution unique to the Qing dynasty, while the rule allowing palace maids to leave after ten years of service was something the Qing had never practiced.

The feudal oppression, however, was consistent across all of them — especially for the women of the imperial city.

Because of this, she had always pretended not to know that Chen Liang Consort was faking. Their ways of thinking were entirely different; trying to force a confrontation would only end badly for herself. After three months of careful observation following her arrival in the novel, she had begun quietly selling small items to save silver — every step considered with great caution.

Su Wan stirred the pot a few times, and when a fragrance began to rise from it, washed her hands, fetched a bowl, ladled out a serving, set it on a tray, and carried it as usual to Chen Liang Consort's room.

In her own way, Chen Liang Consort was something of a remarkable woman — the only consort thrown into the Cold Palace in two years to have survived. The ones who had come before her had hanged themselves or thrown themselves into wells, fading away one by one.

"Today is when this month's stipend should be distributed — go and collect it." Chen Liang Consort looked up at her, a faint glow in her eyes.

Li Shun would be accompanying the Crown Prince to the Imperial Household Department today to select orchids for the memorial to the Empress.

If Su Wan had entered Crown Prince Zhao Heng's dream last night, seeing her in person today would put him on edge — and if he was on edge, he would want to take Su Wan away. If Su Wan was Consort Xu's spy, she would simply be killed, and Chen Liang Consort wouldn't mourn the loss. If Su Wan served no one, Li Shun would handle the next step on his own.

Li Shun had left word that he would send further notice if things went as planned.

One had to try. As things stood, she was as good as dead anyway — she could not let any opportunity slip by.

"This servant will go at once." Su Wan set down the porridge, bowed her head, and withdrew.

Once upon a time, this errand had been handled by Chen Liang Consort's senior matron. After the matron and the head palace maid had been exhausted to death, the task had fallen to Su Wan.

It was thanks to this errand, in fact, that she had been able to turn a small profit each month.

Su Wan went to the back kitchen, collected the sachets she had already packaged, tucked them carefully into her clothes, and set off.

The walk to the Imperial Household Department from Qingning Palace was not short. Su Wan left her exchange signals along the way and reached the outer gate without running into anyone. The guards at the door gave her a glance and didn't stop her.

Su Wan kept her head down as she went in, found the duty eunuch, and stated her business. She was met immediately with a roll of the eyes. "Go wait over there. The matrons and maids from the other palaces haven't finished yet — it's not your turn."

"Thank you for the reminder, sir." Su Wan smiled pleasantly and dipped her head in thanks, then went to stand at the end of the queue.

The eunuchs within the imperial city all had a gift for reading the winds and bowing to those on high while treading on those below. With Chen Liang Consort thrown into the Cold Palace and the old Emperor gravely ill, the Consort's prospects of regaining favour were obvious — no one was going to be pleasant to Su Wan on her behalf.

These minor indignities didn't trouble her.

Consort Xu had gone out of her way to torment Chen Liang Consort — she was the one whose presence in the inner palace meant you could be hit whenever she felt like it, no particular occasion required. She was the one Su Wan actually needed to worry about.

In the year since her arrival, she had lived very carefully. She wanted both her money and her life. What she wanted most was freedom.

Those who came to the Imperial Household Department to collect their own stipends were mostly rough-labor maids and eunuchs from various departments. The stipends of consorts and ladies of higher rank were delivered directly to their palaces — no errand required.

Su Wan waited three quarters of an hour before her turn finally came.

As usual, she stepped forward, pressed her seal, and watched calmly as the duty eunuch skimmed half of the stipend allotted to her and to Chen Liang Consort into his own pouch.

In this imperial city, even the smallest authority could make itself lord and master.

Su Wan did not argue with him. She arranged a grateful smile on her face, murmured a pleasant "thank you for your trouble," and turned to leave.

Back near Qingning Palace, the palace maids who wanted to buy sachets were already waiting. Su Wan quickened her pace, beads of fine sweat gathering at the tip of her nose, her cheeks flushed.

"Su Wan's here." One of the maids spotted her and waved with a smile. Su Wan stopped, still catching her breath, and apologetically produced the sachets from inside her clothes. "Forgive me for keeping everyone waiting."

"Not long — we only just got out ourselves." The one who had called to her leaned in and lowered her voice with the air of someone sharing a juicy secret. "Have you heard? The Crown Prince is going to take a consort."

"They say the Minister has drawn up the list himself — six candidates, to select a primary and a secondary consort simultaneously. It sounds like the palace will be hosting a wedding before long."

"Today is the anniversary of the Empress's passing — everyone mind your tongues, or you'll lose your heads." An older maid cut in quickly.

The few maids who had been eagerly trading gossip fell silent at once.

Su Wan listened, but an odd feeling began to creep up her spine. Six candidates for the Crown Princess — and last night in her dream, the Minister of War had sent her six candidates as well.

Coincidence — or a reflection of something real?

In the novel, the female lead was also one of the six candidates the Minister of War recommended to the Crown Prince. Originally eight women had been put forward. Not wanting to repeat the fate of her previous life — entering the Eastern Palace as a secondary consort and eventually being killed — the female lead had quietly arranged to meet the male lead, who had harboured a secret and unrequited love for her through two lifetimes.

After that meeting, the female lead had manufactured an excuse to convalesce at Fuan Temple outside the capital, traveling with a small retinue of servants. The male lead had arranged for a group of bandits to set upon them on the road; the female lead was thrown into a fright, fell unconscious, and thus escaped the fate of being selected for the palace.

One of the other candidates happened to be in mourning for her mother — considered inauspicious — and was disqualified on those grounds.

In the end, the Crown Princess was still Consort Xu's niece, and no one was selected as secondary consort.

Su Wan exhaled without drawing attention to herself. Her instinct said she was reading too much into it. It was just a dream, and unlikely to recur every night — probably not a reflection of anything. Though come to think of it, her position in the dream and the current Crown Prince's situation in life did share something of a resemblance.

The Crown Prince had originally been intended to be Consort Xu's son. It was the Emperor's guilt toward the Empress that had led him to name his third son Zhao Heng as Crown Prince instead.

As for the first two princes — one had lost the use of both legs and spent his days in a wheeled chair, while the other had been born unable to speak.

Chen Liang Consort had spent ten years in the Emperor's favour without bearing him a single child. Consort Xu, by contrast, had been as prolific as a rabbit — seven children in twelve years, the last still being tended by a wet nurse.

Su Wan couldn't help a private thought: no wonder Consort Xu coveted the position of Empress. Seven dragon balls collected — of course you'd want to summon the dragon.

"Su Wan — this is your silver. My mistress will want the jade-orchid-heart variety in half a month's time, same place." The first maid pressed a small piece of silver into Su Wan's hand. "I'll be going."

Su Wan accepted the silver with a nod and a smile.

The other maids paid their silver and placed new orders, then dispersed.

Su Wan let out a quiet breath, looked both ways, then made her way back to Qingning Palace with an unhurried air.

She hadn't slept well the night before, and her energy showed it — she kept yawning as she went through the gate. Chen Liang Consort was quiet today, without the usual keening and wailing that filled the courtyard.

She left the Consort's share of the stipend with her, then returned to her own room and buried herself in her work.

With the old Emperor gravely ill, the consorts and maids of every palace were on edge, all living in dread of being chosen to accompany him in death. Su Wan was frightened too — but she still had a chance of getting out. The maids who had served their mistresses since the very beginning had no such chance.

By the time she had sorted through all the herbs she needed, the sky had grown dark.

Su Wan prepared dinner and brought it to Chen Liang Consort, waited for her to finish, then went back to her own room and ate a simple meal of porridge and a mantou bun. She washed up, collapsed onto her bed with exhaustion, and closed her eyes.

Please, no more of that dream tonight. Being a helpless puppet of an emperor was even less free than being a palace maid.

chapters.title: Chapter 5
chapters.content:
Su Wan was exhausted enough that she was asleep almost the moment she closed her eyes.

She dreamed of nothing. When she woke, the sky outside had not yet fully brightened. She stretched lazily, rolled around in bed for a bit, and then, once her mind had cleared, got up with purpose.

Sleeping well meant keeping moving — people in this world rarely lived long, especially palace maids inside the imperial city.

When a mistress fell out of favour, a maid fell sick with no right to call an imperial physician. Getting a couple of prescriptions was already considered fortunate.

What this place was most sorely lacking was penicillin. Eating something bad or getting an infected wound could be a death sentence.

Once she was out of this palace, she intended to try extracting penicillin herself — she couldn't let herself die before she ever got to taste freedom.

Su Wan put on her palace dress and went out the door, only to stop short. Chen Liang Consort was standing right outside, dressed in white.

Her heart skipped a beat.

Please, not that. Her orientation was perfectly normal.

"Su Wan, His Majesty says he is coming to collect me today — why isn't he here yet?" Chen Liang Consort smiled and reached out with her claw-like hands, wanting to grab her. "Go and ask His Majesty for me what time he will arrive. Go on."

Little wretch has started guarding herself against me — she bolted the door last night so I couldn't even get in.

Su Wan sidestepped her hands and went straight to the well, her tone flat. "My lady, His Majesty is likely not yet awake at this hour. Please go back inside and wait."

"Not awake?" Chen Liang Consort repeated, and then suddenly began to scream curses. "It must be that pig Consort Xu who has stolen His Majesty's attention again — it must be!"

She grabbed a broom as she ranted and stormed toward Su Wan with it, full of menace.

Su Wan glanced at her, eyebrows lifting calmly. "My lady, there seems to be some commotion out front — perhaps it is His Majesty's head eunuch come to call on you?"

Trying to use a madwoman's act to take out your frustrations on me — not that easy.

"Is that true?" Chen Liang Consort stopped and cocked her ear for a moment, then dropped the broom and ran toward the front, bare feet slapping on the ground.

An entire year, and she had not managed to land a single blow on Su Wan. The girl knew better than she did what the proper shape of madness ought to look like — it was positively infuriating.

Su Wan leaned over to check, saw that she had left the courtyard, and cupped a handful of cold well water to wash her face, then picked up her handmade toothbrush and began to brush her teeth.

Chen Liang Consort was definitely up to something. She didn't usually come running to Su Wan's door two days in a row like this.

Thinking this, Su Wan finished brushing and rinsed thoroughly, then slipped quietly after her.

In the front courtyard, Chen Liang Consort was dancing about like a wraith, chanting under her breath: "Your Majesty, how do you find my figure — better than Consort Xu's?"

Su Wan watched from behind a courtyard pillar for a moment, then shook her head and turned back.

Every woman in this inner palace was pitiable in her own way. Entering this place was like entering a prison — scheming every day just to stay alive, with endless labor on top of it.

Whether maid or consort, every life here was held in the Emperor's hand. Surviving meant walking on a floor paved with the bones of others.

"His Majesty says I am indeed better looking than Consort Xu — stop flattering people, Your Majesty." Chen Liang Consort laughed, stole a glance at Su Wan's retreating figure, and clutched the note Li Shun had sent. In a coy, lilting voice she murmured, "Your Majesty, I am quite tired from dancing — shall we go back inside?"

At that, she hitched up her skirts and ran, gasping by the time she reached her room.

Door shut, Chen Liang Consort leaned against it to catch her breath, then unfolded the note with trembling hands. The Crown Prince had not gone to the Imperial Household Department yesterday. The orchids had been selected by the Department itself and sent to Fengyi Palace. Word from the front was that letters sent north had gone unanswered, and with the situation at the border feared to be deteriorating, the Crown Prince had not slept the night.

Chen Liang Consort read to the end and gave a bleak, hollow smile. She went and lit a paper-spill from the tinder box, held the note to the flame, and watched it burn, her heart as cold as dead ash.

After being cast into the Cold Palace, she had written to her full brother thirteen times. Not one reply had come.

Even if the war in the north was won, her brother would not say a word on her behalf. She had never looked out for the Chen family in her years of favour — and so this ending was her own doing.

When the note had burned away, Chen Liang Consort composed herself and walked numbly to her bed, falling onto it heavily.

There was still hope. The Crown Prince had only just begun his regency, and with the border still unsettled he had no attention to spare for matters of the heart.

Wait a little longer. That Taoist priest's arts had been powerful — he had helped her soar once before, and could surely do so again.

Chen Liang Consort let her thoughts run until exhaustion finally took her and she slept.

Back courtyard.

Su Wan vigorously went through her self-invented exercise routine, resting between each set before continuing. The last of the morning's dim light faded and the sun rose. When she had finished the full routine, she was covered in a fine layer of sweat. She reached down to feel her abdominal muscles — more and more defined — and smiled with satisfaction.

The body was the foundation of revolution. She had decided to break out of this place, so she had better be as healthy as possible.

When the sweat had dried, Su Wan picked some more greens as she always did and returned to the kitchen to start breakfast.

The herbs she had sorted yesterday still needed more time to dry. The maid who had ordered the jade-orchid-heart blend served in Yongning Palace — her mistress was Consort Liang Shu.

The jade-orchid-heart used sandalwood, agarwood, agastache, and nutmeg with sour jujube seed — the fragrance was richly layered and long-lasting, with a calming and sleep-inducing effect, very well suited for those suffering from insomnia.

The trouble was that everything in the palace was distributed by the Imperial Household Department, and gathering even these herbs had taken considerable effort — she had purchased them bit by bit from maids across various palaces.

If she could buy freely, she would have saved far more silver by now.

The previous sachet she had given away as a free trial to the maid in Consort Liang's palace. The maid had placed a proper order yesterday — most likely she had passed the sachet along to her mistress.

Su Wan thought it over and decided that this time she would make the blend even finer, then ask the maid to petition Consort Liang on her behalf — a word from the Consort to have Su Wan transferred back to the Imperial Kitchen should be quite workable.

If it came to it, she would write out the full recipe for the jade-orchid-heart and how to blend it, and offer it freely.

As long as she could get out of this palace, she would develop many more recipes in the future.

Su Wan thought it through carefully and decided the plan was solid. Her internal goal grew sharper and clearer.

Before long, breakfast was ready. Su Wan ladled out a bowl of porridge, added a mantou bun, and carried it to Chen Liang Consort's room. The Consort appeared to have exhausted herself with her performance and was now sleeping deeply. Su Wan exhaled quietly, backed out on light feet, and left.

She put on a daily show of madness — it was exhausting for her too, in its own way. Pitiable.

Back in the courtyard, Su Wan ate her fill, propped a ladder against the palace wall, climbed up, and lowered a small basket over the other side.

The surrounding area was deserted. From the nearby Yichun Palace, she could hear a few maids in the garden playing shuttlecock, their silver laughter drifting over now and then. Su Wan waited until she was certain no one had spotted her, then nimbly climbed back down and tied a small bell to the other end of the rope.

The amount of fragrant herbs each palace received was limited, and few were willing to sell what they had. Earlier this month she had spent a fair sum quietly cultivating a contact with the eunuch in the Imperial Household Department who managed the herb stores. He was currently on duty, and had promised to slip some herbs out to her over the next few days.

She returned to the kitchen, ate her breakfast, cleaned up, went to her room, shut the door, and settled in to work on blending and refining the jade-orchid-heart formula.

With the Emperor gravely ill, Consort Xu was busy eyeing the position of Empress and keeping a close watch on the Crown Prince's selection of a consort — she had no energy to spare for harassing Chen Liang Consort, which gave Su Wan considerably more peace.

Three days passed. Su Wan still had not produced a more pleasing version of the jade-orchid-heart. Chen Liang Consort, aside from drifting up to Su Wan's door every morning like a wandering spirit, had not caused any further trouble.

And the bell hanging on the wall had stayed utterly silent, as though it were broken.

On the fourth night, Su Wan saw Chen Liang Consort settled to sleep and returned to her own room, lying down. As she was drifting off, the bell on the courtyard wall gave a clear ring. She heard it, sat up at once, got out of bed, and went out.

She climbed the wall, hauled up the basket, counted out the silver, took the herbs, put the coins in, and lowered the basket again.

The eunuch waiting below pocketed the silver and disappeared into the night.

Su Wan pulled the basket back up and found a letter inside. She hurried to secure the herbs, climbed back down, and went to her room.

The eunuch had probably assumed, given who she served, that the errand was on Chen Liang Consort's behalf, and had included the letter along with the herbs. The letter said that the candidates for Crown Princess had not yet been decided, and that in addition to Consort Xu's niece, the daughter of Grand Chancellor Xu-Han had been put forward.

Su Wan burned the note, put away the herbs, and sat for a moment in thought.

This diverged from the novel's plot — the Crown Prince was actually refusing to select a consort?

Then again, she thought, it had nothing to do with her. However fiercely the court factions fought, the conflict wouldn't reach Qingning Palace. Crown Prince Zhao Heng had the male lead to help him, and he would ultimately destroy both Grand Tutor Xu and the Minister of War and ascend the throne. Her only job was to plan her own escape, and wait for the new Emperor to take his place so she could leave the palace.

In this world where medicine was scarce and the average life expectancy was perhaps thirty years, her own remaining time was likely not abundant — dying young was the norm, and long life the exception. She had better live well.

Su Wan sighed softly, went to bolt the door tight, blew out the lamp, lay back, and closed her eyes.

She didn't know how much time had passed when she became dimly aware of a voice nearby. She frowned and opened her eyes with reluctance.

In the dim light, a man's face was just inches from hers. High-bridged nose, sharply defined features, and those pitch-black eyes — still as a deep pool — looking quietly at her.

Su Wan swallowed hard, her peripheral vision sliding away to the side.

She was having that terrible dream again.

The man said nothing. He simply watched her, steady and unblinking, his eyes without the faintest ripple.

"You insufferable man — what are you staring at?!" Su Wan sat up with a kick, irritable.
