His arms went around her. His voice dropped low, barely above a murmur, like something whispered against hair: "There, there... that's it..."

He bent his head, and a slow, thorough cascade of kisses fell from her forehead down to the corner of her lips. His palm pressed firm and sure at the curve of her waist, and then he lifted her cleanly off the desk. At her sudden, startled little sound, he settled her neatly onto his own lap.

At some point he couldn't quite identify, Qin Yuan noticed that the chair beneath him had changed. It was now a wide, cushioned reclining chair.

And the surface of the writing desk, which had been bare moments ago, now held a thin book, lying open to the second page.

Late spring turning to early summer. The clothes were light.

Two young bodies pressed close together. Through the thin layers of fabric between them, each could feel the warmth of the other with startling clarity.

Qin Yuan cursed inwardly. He knew perfectly well what was about to happen.

He didn't want any of it. But his body was not taking orders, and its reactions were anything but mild.

...

The reclining chair began to creak in a slow, rhythmic sway.

Jiyao had ridden winged horses in dreams before. But this was unmistakably different.

There was no flying. No clouds beneath her. It was even a little tiring. And yet, with that sense of fullness, of being suspended somewhere between earth and sky, she had only to bow her head to find the young lord's handsome face looking up at her. That alone, for Jiyao, was a sensation unlike anything she had known before. Thrilling, exquisite, entirely her own.

In less than a quarter of an hour, Jiyao's mind went blank. She slumped, trembling, against the young lord's chest.

Perhaps it had simply been too much. The dream ended, abruptly and on its own.

...

In the inner chamber of Zichen Palace.

Qin Yuan jolted awake again. He drew a slow, deliberate breath, and in the privacy of his own mind, cursed several times with considerable feeling. The desire to do violence had never been stronger.

In the dream just now, the woman had done entirely as she pleased with him, and left him in this state on top of it.

By the light filtering into the inner chamber, he cast a brief glance downward, then pushed back the covers, got out of bed, and walked directly to the washing room.

He remained there for quite some time before emerging with any sense of relief.

He had previously resented what he saw as being compelled, in that dream, to take a woman by force. Now, in hindsight, he realized he had been looking at it entirely wrong. There had been no taking by force. It was he who had been used for someone else's enjoyment.

The woman in that dream had simply been satisfying herself. That much was abundantly clear.

Qin Yuan seethed quietly.

Whatever her origins, whoever she was, she would fall into his hands one day. He would make absolutely certain of it.

He would not let it go.

...

Tonight's attendant in Zichen Palace was Chang Shouan, the emperor's most trusted eunuch.

Hearing the emperor linger in the washing room, with the occasional faint, suppressed sound drifting through the door, Chang Shouan, though a man of the inner palace himself, had served the late emperor long enough to have a reasonable idea of what the situation involved.

He dared not make a sound. Only when the emperor emerged did he ask, quietly and with great deference: "Shall Your Majesty have water prepared?"

"Prepare it."

Chang Shouan immediately saw to it.

After bathing, the cold edge of Qin Yuan's temper softened somewhat.

He gave brief thought to summoning the Daoist Cloud Crane back to the palace for another consultation, then dismissed the idea. The old priest's abilities were suspect at best, and his so-called dream-control technique worked only intermittently. Besides, the particulars of these dreams were far too difficult to explain to another person. He put the notion aside.

...

Jiyao lay on her bed feeling rather like a fish that had been flung onto dry land.

Her body was limp and entirely without energy.

She breathed in long, unsteady gulps, her face burning hot.

After a good while, she quietly pushed herself upright and changed out of her inner garments, then drank two full cups of cold tea in quick succession.

The cold tea settled in her stomach and took some of the unnatural heat from her face.

Jiyao lay back down. The scenes from the dream surfaced in her mind without invitation. She raised both hands and covered her burning cheeks, a vague, unaccountable guilt creeping over her.

Had she been a little too bold in that dream?

But the next moment she was already talking herself back: it was fine, it was fine. It was only a dream. No one would ever know. If not in dreams, then when?

And when she thought about it honestly, it really had been thrilling.

Not everything in that little book was exaggeration.

The night lay quiet around her. The sand in the hourglass slipped down, grain by grain. A long time passed before Jiyao finally drifted off to sleep again.

This time it was simple and dreamless.

When she opened her eyes, it was morning.

As usual, Jiyao washed, ate a light breakfast, and made her way to the girls' academy.

By the time she arrived, her fourth and fifth sisters, Pinyao and Qianyao, were already there.

Among the six Fang cousins, the fourth and fifth were unlike any of the others. They were twins, identical in face, identical in dress, inseparable from dawn to dusk.

"Did Second Sister go out yesterday?" Pinyao asked suddenly.

Jiyao could tell them apart not by sight but by sound. Their faces were mirrors of each other, but their voices were distinctly different.

"I did, yes," Jiyao answered, mildly surprised. The twins tended to exist in a world of their own, rarely initiating conversation with the others.

"Were you preparing a birthday gift for Grandfather?" Pinyao pressed.

Jiyao nodded. "Yes."

"What did you prepare? We haven't gone and chosen the same thing, have we?" Pinyao continued.

Jiyao smiled and answered honestly: "I painted a scroll and sent it out to be mounted yesterday. It should be different from whatever you chose."

"Good." Pinyao let out a breath. "It is different. Fifth Sister and I made an embroidered screen together."

The Fang girls had no need to sew for a living, but they had all learned needlework. Qianyao's embroidery in particular was exceptional. The two of them working together on a screen for Grandfather was sure to produce something beautiful.

"That's wonderful," Jiyao said warmly. "Your embroidery is lovely, and it shows your filial hearts. Grandfather will certainly be pleased."

Pinyao smiled, but did not say more.

Jiyao, however, found her thoughts beginning to wander, stirred by the mention of painting. She drifted between memories of yesterday's outing and the painting scene from last night's dream, her face going alternately pale and flushed, until the female teacher walked in and Jiyao forced herself to set aside everything improper and attend to her books.

...

That evening, a light rain crept in without warning.

After dinner, Jiyao asked Shuangxi to light an extra lamp. She took out the chess manual her grandfather had given her a few days ago and began slowly working through it.

Some of the positions inside were unlike anything she had seen before and required careful study.

She had barely settled in when a commotion arose outside.

"Miss, Third Miss is here!"

The words had barely left Shuangxi's lips when Third Sister Zhiyao swept in through the door, draped in a rain cape, trailing damp air and the smell of rain, swaying as she walked. "Second Sister!"

Jiyao stood up in surprise. "Third Sister, what are you doing here? It's still raining outside."

chapters.title: The Beauty
chapters.content:
"I missed you, so I came." Zhiyao laughed and handed her rain cape to Shuangxi. "What are you doing, Second Sister?"

"Reading a chess manual," Jiyao answered plainly.

She didn't quite believe her cousin's excuse. They saw each other nearly every day at the academy. What was there to miss? Something had to have brought Zhiyao out here in the rain at this hour.

But Zhiyao seemed in no hurry to explain herself. She wandered over, picked up the chess manual, leafed through a few pages, then set it back down with a rueful expression. "It's so difficult. I don't know how you can stand reading it."

Jiyao smiled. She knew her cousin well: the girl was lively and restless, and at the first sight of a page dense with text, she would start complaining of a headache. A chess manual was practically a different language to her.

Which made it all the more surprising when Zhiyao actually volunteered to play a game with her.

"Really?" Jiyao was skeptical.

Zhiyao lifted her chin. "Of course it's real. When have I ever said anything I didn't mean? Second Sister, I'll be honest with you: my game has improved enormously lately. I might even be better than you now."

"All right then, let's try." Jiyao brought out the board and pieces.

Unfortunately, Zhiyao's game had not improved quite as dramatically as she claimed. She lost three rounds in quick succession.

"Again!" she declared, refusing to concede.

Not wanting to leave her cousin looking too badly beaten, Jiyao quietly let up, feigning carelessness to lose two games back to her.

"Second Sister, are you letting me win?" Zhiyao asked.

"No," Jiyao said. "I was just distracted. And you caught me off guard with that move..."

Zhiyao's eyes shifted. She said slowly: "Second Sister, do you know you have a habit?"

"What habit?" Jiyao asked, curious.

"When you're lying, you blink very fast."

Jiyao was momentarily speechless.

Did she? She had honestly never noticed.

Then Zhiyao burst out laughing. "Ha! I was teasing you."

Jiyao: "..."

The evening wore on. After a while of laughing and bickering, Zhiyao finally got around to saying what she had really come for, in a halting, hesitant voice: "Second Sister, the truth is... I came because I was afraid you were angry with me."

"Angry?" Jiyao looked up from gathering the chess pieces, genuinely puzzled. "Where did that come from? Nothing has happened between us."

Zhiyao looked embarrassed. "Because of the engagement. I'm younger than you, and yet I was engaged before you. That's one thing. But then with the Wen family too..."

She worried about the order of things, a younger sister engaged before the elder. She didn't know what people outside the family would say, whether they would assume something was wrong with Second Sister, that she had been passed over. And she worried that it might affect Second Sister's future marriage prospects. As for the Wen family business, while it wasn't her doing, the fact remained that their family had valued her and dismissed Second Sister. They were both members of the same family. That kind of unequal treatment wasn't something she could simply overlook.

She had turned it over in her mind for days before deciding to bring it out into the open. Partly for her own peace of mind. Partly because she refused to let outsiders be the reason their bond as sisters was strained.

"I'm not angry with you," Jiyao said, with quiet sincerity. "You haven't done anything wrong."

"You really aren't?"

"Really." Jiyao considered, then added: "Marriage is arranged by the elders. They have their own considerations. As for the Wen family, the fault is theirs, not ours. If I let something like that make me angry, what kind of person would I be?"

Besides, she knew very well that anger was the most useless thing in the world. And even if she were angry, the target of it should certainly not be her third sister.

Seeing the sincerity in her cousin's face, Zhiyao felt the knot she had been carrying in her chest finally loosen. She threw her arms around Jiyao's shoulders. "I knew it. You're the best, Second Sister."

Jiyao smiled. And truthfully, the words weren't wrong. Of all her sisters, she and Zhiyao were closest in age and had always been the most companionable.

Zhiyao gripped her hand and wheedled: "It's too late to go back now. I'll stay the night and sleep here with you. Can I?"

The rain was still falling outside. Jiyao was perfectly glad to have her stay. She nodded at once and told Shuangxi to bring an extra set of bedding, then fetched a clean sleeping robe from her own wardrobe.

The two sisters had never shared a bed before, and there was something exciting about it for both of them.

Especially Zhiyao. With the weight of that long-carried worry finally off her mind, she was in particularly high spirits. She chattered away in bed without stopping, a stream of small girlish thoughts: complaining that her mother played favorites, describing how strict the teacher at the academy had been lately...

Jiyao listened quietly, adding a word here and there, a faint warmth moving through her. There was something she almost envied, though she wouldn't have said so aloud.

Without noticing when it happened, drowsiness settled over her, and she slipped into sleep.

With someone beside her, she was on her best behavior, and let go of any thought of steering the dream. She simply let herself rest.

Zhiyao, however, found it harder to fall asleep in this unfamiliar room. In the dim darkness, she turned her head and looked at her cousin lying beside her, and felt a complicated little ache she couldn't quite name.

Second Sister was the most beautiful of the six of them, graceful and refined, with a figure that drew the eye. She was gentle and composed, never grasping for anything. Whenever any of the sisters needed help, she gave it without hesitation.

It was just a shame that she had lost her parents so young. Zhiyao could only hope that when it came to marriage, Second Sister's fate would not be so much worse than hers or First Sister's.

...

Chang Shouan was one of the oldest of the palace's inner servants.

He had attended the late emperor and had since served the current one. In more than ten years, he had accumulated no particular merit, but committed no serious offenses either.

On this day, the Grand Empress Dowager summoned him to Shoukang Palace, as she occasionally did, to ask after the emperor's welfare.

Three years ago, following a palace upheaval, the emperor's birth mother, Consort Wang, had been sent to a retreat outside the capital. Now the only senior mistress remaining in the palace, aside from the emperor himself, was the Grand Empress Dowager Bai. She was advanced in years and rarely concerned herself with affairs of state. Her one remaining preoccupation was the emperor.

"The emperor is well in all respects, Grand Empress Dowager," Chang Shouan began. Then, for reasons he could not quite explain even to himself, he added: "It is only that, of late, his temper has been somewhat... elevated."

The Grand Empress Dowager frowned. "If his temper is hot, tell the imperial kitchen to prepare cooling dishes. And have the physicians brew a formula to reduce the heat. He must be troubled by affairs of court."

"It isn't that sort of heat," Chang Shouan said carefully.

"Then what sort is it?"

Chang Shouan hesitated, then, steeling himself, pressed forward: "It is... that the imperial harem is empty, Your Highness."

Strictly speaking, it was not his place to say such a thing. But he had served at the emperor's side for many years and carried the man's deep trust, and he felt he could not in good conscience pretend ignorance of the situation, neither for the sake of the imperial health nor the matter of an heir. He had not dared to raise it with the emperor directly. Now that the Grand Empress Dowager had asked, he chose to broach the subject in this roundabout way.

The Grand Empress Dowager sat very still for a moment. "I understand. You may go."

"Yes." Chang Shouan bowed and withdrew.

The Grand Empress Dowager remained unsettled for a long while after.

She was the late emperor's principal consort, not the current emperor's blood grandmother. The relationship between them was a title more than anything else. Years ago, when Prince Jing had held the regency, she had used her influence in the inner palace to quietly shield Qin Yuan on two separate occasions.

After Qin Yuan came fully into his power, he had treated her with great consideration and respect. She, in turn, was sensible enough not to meddle in court affairs, and contented herself with a comfortable retirement, expressing her care for the emperor in small and occasional ways.

Their relationship was, all things considered, a pleasant one.

But now, the Grand Empress Dowager felt that perhaps she needed to do something.

...

That evening.

The moment Qin Yuan returned to Zichen Palace, he knew something was wrong. The inner chamber smelled of face powder and perfume, and there were people in it who should not have been there.

Four young palace women stepped forward as he entered, dropping at once into a low curtsy. "Your servants greet Your Majesty."

The four were varied in height and build, each with a different kind of charm. But they shared two things in common: all four were strikingly beautiful, and all four were dressed in a manner designed to attract attention.

Qin Yuan's brow drew together. "Who sent you?"

The young emperor's authority was formidable. At the first word from his mouth, all four women sank to their knees. "In response to Your Majesty, we were sent by the Grand Empress Dowager to attend upon you..."

"The Grand Empress Dowager?" A cold, humorless smile touched Qin Yuan's lips. She had stayed out of everything for years, and now, on a whim, without so much as a word of notice, she had stuffed four women into his chambers?

And dressed like this, at that. Her intent was obvious.

In the dream, he was already being forced into entanglements with a woman against his will. And now, in reality, four more were being pushed at him at once?

The temperature in Qin Yuan's gaze dropped several degrees. "Where is Chang Shouan?"

At that moment, Chang Shouan was in the middle of teaching his adopted son the precise method of brewing the emperor's preferred tea. He heard the shift in the air and hurried forward. "Your Majesty..."

"Explain."

Qin Yuan's face was composed, his voice giving nothing away.

Chang Shouan felt his heart clench.

He had served this man long enough to know that this particular expression was not a good sign.

He did not dare to lie. He hunched his shoulders, making himself as small as possible, and answered as truthfully as he could manage: "In response to Your Majesty, this servant visited Shoukang Palace today, and mentioned that Your Majesty had seemed... rather short of temper lately, and ventured the private guess that it might perhaps be owing to the emptiness of the inner palace. The Grand Empress Dowager, out of care for Your Majesty, arranged for..."

The emperor's eyes narrowed slowly. The look that settled on Chang Shouan was pointed as a blade. "I did not realize who your true master was."

It was a heavy thing to say. Chang Shouan dropped to his knees with a thud. "Your Majesty, this servant knows it was wrong. This servant had absolutely no such intention. This servant only saw that Your Majesty was..."

"These women, send them back where they came from. As for you..." Qin Yuan cut him off. His gaze rested on Chang Shouan for a long, deliberate moment. "You are no longer needed at my side. Go serve the Grand Empress Dowager."

Chang Shouan's face fell. "Your Majesty! This servant knows it was wrong. Please, Your Majesty, grant your mercy!"

The Grand Empress Dowager's position was unimpeachable, certainly. But Shoukang Palace was essentially a place of quiet retirement. Serving there was nothing compared to serving at the imperial side.

Yet he knew well that once the emperor made a decision, no one could undo it. He could only console himself with a thin thread of hope: the emperor had merely reassigned him, not dismissed him entirely. Perhaps, someday, there might be a chance to return.

Chang Shouan's heart was full of bitter regret. He cursed his own moment of foolish overreach. He knew better than to press his case further at a moment like this, and so he held his tongue and led the four women out of Zichen Palace toward Shoukang Palace to report back.

The Grand Empress Dowager had not yet retired for the night.

She had just finished removing her ornaments when the news reached her. She sat very still for a moment, wondering if she had misheard. "All of them sent back?"

"Yes."

"Not a single one kept?"

She found it difficult to believe. She had selected those four women herself, with great care. They were all genuinely beautiful, and she prided herself on having an eye that had not dimmed with age. And Chang Shouan had implied that the emperor...

"Yes," the attendant confirmed. "Not one was kept. And Chang Shouan himself has been assigned to Shoukang Palace."

The Grand Empress Dowager was quiet for a long time. "I see. See to it that the women are properly settled. And arrange lodgings for Chang Shouan as well."

The old woman turned it over in her mind, and understood: the emperor had been displeased by her sending beauties to his chambers.

He had not lashed out. He had simply returned them all. That, at least, meant he was still giving her some measure of face.

But the Grand Empress Dowager truly could not fathom the reasoning behind it. The emperor was young, vigorous, and in the full heat of his years. How could he refuse beauties? Even if he had no intention of using them, surely having them there to look at was no hardship.

It couldn't be a physical matter, or Chang Shouan's words would not have implied what they did.

The Grand Empress Dowager shook her head, baffled, and let out a long, heavy sigh.

chapters.title: Restraint
chapters.content:
The matter did not stir much of a ripple within the palace.

That the emperor did exactly as he pleased was something everyone had long since accepted. What no one had anticipated was that he would refuse even the Grand Empress Dowager's gesture without a second thought.

Zichen Palace was very quiet. Several attendants stood with their hands at their sides, heads bowed.

After his bath, Qin Yuan could still seem to catch a trace of powder and perfume lingering in the air. He found it profoundly irritating.

His eyes narrowed. "Open the windows," he said, his voice cool and flat.

The attendants moved at once to comply.

A mild night breeze drifted in, and the air inside the chamber freshened immediately.

Qin Yuan closed his eyes briefly.

He disliked the scent of powder. He disliked the scent of peach blossoms.

The latter was a more recent addition to his list.

That night, perhaps heaven itself had taken pity on him. Qin Yuan did not dream of the peach grove.

He slept soundly until morning.

...

That same night, Jiyao also slept well.

Though because she and her cousin had talked into the small hours, both of them fell asleep late. The following morning, they overslept entirely. It was Shuangxi who woke them.

Opening her eyes to the brightness beyond the bed curtains, the two sisters sat up in alarm and scrambled to wash and dress.

Early in the morning, the Third Household sent over the clothes and book bag Zhiyao would need for the day.

The two of them rushed through a hasty breakfast and hurried off to the academy at a near-run.

They made it just in time. They had barely settled into their seats when the female teacher made her unhurried entrance.

The sisters exchanged a look, and the same small smile passed between them, before they simultaneously, and without a word, looked away.

That had been close.

Life for the Fang girls was simple and full.

The days went on, and another one slipped by before Jiyao quite noticed.

That evening, she took out the chess manual she hadn't finished the night before and returned to it slowly. It was nearly the hour of hai before she finally set it aside and went to bed.

Lying under the covers, her thoughts drifted without direction.

She thought of Grandfather's birthday. She thought of the scroll she had prepared. She thought, in a vague and wandering way, of that little illustrated book.

Without knowing when sleep came, she was simply inside a dream.

It was the fourth month now, and the real peach blossoms had long since fallen. But in the dream, they blazed as bright as ever.

She must have gotten too absorbed in the chess manual before bed. In the dream, she found herself playing chess. And the one sitting across from her, the one she liked so dearly, was the young lord.

Seeing him, Jiyao felt her cheeks warm at once, the scenes from the last dream rising unbidden in her mind.

And with that warmth came a flicker of guilt.

She remembered that she had meant, in that dream, to simply let things go where they would on their own, not to steer anything. But in the end she hadn't been able to resist taking the reins.

Well. What was done was done.

This was her dream, after all. She was the one in charge. And that last dream had been, if she was honest, genuinely thrilling.

That thought settled something in her, and the faint tension dissolved into something closer to shy anticipation. She looked down at the board and realized that what the two of them were doing could barely be called playing chess. They were essentially following the chess manual step by step.

That kind of game, where the outcome was already visible, held little appeal for Jiyao.

She raised her eyes and looked at the young lord across from her, and felt a sudden stirring of intent. She pressed her hand gently over his, just as he was about to set a piece down, and said slowly: "I don't want to play chess anymore. Let's do something else."

She had tried two things from that secret book in her dreams now, and both had been exhilarating. Especially the last one. Her curiosity was at its height, her interest sharp and eager. She was like a child who had just discovered a new toy and couldn't wait to find out all the ways it could be played with.

But the young lord looked at her without any apparent comprehension. "Something else? Like what?"

Jiyao looked at him sideways, eyes glinting with subtle suggestion. "What do you think?"

Honestly. Did she have to spell it out for him?

...

Qin Yuan had gone to bed late.

He wasn't even sure at what point he had fallen asleep. Somewhere in that hazy in-between, he caught a trace of a fragrance, faint as a memory. He collected himself. And found he was standing in the peach grove again.

A hand was resting over his on the chess board. Across from him, a woman's eyes were curved with laughter, full of a warmth that seemed to bloom from within. "What do you think?" she said.

Qin Yuan could not retain her face. But her brows moved with such life, and the voice was unmistakably familiar. He recognized her at once.

And he knew with equal certainty that he had fallen into that strange dream again.

The scenes from last time rushed back to him. The chill that settled over his features was immediate and unmistakable.

Here again.

Finding that he could move, Qin Yuan pulled his hand free without hesitation and stood. "Think of what?"

Jiyao blinked. Something had gone sideways.

This was not where things were supposed to go.

But she recovered quickly, and rethought the matter. Perhaps somewhere deep inside, she had decided the dream felt too easy, too predictable, and wanted it to have a little more resistance, a little more edge.

Ordinarily, Jiyao would have been happy enough to let the dream unspool on its own for a while, to let it build its own texture and detail. But right now there was something she wanted more. She had no patience to spend herself on minor complications.

So she said nothing. She simply looked at him, steady and unhurried, and thought quietly to herself: He knows. Not only does he know, he's glad, and he's going to carry her inside and explore all the rest of this with her, together.

Sure enough, the moment the thought took shape, the young lord gave a soft, low sigh. There was something indulgent in it, something resigned, and something that might have been tenderness. "You. What am I going to do with you."

Qin Yuan discovered, in almost the same instant, that he had lost control again.

He didn't understand what had triggered the shift. He could only feel himself moving toward her, without choosing to, bending down, and lifting her cleanly into his arms.

The way he held her was like holding something irreplaceable. Steady, careful, deliberate, he carried her at a brisk pace toward the room.

Inside, he set her down gently on the bed and latched the door.

The sky outside had darkened at some point, though when, neither of them could have said.

The room was lit by several lamps. Their amber glow fell over everything, softening the edges, casting a warmth that shimmered with something else beneath it.

Jiyao reached under the pillow embroidered with mandarin ducks and drew out the thin little book. She looked at him and beckoned.

Qin Yuan's eyelid twitched. He knew what it was from the cover alone.

He had no interest in it whatsoever. In fact, something closer to revulsion stirred in him at the sight of it.

But he had no say in the matter. He sat down beside her and was made to look at the book with her, page by page, while she turned each one with unhurried deliberation, until she reached the third.

"This one." Jiyao pointed to the illustration, then looked up at him, her eyes bright with curiosity. "What do you think about this one?"

The first two had both been quite pleasant. The third ought to be fine as well.

The vein at Qin Yuan's temple jumped. So she intended to work through the whole thing, illustration by illustration?

He had heard the Daoist Cloud Crane say with confidence that he was the Son of Heaven, that his constitution was sound and his person free of any spiritual entanglements. Yet Qin Yuan could not help associating this woman with all the creatures he had ever heard of: the peach blossom spirit, the fox maiden, the lascivious female ghost...

If she were a palace maid, or anyone else who existed in the real world where he had power, he could simply have her removed.

But here, he nodded, with every indication of sincere enthusiasm, his voice dropping into something warm and intimate: "I think it very fine as well."

And then, like a man wholly given over to desire, he kissed her face with something that looked like reverence, with something that looked like love, and while she was still lost in that, gently eased her out of her robes.

The room was neither too warm nor too cool. Everything was just right.

Qin Yuan stood at the edge of the bed, cursing himself silently, and lifted her with arms that did not belong to him, arranging her so she faced him.

...

A tremor moved through Jiyao's body.

She was a little excited. And a little frightened. Terrified, actually, of losing her balance.

She locked her arms tightly around his neck and said in a rush: "Be careful. Don't let me fall."

Her voice came out soft and plaintive, half a command and half a complaint.

The moment the words were out, Jiyao felt a flicker of embarrassment. That had been unnecessary. This was her own dream. How could she possibly fall?

Sure enough, she heard the young lord say, in a low, steady voice: "You won't fall. I won't let you."

Jiyao smiled, bright as a lamp suddenly lit. She kissed the tip of his nose, then tilted her head and breathed softly against his ear.

It was a small trick she had learned from the notes beside one of the illustrations. According to the text, it had its uses.

It evidently did. Because in the very next instant, she felt a clear and unmistakable change in him.

The tips of his ears went red. His grip on her tightened sharply, and with one swift, fluid motion he shifted her upward and settled her again, more firmly than before. What had already been a close and complete union became something closer still.

Jiyao very nearly cried out. Her arms tightened instinctively around his neck, and she became acutely aware of his breath, hot and unsteady, spilling directly against the hollow of her throat.

That sensation, warm and strange and slightly maddening, spread through her entire body in a slow wave.

But she couldn't attend to it properly. Not now. She could only hold on, her mind emptied of everything, dissolving into the warmth of him.

...

Whether he had any control over the dream or not, in this strange place Qin Yuan always found himself fully present, every sense alive, the experience indistinguishable from reality.

He despised this, the helplessness of it, the way he was moved and used like a puppet with no say in the matter. And yet the soft, pliant body in his arms, the faint, clean fragrance that drifted around him, the sensation of being suspended somewhere above the ordinary world...

There was no denying that it was unlike anything else. Something new. Something unexpectedly acute.

And so even as Qin Yuan's mind pulled back in revulsion, his body was, without question, experiencing a pleasure that had no easy name.

Then the woman in his arms trembled once, spent and heavy, and collapsed against his chest.

In that moment, Qin Yuan realized he had regained control of the dream.

The sensible thing, he thought, the thing he should do, was push her away. He could not harm her within this dream, but at the very least, he could put a stop to what was still happening.

But his whole body was wound tight, his mind buzzing, and this was very much not the moment for sensible decisions.

His body moved before his mind could catch up with it. He kept going, without meaning to, without choosing to, until the sensation crested and broke over him completely.

...

The night was very dark.

Qin Yuan opened his eyes in the blackness. His expression was shadowed. His face looked as it had never looked before.

He had always believed his self-control to be beyond what ordinary men could manage. It was one of the few things he had never doubted about himself. And yet just now, in the final moments of that dream, he had failed to hold the line.

He had been wide awake. And yet.

Perhaps he could not entirely blame himself. It had happened too quickly. He had not had time to react.

If there was a next time...

No. There should never be a next time.

He drew a slow breath and closed his eyes for a moment. He pushed everything else down, got up, and walked to the washing room.

chapters.title: An Encounter on the Road
chapters.content:
The room was very quiet.

The bed curtains were drawn tight, letting in not a single thread of light.

Jiyao lay perfectly still, not moving at all.

The scenes from the dream played back before her, one after another, vivid and unyielding.

Her cheeks burned, and her heart was beating far too fast.

Thrilling, yes. Genuinely thrilling. But in the wake of it, she felt strangely hollow, her mind washed clean of thought.

After a while, she quietly sat up, tidied herself, and changed her inner garments.

She moved as gently as she could, but even so, Shuangxi, sleeping in the outer room, stirred. Drowsy and murmuring, she asked: "Does the young miss need something?"

"No, no, go back to sleep. I'm fine." Jiyao answered quickly, flustered and embarrassed all at once.

However bold she was in dreams, in waking life she was still a sheltered young woman of a respectable household. If anyone ever found out about such things, she would never be able to face the world again.

Fortunately, Shuangxi was still thick with sleep, and did not ask anything further. She turned over and drifted off again.

Jiyao let out a long, quiet breath, and padded softly back to bed.

A glance at the hourglass told her there was still some time until dawn. She made no attempt to direct another dream, and simply went back to sleep like a reasonable person.

The next morning, she went to the academy as usual.

During a break, her youngest sister Mengyao came to her with a request: "Second Sister, how many different forms of the character 'longevity' can you write?"

"Hmm?" Jiyao looked puzzled. "What do you mean?"

Little Mengyao pulled a face. "Grandfather's birthday is coming up. I want to give him a Hundred Longevity scroll as a gift. But you know how it is, a Hundred Longevity scroll needs a full hundred different versions of the character, and I can't come up with that many on my own. Second Sister, please help me."

Jiyao smiled. "All right. I happen to have some ready-made ones. After school, I'll send them over to you, shall I?"

"Yes, please! Thank you so much, Second Sister." Mengyao beamed and curled her arm around her cousin's, visibly relieved. She had known that Second Sister would be easy to ask. Second Sister never said no to this sort of thing.

After school, Jiyao returned to Haitang Court and dug out the hundred different forms of the longevity character she had prepared two years ago when she was making an embroidered longevity piece of her own. She had them sent over to her youngest sister.

The messenger had not yet returned from Sixth Miss's courtyard when Haitang Court received another unexpected visitor.

It was her second elder cousin, Fang Lin.

Fang Lin was the second son of the eldest branch, three years older than Jiyao. Like the other Fangs, he had been given a handsome face. Young as he was, he had already passed the prefectural examinations. He was preparing for next year's provincial exams and spent his days either buried in books or calling on distinguished scholars for guidance. He had little interaction with the female cousins.

The last time Jiyao had seen him was on the anniversary of her father's death, when he had accompanied her to the family grave site outside the city out of kindness.

So his arrival now surprised her. "Second Brother, what brings you here?"

"These are sweets from Xingfang Confectionery. See if they suit your taste." Fang Lin set the sweets down first, then explained his real purpose: he wanted to borrow a book.

"Which book?"

"Master Zhoushan's 'Treatise on Rivers and Seas.' Very few copies exist in circulation. Grandfather mentioned that Second Uncle's collection might have one. I'd like to borrow it, if it isn't too much trouble."

"Not at all." Jiyao nodded. "Wait here a moment, Second Brother, and I'll go find it."

"I'll come with you." Fang Lin stood, preparing to follow.

Jiyao startled and waved her hands quickly: "No need, no need. You wait here, I'll be right back."

Her father's study contained more than respectable books.

Though they were tucked away out of sight, if her second brother happened to see something that should not be seen...

Absolutely not. Out of the question.

Fang Lin was mildly surprised by her reaction, but asked nothing further and simply nodded. "Then I'll trouble you, Second Sister."

Jiyao went to her father's study and searched for quite a while before finally locating the "Treatise on Rivers and Seas." She brought it out to her cousin.

Fang Lin accepted it carefully. "Good. I'll take this home and return it in a few days."

Jiyao gave a small smile.

By the time she saw her second brother off, night had already fallen.

Perhaps because she had gone into her father's study, she felt distracted and unsettled all evening. She had half a mind to move that little illustrated book to a different hiding place, but on reflection, decided there was probably nowhere more discreet than where it already was.

She left it where it was.

That night, lying in bed, Jiyao thought about the recent stretch of evenings: she had been so absorbed in the dream's more exciting diversions that she had not properly spent time with her parents in quite a while. A quiet pang of guilt moved through her.

Over the several nights that followed, she took deliberate control of her dreams, letting herself simply be with her parents, at their side as a daughter should be.

For her, those dreams were gentle rather than exciting. But they carried their own quiet comfort.

...

Qin Yuan had been in reasonably good spirits lately.

He was the Son of Heaven, with all authority in his hands. Beyond the matters of court, there was little in his daily life that genuinely troubled him.

Three consecutive nights without that strange dream made things even lighter.

He was in such a settled mood that even when a court official invoked the virtue of filial piety and suggested that his birth mother be brought back to the palace, Qin Yuan did not lose his temper. He dismissed the proposal with a single, measured line: "The Empress Dowager's health is delicate. She requires the quiet of her retreat outside the city."

To stop officials from making an issue of filial devotion, Qin Yuan was especially attentive toward the Grand Empress Dowager, showering her with every mark of respect.

When the Grand Empress Dowager saw that the provisions for Shoukang Palace had, if anything, increased rather than diminished, she relaxed completely. She had been worried for days that she had angered the emperor. Now it seemed there had been no lasting change in how she was treated.

All was well.

With time on her hands, the Grand Empress Dowager summoned Chang Shouan for a chat.

Chang Shouan had, of late, been attending to duties in Shoukang Palace, so her summons were easy enough to accommodate.

"Don't look so miserable," she told him. "When the time is right, I'll put in a word with His Majesty on your behalf. It's possible he'll let you return."

Chang Shouan nearly leaped with relief. He dropped to his knees and thanked her profusely.

"Don't be so formal." The Grand Empress Dowager waved a hand. "If anything, you were caught up in my business..."

Before she could finish, Chang Shouan was on his knees again, insisting repeatedly that he would never presume to say such a thing.

The Grand Empress Dowager sighed and decided not to dissect the question of who bore the greater responsibility. She asked instead, in the easy tone of idle conversation: "Tell me honestly, do you think the emperor was angry that day because those women I sent were palace maids?"

She knew only fragments of what had happened in the palace upheaval years ago, but she had heard enough to know that among those involved, aside from Consort Wang, certain palace women had also had a hand in it. A great number of people in Zichen Palace had been put to death afterward, enough that it might fairly be called a purge. The emperor's habit of refusing female attendants perhaps had something to do with that.

Chang Shouan managed a strained, uncertain smile, not quite sure what to say.

In his own private estimation, the more likely explanation was that His Majesty had been furious at them both for taking matters into their own hands. But he could hardly tell the Grand Empress Dowager her guess was wrong. He hesitated, then offered a diplomatic noncommittal: "As for that, this servant honestly cannot say."

The Grand Empress Dowager gave a small frown. "Never mind. Whatever he does, I'm not going to interfere anymore."

She said it, but she also knew that with the Empress Dowager absent from the palace, there were certain things that still fell to her, whether she wanted them to or not.

...

Time moved quickly.

Before Jiyao knew it, another rest day had arrived.

By her calculation, the Longevity Offering scroll she had left at the mounting shop should be ready. Grandfather's birthday was imminent, and she needed to go collect it.

After the unpleasant encounter last time, she thought carefully and decided she would bring a guard along this time.

She changed into an appropriate outfit, collected her receipt slip, and was just about to inform her Third Aunt when she stepped out of Haitang Court and ran directly into her second cousin, who had come to return the borrowed book.

"You're going out?"

"Yes."

"Where to?"

Jiyao explained briefly.

Fang Lin laughed. "Perfect timing. I've had enough of books for one morning and wanted some fresh air anyway. I'll come with you, and you won't need to trouble a guard."

"Thank you so much, Second Brother." Jiyao was genuinely pleased.

She had been mildly dreading the conspicuousness of bringing a guard along. Having her cousin as an escort was far better in every way.

Fang Lin rode on horseback while Jiyao traveled by carriage. They reached the mounting shop without incident, and she collected her scroll.

The mounting was done beautifully, exactly as she had hoped. Fang Lin admired it generously, praising both the painting itself and the quality of the craftsmanship.

The whole outing went smoothly. What no one had expected was that on the way home, they would encounter the imperial procession.

From a distance, two outriders came thundering forward on horseback, shouting in carrying voices: "Make way for the Emperor! All civilians clear the road!"

The people on the street reacted at once, parting like water to either side.

Inside the carriage, Jiyao heard the clamor and felt a sudden spike of alarm. "Second Brother! Our carriage..."

She did not often venture out, but she knew well enough that commoners were expected to step aside when the emperor passed.

The problem was that the sides of the road were narrow, and the carriage was wide. There would not be room to pull over easily.

"It's all right." Fang Lin's voice was quick and calm. "There's a side alley just ahead. We can take shelter in there. We have enough time."

"All right." Jiyao settled slightly.

The Fang family's carriage withdrew into the nearby alley.

Out on the main road, the imperial guard cleared the way, and the emperor's procession swept through at a brisk pace.

Standing there, Jiyao found her thoughts drifting unbidden to the rumors she had heard about the emperor over the years.

He had ascended the throne as a youth. He had outmaneuvered the regent prince. He had suppressed the Buddhist temples, imprisoned his own mother, executed his brother...

Grandfather strictly forbade any discussion of court affairs in the household, but some stories were simply too startling to be entirely contained. Even a girl of the inner chambers heard things from time to time.

Jiyao was tempted, briefly, to sneak a glance, to see for herself what this famously cruel and fearsome emperor actually looked like. But her nerve failed her. She kept her head dutifully lowered and waited beside the carriage.

The whole street was hushed. Only the beat of hooves on stone could be heard.

After a long while, the procession had completely passed, and the road filled again with its usual noise and life.

Jiyao exhaled and climbed back into the carriage.

"Strange," Fang Lin murmured to himself on horseback, frowning. "What would bring him out of the palace at this hour?"

His voice was barely audible, but the moment the words left his mouth, he seemed to realize he had overstepped. He cleared his throat with a quick, covering cough.

Inside the carriage, Jiyao caught the faint shape of his voice but not the words. She made no comment.

She didn't know either.

But the next day, she found out.

chapters.title: Satisfied
chapters.content:
It was her second cousin Fang Lin who told her.

The following evening, he came to Haitang Court and, without even pausing for tea, leaned in and lowered his voice: "Second Sister, can you guess what that procession yesterday was for?"

"I couldn't begin to guess," Jiyao said, shaking her head.

She understood perfectly well who "that person" referred to, but as for the purpose of his outing, she had no idea at all.

"Have you heard of General Huo, the old general?"

Jiyao nodded. "I have."

Who in this dynasty had not? The Huo family had served the crown with distinction for generations. The commander who had been sent to reclaim the southwestern territories was the old general's own son.

"They say the old general fell gravely ill. He was at death's door. When that person heard the news, he personally went to the Huo residence to pay his respects, a gesture of remarkable honor." Fang Lin leaned in a little closer, his expression conspiratorial. "And then, can you guess what happened?"

Jiyao blinked. "What happened?"

"The old general had been deeply unconscious. But when all the commotion reached him, he apparently woke up. The shock was so great he vomited blood on the spot..."

"What?" Jiyao stiffened. "He vomited blood?"

Fang Lin continued, unhurried: "Yes. But here's the thing: after he vomited the blood, the danger passed. He pulled through."

"That can actually happen?" Jiyao stared at him, eyes wide. "Well, that's good then. That's a good outcome."

"Exactly, which is why I came to tell you." Fang Lin smiled.

Though that was not his only reason.

Fang Lin had always had a lively temperament and an ear for news. Grandfather strictly forbade the younger generation from discussing court affairs, but after learning of this, he had been burning to share it with someone and had nowhere to put it. Telling people outside the family would be unseemly. On reflection, he had thought of the cousin he had been out with the day before.

Second Sister was quiet and reserved, and she never gossiped. Telling her was safe.

"I heard the Huo family is extraordinarily devoted to that person, and that when they helped bring down..." Fang Lin got a few words further before catching himself, and cut off the sentence with a deliberate cough.

Jiyao offered a mild, uncomprehending smile, as though she hadn't registered a thing.

Even so, Fang Lin made sure to remind her: "Second Sister, this goes no further. You mustn't tell anyone."

"I won't say a word." Jiyao gave him a sincere nod. "Trust me, Second Brother."

Fang Lin drained his tea and left, visibly satisfied.

True to her word, Jiyao said nothing to anyone about the old general.

But the story was hardly a secret to begin with. Within a few days, it had spread throughout the capital on its own.

Some said the Huo family had already prepared a coffin. For the old general to wake up now was surely divine protection, or perhaps the blessing of the emperor's own celestial aura. The explanations multiplied and blurred together, and no one could say for certain what was true.

What was beyond dispute was that the emperor was in high spirits. He dispatched a number of imperial physicians to the Huo residence and sent a continuous stream of valuable tonics and rare medicines to the household.

None of which, of course, had much to do with Jiyao.

The emperor and the old general both existed in a world far removed from hers. She was genuinely glad to hear the general had turned the corner, but that was the extent of it.

Her own life went on as it always had.

That night, Jiyao dreamed again.

She was reading a chess manual by the window when she looked up and saw the young lord walking toward her.

She paused, and set the manual down.

She had been spending her recent dreams with her parents, focused and deliberate. It had been several nights since she had dreamed of him.

Now, seeing him unexpectedly, she took in those cool, clear features she knew so well, that bearing that had always pleased her. His face was still exactly the way she liked it.

She hesitated for a moment, then made no effort to send him away. She let the dream continue as it would.

She opened her arms to him, smiling brightly: "Come here. Hold me."

...

The pleasant mood Qin Yuan had been carrying for days dissolved the instant he saw the woman in the dream.

The past few days had been smooth, nothing troubling from court, and even the gravely ill old General Huo had improbably pulled through. Everything had been going quietly well.

And now, tonight, here he was in that dream again.

He had lost count of how many times this had happened. He could never remember her face, but her voice had become unmistakably familiar.

The words "come here, hold me," and in particular that last word, brought the previous dream rushing back with unwelcome clarity. He remembered holding her, acting against his will, and in the final moments, failing to hold the line despite having control of the dream.

The memory darkened his expression immediately.

He stood where he was without moving. Jiyao tilted her head, puzzled. Something was off. Why was he being strange again?

But it didn't matter. Small complications only made things more interesting.

She rose and stepped toward him, smiling. "What's the matter? Are you upset with me for not seeing you these past few days?"

Even as she said it, she was already thinking: he's a little cross with her, but he can't quite bring himself to stay cross. He's going to pick her up and hold her, and spin her around.

She pictured it precisely: the skirts lifting as he turned, spreading outward like a flower in bloom.

The moment the thought fully formed, Qin Yuan found himself robbed of control again.

He stepped forward, unable to help himself, and pulled her into his arms.

It was not the first time he had held her, but he was still caught off guard by how slight she was, how soft, barely anything to hold onto.

Without entirely knowing why, his mind leaped back to the reclining chair in the study from that earlier dream. The way her waist had felt in his hands then...

His expression remained flat, but something tightened in him. He held her and turned in place, wordlessly, once.

Her sleeves and skirt billowed, and her laughter rang out bright and clear as silver bells.

The sound of it conjured, unbidden, a very different sound from a very different moment.

Jiyao had no idea what was going through his mind. She laughed and said: "All right, all right. You can put me down now."

Before he did, she was moved by a small impulse. She pressed a quick kiss to his cheek.

Qin Yuan glanced at her, and in that instant he found he had regained control.

Without a word, he raised his fingers and wiped the faint dampness from his cheek.

Jiyao saw it.

She blinked, and felt a flicker of indignation. What was that supposed to mean?

She made a small, disgruntled sound, leaned forward, and kissed him on the lips. She even gave the corner of his mouth a pointed little nip.

And she thought: He should be very moved by that. Very pleased. He should deepen the kiss. Then kiss her collarbone, her earlobe, and a few other places besides. A dream lover conjured from her own imagination should, by all rights, be entirely devoted to her and attuned to her every wish.

This was her dream, and in it, she was sovereign. Whatever she wanted strongly enough would always come to pass.

This time was no different.

Qin Yuan discovered almost at once that he had lost control of the dream again.

His hand closed around her waist, pressing firmly, as he deepened the kiss with considerable force. His other arm held her locked against him, as though he intended to press her into himself entirely.

Everything in the dream was real in the most immediate, physical sense. Jiyao felt as if something had lit a small fire: wherever he had touched, wherever he had kissed, her skin felt faintly feverish, faintly itching with warmth. She trembled, and something secretive and eager stirred inside her.

Her thoughts drifted, soft and unhurried: perhaps the fourth page of the illustrated book, then?

She hadn't planned on any of that tonight, but the atmosphere had shifted and it seemed entirely natural to keep going. After all, it was only her dream. She could do as she pleased.

The light went out. The room filled with the warm glow of red candles. The bed curtains stirred in the still air, heavy with suggestion.

Jiyao gestured for him to look at the table.

Qin Yuan followed the direction of her hand, and his gaze landed on the book that had appeared at some unknown moment, fallen open to the fourth page.

His eyelid twitched. His suspicion was confirmed: she was working through the illustrations one by one.

He had genuinely no idea who she was or what kind of woman would be this absorbed in such a pursuit. But the time for wondering was past. Unable to help himself, he bent his head, his lips finding her earlobe with precise deliberateness, kissing it repeatedly while his fingers worked steadily and with practiced ease at the layers of her skirts and robe.

The skin he uncovered was pale as fresh snow, almost startling in its clarity.

Jiyao lay on the tall curtained bed, curled like a crescent of new snow, held by someone who had gathered her close.

A cascade of kisses fell along the back of her neck, warm and unmistakably intent, moving gradually downward until they settled, lingering, at the graceful hollow of her shoulder blades.

Waves of heat came one after another.

Jiyao trembled without meaning to. She could not see the face of the person behind her, and could only feel herself slowly dissolving, warmth spreading to every part of her body. Her mind was somewhere between bewilderment and a joy that bordered on panic, uncertain whether she wanted to pull away or hold on.

In the end, instinct was all she had left to act on.

Very soon, something like a white flash crossed her mind, and everything went blank.

...

Qin Yuan looked at the woman in his arms.

The flush had not yet faded from her pale skin. She lay curled against his chest, boneless and still.

This woman was, without question, utterly detestable. And yet in this moment, there was something about her that was oddly... pitiful.

Qin Yuan became aware, then, that he had regained control of the dream.

Was this where it ended? he asked himself.

He could disengage now. He still had time.

He looked down.

She was satisfied. He was very much not. In fact, he was in considerable discomfort. And with the two of them pressed this close together, even the slightest shift drew a sharp breath.

He supposed there was no point in this position, at this stage, in doing anything by halves. Better to close his eyes and get through it as quickly as possible.

Anything was better than being suspended between this and nothing.

Qin Yuan set his jaw, turned her to face him, and continued.

chapters.title: A Strange Pleasure
chapters.content:
Jiyao's mind was an absolute blank. Her body had nothing left in it.

She was still drifting somewhere above herself when the world tilted and she was suddenly pressed beneath him, the change arriving so swiftly she hadn't caught up with it yet.

"Ah?"

What started as a question immediately changed into something else entirely. Jiyao blinked, dazed and bewildered, her thoughts stumbling: is this...

Wait. Wasn't it over?

How was it starting again?

And this position wasn't right either. This wasn't from the fourth page. It wasn't even from the fifth page...

"You..." she said, forgetting entirely to control the dream, speaking on pure instinct, and the sound that escaped her on that one syllable nearly became something much louder.

She bit down on her lip, hard, terrified of making a sound even within a dream.

But the young lord seemed to be doing it on purpose, varying the pace with maddening inconsistency.

Jiyao's patience finally broke. She glared at him as fiercely as she could manage, which, under the circumstances, had precisely zero intimidating effect. She gave up on glaring and dug her nails into his back instead.

Qin Yuan made a sharp, short sound and pinned her offending hand.

He had been through this strange dream many times now, but this was the first time he had engaged in it while in full control.

Whatever the motive, whether to relieve frustration, whether it was something like revenge, or whether it came from some other obscure corner of himself, the fact was: this time, for the second half, he was setting the pace. He did not arrive at complete satisfaction, but it was considerably more gratifying than the helpless, passive experience he'd been subjected to before.

After he woke, Qin Yuan lay in the water and reflected on what he had done in that dream with something approaching disbelief.

He had been entirely resolved to end it quickly. How had he ended up staying that long, wide awake the whole time, and then calling it satisfying on top of everything?

What was there to find satisfying about being compelled into something against one's will? He must have lost his mind entirely, to have entertained even the ghost of such an idea.

...

The night was very dark.

Jiyao pressed her hands over her still-burning face.

So that kind of thing could apparently happen more than once.

Thrilling. Genuinely, absurdly thrilling.

At least she hadn't screamed in the dream. The thrill was entirely hers, known to no one else.

Small mercies.

Whatever she got up to in dreams, in daylight Jiyao was always the quiet, well-mannered second miss of the Fang family, composed and proper as anyone could wish.

And then, before she quite realized it, Grand Secretary Fang's birthday arrived.

It fell, by good fortune, on a rest day.

Just as Jiyao had expected, there was no grand celebration. The family simply gathered for a quiet meal together.

At the table, her second cousin rose to present his gift first: a composition he had written himself, elaborate in language and genuine in feeling.

The eldest cousin was serving as an official in the provinces and was not in the capital, so the second, Fang Lin, naturally took precedence among the grandchildren.

Jiyao and the rest of her brothers and sisters followed, each presenting their gift in turn.

She watched with quiet attention as they came forward, one by one. None of the gifts were extravagant: calligraphy, paintings, compositions, embroidery, handmade pieces. But it was plain that every one of them had been made with care.

Grand Secretary Fang stroked his beard, visibly pleased, and commented on each gift with genuine interest and warmth.

The whole scene was one of easy harmony.

His daughter, Fang Pei, had also come with her son to offer her birthday wishes. After the family banquet ended, she went with her father to his study and raised the second matter she had come about: "Father, I'd like Jin De to study at the Fang family academy, if that's all right. Can you make a place for him?"

"Why wouldn't it be all right? He may be a Zhao by name, but he's still a Fang grandson on his mother's side. Tell him to come tomorrow."

Fang Pei hesitated, then added: "There's also someone else who has come to me with a request."

"Oh?" Grand Secretary Fang's brow lifted. "Who?"

"Jin De's eldest paternal aunt." Fang Pei sighed.

Zhao Jin De had three paternal aunts, all married to families in the capital and all closely connected to the Zhao household. The eldest had married a military official by the name of Lu, who had died young, leaving three sons. The first son had died in childhood. The second had inherited a military post. But when it came to the third, Zhao Jin De's eldest aunt had refused absolutely to let him follow the same path. She was determined to have this son pursue the civil examinations instead.

The boy had proven himself capable enough. He had passed the county examinations at seventeen. But to advance further, he needed instruction from a proper teacher, and the Lu family had no connections in that world. His mother had run out of options and turned to her own younger brother and his wife for help.

"Father, you know what it was like when I first came to the Zhao family. The eldest sister-in-law helped me a great deal back then. She rarely asks for anything. I couldn't bring myself to refuse her..."

Grand Secretary Fang considered. "I understand your meaning. Have the boy come along tomorrow as well. I'll look at him first. If his character is sound and his foundation is solid, he can stay."

Fang Pei was overjoyed. "Thank you, Father!"

...

Jiyao heard about all this the following day.

During a break at the academy, her youngest sister Mengyao announced to the group: "Cousin Jin De is going to study at our family academy too. He'll be with Fourth Brother and Fifth Brother and the others."

"Ah." Jiyao responded with mild, unaffected approval. "That seems good. The cousins can encourage one another."

"And there's another person, apparently. Someone who's... cousin Jin De's cousin..."

The girl said "cousin" twice over in the same breath, and Third Sister Zhiyao, who was listening, burst out laughing. "What? A cousin's cousin?"

"Yes, his cousin's cousin! That's exactly what I said!" Mengyao was a little flustered. "Don't believe me? Ask Second Sister. Second Sister will know for sure."

Both younger sisters turned to look at Jiyao at the same moment.

Jiyao kept her composure. "Perhaps Sixth Sister means a relative from cousin Jin De's aunt's side of the family?"

"Yes, exactly!" Mengyao nodded vigorously. "His eldest aunt's son, apparently. The surname is Lu."

Zhiyao said nothing, and instead reached over to pinch Sixth Sister's ear.

Jiyao watched the two of them with a quiet smile and thought: surnamed Lu. Could it be Lu Ming, the one she had briefly met before?

The thought passed through her mind and moved on.

The Fang family's male and female students studied in separate buildings. A few new faces joining the boys' academy would make no practical difference to the young women.

As it turned out, though, she ran into Lu Ming that very afternoon.

After school, she had barely returned to Haitang Court when she was told that Grandfather wished to see her on some matter. She went quickly.

Just as she reached the front courtyard, she spotted two figures walking together in quiet conversation: her cousin Zhao Jin De, and Lu Ming.

Zhao Jin De looked up and saw her first. "Second Cousin Sister!"

He jogged over and bowed, clearly pleased with himself. "I'm going to be studying here from now on. Grand-uncle just examined both my cousin's work and mine, and said we could stay."

Grand-uncle had originally only intended to examine the cousin, but not wanting to show obvious favoritism, he had tested Jin De as well. A word of praise from a man who had placed third in the imperial examinations was no small thing, and Jin De was quietly delighted with himself.

"That's wonderful. We'll be seeing each other often, then." Jiyao smiled, and as Lu Ming had by now reached them, she gave him a small nod of acknowledgment. "Mr. Lu."

Lu Ming was momentarily caught off guard, then returned the greeting with a nod of his own. "Miss Fang."

"Where are you off to, Cousin Sister?" Jin De asked curiously.

Jiyao gestured toward the study ahead. "Grandfather has something to discuss with me."

Jin De understood at once. "Go on then, don't let me keep you."

Jiyao nodded to both of them and walked on quickly.

She arrived at her grandfather's study shortly after.

What Grand Secretary Fang wanted was nothing particularly urgent. He had received her gift at the birthday banquet, and with all the grandchildren around, had only managed to express simple approval. But inwardly, the painting had stirred a great deal more in him: he had thought of her father, his second son, gone too young.

That night, the Grand Secretary had taken out several of his second son's early paintings and studied them for a long while before finally deciding to entrust them to Jiyao.

"These are paintings your father made during his lifetime. I have kept two for myself. The rest I am giving to you to look after."

Seeing the grief in her grandfather's eyes, Jiyao felt a sharp ache in her chest and had to blink back tears. She received the scroll paintings with both hands and answered with a quiet bow of acceptance.

She could see her father in her dreams. But she knew, with perfect clarity, that he had long since left this world.

"You have some natural ability in painting," Grand Secretary Fang continued. "It would be a shame to let it go to waste. Both of your aunts by marriage are skilled in that art. In your spare moments, you might go to them for guidance. Don't always keep yourself shut away in Haitang Court."

Jiyao held back the sadness in her throat and said yes once more.

Grand Secretary Fang waved a dismissal. Jiyao curtseyed and took her leave, the scroll paintings in her arms.

The sun had already set. The western sky was vivid with afterglow, a red so deep and brilliant it was almost painful to look at.

Back in Haitang Court, Jiyao sat looking at her father's paintings for a long time before finally putting them away with great care.

That night, lying in bed, she dreamed, as she had known she would.

In the dream she was searching for her parents, but when she looked up, she found the young lord sitting across from her instead.

Their eyes met.

Jiyao frowned, hesitated for a moment, then thought simply: I don't want to see you right now. Leave. Go quickly.

The moment the thought formed, the young lord vanished from before her.

At the same instant, in the inner chamber of Zichen Palace, the young emperor's eyes snapped open, his expression distinctly peculiar.

chapters.title: Cherries
chapters.content:
Qin Yuan was genuinely surprised.

Not because he had fallen into the strange dream again, but because this time it lasted only a matter of seconds.

It was almost like a trick of the mind.

But he was certain it had been real. He had entered that dream once more, and when the woman in it looked at him, she had done so with an expression he could only describe as... inconvenienced. The same way someone looks at an unexpected nuisance.

He couldn't remember her face. But that look, in that instant, he had no doubt whatsoever about.

A formless, mounting fury rose in him.

He spent a long moment subduing it before closing his eyes and telling himself: leave it. For him, not dreaming that dream at all was the preferable outcome.

But for reasons he could not account for, sleep refused to come back. In the end, he had no choice but to call for the calming incense to be lit again.

...

Once the young lord had obligingly disappeared, Jiyao realized, somewhat belatedly, that her reaction had perhaps been a little hasty.

It wasn't as though she could only do one kind of thing with him in these dreams. Spending time with her parents with him quietly there alongside her could have been perfectly pleasant too.

She was the one being foolish. She had been overthinking things lately, and it had muddled her judgment.

Fortunately, the young lord was nothing more than a figment of her imagination, without any awareness of his own. It made no real difference.

And there was no need to call him back. She would simply be more thoughtful next time.

That night, Jiyao directed her dream with intention, letting herself spend the hours simply being with her parents.

She sat with her father and practiced brushwork. She sat with her mother and learned embroidery. As though, by doing so, they were still beside her. As though she was still someone with a father who loved her and a mother who cherished her.

The dream was sweet. Waking from it, though, always left a faint residue of sorrow.

Jiyao steadied herself and pulled her emotions back into order, then dressed and went to the academy as usual.

The curriculum at the Fang girls' school was fairly relaxed, and Jiyao had plenty of free time. In the past she would have spent any spare moment in Haitang Court working through chess problems. But Grandfather had specifically encouraged her to pursue her painting, and she couldn't very well ignore that.

After some thought, Jiyao spent a morning in the kitchen making a small selection of sweets, and went to pay a visit to her Fourth Aunt in Muxiuan Courtyard.

Fourth Aunt was surnamed Chen, given name Wenjun. Compared to Third Aunt, who managed the household's domestic affairs, Fourth Aunt had considerably more leisure time.

Jiyao was reserved by nature and had spent most of her years at the academy, so while she got along pleasantly enough with all her aunts, she had never been particularly close to any of them. Calling on Fourth Aunt out of nowhere felt presumptuous, and it took considerable effort to work herself up to it.

She stood outside the gate of Muxiuan Courtyard for a good while, gathering her nerve, before finally taking a breath and stepping inside.

The courtyard was quiet. No servants bustled about. The only sign of life was a small cat stretched out lazily in a patch of sunlight.

She had barely stepped through the gate when a voice reached her from inside the room, unmistakably Fourth Aunt's, and unmistakably displeased: "Her husband's family's nephew gets to study at our academy, but when my own family's nephew asked two years ago, the answer was no. How does that make sense?"

Jiyao stopped where she was.

"I've told you," came the reply, most likely Fourth Uncle's voice, "Lu Ming was only admitted after Father examined his work personally and found it satisfactory. It wasn't arbitrary."

Fourth Aunt made a cold, dismissive sound. "Examined his work, he says. More like playing favorites. Father looks down on my family. No, that's not right either. He doesn't look down on my family. He looks down on you."

"Lower your voice, for heaven's sake. What if someone hears?" Fourth Uncle sounded alarmed.

"So what? Your family does the favoring and I can't even say the word?"

...

Jiyao stood with her eyes wide, simultaneously embarrassed and deeply uncomfortable. This was absolutely not the moment to step forward.

Not only should she not step forward, she should leave and pretend she had never come at all.

She retreated as quietly as she possibly could, holding her breath with every step.

She had actually heard something about this before, vaguely: apparently Fourth Aunt's nephew from her birth family had wanted to study at the Fang academy. Grandfather had met with the boy privately, decided against admitting him, and arranged for him to attend a different school instead. At the time, Fourth Aunt had seemed to accept it without protest, and Jiyao had assumed the matter had been settled agreeably. She had not realized the resentment had been sitting there ever since, quietly festering.

Jiyao let out a soft sigh as she walked away. Human relationships in the real world were, she thought, far more tangled and exhausting than anything in her dreams.

Back in Haitang Court, she handed the sweets to Shuangxi without explanation.

Shuangxi blinked. "Miss, weren't you going to..."

"Not anymore. If anyone asks, just say I've been here in Haitang Court all afternoon."

Shuangxi didn't understand, but nodded. "Yes, miss."

Jiyao went to her father's study and decided she would find something on painting to read on her own. She searched through the shelves for a while and eventually turned up several useful volumes.

She was about to leave when her gaze drifted, without quite meaning to, toward the thick book resting at the top of the bookcase.

She hadn't taken it down. She hadn't looked at the illustrations again. But the images from inside it kept surfacing in her mind anyway, vivid and fully formed.

Just thinking about them was enough to make her face go warm.

She went back to her room and drank two cups of tea in succession before the inconvenient warmth inside her finally subsided.

That night, she entered a dream once again.

It began in a courtyard. Peach blossoms were blazing in full bloom.

Her parents were seated together, drinking tea.

Jiyao brought a new painting to show her father. "Please tell me what you think, Father."

Her father considered it for a long moment, then began his commentary. His observations were so precisely aligned with her own unformed instincts that she found herself nodding again and again.

Then her mother, who had been sitting quietly beside them, said suddenly: "Sweetheart, where is your husband? We haven't seen him these past few days."

Jiyao wasn't sure whether this was some hidden corner of her own thoughts speaking through her mother's voice, but she answered vaguely: "He's in the room."

"Is he? Well, the hour is getting late, my dear. You should go and rest." Her mother's smile was full of warmth and a hint of mischief. She tilted her head meaningfully. "You don't need to keep us company every moment, sweetheart. You've been here with us a long time already."

Jiyao didn't say anything, but she felt a small stirring of interest.

She leaned against her mother's shoulder and lingered with them for a while longer, reluctant to leave, before finally saying her farewells and turning back toward the room.

The room, when she arrived, was not quite as she remembered it. Something had been added: an alabaster bathing pool, carved from white jade, had appeared in the middle of the space. Gauzy curtains hung around it. The water inside was clear and clean, soft tendrils of steam rising from the surface.

Jiyao made a small, wondering sound, then recalled that the teacher at the academy had mentioned bathing pools during the day's lesson. That must be why it had appeared.

She walked over and crouched to test the water. The warmth flowed over her palm in a pleasant rush, and she half-closed her eyes. In another moment, she was simply in the water, having thought herself there.

She considered, and petals began drifting in from somewhere unseen, spinning lazily as they settled on the surface.

In the waking world, Jiyao did not know how to swim. In the dream, she could. Not just a little, but freely and with ease.

She let herself imagine the rest: herself playing in the warm pool, the young lord standing at the edge holding a tray, offering her pieces of fruit or a cup of hot tea.

Yes. Just like that.

The thought took shape, and she looked up to find the young lord stepping out from behind the gauzy curtains, tray in hand.

He was dressed all in white, his collar slightly loose, a small glimpse of skin at his chest. His expression remained, as ever, cool and composed.

Jiyao smiled and beckoned with a playful pout: "My lord. I want some cherries."

...

Qin Yuan found himself in that strange dream again, and this time without a properly fastened robe.

Before him was a bathing pool. In the pool, a young woman was swimming.

The water moved and shifted around her. Her pale, soft form was visible through it, more so than less.

The vein at Qin Yuan's temple pulsed steadily. He formed a fairly clear guess about where this was heading: she wanted to try something new again.

A bathing scene? Or something in the water itself?

Either way, it would inevitably end in the same place.

This woman really was...

"My lord, I want some cherries," she said.

Qin Yuan permitted himself a brief, cold inner laugh, and then, helplessly, moved toward the edge of the pool. He selected a single cherry, vivid red and still jeweled with water droplets, and held it to her lips.

He stood at the edge of the pool, and within his field of vision: the clear, still water, and within the water, the young woman's form, present but not entirely, there and not there.

Her hair was pinned high. A loose strand or two had fallen and been wetted, and they lay damp against her cheek. A single water droplet traced a path along her collarbone, hesitating at the edge before deciding whether to fall.

Qin Yuan's breath caught.

He had never retained her face. But her body he remembered entirely. Eyes closed, he could trace its every line.

And then, at precisely that moment, she leaned forward to take the cherry from his fingers, and the tip of her wet tongue, whether by accident or design, brushed across his hand. A tingling current shot from his fingertips through his entire body in an instant.

Qin Yuan went rigid, and found, much to his own private disgust, that he was faintly anticipating whatever she was going to do next.

He caught himself less than a breath later.
