Fang Can shook his head again, regret in his voice. "It was a chance encounter -- I had no name, no address, nothing to go on. And I was in the middle of returning to the capital and could not delay. Only that she appears to be in Yizhou."

Minister Fang was silent for a long moment. "Then we will send someone to inquire," he said at last. "If it turns out to be her..."

He did not finish the sentence. He only thought: whether it was her or not, Jiyao deserved an answer.

After a pause, he added, "Say nothing of this to Jiyao for now."

So many years had passed. The child had already come to terms with her mother's disappearance. An uncertain piece of news would do nothing for her now except keep her lying awake with worry.

"I understand." Fang Can nodded.

That was the same reason he had said nothing to his cousin tonight, no matter how many times he had come close.

...

Jiyao knew none of this.

The wine had caught up with her properly now. Things were beginning to double at the edges. Every few steps she had to pause and shake her head. Afraid she might stumble, she held tight to Shuangxi's hand and walked with great, deliberate care.

"It's all right, miss. You'll be fine."

"Mm." That plum wine, Jiyao thought, was terrifyingly strong. She was never touching it again.

The moment she was back in Haitang Courtyard, she sank into a chair at the table, her head listed to one side, and nearly slid straight into sleep.

"Miss. Miss." Shuangxi saw and gave her a gentle nudge. "You haven't washed up yet."

"Oh. Right. Yes." Jiyao stirred and murmured a response, and thought vaguely: did she really need to wash up? Couldn't she just blink, and everything would be as it should be?

She thought about it. And thought about it again. And still nothing happened.

After a long, blank moment, she finally realized, belatedly: she was not in her dream. This was real life.

Goodness, her mind was truly gone.

Shuangxi brought over a cloth wrung out in cool water and gently wiped her face.

The cold cleared her head a little. She endured the drowsiness just long enough to wash up properly, then climbed into bed.

She was so deeply tired that the moment her head touched the pillow, she was asleep.

In that hazy space between waking and dreaming, a thought drifted faintly through her mind: was there something she had forgotten?

Never mind. It was probably nothing important. Tomorrow would do.

...

The moon lay soft and hazy in the sky.

In the inner chambers of Zichen Palace, the calming incense had been lit early.

In recent days Qin Yuan had been following Daoist Yunhe's advice, adjusting his sleeping time and position in an attempt to keep the strange dream away. But tonight, he had deliberately changed everything back.

He remembered what she had said in the dream that afternoon: "Tonight, we'll talk about tonight. Tonight we can..."

He was certain the dream would come again tonight.

Once, he had wanted nothing more than to be rid of it. But now, quietly, he found himself waiting for it.

Not because of anything that happened between them in the dream -- he told himself that emphatically. Only because he had made up his mind: tonight, he would find out who she was.

The calming incense was supposed to help with sleep, but whether it was because he had already rested during the day, or because his mind was too preoccupied tonight, Qin Yuan found himself staring into the dark, sleepless -- an old affliction he had not suffered in some time.

It was nearly the third watch before he finally drifted off.

By the time he woke, it was already time for the morning court.

He opened his eyes and lay there for a moment, unmoving. Then his expression darkened, and a slow, sharp anger rose in his chest.

Was that woman toying with him?

He drew a long breath and pressed everything down with effort, telling himself: it is fine. If not tonight, then the next night. He would find her eventually.

And when he did -- old scores and new could be settled all at once.

chapters.title: A Clue
chapters.content:
"Miss, time to wake up."

Jiyao opened her eyes. Through the thin gauze curtain, the room was filled with light.

She startled. "What hour is it?"

"Past the hour of Chen. I wouldn't have come to wake you otherwise." Shuangxi smiled and drew back the curtain.

Jiyao sat up and pressed her fingers to her brow. "I slept that long," she murmured.

She would have to be more careful with plum wine in the future. Just because it went down like fruit juice did not mean she should treat it as one.

She had no time to dwell on it. Jiyao dressed quickly, tidied herself, and hurried off to the women's academy.

She had barely reached the entrance when she saw Fourth Cousin Pinyao and Fifth Cousin Qianyao walking toward her.

Just like yesterday, the twins looked straight through her and turned their eyes away.

Jiyao lowered her gaze and went quietly to her seat.

She was not the kind of person who talked much in real life anyway. If they would not acknowledge her, she simply would not acknowledge them either.

During the break, Third Cousin Zhiyao came and sat beside her, whispering, "Second Sister, did you and Fourth and Fifth Sister have a falling-out?"

"No." Jiyao shook her head.

"Well, that makes sense -- what are the chances you'd argue with anyone?" Third Sister thought for a moment. "So what happened? Something seems off between you."

"I'm not entirely sure myself," Jiyao said vaguely.

"You're all cousins under the same roof. It's not good to have bad feeling between you. Would you like me to try and smooth things over?"

"It should be fine on its own. Give it a couple of days." Jiyao considered it and decided that was probably true.

She thought: in all honesty, if they never reconciled, it would not affect her much either way.

Zhiyao nodded at that and let the matter drop.

The days of the Fang daughters passed in a full and quiet rhythm.

Before she knew it, another day was gone.

When evening came and she was settling in for bed, Jiyao remembered that she had originally intended to shape her dreams the night before. Two cups of plum wine had made her forget entirely.

But these things were never urgent. If not last night, then tonight.

She lowered the curtain, closed her eyes, and gradually fell asleep.

Before long, she was dreaming again.

During the day, she had paid little mind to her cousins' cold behavior. But that night she dreamed she was in an argument with someone -- she could not even tell whether it was Pinyao or Qianyao.

In the dream she felt frantic, and yet could not get a single word out.

Just as the frustration peaked, she realized she was dreaming. Jiyao almost laughed at herself. She had no interest in wasting her dream on this. With a small shift of thought, the scene vanished entirely.

Everything before her dissolved in an instant, replaced by a lotus pond.

The pond was vast. Lotus flowers bloomed across its entire surface in a sweep of red petals and green leaves that stretched as far as the eye could see.

At the water's edge stood a pavilion, and inside it, a low couch. On a small table beside the couch sat an assortment of seasonal fruit. Jiyao reclined against the cushions and gently patted the space beside her. "Husband, come sit here."

She knew that in the next instant, he would simply appear, seated at her side.

And sure enough, in the blink of an eye, someone was there.

Jiyao did not need to look. She leaned back slightly, resting against him, and raised one slender hand to gesture across the blooming pond. "Isn't it beautiful?"

"It is."

...

Qin Yuan found himself in the strange dream again without warning.

This time, he felt no particular irritation. There was even a quiet sense of anticipation.

He had a clear objective: gather more clues. Identify her as soon as possible.

When she asked him the question, Qin Yuan lowered his gaze, schooled his expression, and answered with perfect ease. "It is."

"Isn't it?" Jiyao smiled brightly and turned to kiss the corner of his mouth.

This lotus pond was her way of making up for what she had missed in real life.

Since she was not actively shaping the dream, Qin Yuan could move freely. He did not pull away from the kiss -- only touched his fingertip almost imperceptibly to the spot she had kissed and gave a quiet hum of acknowledgment.

Her hair fell soft against his arm. He asked, as casually as one might remark on the weather, "Are you from the capital?"

"Me?" Jiyao looked up at him, a little surprised, then shook her head. "No, I'm not from the capital."

She had been born in the capital and raised there -- but her grandfather's ancestral home was in Bingzhou. She supposed that technically she was not a capital native.

"Where are you from, then?" Qin Yuan asked.

Jiyao hesitated. Her family's registered home was Bingzhou, yet she had never once set foot there. Calling herself a Bingzhou native seemed equally strange.

It was a difficult question. Rather than answer it, Jiyao simply leaned up and kissed him, then tucked her head into the curve of his arm and said with a smile, "What does it matter where I'm from? I'm yours."

"You --" Qin Yuan's brow furrowed. He was distinctly unsatisfied with that answer.

But then she added with a laugh, "And you're mine."

Qin Yuan said nothing. His eyes turned unreadable.

Was she teasing him? Or had she somehow sensed his purpose and was deliberately deflecting?

It did not matter. There were other ways to find things out.

Jiyao puzzled over why her husband would ask such things in a dream. Then again, when she was not deliberately controlling the dream, all kinds of strange things could happen. The conversation they were having right now was already unusually coherent by dream standards.

She did not think further on it, and parted her lips softly to ask, "Husband, do you want to keep looking at the lotus flowers?"

The implication was clear. She was ready to do something else.

Without waiting for a reply, Jiyao let her thoughts shift, and in an instant the two of them were inside, on a bed.

Qin Yuan blinked.

The young woman's dark eyes were bright and steady, fixed on him with an unwavering gaze. Her slender hand lifted to point at the window, and she murmured softly, "It's already evening now."

Her voice was low. The implication unmistakable.

Qin Yuan's heartbeat quickened. He understood immediately what she wanted.

This woman really was...

The red candle swayed. Jiyao pressed a kiss to the shifting line of his throat. As her eyes dropped, she unsurprisingly caught sight of the change in him.

Her eyes curved.

She had known it. The moment she touched his throat, something always happened -- it seemed even more reliable than breathing into his ear.

Qin Yuan drew a sharp breath. His throat moved involuntarily.

It was obvious that his body in this dream could not withstand her provocation.

And she was still looking at him like that.

"Shall we try this?" she asked, producing the erotic manual from somewhere and flipping through a few pages until she pointed to one. "This one."

She said it as though consulting him. But Jiyao had already made up her mind.

If he agreed, wonderful. If not -- she would make him agree.

Qin Yuan's brow drew together.

His instinct was to refuse, and the refusal almost reached his lips before he swallowed it back down.

It was not that he was beginning to give in to these things. It was that experience had taught him: in this dream, he was rarely the one who got to decide, unless she was already satisfied. And every time he resisted, he lost control entirely.

Better to play along and keep his grip on the dream.

Besides, there had already been so many times. One more or less hardly made a difference.

With that, Qin Yuan gave a small nod. "That one, then."

Jiyao smiled. Though she could shape the dream however she wished, if things were already going exactly as she wanted, she had no desire to force every word from her husband's mouth.

She held out her hand to him, coaxingly. "Then carry me."

Qin Yuan's expression remained perfectly flat as he picked her up and set her on the edge of the bed, then stood at her side.

Oddly enough, the tall canopy bed seemed to have risen in height at precisely the right moment.

And yet, though Jiyao had chosen the style herself, when the time came she proved remarkably uncooperative, drifting backward by degrees without quite seeming to mean to.

Qin Yuan's patience wore thin. The vein at his temple began to throb. He gritted his teeth, tightened both arms around her waist, and held her firmly in place.

The sensations in this dream were far too real.

Jiyao glanced down, and could even see the clear change in her own shape.

The double force of sensation and sight was almost too much to bear. She trembled and reached for him, meaning to ask him to be gentler, but when she opened her mouth, nothing came out that could be called words.

Her pale skin had taken on a faint flush of pink without her noticing. A light sheen of moisture had appeared at her brow, and there was the glimmer of tears at the corners of her eyes.

Through the haze, Jiyao thought: if she had known it would be like this, she should have simply sat astride him from the start. At least then she could have set her own pace.

But stopping now and switching would be a waste.

Later, Jiyao's mind went entirely blank. She clung to his arm and sobbed quietly against him.

Qin Yuan's eyes flickered. He had not been fully satisfied, but he did not push further.

He remembered his new goal, and asked again, "What is your name?"

Jiyao's body was still trembling faintly. She heard the question and lifted her head, looking up at him with hazy, slowly-clearing eyes.

When she was very small, she had heard people say: if someone calls your name in a dream, never answer. A passing ghost officer might hear and imitate a familiar voice to lure away your soul.

So in her dreams, Jiyao never spoke her own name. Even her parents had always called her the affectionate pet name "Little Darling."

And now, faced with the husband of her imagination, she certainly was not about to reveal her real name. She opened her eyes -- still misty -- and said in a trembling voice, "Little Darling. Don't you all call me Little Darling?"

"You --" Qin Yuan's expression shifted. A vein at his temple jumped.

Again. That same answer.

Jiyao's mind gradually cleared. With a small shift of thought, the two of them were properly dressed again. She tugged at his hand and added helpfully, "Of course, you can also call me Wife."

She remembered -- in the dream, the identity she had given him was that of a husband who had married into her family.

Qin Yuan gave a thin smile. "Your surname?"

Jiyao did not like that he was asking again. She frowned. Why was he still at this?

But she was in a good mood right now, and she was not ready to end the dream. She did not want to get into it. Instead she simply reached out and pointed at the jewelry case on the dresser. "Husband, hand me the lip rouge."

She imagined: he agrees at once, walks over promptly, and picks out the one I like best.

Qin Yuan found he had lost control of the dream again.

"All right." He answered without meaning to, crossed to the dressing table, opened the case, and among all the little boxes and pots, lifted out a thin, round one.

He was inwardly furious at his own helplessness, but could do nothing about it. He carried it back to the bed and held it out to her. "Here. Your lip rouge."

Jiyao reached up to take it. With the motion, the twisted silver bracelet on her right wrist slipped a little down her arm.

Qin Yuan's gaze sharpened.

He had seen that bracelet before.

In one of the earlier dreams -- in the study, when she had been grinding ink for him -- it had hung at her wrist, catching the light with every movement. He had only glanced at it once before looking away.

But now, from his angle, he could make out three small, unassuming characters on the inside of the band.

His mind worked quickly, silently turning those characters the right way around, and then something shifted in his chest.

Liuyun Workshop?

It was from Liuyun Workshop?

Liuyun Workshop was the largest jeweler in the capital, renowned for its original designs and exquisite craftsmanship. Its pieces had become highly sought after by the noblewomen of the capital in recent years.

The year before, Qin Yuan had ordered the seizure of a corrupt official's assets. Among the confiscated property: five hundred and seventy-one pieces of gold and jade jewelry from Liuyun Workshop.

The silver bracelet bore the mark of Liuyun Workshop on its inner face. It had to be theirs.

The frustration in Qin Yuan's chest dissolved in an instant. A stroke of luck, and it seemed even the heavens were helping him.

With this clue, the scope of the search had narrowed considerably further.

Jiyao accepted the lip rouge and looked at it with interest. "Let me put some on you. All right?"

"What?"

Without waiting for his answer, she dipped one fingertip into the color and carefully applied it to his lips.

He was already handsome beyond fault -- every feature of his face suited her perfectly. But with the lip rouge, the color was simply too vivid. Jiyao looked at him and found it oddly unsettling. She quickly reached up and wiped it away.

She was gentle about it. "I'm sorry, I didn't do it well. Please don't be angry."

Then she leaned in and kissed him on the lips.

In Jiyao's imagination, he would never be angry with her. He would simply call her Little Darling and fold her into his arms.

And that was exactly what happened.

Qin Yuan bent his head and drew her gently against him, his voice soft as she had never heard it. "Little Darling. How could I ever be angry with you?"

Jiyao reached around and held his waist.

Summer nights were short. Not wanting to lose too much sleep, Jiyao did not let the dream go on much longer.

She ended it and woke.

The night was perfectly still.

She tidied herself briefly and fell back asleep.

...

In the inner chambers of Zichen Palace.

Qin Yuan woke from the dream.

After so many strange dreams in recent weeks, he had settled into something like a routine.

Wake. Go to the bathing room. Bathe and change.

Tonight was no different.

When he emerged, it was only the fourth watch -- too early for morning court. He did not go back to sleep. Instead he had paper and ink brought out.

The palace lamps burned steadily. The young emperor bent over the desk and began to draw.

He was no artist, but reproducing something from memory was not especially difficult for him.

Before long, a bracelet took shape on the paper.

"Summon Zhang Zan."

Zhang Zan was the head of the imperial intelligence network. One of the emperor's most trusted men.

He arrived promptly, and found the emperor watching him with eyes like still, deep water -- calm on the surface, but carrying an unmistakable sense of certainty. "Take this drawing to Liuyun Workshop. Find out who bought this bracelet."

"Yes, Your Majesty." Zhang Zan bowed and withdrew.

Dawn was beginning to lighten the sky.

Qin Yuan glanced at the incense holder, where the last stick had long since burned away, and thought: when you are truly determined to uncover someone's identity, there is always a way.

chapters.title: Fox Spirit
chapters.content:
On the third day after her eldest cousin's family returned to the capital, Jiyao met her eldest female cousin, Fang Ruoyao.

The eldest Fang daughter had married the previous year, into a family within the capital. Now, hearing that her brother and his wife had come home -- and being far enough along in her pregnancy to be settled -- she had come back to her family home in a palanquin.

The reunion was full of warmth and feeling.

After seeing her parents and brother and sister-in-law, the eldest Miss Fang made a point of spending time with her younger cousins.

She had always been attentive and loving as an elder sister, and it did not take long for her sharp eyes to notice that something was wrong.

There was some difficulty between Second Sister and Fourth and Fifth Sister.

She wanted to get to the bottom of it and help smooth things over. But the evening was growing late and her husband's household had already sent someone to collect her. She could not linger too long, and she did not want her husband's family to see discord among the Fang daughters.

So she held her tongue for now and, just before she left, offered a few tactful remarks about respecting one's elders and standing together as sisters.

Jiyao felt a little self-conscious listening to it. Was it really that obvious? Third Sister had noticed just two days ago, and today Elder Sister saw through it at a glance?

Though in truth she had not taken the whole affair to heart. She and Fourth and Fifth Sister had never been particularly close to begin with. If they wanted to stop exchanging pleasantries, so be it.

She was perfectly content on her own.

As it turned out, after Elder Sister left, Jiyao encountered Fourth and Fifth Cousin on her way back to Haitang Courtyard.

The two girls were identical in appearance and dressed the same besides. At a glance, it was nearly impossible to tell them apart.

They were standing beside the path, looking at flowers.

When they saw Jiyao, neither moved aside nor looked away. One of them gave a soft, deliberate cough, exchanged a glance with her twin, and the two of them began to speak to each other as though Jiyao were not there.

Fourth Cousin said, "It's not as though there's any real grudge between us. Going on like this, not acknowledging each other -- isn't it a bit much?"

"It is a bit much, but what can we do? You know we can't go against Mother, and Mother is still upset."

"I know." Fourth Cousin sighed. "I suppose we just have to wait for her to cool down."

Fifth Cousin Qianyao gave a quiet murmur of agreement.

With that, the two exchanged a look and walked away together.

Jiyao stared after them, genuinely astonished.

They had said nothing, then said everything -- timing it perfectly so that by the time she was close enough to hear, every word was audible. It could only have been for her benefit.

She had already more or less guessed why her cousins had been avoiding her, and she had not particularly minded. But this little performance -- the longer she thought about it, the funnier it seemed.

And then, beneath the amusement, something small and quiet ached.

Her cousins kept their distance because of their mother's feelings. As for her own mother -- where was she?

Jiyao dreamed of her parents often. But even the most vivid dream was not the same as the real thing.

Back in Haitang Courtyard, she sat at the table and could not find the heart to study the chess manual. Instead she turned the twisted silver bracelet on her wrist over and over in her fingers, lost in thought.

There were other pieces of jewelry in her possession, nicer ones. But she always came back to this bracelet, because she had found it in her mother's jewelry box.

She had kept it carefully polished all these years. Wearing it made her feel as though her mother was still nearby.

...

Liuyun Workshop was the largest jewelry house in the capital, busy with customers every day.

That afternoon, a group of unusual visitors arrived.

They were dressed head to toe in black, their expressions flat and unreadable. Their leader did not say a word before reaching into his robe and setting an imperial palace token on the counter with a sharp crack.

The shop boy went pale and hurried to fetch the proprietor.

The proprietor was a seasoned man. One look at the palace token and he was all bows and smiles. "Officers, how can I assist you today?"

"Check your records." The leader -- Zhang Zan himself -- produced a folded drawing from his robe and laid it on the counter. "Find out who you sold this bracelet to."

The proprietor took it carefully, examined it several times, and his expression grew troubled. "I won't deceive you, sir -- this twisted silver bracelet has been part of our inventory for well over a decade. We've sold more than a hundred pairs of this exact design. As for who bought each one, I'm afraid we simply don't have that information."

"You don't have it?" Zhang Zan's expression went cold. "You don't know who you sold to?"

"Truly, we don't. Here, let me show you the old ledgers."

The proprietor brought out the records from more than ten years back and showed them entry by entry.

Liuyun Workshop was a business. The twisted silver bracelet was well-made, but inexpensive by their standards and not among their featured pieces. They recorded the sales, yes -- but in the simplest terms.

Each entry read only: on such and such a date, one pair of twisted silver bracelets sold, for twelve taels of fine silver.

There were also entries for individual bracelets sold as singles.

One could hardly expect a shop to ask every customer for their name and household details.

The few entries that did name a specific buyer were all major clients who had come in and purchased substantial quantities of jewelry, with one or two pairs of silver bracelets tucked in among the rest.

Zhang Zan flipped through quickly, wasted no more time on conversation, and took the relevant ledgers back with him.

...

Qin Yuan was in reasonable spirits that day.

He had made that strange dream again the previous night, and it had involved the usual disruptions. But stumbling across those three characters -- "Liuyun Workshop" -- on the inside of the bracelet had led him to a new thread.

A thread meant finding her was considerably less impossible.

It was surely only a matter of time before she stood in front of him.

He let himself imagine it for a moment, and the corner of his mouth lifted slightly.

Zhang Zan arrived at the palace to report while the emperor was out in the practice grounds, running through mounted archery.

The young emperor rode at full gallop and loosed arrow after arrow. Each one found its mark -- precise, powerful, without a single miss.

He spotted Zhang Zan from a distance, pulled up, and dismounted, tossing the bow to an attendant with a careless flick of his wrist.

"Your Majesty." Zhang Zan steadied himself and came forward with a respectful bow.

The emperor made a quiet sound of acknowledgment and moved to the nearby basin held by an attendant, leisurely washing his hands, unhurried, wiping away the water with a cloth before he asked, "Well?"

Zhang Zan lowered his head, his expression pained. "This subject has failed."

At the word failed, Qin Yuan's hand stilled. His eyes narrowed slightly, and his voice dropped. "Hm?"

Zhang Zan's heart lurched. He hastily explained what had happened, then continued, "Your Majesty, that twisted silver bracelet -- over the past decade and more, Liuyun Workshop sold a total of one hundred and twenty-eight pairs. Of those, thirty-nine pairs were split and sold as individual pieces. Of the rest, there are only twelve buyers for whom there is any traceable record."

"Twelve." The coldness in Qin Yuan's expression was quiet and precise. Disappointment settled in slowly.

"Yes, Your Majesty." Zhang Zan presented the list of those twelve names, adding, "Because the bracelet is not a particularly valuable item, Liuyun Workshop did not make a point of recording each buyer at the time of sale. Given how many years have passed, the others are extremely difficult to trace."

An attendant took the list and offered it to the emperor.

Qin Yuan glanced at it, and a faint weariness stirred beneath his composure.

He should have anticipated this. The bracelet was not an uncommon design -- the likelihood of it being unique to one person had never been high. What he had not expected was for it to be this ordinary. And from over a decade ago at that.

A single bracelet was not going to lead him to her easily.

On the other hand, it was not entirely bad news. At the very least, it confirmed: the bracelet genuinely was from Liuyun Workshop. Some details from the dream could serve as real clues.

He was not heading in the wrong direction.

Seeing that the emperor had been silent for some time, Zhang Zan grew increasingly uneasy. He gathered his nerve and carefully asked, "Your Majesty, shall we continue investigating these twelve individuals?"

"Of course we continue." Qin Yuan's eyes narrowed slightly. "And not only the twelve. Find out who is currently wearing a bracelet like this one."

Zhang Zan thought, with some inward anguish: a silver bracelet is obviously a woman's ornament. Investigating this discreetly would be no easy matter -- not without the emperor making a public proclamation.

And a proclamation would create its own problems. If the bracelet's owner grew frightened, she might simply hide it or have it melted down.

Zhang Zan understood the difficulties all too well. But the order had been given, and he had no choice but to accept it. "This subject obeys."

The emperor waved a hand in dismissal.

Zhang Zan bowed and withdrew quickly.

A mild breeze moved through the air, carrying a thread of coolness.

Qin Yuan had lost all interest in returning to the archery range. He closed his eyes briefly and told himself: it does not matter. The investigation continues.

He refused to believe she could not be found.

...

The lotus flowers in the Fang family pond had finally opened.

Third Cousin Zhiyao invited Jiyao to go and admire them together.

Jiyao had been looking forward to it for a long time and agreed at once. After the academy let out, the two cousins walked over to the pond together.

Willow branches trailed long and graceful along the water's edge. Nearly half the lotuses had bloomed, their red heads catching the slanting evening sun in a sweep of vivid color.

"What a shame our pond is so small," Third Sister sighed. "If it were a lake, that would be something."

Jiyao offered what comfort she could. "It is a little small, but small has its advantages."

"What advantages could small possibly have?" Third Sister tilted her head.

Jiyao thought about it for quite a while before answering. "It costs less to build."

Third Sister blinked, then burst out laughing. "Don't let the tutor hear you say that."

Land in the capital was worth a fortune -- a pond did cost considerably less than a lake. But a well-bred young lady was not supposed to have "saving money" anywhere near her list of values.

As their tutor would have said: that was common.

Jiyao only smiled quietly. In front of the tutor, she knew better.

"The thing is, Second Sister -- what I meant was, if it were a lake, we could go out in a boat." Third Sister waved her hand in an approximation of rowing and sighed again. "I've never been on a boat."

At the Duanwu festival she had badly wanted to go out and watch the dragon boat races, but her mother had said the lakeside would be too crowded and kept her home. She still felt a pang of regret when she thought of it.

Jiyao murmured in agreement. "Neither have I."

But she thought: perhaps tonight she could try it in a dream.

For her, it would not be very difficult at all.

...

That night.

Jiyao settled in early.

When she realized she was dreaming, she let her thoughts shift, and in an instant she was standing on a boat.

She had never sailed in real life, but she had read about it, and so in the dream the hull rocked gently on the water's surface.

Above her, the sky was thick with stars. Mist hung close over the water on all sides, and a cool night breeze carried the clean scent of lotus blossoms against her face.

Now and then a fish leaped from the water with a splash, and then disappeared again beneath the surface.

Jiyao sat with her knees drawn up at the stern, sipping tart plum juice. She thought: well, it's pleasant -- but perhaps that's all it is.

Maybe it was because she was alone.

Hmm. What this scene needed was someone standing at the prow, playing a flute for her.

Her thoughts turned at once to the obvious choice. Who could be better suited than the husband of her dreams?

She sent out the thought: come out from the cabin, husband, playing as you walk.

In the next instant, the sound of a flute rose from somewhere on the boat -- clear and winding, a melody that turned and soared.

Jiyao looked around. And there was her husband, dressed in unadorned white, stepping out from the cabin into the open air.

Moonlight pooled around him, and for a moment he looked not quite of this world.

Jiyao propped her chin in her hand and watched him with a smile, thinking: just as she had hoped. Whatever skill she wished him to have, he always had.

...

Qin Yuan discovered he was in the strange dream again without warning.

He had studied the qin briefly as a boy, but he had no real knowledge of the flute. And yet here he was, playing one -- and playing it well.

Only when the song ended did he regain control of himself.

Jiyao clapped lightly. She tilted her head back to look at the sky overhead. "Look -- the stars tonight are so beautiful. In a little over twenty days, it will be Qixi."

Qin Yuan thought: the date she named matched real life.

That time she had said the daytime was not appropriate -- in the real world, it had also been daytime.

Combined with the standard speech, the streets that resembled the old Eastern Market, the Liuyun Workshop bracelet... he no longer had a single doubt that she was a real person.

He smiled slightly and said on purpose, "Do fox spirits celebrate Qixi?"

Jiyao shot him a look and corrected him at once. "What fox spirit? I'm a person. A person."

Honestly.

"Mm, you are a person," Qin Yuan agreed, and then, as though the thought had just drifted by, asked, "What year were you born?"

Jiyao frowned. A flicker of impatience crossed her face.

Was this not the time to be quietly enjoying the scenery? Why was he suddenly asking about her age?

It was as though he were not really her husband in this dream. How could he not know something so basic?

In fact, Jiyao had lately found herself preferring the way he had been in the early dreams -- when she did not have to control every word, and he simply seemed to know what she wanted. These days something felt subtly off, though she could not quite put her finger on what.

But she was too comfortable and too lazy to think hard about it. Dreams were meant for relaxing. Why would she spend one worrying?

She met his eyes and silently willed: he stops asking questions, and instead lets me lie with my head in his lap while he combs out my hair.

With that thought, Qin Yuan found he had lost control of the dream again.

His mood sank. But against his will, he settled beside her, let her lay her head in his lap, took the comb she handed him, and began drawing it gently through her hair.

Her hair fanned out loose and dark, like a length of fine black silk -- smooth and soft, with no ornament anywhere to interrupt it.

Qin Yuan had intended to keep searching for clues in this dream. Instead he could only sit with the comb in his hand, working through one long, unhurried stroke after another.

Jiyao loved having her hair combed. Every time, it made her feel as though the tension left her body all at once, and she grew drowsy and content.

At some point, without quite meaning to, she shifted and rolled into his arms.

They were very close together, and summer robes were thin. Jiyao noticed, with no great surprise, the obvious change in him.

She half-tipped her head back to look at him, dark eyes catching the moonlight, flower-petal lips parting softly. "Husband, shall we try doing it on a boat?"

Qin Yuan's lips pressed together. His throat moved without his permission. Fox spirit, he thought.

But before he could answer, Jiyao was already second-guessing herself: no, no. Even if it was a dream, even if there was no one else around -- they were on a lake, on a boat, out in the open. How could she do something like that out here?

So she only said, "Never mind. Forget I said it. Just keep combing my hair."

Qin Yuan closed his eyes and drew a long breath.

Fox spirit, he thought again.

chapters.title: Probing
chapters.content:
Like so many times before, Qin Yuan woke and went directly to the bathing room.

He called for water and submerged himself.

With his eyes half-closed, he turned the dream over in his mind, and the more he thought about it, the darker his expression grew. For one brief and rather alarming moment, he was seized by the urge to issue a proclamation across the entire empire, commanding every locality to find a young woman with a red mole behind her ear.

The impulse lasted barely a heartbeat before he crushed it.

He had been emperor long enough to know exactly what would happen. If he issued a decree like that, the people below him would scramble to interpret his intent, and the women brought before him would almost certainly not be the one he was looking for.

And something so heavy-handed would inevitably fall on the shoulders of ordinary people. Causing suffering for the sake of the empire was one thing -- regrettable but sometimes necessary. Causing it for purely personal reasons was something else entirely, and something Qin Yuan would not stoop to, whatever his reputation said about him.

He had a name for brutal in the court. He did not think he had yet become shameless.

No -- he would continue gathering information quietly, and identify her himself.

He had far too little to go on.

Her name: unknown.

Her age: unknown. From her voice, he could only estimate -- past fifteen, not yet twenty.

Her appearance: unknown. He knew only that her skin was very fair, that she had gently arching brows, and a small red mole behind one ear.

Her origins: unknown. But she was likely living in the capital, or had been.

Her family...

Qin Yuan caught himself. He had nearly overlooked something. This woman was not the only person who appeared in that dream. Aside from the street vendors they had passed that one time, there were her parents.

He remembered -- in the earliest dreams, he had seen her parents with his own eyes. He had even, to his profound humiliation, declared in front of them that he would marry into her family.

The trouble was that at the time, he had still been too disoriented to look carefully. He could recall only a vague impression of her father -- a few wisps of beard, a pleasant, refined face.

He could not reconstruct the features precisely enough to draw them.

Still, it was something. A rough outline at least, which was more than he had with the woman.

Qin Yuan opened his eyes. Perhaps, he thought, her father was the better starting point.

He could not produce a likeness of her. He might be able to produce one of her father.

And a man was, in any case, easier to track down than a woman hidden away in the inner quarters of a household.

With that thought, a quiet thread of renewed confidence settled over him, and with it, a cautious sense of anticipation for the next dream.

...

Into the sixth month, the heat grew relentless.

The women's tutor fell ill, and the Fang family's academy closed temporarily.

With the sun blazing outside, Jiyao had no desire to go out. She spent her days lazily in Haitang Courtyard, studying chess manuals or reading and practicing her calligraphy.

Perhaps it was the heat, but she had little appetite, and a vague, formless unease sat somewhere in her chest that she could not quite name.

One afternoon, Third Cousin Zhiyao came to find her and had barely stepped inside before she started complaining about the warmth.

Jiyao rose and asked Shuangxi to bring a cup of sour plum soup, smiling as she said, "In weather like this, why aren't you resting? Why are you running around?"

Third Sister accepted the cup and drained it in one breath, then picked up a fan and started waving it. "Second Sister, you don't know -- I would love to stay home and rest, but my mother keeps..."

She seemed to catch herself. The sentence cut off abruptly.

Jiyao only smiled and did not press.

Third Sister went on anyway. "My mother has been in a bad mood lately and keeps finding fault with me."

"What's the matter with Third Aunt? Is it the heat making her irritable?"

"No." Zhiyao waved her hand, clearly struggling with how to put it, and ended up only saying vaguely, "It's just -- various small things. Never mind, I don't want to talk about her."

She could hardly explain that because First Aunt had been in poor health for years, her own mother had been managing the Fang household. Now that Eldest Cousin and his wife had returned, First Aunt had suggested that First Cousin-in-law help share the domestic duties -- and Third Aunt, though she said nothing openly, was seething. She was convinced this was First Aunt directing her daughter-in-law to take over the household management.

With no one outside the family she could vent to, Third Aunt kept it all bottled up and then periodically let it out on those closest to her. The past couple of days, Third Sister had been sitting with her mother, and the slightest misstep seemed to set her off.

She could not sit still at home any longer. Coming to stay with Second Sister was a refuge.

Jiyao had always been quiet and uncomplaining. If her cousin did not say, she would not ask.

Third Sister chattered on -- about not sleeping well lately, about having just gotten engaged and already needing to start embroidering her wedding clothes...

Jiyao listened in companionable silence, chiming in with a word or two every now and then, and refilled her cousin's cup of cooled tea at the right moment.

Third Sister stayed until early evening before finally leaving.

Jiyao breathed out slowly and thought: everyone carries their own worries. Even cheerful, carefree Third Sister had her troubles.

Though -- Third Sister was already embroidering her wedding clothes?

Jiyao shook her head and pushed the thought away.

The evening light was deepening, and Shuangxi brought in dinner.

Jiyao ate only a few bites before setting it aside. She was about to return to the chess manual when a sudden clatter of sound came from outside.

A downpour had arrived without warning.

The rain came fast and heavy. It swept away the oppressive heat and, with it, something of the vague unhappiness that had been sitting in Jiyao's chest all day.

She did not go back to the chess manual. Instead she stood by the window and watched the rain.

The sky and earth blurred together in the dusk, one vast grey curtain. Rain struck the ground in sheets, and she felt strangely, quietly glad.

That night, Jiyao shaped her dream once more.

Outside, the rain was still pouring.

Even inside the room, the sound of it came through faintly.

Jiyao was playing chess with her husband.

She studied the board with a downward glance -- they had each placed only one stone. She smiled and placed another. "Your turn."

...

When Qin Yuan found himself in the strange dream without warning, he felt no surprise at all.

He thought of the heavy rain when he had gone to sleep, and heard the same rain outside the dream now. His certainty solidified: this woman was somewhere in or near the capital.

Since Jiyao was not actively shaping the dream, he could move freely.

He picked up a stone and set it down with a quiet click.

A small sound of surprise escaped Jiyao. She had not expected that move.

She had played chess in her dreams before, or watched others play, but it had nearly always been familiar formations straight from the manuals, or routes she knew well.

This move from her husband was something she had not anticipated.

Jiyao placed a stone. And then another exchange, and another after that.

The further they played, the more delighted she grew. This really was different from usual.

Could it be that somewhere in her depths, there were things she had never consciously noticed? Things that only surfaced in dreams?

She had read once in a collection of miscellany about ancient scholars who had achieved enlightenment in dreams. The thought made her sit up straighter with a flicker of genuine excitement.

Qin Yuan was surprised too.

He had spent enough time in this strange dream to have formed some picture of this woman: spoiled, prone to tears in intimate moments, someone who liked provoking a response but could not endure very much herself. He had not expected her to play chess like someone building a fortress -- steady, careful, impossible to dismiss.

Solid defense, methodical advancement. He had underestimated her.

Jiyao was quietly puzzled as well.

That sweeping, incisive style -- where had she seen it? Which school of chess was this? And it was appearing in her dream?

One attacked, the other defended. Their styles were entirely different. But somehow in this dream, they wound and wound around each other in a match that went on for a long time.

Then a crack of thunder shook the air, and Jiyao suddenly remembered.

She had entered this dream tonight intending to do something else entirely with her husband.

Her mind had been heavy and restless for days. The rain outside had made her want a different kind of thrill.

How had she gotten so caught up in chess that she forgot?

She set down her stone and smiled. "We'll finish another time. While the rain is still falling, let's do something else first."

"Something else?" Qin Yuan's thoughts jumped, and he had a fairly good idea what she meant. He kept his tone neutral. "What's the rush? We haven't even finished the game."

Though he had to admit -- that she could hold her own against him for this many moves said something real about her ability.

Jiyao blinked. What did he mean, what was the rush? She was the one who had imagined him. Why would he care about finishing a game?

She did not say this aloud.

She stood, walked around to his side of the table, and wrapped her arms around him from behind, pressing soft words against his shoulder. "But I want to try it now..."

She had never done it while it was raining.

The chess would keep. If the rain stopped, the moment would be gone.

The young woman's soft body pressed close against his back, and Qin Yuan went very still. He knew he ought to push her away. But a thought crossed his mind: was there any point?

He could not resist in the end anyway. And he had already decided to play along and use the opportunity to gather more information.

So he did not move. He only asked, "Try what?"

"You know perfectly well," Jiyao said with a hint of fond reproach. Her thoughts shifted, and a booklet appeared in her hands. She came around to his side and leaned against him. "This one, this one, and this one. Pick one of the three."

Without waiting for his answer, Jiyao had already decided, pointing to one of the pages. "This one. Let's do this one."

Qin Yuan smiled to himself.

Exactly as he had known. What did it matter whether he answered or not?

But in the next instant he caught himself: what was he thinking? He was playing along with her, not actually interested in any of this. Why was he giving any thought at all to which style she chose?

...

The thin gauze curtain fell around them.

Outside, the rain went on. Inside, Jiyao was turned away from him, drawn back against his chest. A trail of kisses moved down the pale line of her neck.

Jiyao's feet arched without her meaning them to.

With the rain outside to cover the sound, her voice was barely audible.

...

After some time, the rain finally stopped.

Jiyao lay where she was, content and hazy, not wanting to move a single inch.

She had always found that the intensity became too much and ended the dream before she was ready. But lately she had discovered that a little quiet time together after -- just resting, without any particular intention -- had its own gentle, understated sweetness.

To keep things from getting out of hand again, Jiyao even directed the dream to restore their clothing at once.

Then she asked him to draw her eyebrows.

Her brows were naturally well-shaped, soft arches like distant hills -- she had no real need to enhance them. But this was a dream, and she wanted to try what the books described as the pleasure of having one's brows drawn by someone you loved.

They sat together in front of the mirror.

Strangely, the polished bronze surface was slightly clouded. The figures reflected in it were indistinct.

Qin Yuan's attention sharpened. He had nearly forgotten what he was supposed to be doing here.

He said, as though it had just occurred to him, "I haven't seen your parents in a while. Should I go and pay my respects?"

Jiyao stiffened slightly.

She was still a little soft from earlier, and he had chosen this particular moment to bring up her parents?

"Some other time," she said casually. "Father isn't home."

"Not home?"

"He's on duty at his office tonight." Jiyao found the reason quickly.

In her dream, her father was alive. And since he was alive, he would naturally still be serving as an official -- not sitting idle at home. She had said it without thinking, just the first plausible excuse that came to mind.

But Qin Yuan's mind caught on it immediately.

On duty at his office. Which meant her father held a position in the court. But given how plain the silver bracelet was, his rank was probably not high.

Qin Yuan was about to press for more when the dream ended abruptly.

...

Jiyao opened her eyes and breathed out slowly. She tidied herself, lay back down, and settled into sleep.

Thinking back on the dream, she felt a faint, inexplicable awkwardness. A small thread of something like embarrassment.

In her dreams she moved between two worlds -- her parents in one, her husband in the other. But aside from that very first dream, something in her had never quite been willing to let those two worlds meet.

It was as though, if her parents knew what she got up to with her husband, they would be disappointed in her.

Jiyao touched her still-warm cheek and sighed softly.

She thought: there was no real reason to feel this way. In the dream she was a married woman, after all. Her parents knew about her husband. They had been there.

There was nothing to be embarrassed about.

chapters.title: Dreaming
chapters.content:
Qin Yuan came awake without opening his eyes.

He lay still, sifting through everything -- what was real, what was dream, what might be used.

Put together, the scattered fragments pointed somewhere specific: she was very likely the daughter of a minor official somewhere in the capital.

Minor, because of the plain silver bracelet. And for another reason: the one time he had caught a glimpse of her father in the dream, he had not recognized the man. If her father had been a senior official who attended morning court regularly, Qin Yuan would have known his face.

Still, the only way to be certain was to see him again.

...

The emperor had been paying unusual attention to the officials of the various ministries in the capital.

Some at court speculated that he was planning a purge of the civil service. Given what they knew of his methods, the mood both inside and outside the government turned cautious.

One morning, while Qin Yuan was working through a pile of memorials, a eunuch arrived from the Shoukang Palace with word that the Empress Dowager Grand Empress was unwell.

His hand paused on the paper. He did not look up. "Unwell?"

"Yes, Your Majesty." The eunuch replied carefully.

"Has a physician been called?"

"Yes, Your Majesty. The physician says it is heat affecting the heart, combined with suppressed internal fire."

The emperor made a quiet sound. "Understood. You may go."

The eunuch bowed and hurried out.

Qin Yuan finished the memorial he was working on. After a while, he rose and made his way to Shoukang Palace.

Over the years, he had been dutiful in sending gifts -- rare and precious things, a steady stream of ice through the summer months, never once missed. And now the palace physician had the nerve to say she was suffering from heat?

That was quite something.

He noticed the coolness the moment he stepped inside.

Qin Yuan's expression flickered.

The eunuch Chang Shouan, who had been transferred to Shoukang Palace, quickly led the others in hurrying forward to greet him. "We pay our respects to Your Majesty..." His voice cracked, and his eyes went red within the first few words. Nearly two months. He had finally seen His Majesty again. He had not been mistreated here -- no one had dared to treat him badly -- but the loneliness and quiet humiliation of his situation was something only he could fully know.

Qin Yuan's gaze passed over him without pausing. "How is the Grand Empress?"

"She took her medicine and rested a while, Your Majesty. She has just woken."

Before the eunuch had finished speaking, a delighted voice came from the inner chamber: "Is that the Emperor? Quick, please ask him in."

Qin Yuan's expression shifted very slightly. He went inside.

In the center of the inner chamber, a large ice basin was breathing out cool mist.

It was noticeably more comfortable than outside.

The Grand Empress was propped against pillows, a light coverlet drawn over her. Without her usual careful makeup, a few signs of age showed through her normally composed features.

"Is Grandmother feeling better?" Qin Yuan came to her side and asked.

"Much better. Really, there was nothing wrong with me to begin with. Those below me shouldn't have alarmed you over something so trivial." She sounded genuinely flustered.

Qin Yuan replied with complete courtesy. "Nothing concerning Grandmother is trivial. It is all important business."

The Grand Empress smiled, and then sighed.

"I hear that Grandmother's indisposition was due to suppressed fire and the heat." Qin Yuan's expression became mildly grave, and his gaze swept cold over the palace attendants and eunuchs. "Has anyone in her service been negligent?"

Every person in the room felt a chill. They dropped to their knees, one after another, crying out that they had done nothing wrong.

Within moments, the hall was full of kneeling figures, all pleading their innocence.

The Grand Empress startled. "It isn't their fault. They have all been very attentive. It is I -- I have been troubled lately."

"Troubled?" The emperor's expression shifted slightly, as though puzzled. "What could Grandmother be troubled about?"

She hesitated. "I have been dreaming a great deal lately. Often of my parents and my younger brother. My parents are gone now, and I only have the one brother left. Whenever I think of it, I feel sad."

"That is easily addressed." Qin Yuan said it without a moment's pause. "Summon the Marquis of Cheng'en to the palace at once."

The words were barely out before an attendant had already gone to carry out the order.

A smile appeared on the Grand Empress's face.

Not only because she would see her brother -- but because of what it meant that the emperor had come at all.

After the incident with the palace women, the emperor had continued to provide for her without any change in the material sense. But he had not set foot in Shoukang Palace, had not come to offer his morning and evening greetings. At first she had told herself it was nothing. As time stretched on, a quiet anxiety had begun to take root.

Had she truly offended him?

Now he had come to visit her when she fell ill, and he had even allowed her brother to enter the palace to see her. The weight she had been carrying quietly released itself, and her face visibly brightened.

She smiled with genuine warmth. "The Emperor must take care of himself. Affairs of state are important, but rest is important too."

"Grandmother is quite right." He inclined his head with an expression of dutiful attention.

She gave him a few more careful pieces of advice, all of which he accepted agreeably.

The atmosphere was warm and easy.

Seeing that the emperor seemed to be in decent spirits, the Grand Empress ventured to raise another matter. "For the sake of the imperial succession, the Emperor should expand the court ladies. If a full imperial wedding feels too much of an undertaking, a few consorts could be arranged first..."

She had always intended to keep to herself and not meddle in things. But she was still the Grand Empress, and with the inner palace empty and no heir in sight, her own position was uncertain. She felt she had to speak, when the moment arose.

Qin Yuan smiled faintly and said, with the air of someone making idle conversation, "There is no urgency."

A wedding? Consorts?

He was already thoroughly occupied with the matter of the dream. He had no patience for anything else.

The Grand Empress paused. No urgency? What exactly was not urgent -- the wedding, or the consorts?

She collected herself and asked, "The last time, with those palace women -- was it that the Emperor found them too lowborn?"

Qin Yuan's expression tightened slightly. He remembered exactly what she was referring to. The business of being forcibly presented with those women still irritated him when he thought of it.

But the Grand Empress was watching him with genuine concern, and she was unwell. Qin Yuan had no interest in going into detail. He made a vague sound of acknowledgment and looked for a way to excuse himself.

"I understand," the Grand Empress sighed. "I did not think it through carefully enough. The first woman in the inner palace ought to be from a scholarly or official family..."

Qin Yuan's thoughts snagged.

An official's family. Well, that description could apply to someone -- like the woman in the dream, for instance --

No. Why was he thinking about her again?

"Perhaps I could select a few young ladies from official families to be placed in the palace," the Grand Empress continued.

"There is no need. I have my own thinking on this matter, and I would not have Grandmother concern herself." Qin Yuan pushed the thought aside and cut her off gently but firmly.

He had no desire for a repeat of last time.

He had no intention of being close to any woman until the matter of the dream was settled.

"Grandmother should rest," Qin Yuan said, composing himself. "I have affairs to attend to."

He rose and left.

After the emperor had gone some distance, the Grand Empress noticed Chang Shouan standing nearby and let out a small sound of guilt. In the conversation just now, she had meant to put in a word on his behalf -- and had completely forgotten.

Well. If she had not truly offended the Emperor after all, there would be other opportunities. She could speak for him another time.

As for helping select new ladies for the palace -- the emperor had said he had his own thinking on the matter, and she was left with no choice but to let it rest.

...

After leaving Shoukang Palace, Qin Yuan returned to his memorials.

That evening, he had calming incense lit and retired early.

He had made up his mind: to confirm her identity in his dreams, he could not afford to miss any opportunity.

That night, Jiyao stayed up later than usual.

She had been caught up in thinking through the chess game she had played with her husband in their last dream, and had spent the day absorbed in reviewing it, her excitement growing. Then, to make things even better, her eldest cousin had sent over a chess manual as a gift.

Jiyao read until the hour of Hai before finally hurrying off to sleep.

Perhaps because she had been looking at the chess manual just before bed, she found herself in the dream studying one too, seated by a window.

When she realized she was dreaming, she deliberately shifted the scene, picturing her husband and asking him to come and continue the game.

In an instant, she was seated in a pavilion.

Not far away was a pond of lotus flowers. A gentle breeze carried traces of their scent, and across from her sat her husband.

The board between them held exactly the position from where they had left off in the previous dream.

He was sitting very still, expression unreadable. Jiyao smiled and gave him a nudge. "It's your turn. What are you thinking about?"

...

Qin Yuan heard her voice and felt the familiar shift. He was in the dream again.

A lotus pond, a pavilion, a light breeze.

The two of them seated across from each other.

Ah -- they were playing chess.

He glanced down at the board, picked up a stone, set it down, and asked in a tone of pleasant unconcern, "Can we go today?"

Jiyao blinked. "Go where? Who are you talking about?"

"Your parents."

Jiyao's brows drew together slightly. She thought about it, and then could not help correcting him. "You ought to call them your in-laws."

Of all things -- just the other night after waking from that dream, she had been vaguely thinking that she might let him be formally introduced, have him present tea, perform the proper courtesies. And here he was opening with "your parents"?

That was not right. It was very impolite.

It was strange, actually. In the beginning, her imagined husband had seemed to know exactly what she wanted without her having to direct him at all. Lately she kept noticing these small ways in which he did not quite get things right.

Still, with a face like his, it was forgivable.

Qin Yuan kept his thoughts to himself. In-laws? He was the emperor. Even in a real imperial marriage, his wife's parents would address him as subject and lord. He might, as a courtesy, call her father by the term -- out of kindness to the empress. But this man in the dream? The thought alone was almost comical.

He said nothing. He placed another stone on the board.

Jiyao did not pursue it. She made a generous wave of her hand. "Never mind. Chess first, we'll deal with the rest after."

She was here for the chess.

Qin Yuan had no interest in playing. If the plan was to meet the parents "after the game," the simplest solution was to throw the match and end it.

So he made a few deliberate, careless moves and walked himself into a loss.

Jiyao could not believe it. She had spent the whole day going over the game, thinking carefully about every move. And it ended like that?

That quickly?

She steadied herself. "Again."

But Qin Yuan was reluctant, and said vaguely, "The game is over. Shall we not go and see them?"

He could not bring himself to say "in-laws." He simply could not make the word leave his mouth.

"One more game first."

Jiyao could see he was not willing, and felt a flicker of annoyance. She turned the thought over: he is not to bring up my parents again, he is happy to play another game with me.

With that, Qin Yuan found he had lost control of the dream.

Inwardly furious, he could do nothing but settle in front of the board, wearing a faint, automatic smile, and go on playing.

He genuinely did not want to let her have her way -- so when he realized he still had some influence over the individual stones he placed, he quietly began to sabotage himself. If she wanted chess, he would give her chaos.

Jiyao noticed something was wrong almost at once, puzzled. What had happened? He had been so good last time.

She tried again. Still wrong.

Again. The same result.

After several games in a row, she had confirmed it: his playing had collapsed entirely. There was not a trace of the brilliance from that other dream. He was, quite simply, terrible.

She looked at him with something she could not quite bring herself to say. "You..."

"What is it?" Qin Yuan raised a faint, innocent eyebrow.

"Nothing." Jiyao thought it through carefully. Perhaps that was just how dreams worked -- unpredictable and inconsistent. She had wanted to play chess with him, but had not directed every move. And deep down she did not want to repeat the patterns she already knew. So maybe his poor play right now made a kind of sense.

No. That was wrong.

Because then how had he played so brilliantly in that last dream?

She remembered vividly -- his style had been sharp and incisive, and they had played for a long time.

Could it be that she really was like those scholars from the old books, achieving a flash of insight in a dream?

If so, that kind of thing was rare and could not be summoned at will.

The thought made her regret the last dream a little. She should not have wasted it. She should have kept playing.

But Jiyao had always been good at not letting things she could not change ruin her mood.

She closed her eyes for a moment and redirected her thinking.

For the remaining games, she began to consciously direct each of his moves.

And yes -- when she directed him, he played at his real level.

But she found the feeling hollow. This was no different from playing against herself.

The joy went out of it. She lost interest in continuing.

She looked at him, and ended the dream with a faint sense of disappointment.

...

In the inner chambers of Zichen Palace.

Qin Yuan's eyes flew open.

The single lamp left burning in the room gave off a soft, unsteady light.

For once, he did not go straight to the bathing room. He lay where he was.

The dream played back clearly in his mind. The young emperor's feelings were complicated.

He had obviously, infuriatingly, forgotten himself. He had meant to play along -- and then spent his time in the dream taking petty revenge like a child.

Had he lost sight of what he was actually there to do?

He had wasted the entire opportunity.

And her expression at the end. That look. Was that disappointment?

He might not be able to hold onto her face, but expressions were another matter.

It was still early -- nowhere near morning court. But sleep did not come. Qin Yuan gave in and called for another stick of calming incense to be lit.

The faint, gentle scent drifted through the chamber. He lay with his eyes half-closed and eventually drifted off again.

The dream seemed to pick up where it had left off.

They were playing chess, he had been making a mess of it on purpose, and she was displeased -- she shot him a look, said something he could not quite catch, then stood up and sat herself in his lap, lifting her face to kiss him while her hands moved downward and closed around him...

Qin Yuan jolted awake, heart hammering, his expression deeply unhappy.

Not the strange dream.

He knew immediately. This was different from the dream he could not control -- this was something he had drifted into himself, half-asleep. It was hazier, more indistinct, like looking through a layer of gauze. Nothing like the vivid, almost tactile reality of the other dream.

Qin Yuan pressed his fingers to his temple.

He was losing his mind. An ordinary dream, and it was still about her.

chapters.title: Expedience
chapters.content:
This was not the first time Qin Yuan had dreamed something like this on his own.

He was a young man in reasonable health. He had occasionally had such fragments before -- but always dim, always faceless.

This time he still could not hold onto her face, but he knew with certainty it was her. The scene had even carried on directly from the strange dream.

The young emperor lay in the darkness, his eyes unreadable, his expression dark.

Being pulled into the strange dream against his will was one thing. But dreaming this on his own -- what did that say?

Had the strange dream simply become habit?

He did not linger on the question. He got up and dealt with the aftermath, then went to the bathing room as usual and called for water.

In the bathing room, Chang Fu -- on duty again tonight -- quietly exhaled when he heard the water begin.

He had been making sense of all these midnight baths, privately and with some sympathy for his adoptive father Chang Shouan. If the emperor kept having his temper stirred up at this rate, it was not unreasonable that Chang Shouan had thought to mention it to the Grand Empress and ask her to arrange something. It made a certain kind of sense.

What no one had anticipated was that it would enrage the emperor so thoroughly. And here Chang Shouan still was, stuck in Shoukang Palace with no way back.

Truly unfortunate.

Of course, Chang Fu kept every single one of these thoughts tucked firmly inside his head. He was not about to let a word of it out -- not while he still had a post to keep.

...

At the Minister's residence.

Jiyao opened her eyes and breathed out slowly.

She was not entirely satisfied with that dream. But it was a small thing. Just a dream.

She composed herself, closed her eyes, and went back to sleep.

This time, she let herself drift without trying to shape anything. Just rest.

When she woke again, it was daylight. She tidied herself and went to the academy.

The tutor had recovered, and classes had resumed.

Fourth and Fifth Cousin still looked past her as though she were not there. Jiyao paid it no mind.

She spent her days reading at the academy or working through the new chess manual at Haitang Courtyard, thoroughly occupied and thoroughly content.

Though, admittedly, a little tired.

The days were still long and the nights short, and Jiyao felt perpetually short on sleep. For several nights in a row, she did not shape her dreams at all.

Finally, the day before a rest day, she decided that tonight she would let herself go a little in the dream.

But just after dinner, Third Cousin Zhiyao arrived at Haitang Courtyard, bright-eyed and smiling the moment she stepped through the door. "Second Sister, come out with us tomorrow?"

"Where? Who's going?"

"Ziyun Temple on Qiyun Mountain, to pray." Zhiyao lowered her voice. "It's really my mother who wants to go and burn incense. I asked her if she'd bring you along, and she said to come and ask whether you'd like to join us."

Third Sister's eyes were wide and expectant.

Jiyao felt the pull of it at once.

She rarely went out. The last time had been for Grandfather's birthday gift. This time there would be an elder accompanying them, which made it altogether more proper -- and more rare.

"Yes, of course -- I'd love to," Jiyao said without hesitation.

"Then get some rest early, and we'll go together tomorrow."

"I will." Jiyao nodded firmly.

With everything settled, Third Sister rose and left.

Because of the outing tomorrow -- to a Daoist temple, a place calling for a certain reverence -- Jiyao did not feel right about spending the night in the dream seeking the kind of excitement she usually looked for. She went to bed early.

The next morning, tidied and ready, Jiyao joined Third Aunt and her daughter in a carriage headed for Ziyun Temple in the hills outside the capital.

The carriage moved smoothly.

Third Aunt Jin Xiaoyue gave both girls careful instructions as they rode. "When we get inside the temple, stay close to me. Don't wander off, and don't speak carelessly -- we don't want to offend the gods..."

Both Jiyao and Zhiyao agreed meekly.

Jin Xiaoyue smiled, pleased with their response.

The household management situation had been sitting heavily on her for days, and with no one she could properly confide in, she had seized on the excuse of a prayer visit to get out of the house. She had originally planned to bring only her daughter, but her daughter had asked if Jiyao could come. It was no great trouble to add her.

She had always felt a quiet sort of pity for this niece. Jiyao and Zhiyao were close in age, but such different creatures. This child had lost her parents and gone through it all without a fuss. In nearly ten years of managing the Fang household, Jiyao had never once caused her a moment of difficulty.

On that basis alone, Jin Xiaoyue thought: bringing her along costs me nothing.

After they left the city gates, the carriage rolled west. Before long, they reached the foot of Qiyun Mountain.

Ziyun Temple sat at the halfway point of Qiyun Mountain, outside the capital, dedicated to the Three Pure Ones and an assortment of other deities.

The temple had not drawn many worshippers in years past. But after the current emperor's campaign against Buddhism -- dismantling monasteries, reclaiming their lands, compelling monks to return to secular life and pay taxes -- Ziyun Temple had seen a steady and growing stream of visitors.

Today was no exception. The temple was busy.

Third Aunt rallied herself, led both girls through the incense offering and the prayers and the wishes, and drew a fortune slip.

Everything went smoothly, except for a small delay at the end -- interpreting the slip. Everyone, it seemed, wanted Daoist Yunhe to read theirs, and there was quite a queue.

They settled in to wait patiently.

Third Cousin Zhiyao grew bored and turned to her cousin. "Is Daoist Yunhe very skilled? Why is everyone asking for him specifically?"

"That's..." Jiyao hesitated, unsure how to answer. She had never interacted with Yunhe herself and had no way to know.

She was composing a careful maybe when a familiar voice came from just behind them.

"He is very skilled. They say he's a living immortal -- able to commune with the gods, read fortune and misfortune. Even people from the palace have summoned him for consultation."

Jiyao turned in mild surprise. It was Lu Ming.

She had not expected to see him here of all places.

Zhiyao recognized him too but could not quite place the name. "You -- wait, it's you -- you're..."

Jiyao murmured helpfully, "Young Master Lu. Jin De's elder cousin."

"Right, right, of course." Zhiyao remembered. Zhao Jinde's cousin, the one currently studying at the Fang family school.

Lu Ming stepped back slightly and bowed to both of them. "My respects to the two young misses."

He had brought his mother to Ziyun Temple today to offer incense, and while waiting for their fortunes to be read, had run into people he knew.

Two young ladies was one thing -- but there was an elder present. Third Aunt, no less.

Third Aunt managed the inner workings of the Fang household and kept close attention to the family school. She had specifically arranged for tea, refreshments, and seasonal fruit to be provided daily. As one of the beneficiaries, Lu Ming felt genuine gratitude, and he bowed to her with genuine respect.

Third Aunt smiled warmly. "You are far too formal, child."

Her eyes then landed on Lu Ming's mother, Zhao Yuanniang, and the two of them fell into conversation. They had met a few times at the Zhao household and had always gotten along well.

It was unusual to run into acquaintances like this, and they were family besides. With both women at leisure, they found more and more to talk about.

Zhiyao still had the earlier topic on her mind and leaned toward her cousin. "People from the palace? Which people from the palace? The Grand Empress?"

As far as she knew, the emperor had no empress and no consorts. The empress dowager was in retreat at a detached palace. The only two truly significant people in the palace were the emperor himself and the Grand Empress.

Jiyao had no idea. She almost never left the house, and most of what she knew came from books, classes, and what relatives mentioned in passing.

She shook her head and said nothing.

Lu Ming sighed. He knew he should probably not have said anything, but he could not help adding quietly, "It was His Majesty."

He had overheard one of the young Daoist novices mention it during an earlier visit with his mother.

"Oh..." Third Sister let out a small involuntary sound of surprise. "But how could he..."

Jiyao's eyes had gone wide too.

She had heard about the emperor's campaign against Buddhism -- the demolishing of temples, the reclaimed land, the forced disrobing of monks. She had assumed this emperor had no faith in the divine or the supernatural. That he would consult a Daoist priest seemed genuinely impossible to her.

Lu Ming, perhaps reading their expressions, added quietly, "The thoughts of those above us are not for people like us to guess at."

Jiyao nodded. That seemed very true.

All of this was, in any case, very far from their world. Jiyao took it in and let it pass.

The line for fortune-reading had dwindled. Finally it was their turn.

The fortunes were favorable for all of them. Both aunts were in excellent spirits and made offerings accordingly. They stayed for a vegetarian lunch in the temple's dining hall and each received a protective talisman and a sachet before they left.

It was mid-afternoon by the time the group descended from the temple.

The two families parted at the city gate and went their separate ways.

Inside the Lu family's carriage, Zhao Yuanniang turned to her son. "The two Fang girls we saw today -- are either of them promised?"

"One of them is engaged, I think. The other isn't yet," Lu Ming said vaguely.

Zhao Yuanniang gave a small hum and murmured, "How lovely."

Lu Ming was puzzled. Lovely? What was lovely?

But he did not ask. Something told him, with a vague and slightly alarming certainty, that if he pressed further, he would be stepping into territory that was not quite proper.

The thought of that territory made his heartbeat, against his will, quicken slightly.

...

Inside the Fang family's carriage.

Third Aunt Jin Xiaoyue stroked the fortune slip, her mood still bright.

Jiyao, on the other hand, felt a quiet pang of regret.

It had been a rare outing, and the mountain scenery had been beautiful, but they had moved through it all in a rush, with no time to truly take anything in.

She shook the feeling off quickly.

Never mind. There was tonight. She would dream it.

That night, after bathing, Jiyao changed into a thin sleeping robe and drew the gauze curtain carefully around her.

Lying in bed, she realized belatedly: she had originally planned last night to let herself go a little in the dream. Tonight she wanted to go out and play instead.

Which to choose?

She thought about it. Then decided: why not both? Go out during the dream's daytime, come home and indulge a little when it gets dark. That was perfectly sensible.

Dreams had their own sense of time anyway -- it was not like the real world.

She had gone days without shaping her dreams. This time, she might as well make it worthwhile.

With her mind made up, Jiyao closed her eyes, let her thoughts go, and drifted into sleep.

The dream began somewhere unfamiliar.

Red walls, green-tiled roofs, halls and towers rising in tiers. It looked like a palace or perhaps a temple. Somewhere in the distance, voices murmured -- too far away to make out.

Jiyao was disoriented for a moment. The place stirred a vague memory -- it reminded her a little of where she had first encountered her husband in a dream.

At the thought of that face, which had settled so completely into her heart, she found it easy to forgive him for whatever had happened with his chess.

Forget it. It was a small thing. In the next dream she would just guide him to play properly. Easy enough.

Jiyao let her thoughts shift, and in an instant she was standing in the peach grove of Haitang Courtyard.

She centered herself and called out silently: come out, husband -- just as you looked the second time I saw you.

She remembered clearly: the second time she had dreamed of him, he had his dark hair bound high, and stood holding a sword, dressed like a wandering swordsman. That was how she had first imagined him -- a free-spirited wanderer who had married into her family willingly. He had danced with the sword for her. He had brought her flowers.

A traveling companion like that was just what this outing called for.

She steadied herself and walked quickly around to the back of a broad, sturdy peach tree. And there he was, stepping out from behind it.

Dressed exactly as she had imagined. Easy and assured, all natural grace and quiet strength.

...

Qin Yuan had gone several days without the strange dream.

That was normal. The dream had never come every night. And frankly, the nights without it were quieter.
