And yet, after five or six days of nothing, a restless dissatisfaction had begun to settle in him that he could not quite name or explain.

It was not that he missed the dream. Only that he still had not confirmed her identity, still had not exacted any kind of revenge. The idea of it just... ending, without resolution, was intolerable.

He needed to identify her, and soon.

But for some reason he kept returning to the end of that last dream -- her expression, that small flash of disappointment in her eyes.

Tonight, Qin Yuan had the calming incense lit as usual and went to bed early. Without warning, the strange dream took him.

He had not even finished collecting himself when she was right in front of him.

Before he could think, the words were already out: "I can play chess."

Jiyao blinked. "Chess? What do you mean?"

She wondered: why had he brought up chess without any context? Could it be because she had been thinking about forgiving his playing?

"Never mind," Qin Yuan said at once, regretting the words the moment they were spoken. He closed his mouth.

What was he saying? Why had he said that at all?

"We're not playing chess today." Jiyao had other things on her mind entirely. Her eyes lit up. "Husband, let's go somewhere. Let's go to Qiyun Mountain -- the scenery there is beautiful."

Qin Yuan's mind moved quickly.

His first instinct was to refuse. But the memory of that last dream was still fresh, and he knew exactly what happened when he refused. He lost control entirely and became little more than a puppet. And besides -- she had mentioned Qiyun Mountain. That confirmed she was in the capital.

Better to agree, go along with whatever she wanted, and look for openings.

He said, slowly, "I'd be glad to go. But shouldn't we let your..." he paused for just a fraction of a second, "...in-laws know first?"

The words in-laws. He had thought he would never say them. But now that he had, they came out easier than he had imagined.

He told himself: this is expediency. The same way he had once endured the regent, calling him respectfully Uncle Emperor through gritted teeth. Short-term tolerance in service of a longer objective.

The dream was not a place for pride. Once he had found her -- if her father turned out to be a decent official, he would be transferred far from the capital. If he turned out to be corrupt or foolish, there would be no need to leave him there at all.

The word in-laws pleased Jiyao visibly. She rose on her toes, kissed the corner of his mouth, and murmured, "You're right. But if we tell them, they'll only try to stop us going..."

Qin Yuan's expression shifted slightly.

"Although..." Jiyao's eyes moved, considering. "We could always ask forgiveness after. Go first, and apologize when we come back."

Qin Yuan's pulse gave a small, involuntary kick. He kept his tone easy. "Apologize in person?"

"Of course," Jiyao said. "Though it would also depend on what they want."

What she was actually thinking was: it would depend on how her husband conducted himself. If he continued to be as good as he had been, letting him properly pay his respects to her parents -- present tea, show his manners -- might not be entirely out of the question.

chapters.title: Indulgence
chapters.content:
For this outing, Jiyao decided not to travel in a carriage. She would ride.

She had never ridden a horse in real life. But her husband certainly knew how.

With a thought, the two of them were already outside.

The street was nearly empty, with hardly anyone in sight.

Qin Yuan's gaze moved over the surroundings. He did not recognize where they were.

"Let's share a horse," Jiyao said, pointing to the single horse standing nearby, eyes bright with anticipation.

Unfortunately, her husband did not seem to read her anticipation at all. He glanced at her once, then turned to look at the street around them.

He was trying to note the location.

Jiyao sighed quietly.

She formed the thought: pick me up and set me in the saddle, then mount behind me and hold the reins with both arms around me.

With that, Qin Yuan lost control of the dream. He pushed his thoughts aside, said nothing, lifted her into his arms, set her carefully onto the horse's back, and swung himself up behind her. With the reins gathered in his hands, his arms encircled her completely.

"Hiyah!"

The horse leaped forward. The scenery blurred past on either side.

Qin Yuan had trained in martial arts since childhood; riding and archery were second nature to him. But he had never carried anyone on horseback before.

The woman leaning against his chest was thoroughly restless -- now tilting her head, now shifting her weight. Her loosened hair blew back against his face, and her soft body pressed and shifted against him.

Qin Yuan felt a response stirring in him almost at once.

He was quietly furious.

The body in this dream truly could not withstand any provocation.

And she kept moving.

The vein at his temple was beginning to pulse. He gritted his teeth and finally said, low, near her ear, "Stop moving."

"Oh." Jiyao noticed the change behind her and blinked, taking a moment to understand what was happening. She felt slightly like laughing, and also slightly puzzled.

It was not as though she had been thinking about anything. Why had that happened?

But the thought was gone almost before it formed. Something else had caught her attention.

Riding a horse was not as much fun as she had imagined. It was actually rather uncomfortable.

She did not like it. It compared poorly, she thought, to riding a heavenly steed -- that was true freedom.

Since horseback riding was not enjoyable, there was no reason to keep going.

Jiyao let her thoughts shift, and the distance collapsed. In moments, they were at the foot of the mountain.

Qin Yuan noticed with quiet astonishment that the mountain before him was identical to the real Qiyun Mountain -- down to the height of the trees and the stones along the path.

Even the temple halfway up the slope was exactly the same.

Jiyao turned her head. "Carry me down."

Qin Yuan drew a slow breath, put one arm around her waist, and dropped them both from the saddle in a single controlled motion.

Once on the ground, Jiyao took hold of his arm and pulled him toward the mountain path.

He said nothing. He wanted to see what she was actually going to do.

She wanted, it turned out, to look at things.

Mountains, water, trees, flowers.

When they reached Ziyun Temple, Jiyao walked around it.

"Why not go inside?" Qin Yuan asked.

He thought of Daoist Yunhe somewhere within those walls -- who had a reputation as a living immortal, and yet could not even guess where she came from.

Jiyao thought: obviously she could not go in. Even at her most reckless in a dream, she retained some instinct for reverence in certain situations.

Besides, she had already been there today.

"I don't want to," she said quietly. "We're here to enjoy ourselves, not to pray."

So she played. She waded in the water, tried to catch fish, chased butterflies. Everything she had wanted to do on the real visit but had not.

Qin Yuan stood to the side, arms folded, watching with an expression somewhere between impatient and baffled.

This was it?

She had said they were going to Qiyun Mountain to play, and this was what she had meant? These things that children did?

He had known she was enthusiastic about a certain kind of activity. He had not expected this other, entirely childish side of her.

But he had made his decision to go along with her, so he said nothing and endured it -- watching her play.

Then Jiyao turned, caught sight of him standing nearby with his arms folded over the sword at his side, and waved him over with a bright smile. "Come and play too."

"Not--" He got one syllable out before feeling the familiar shift.

He had lost control again.

Qin Yuan told himself grimly: endure this. When he had found her and dragged her in front of him, he would repay all of it in full.

Thinking this, he proceeded to chase butterflies against his will.

His body in the dream seemed even more agile than in real life. He actually caught one -- a butterfly as wide as a bowl, its dark wings shimmering in the sunlight as it fanned them against his palm. Everything felt unnervingly real.

Jiyao said urgently beside him, "Be careful, don't hurt it."

The butterfly opened its wings and drifted away, growing smaller until it disappeared.

Qin Yuan was made to play games he could not stop -- floating down the stream on a bamboo raft, walking fast through the mountain paths, and finally, lying flat on his back in a meadow looking up at the sky.

He was the emperor. When he was tired of government affairs, he went to the practice grounds to ride and shoot. The first time he had ever done something this undignified, this pointless -- it was in a strange dream.

And the sensations were too real. On the stream, the current pushed fast against the raft and his heart rate went up with it. Lying in the grass in the sun, he could actually smell the warm green scent of it.

For him, it was entirely without precedent.

For just a moment, Qin Yuan had the disorienting sensation that he had genuinely left the machinery of the court behind, and was simply here, in the middle of mountains and water.

It lasted only a moment. He shook it off. Even if he actually went into the mountains for leisure, it would never be like this. Not this undignified.

Jiyao, oblivious to his thoughts, had glanced at the mountain stream and had a new idea.

The water was clear enough to see the bottom.

She sat at the edge, took off her shoes and stockings, and carefully dipped both feet in.

The current moved cool and slow against her soles, faintly tickling.

Jiyao felt so comfortable she almost sighed aloud. Her eyes half-closed.

When she found something good, she was always generous about sharing it.

She thought: sit beside me and soak your feet, right here.

This was her dream. What she wanted, she got.

So it was. Qin Yuan settled beside her, mirroring her posture.

He had taken many cold baths. But sitting barefoot at the edge of a mountain stream, feet in the water -- this was entirely new.

The current rushed cheerfully past his feet. Occasionally a small fish swam close and grazed past, cool and quick as a breath.

The surface of the water caught the light in shifting patterns. Then the young woman across from him slowly, deliberately stacked both of her pale feet on top of his.

The sensation was smooth and cool and entirely different from the fish.

Qin Yuan went rigid.

Jiyao glanced at him sidelong. A mischievous impulse rose in her, and she let her foot slide deliberately upward along his ankle.

Qin Yuan instinctively wanted to push her away and stand up. But at this moment he still could not control himself -- he could only sit there and feel that cool sensation moving up his leg.

It was cool. And yet something like a spark ignited in his chest, and spread fast through his whole body.

He said it to himself again: fox spirit.

She was supposed to be a well-bred young lady. How did she keep finding new ways to do this?

They were sitting very close, and the summer robes were thin. Jiyao could see the obvious change in him at a glance.

She let out a small, surprised sound, thinking she had imagined it, and nudged it lightly with her foot to check.

Burning.

Her foot was still damp from the stream.

His robe was half-damp now too, which only made things more apparent.

Her husband let out an involuntary hiss of breath. His face had gone red, beads of sweat at his brow. His throat shifted in a visible effort to hold himself still.

Watching him hold on -- the determined line of his jaw, the effort in his eyes -- Jiyao felt a sudden warmth stir in her.

She remembered: when she had shaped this dream tonight, she had planned it out. Go out and play in the daytime. Come home in the evening and enjoy herself a little.

They had been out long enough. It was time for the sky to darken.

That thought, and the light shifted.

In the blink of an eye, the two of them were inside, in Haitang Courtyard.

The familiar room. The familiar bed.

In exactly the same position they had been sitting in at the stream's edge.

Qin Yuan's mind registered the abrupt change with a jolt. It was not the first time she had transported them without warning, but this time it was unusually stark.

She seemed to have no interest in concealing it. It made him more curious than ever about who she was.

But this was not the moment to think about that.

The vein at his temple was jumping. His body felt like it was about to combust. And she chose that moment to give him another light tap with her foot.

It did not help. It made everything worse.

"What about this one?" Jiyao pulled her foot back, leaned against him, and pointed to a page of the erotic manual, eyes soft with anticipation and a trace of eagerness.

In that moment, Qin Yuan suddenly found he had regained control.

Jiyao asked again when he did not answer. "I'm asking you. Say something."

Qin Yuan closed his eyes for a moment. Something like "not particularly" was on the tip of his tongue, and then he changed it. "Whatever you like."

He had made the decision to play along. He could not let his control of the dream slip again over something as trivial as this. And he had barely managed to get it back.

Besides, he genuinely did not care either way.

Jiyao smiled and kissed the corner of his mouth. "I knew it."

That was better. Her preferences were what mattered.

...

The gauze curtain fell around them.

Qin Yuan noticed, as things unfolded, that whether or not he had agreed made little practical difference.

These things were going to happen regardless.

Though -- there was some distinction.

Right now, for instance, he had not followed the manual's illustration precisely. The manual showed her legs lifted over his shoulders. He had arranged things so that those two pale legs were wrapped around his waist instead.

And then, holding her, he moved with the same steady, accurate force he brought to archery practice. Every arrow to the center of the target.

Perhaps because she had gone so many days without shaping this kind of dream, Jiyao felt everything far more intensely than usual.

Her hair had come loose around her face. Her cheeks were flushed. At some point, a glimmer of tears had appeared at the corners of her eyes.

Later, Jiyao lay with her face against his shoulder, crying softly, her mind almost completely blank.

Qin Yuan gave a quiet, dry laugh to himself and settled her back onto the bed.

He had always known it. She loved to provoke a response, and then could not endure very much herself.

Her body was still trembling faintly. She recovered a little, looked at him, and leaned in to press a kiss to his cheek, murmuring, "I like you so much..."

After all, he was the husband she had conjured from her own imagination. He suited her perfectly in every way. Including this.

Perhaps because it had been too intense, Jiyao was pulled hard out of the dream and woke abruptly.

The night was deep and dark.

She lay staring up at the canopy of the bed for a while.

When she felt steadier, she got up, tidied herself, and lay back down.

Jiyao touched her still-warm cheek and thought: she had set out to find a thrill, but that had been rather more of a thrill than she had bargained for.

It was a good thing she did not dream like this every night.

...

In the inner chambers of Zichen Palace.

The young emperor opened his eyes.

For once, he had been fully satisfied. His body did not give him much trouble.

But then that phrase surfaced in his mind -- I like you so much -- and something in his chest gave a sudden, inexplicable sting.

He could not name what the feeling was.

Like? What kind of liking? Did she mean him?

A few moments passed. Then Qin Yuan remembered with a jolt: she had said she would apologize to her parents in person. And he had forgotten entirely.

How had he let something that important slip?

Qin Yuan closed his eyes. Perhaps it was not that he had forgotten, he thought. Perhaps it was simply that she had never given him an opening -- pushing it off, delaying it at every turn.

She had done it on purpose.

chapters.title: Strange
chapters.content:
Could it be that she had guessed his intentions? And was deliberately hiding her identity as a result?

No. If that were the case, why keep returning to the dream, again and again, and taking such risks? She could simply stop.

Could it really be because of that word she had used -- that she liked him?

The thought crossed his mind and was gone in an instant. Qin Yuan dismissed it completely.

Impossible. That woman's words could not be trusted. Especially anything said in the middle of... that. Those words in particular were never to be believed.

Then what was the reason?

He pressed his fingers to the dull ache at his temple and stopped thinking about it. He got up and went to the bathing room.

The next day, when he had a free moment, Qin Yuan changed into plain clothes and set out with two guards for Qiyun Mountain.

Qiyun Mountain was just outside the capital, not far from the palace. But Qin Yuan's days were full, and he had been there only a handful of times.

The scenery was exactly as it had been in last night's dream. The trees and stones along the mountain path were at precisely the same height and in precisely the same places.

Rocks, streams, meadows, the temple halfway up the slope. Not a single detail differed.

If not for the guards walking behind him, Qin Yuan might almost have thought he was still in that dream.

But everything he did today was the deliberate opposite of the dream.

He did not stop at the stream. The thought of chasing butterflies, wading in the water, or lying in the grass was out of the question.

When he reached Ziyun Temple, he walked straight in.

The temple was busy. Daoist Yunhe was at his usual post, patiently reading fortunes for a line of worshippers.

He glanced up without thinking -- and went still.

Not far away, a man was watching him with a blank, level expression. Clear-featured, with an air that pressed down on the surrounding space like a weight. The current emperor, unmistakably.

A cold sweat broke over Daoist Yunhe despite the heat of the sixth month.

Three Pure Ones above -- what was he doing here?

His concentration evaporated. He murmured a few words to the novice beside him, handed off the remaining queue, and hurried toward the emperor.

"My respects to--" He began to bow.

Qin Yuan stopped him with a gesture. "I am traveling incognito. No ceremony."

"Yes, yes, of course." Yunhe straightened quickly.

Qin Yuan's gaze moved to the queue of people waiting for their fortunes.

Yunhe immediately offered, "My apprentice is also capable of reading the slips."

Qin Yuan gave a quiet sound of acknowledgment. He had little faith in the supernatural and rarely visited Daoist temples. Today he had come partly out of a deliberate impulse to do the opposite of everything in the dream.

Looking around now, the bustle and incense of the place did remind him, uncomfortably, of the Buddhist temples before the crackdown.

The emperor's gaze swept the hall, cool and measuring.

Daoist Yunhe's heart sank with a lurch.

He had heard that before the emperor moved against Buddhism, the emperor had visited several monasteries in plain clothes. If the same thing was happening here at Ziyun Temple now...

No, surely not. Their reputation was notable, but their land holdings were modest. They were unlikely to follow the same path as the Buddhists.

He was still thinking this when he heard the emperor ask, "Do you play chess?"

Yunhe blinked. "A little, Your Majesty."

"Find somewhere quiet. Let us play a game."

"Of course."

When the emperor commanded, Yunhe dared not refuse. He quickly found a small, private meditation room and sat down across from the Son of Heaven.

Though a man of the Daoist path, he was not entirely removed from worldly concerns. He deliberately played poorly.

Qin Yuan saw through it almost immediately. His gaze lifted, cold. Then he dropped the piece he was holding back into the pot. "This is pointless. I'm done."

He should not have come to Qiyun Mountain at all today. He had seen enough of it last night.

Yunhe felt awkward, and was still forming an explanation when the emperor had already stood and turned toward the door, leaving only a retreating back.

Yunhe left the chess set where it was and hurried to follow.

The temple was full of incense smoke.

Without meaning to, Qin Yuan found himself thinking back to that game against the woman -- and the one before it, when she had played seriously against him.

Her chess was genuinely good. She gave everything when they played together.

It was a pity that this particular quality was thoroughly overshadowed by everything else she had done.

Seeing the emperor's expression turn stormier, Yunhe ventured, with some courage, to break the silence: "Does Your Majesty still find himself troubled by the strange dream?"

Qin Yuan's eyes narrowed slightly. "What are you trying to say?"

Yunhe had been about to share his suspicion about shared dreaming. But the words were already at his lips when something made him stop.

Shared dreaming meant there was another person involved. The current emperor had a reputation for ruthlessness. If he believed it and became determined to find the other dreamer and punish them, the blame would fall squarely on Yunhe for having said so.

He could not mention shared dreaming. Not under any circumstances.

He swallowed the words and managed an awkward smile. "I only wanted to know whether the Dream-Forgetting Pill and the sleeping techniques have been of use."

Qin Yuan did not answer.

Perhaps they had helped, he thought. He had never tried the pill. And he preferred the idea of finding the woman in reality to the self-deception of simply forgetting. However long that took, it would happen eventually.

Qin Yuan did not linger at Ziyun Temple. He had come partly to deliberately invert the dream's logic, and that was done.

He left and returned to the palace.

Over the following nights, he retired early. The strange dream did not come.

...

Jiyao's life continued to be full and quiet.

She moved back and forth between the academy and Haitang Courtyard -- reading, or working through chess manuals.

Only at night, in her dreams, was she bold and free and capable of anything.

After that last dream's intensity, she had no appetite for that kind of thing for quite some time. Her evenings in the dream were mostly spent with her parents -- sometimes in childhood, sometimes imagining what growing up with them might have looked like.

On other nights, when the mood struck her, she flew high above the ground or swam through deep water -- unencumbered and at ease.

During the day, she was still the quiet, well-behaved Second Miss of the Fang household.

The seventh month arrived, and with it, the Qixi festival.

The Fang household had many daughters in this generation, and the festival was taken seriously. In previous years, Third Aunt had led the girls through the ritual offerings to the Weaving Maid.

This year, Third Aunt said she was unwell, and it fell to the eldest cousin's wife to take the girls through the ceremony.

In large gatherings like this, Jiyao tended to fade into the background -- she was there, but barely noticeable.

When the ceremony ended, everyone returned to their rooms.

After bathing, Jiyao lay down to sleep.

She was nearly asleep when a thought surfaced: Qixi was not only the festival of skilled hands. It was also the night, in legend, when the Cowherd and the Weaving Maid were finally allowed to meet.

If it was a festival, she ought to see her husband as well as her parents. It had been quite some days since she had dreamed of him.

With that decided, Jiyao closed her eyes and let herself drift.

In the dream that night, her parents sat together in the courtyard -- one playing the qin, the other keeping time with soft claps, entirely absorbed in each other.

Jiyao sat on a nearby stool and listened with a quiet smile.

When the piece ended, she applauded. "Let me try! Let me have a turn."

"You? Go ahead then." Her mother rose, smiling, and gave up her seat.

Jiyao sat at the instrument. She had studied the qin at the academy, but her skill was unremarkable. In the dream, however, her playing was effortless -- clear and beautiful, the notes flowing like water.

Her parents praised her warmly. Her mother even sat beside her to correct her fingering.

She spent a good while with them before finally going back to her room to begin the second half of what she had planned.

She called out silently: come out, husband.

Then, after a moment's thought, she added: after bathing, with his hair still slightly damp at the ends, his collar a little open, with just a sliver of skin showing.

He is to slip in without warning and take me by surprise from behind.

With that thought, Jiyao was suddenly caught in a warm embrace.

Through the thin layer of fabric, her back pressed against his chest, heat radiating into her.

She gave a small shiver and turned, rising on her toes to kiss him -- but he had already pulled her in tight.

...

Qin Yuan fell asleep late that night, well into the hour of Hai.

He had barely been asleep when he found himself in the strange dream.

And at a particularly inconvenient moment.

The gauze stirred. The candlelight swayed.

Before him was dazzling white. In his nose was a scent he knew. Against his lips was warm, soft skin.

The woman's collar had come open. New-fallen snow.

And he was kissing it, carefully, attentively.

Qin Yuan felt his mind fill with a sudden bright ring of static. Every drop of blood surged upward. His temple throbbed.

He had been gone from this dream for a long time. How had he walked straight into this?

The woman was arching faintly, one hand at his shoulder -- not quite pulling away, not quite pressing herself fully against him, somewhere uncertain between the two.

"Husband," she murmured. "Husband..."

Her voice was honey-wrapped and soft, carrying a full and drowsy sweetness. Like two small hooks, catching at something inside him and tugging.

Qin Yuan closed his eyes. Something resigned settled over him: fine. Sooner or later, it always came to this.

Better to get through it first, and then ask his questions.

So instead of continuing what he had been doing, he reached down and untied the sash of her robe.

...

Jiyao looked at him with a trace of confusion. She had not expected this, but she did not ask. She simply did what she had done before -- arms around his neck, legs around his waist.

Once was enough. Qin Yuan did not continue.

Experience had taught him: push too far, reach full satisfaction, and the dream tended to end. He could not waste the opportunity.

Jiyao lay where she was, too comfortable to move. It had been many days since she last dreamed of him, and now that she had, she wanted to simply stay close a little longer.

He spoke. "What do you like about me?"

Jiyao blinked. After a moment, she understood -- it was something she had said, lost in the haze of that other dream.

She thought about it. A small smile. "Lean in -- I'll tell you."

Qin Yuan did.

Jiyao kissed his ear and murmured, "I like you. All of you. Everything about you."

After all, he was a man she had imagined into being. Apart from the occasional small imperfection, he suited her in almost every way.

Though she had to admit -- the more times she did this particular thing, the less new it felt. It was still thrilling, but not the way it had been at the beginning. She did not dream of him as often as she had at first.

The woman's breath was warm against his ear -- warm and soft and faintly tickling. Qin Yuan went rigid. He ignored his body's response and kept his tone completely flat. "Is that so. Then why do you keep not letting me meet your in-laws?"

The word in-laws came out much more naturally now. The second time was easier than the first -- like the way he had once called the regent Uncle Emperor with practiced steadiness, every single morning, until it meant nothing at all.

Jiyao was genuinely startled. Her imagined husband was still thinking about this? Still bringing it up?

Was it her own heart, reminding her through his mouth that this was somehow irregular?

She blinked slowly and said, "I haven't been keeping you from meeting them. You met Father this afternoon, didn't you?"

In a dream, whatever she declared to have happened simply had. She said they had met during the day -- so they had met during the day, even if she had not staged it consciously. That was the neat efficiency of the dream world.

This way, she did not have to go to the trouble of arranging a proper meeting scene.

But to her surprise, he frowned. "I don't remember meeting anyone this afternoon."

Qin Yuan was genuinely close to laughing. How did she manage to say complete nonsense with such complete composure?

"Hm?" Jiyao was baffled.

He said, patiently, "I did not meet anyone this afternoon."

Jiyao was confused. That was not right. This was her dream. If she said it had happened, it happened.

She sat up slightly and cupped his face in both hands, kissed him once, and said lightly, "Then I'll take you to see Father tomorrow. All right?"

Qin Yuan said nothing.

Jiyao took his silence as agreement. But she was still turning it over in her mind.

Something was not adding up. Everything in the dream was supposed to follow her wishes. So why was there now a voice in the dream that disagreed with what she said?

She could not work it out. But she was growing drowsy, and she could not be bothered to think harder about it in the dream. She ended it and let herself wake.

chapters.title: Anticipation
chapters.content:
Qin Yuan woke from the dream with an expression like a storm.

He went to the bathing room. Called for water.

Submerged in the bath, eyes half-closed, his anger still had not cooled: she had done it again, and again, and yet again. His patience was nearly gone.

If her father could not be reached through the dream, he would find another way.

He could not keep letting the days slide by like this.

...

For Jiyao, dreams were dreams and reality was reality.

She had always kept a clear line between them.

After waking from the dream, she tidied herself briefly and went back to sleep.

With the seventh month came cooling weather. The Fang household had new autumn clothes made for each of the young ladies.

Jiyao had barely put on her new robe when Shuangxi came to tell her Grandfather Fang was asking for her.

"I'll go at once."

She considered for a moment, then brought a chess manual along to the study. Grandfather had once said that if she had questions while studying, she was welcome to ask him -- but she had always felt awkward about taking up too much of his time.

She was nearly at the front study when two figures came toward her: Second Cousin Fang Lin and Lu Ming.

Jiyao was mildly surprised. She had run into Lu Ming twice before, both times with her cousin Zhao Jinde. This was the first time she had seen him with Second Brother.

But it made sense, she supposed -- they were both at the Fang family school, and close in age. It was natural enough that they would know each other.

As the two groups met on the path, everyone gave a small nod of greeting.

Then Lu Ming noticed the manual in Jiyao's hands and looked startled. "Is that Gu Songyi's Tuichuang Manual?"

"It is."

His expression was unmistakably interested. Jiyao saw it, hesitated for a fraction of a second, and then said, as though she had not noticed, "Grandfather is waiting for me -- I should go." She walked on.

After she had gone, Fang Lin glanced at Lu Ming with a grin. "What's that look for? Want to borrow it?"

"Nothing like that." Lu Ming shook his head. "I was just surprised. Miss Fang is quite young to be reading that."

He caught himself and added, "I mean -- the Tuichuang Manual is not widely circulated."

"It isn't. But Grandfather happens to have a copy, and she happens to love chess." Fang Lin smiled. "Don't let her age fool you. Her chess is not bad at all."

He knew there were servants who talked about his Second Sister behind her back -- quiet, timid, unremarkable. But speaking of her to an outsider, he naturally gave her every credit he could.

Lu Ming gave a small smile. That makes sense. A person who keeps things inward tends to excel at chess. It follows.

When Fang Lin glanced over, though, he had already smoothed his expression into something appropriately neutral and gave a quiet nod.

Fang Lin thought nothing of it.

Jiyao thought nothing of it either. She excused herself from the two and went hurrying to her grandfather's study.

After greeting him properly, Grandfather pointed to the chair by the window. "Go sit there."

Jiyao was puzzled. "Grandfather?"

"Sit."

She did not understand, but she obeyed.

A moment later, there was a knock -- three quiet raps on the door -- and a clear female voice: "Grandfather."

Jiyao's heart gave a small start. That was Fourth Cousin Pinyao's voice.

Grandfather glanced at Jiyao before answering, "Come in."

The door swung open, and Fourth Cousin Pinyao and Fifth Cousin Qianyao walked in together.

They saw Jiyao and looked briefly surprised, but said nothing. Both curtsied to their grandfather. "Granddaughters pay their respects."

"Mm."

Minister Fang did not speak.

The study went quiet.

Pinyao felt the unease building and asked softly, "Grandfather, you asked us to come -- is there something you needed?"

Minister Fang frowned. "You walked in here and you didn't see your Second Sister?"

Jiyao felt thoroughly uncomfortable -- neither standing nor sitting seemed right.

The twins exchanged a look, and their expressions grew even more awkward.

Seeing them like this, Minister Fang let out a sigh. "I thought the family was getting along well. It seems I was blind. Two months of this, and I only find out today."

That landed heavily.

All three girls said at once, "Grandfather!"

Jiyao even rose to her feet.

"Sit down." One look from him, and she sat back down.

"Who taught you to treat your elder sister this way? Your father, or your mother?" He looked at the twins with an expression of unmistakable disappointment. "What have you been studying at the academy all this time? If your parents give you instructions that are right, then follow them. If they are wrong -- even if you cannot stop them, you can at least find a way to be discreet."

Pinyao and Qianyao's eyes went red. Tears trembled at the edges.

"Grandfather, actually we--"

"What -- are you saying you have not been ignoring your sister?" He cut them off, the sternness rare and startling on his face.

Jiyao said quietly, "The two of them did explain themselves to me in private."

She had to be fair to them. They had let her hear their exchange, clearly intending her to. It would be wrong to leave that out.

Minister Fang gave a soft, humorless sound. "They explained in private and kept on doing it in public. If I hadn't found out, how long would this have gone on?"

All three were silent.

"Have you no thought for your own dignity? For the family's dignity? What will people think when they hear of this? As daughters, you did not know to give your parents good counsel. As sisters, you did not know to treat your elder with respect..."

He rarely interfered in household matters, and he had never once raised his voice to the granddaughters. That he was saying any of this now made the twins press their lips together to keep from trembling.

He looked at them and felt something soften in spite of himself.

He sighed, and some of the edge left his voice. "You are sisters. You should be each other's steadiest support. How can you let something so small put a wall between you? I am still here now, and you are already like this. When I am gone, will you truly not speak to one another for the rest of your lives?"

That last sentence changed all three girls' faces instantly.

"Grandfather!" all three said together.

Jiyao was especially shaken. Others had their parents to lean on. She had only this one grandfather.

Minister Fang steadied himself and turned to the twins. "Go now. Give your Second Sister a bow, and we'll call this settled."

Pinyao and Qianyao exchanged a glance. They stepped forward, and both dipped into a curtsy. "Second Sister..."

Jiyao hurried to her feet and returned the gesture. "Fourth Sister, Fifth Sister."

"Good. Go -- there are gifts on the table for you. Your parents don't need to worry; I'll speak to them myself." He knew something of the background, and he did not want to put the twins in a harder position than necessary.

The twins' shared birthday was two months away. The gifts were early, and generous.

The girls looked, and both went quietly wide-eyed.

"Yes, thank you, Grandfather." Both curtsied and took their leave.

Jiyao moved to leave with them, but Grandfather called her back. "Jiyao. Stay."

"Yes." She stopped where she was, standing respectfully.

With the twins gone, it was only the two of them.

Minister Fang sighed. "You, child -- why do you never tell your grandfather anything?"

Her Fourth Aunt's matchmaking scheme -- she had said nothing. The twins freezing her out -- she had said nothing.

"I thought it wasn't worth troubling Grandfather over," Jiyao said quietly.

From her perspective, it had also resolved itself. It had not truly affected her. She had not been keeping it inside -- she had simply not thought it mattered. When Third Sister had offered to smooth things over, she had gently turned down the offer.

And now Grandfather had stepped in on her behalf, and she was genuinely grateful.

"If you being mistreated isn't worth troubling me over, what is?" He frowned, clearly not approving.

He had been occupied with official affairs and barely attended to things inside the house, which was why it had taken two months for him to hear about this at all.

Small skirmishes between cousins happened. But two months of no acknowledgment whatsoever was not a small skirmish. And it involved Jiyao specifically -- a child without a father or a mother, without brothers or sisters. By any reckoning, this was a case of bullying someone without family to stand up for her.

While he was still here, his own attitude toward her needed to be visible. Only then would those below him not dare to look down on her.

He had a few more things he wanted to say, but he noticed that her face had gone very pale and her eyes were shining suspiciously. His expression softened despite himself.

He knew this child. She would never come to him with complaints.

He glanced at the chess manual in her hands. "Did you bring that because you had questions?"

"There is one thing I couldn't work out. I was hoping to ask Grandfather."

"Let me see."

Minister Fang had loved chess in his youth. He and his wife had fallen in love over a game. In recent years he had stopped playing, but his eye for the game had not dimmed.

He read through it carefully and explained the difficulty to her.

Jiyao grasped it almost immediately and was able to extend the logic further on her own.

Minister Fang was very pleased with that. And then felt a pang: if only his wife were still here, there would have been no falling-out among the cousins in the first place. If only his second son had lived, Jiyao would have grown up bright and easy.

But things as they were had their own kind of goodness too.

When he had explained everything, he waved her off to go. Then he called his fourth son, Fang Jing, in.

Fang Jing had a well-known gentle temper. He was agreeable with everyone -- his wife, his father, everyone. When his father gave him a thorough dressing-down, he had nothing to say in his own defense, only accepted it one apology at a time.

Minister Fang looked at his son. "Go and have a word with your wife. She's a mother herself now, and a generation older than these girls. She ought to carry herself accordingly."

"Yes, yes, I will." Fang Jing promised repeatedly. "I'll speak to her today."

Back in Muxi Courtyard, he braced himself and brought the matter up. "At the very least, don't put the children in a difficult position."

"So you're blaming me." Chen Wenjun felt both stung and aggrieved.

She was not without some awareness that forbidding her daughters to associate with their cousin had been an overreach. But being scolded for it was another matter entirely.

"I'm not blaming you. You know very well that what we have here depends on Father. And my rank is nothing -- a seventh-grade official in the Ministry of Works. Nothing close to what Father has achieved. If Father turns against us, when it comes time to find matches for Pinyao and Qianyao--"

"Which is only because you haven't made anything of yourself," Chen Wenjun said flatly.

"I know. I can't compare with Father or with my brothers. But with Father's backing, the girls will be seen more favorably when they marry. If we truly offend him..."

He reasoned with her until she finally said, with rather poor grace, "All right. I understand. You're all Fangs, you're family, you can be as close as you like."

Not a gracious concession, but it meant she would no longer prevent her daughters from having a normal relationship with their cousin.

Fang Jing also sent a basket of fruit and pastries to Haitang Courtyard in her name.

The matter was considered closed.

...

In truth, Jiyao had not spent much energy worrying about her relationship with the Fourth Branch.

The whole business had, however, done her some good.

After this, everyone in the household understood that Minister Fang watched over her especially. The servants treated her with noticeably more care.

She even overheard two of them one afternoon saying that she was the granddaughter Grandfather loved most of all, and that the reason her marriage had not been arranged yet was because he was privately holding out for the best possible match for her.

Jiyao listened to this, faintly astonished.

If she had not personally experienced the ordeal of the candidate selection behind a screen, she might almost have believed it.

Still -- as things stood, the rumor was rather entertaining.

Beyond Qixi, July held one more day that mattered greatly: Zhongyuan, the Ghost Festival.

The Ghost Festival was for honoring ancestors and paying respect to the departed.

Her father had been gone for many years. Jiyao marked the occasion with care.

She began preparing days in advance: spirit money and paper offerings, fresh flowers, candles. She folded paper ingots by hand. She cleaned the ritual vessels herself, trusting no one else with that task, and observed a three-day fast beginning beforehand.

She also paused her dream-shaping for the duration.

On the afternoon of the fifteenth, with three sacrificial meats, four seasonal fruits, pastries, cooked food, and paper gold and silver assembled and offered, the ceremony was complete at sunset.

That night, Jiyao lay in bed, thinking of her father, gone so young. Thinking of her mother, who had simply disappeared.

When her mother first vanished, Jiyao had been small. She had prayed often, hoping she would be found quickly. As the years passed, she had stopped hoping for that. She only wished, quietly, that her mother was alive somewhere and safe.

Even if she could not come back, that would be enough. Just let her be alive.

Perhaps because of the Ghost Festival, many long-buried feelings had surfaced. That night she dreamed of her childhood, her parents both there, entirely present.

She was happy in those dreams. She did not shape them, only followed where they went. For several nights afterward, she went on dreaming in that same vein.

Then, in the last days of the seventh month, she shifted deliberately back to the present -- still sixteen in the dream, just as she was in real life.

The difference was that in the dream, she had her parents, and her husband.

Thinking of her husband, she found herself remembering the strange moment from that last controlled dream. She could not understand it, and decided to try again.

In the dream's courtyard, Jiyao turned to her mother. "Mother, how was the red bean cake earlier? Did you enjoy it?"

"It was fine. Just a little too sweet for me, you know how I am."

Jiyao smiled. "I'll ask them to use less sugar next time."

She had not staged the scene of her mother eating red bean cake at all. But she felt it had happened, and so it had.

Everything seemed normal. Nothing strange.

Jiyao thought: now test the other side.

"I'm going in to check on my husband." She smiled at her mother and went inside.

With a small thought, she pushed open the door, stepped in, and asked the figure standing by the window, "Husband, what did Father say to you just now?"

...

Qin Yuan had gone nearly twenty days without the strange dream.

The longer it stretched, the more restless he became.

The clues from the dream were thin. Zhang Zan had tracked down the twelve buyers of the bracelet, and none of them matched.

About two weeks ago, Qin Yuan had given up waiting for new dream clues and ordered a systematic search of the households of officials in the capital.

There were many officials to cover, and inner-household female members were not easy to investigate discreetly. He had the search begin with officials below the third rank.

Her father had appeared in the dream once, and Qin Yuan had not recognized him. If he had been a senior official who attended morning court regularly, recognition would have been immediate. So below third rank, possibly considerably lower.

Other possibilities existed, of course. He would work through them one by one.

The emperor's people were capable. In two weeks, much of the obvious dead-end territory had been cleared away, even if a specific person had not yet emerged.

That night, Qin Yuan retired early.

Without warning, the strange dream came.

The door creaked. She stepped inside, smiling. "Husband, what did Father say to you just now?"

Qin Yuan turned to look at her. His expression was perfectly neutral. Inside, a dry amusement stirred.

What had her father said? He had arrived in this dream one instant ago. The first and only person he had seen was her. There was no father anywhere. What could her father possibly have said?

She was already forming the thought: he answers that Father told him to treat me well and never to bully me.

With that, Qin Yuan lost control again, and his mouth shaped the words without him: "He said to treat you well. Not to bully you."

Jiyao's smile broadened. "I knew it."

Good. Everything was as it should be. Her control was working perfectly.

That earlier incident must have been a fluke.

Qin Yuan closed his eyes. Rage moved in waves through him.

He hated this feeling -- this complete, helpless absence of control.

And in this dream, when control failed, there was nothing to be done.

He could only tell himself: do not rush. Keep investigating. One household at a time. Spare no expense. She will be found.

Jiyao, unaware of any of this, came forward and took hold of his hand. "Husband, what book are you reading?"

She looked. Her gaze landed on what he was holding -- the erotic manual.

Well then.

It had been nearly twenty days since that kind of dream. Her monthly time had ended five or six days ago. Now that she thought about it, perhaps she was feeling the very faintest trace of inclination.

Seeing the familiar booklet, Jiyao was not particularly surprised.

Qin Yuan's expression twitched: again?

Twenty days of nothing, and this is what he walks into?

The young woman's lips parted, her voice soft and slightly expectant. "Shall we try this?" She pointed to the page.

Without waiting for his answer, she leaned up and pressed her lips to his throat.

Warm and damp. The faint, familiar scent that by now he knew too well.

Perhaps it had been too long, or perhaps this dream-body truly could not withstand even the lightest touch. That one small, brief kiss, and Qin Yuan felt the change in himself immediately.

chapters.title: Drawing Her Out
chapters.content:
Qin Yuan's whole body stiffened.

Jiyao said nothing and rose on her toes to bite lightly at his lip.

The pressure was light -- more of a tingling numbness than anything that could be called pain.

That faint sensation spread quickly, moving through him in waves, reaching the tips of his fingers and the soles of his feet.

Qin Yuan's body went taut all at once. He swore under his breath, and the booklet slipped from his hand. One arm shot out without his intending it, and he pulled her hard against him.

The style on this particular page was a little peculiar.

In practice, it was more so.

One standing, and the other also standing.

Jiyao had barely managed it for a moment before her legs began to give. She trembled, wanting to retreat and unable to.

In that moment, Qin Yuan regained control of the dream. The vein at his temple throbbed. He set his jaw and simply reached down and lifted her leg.

Jiyao was caught off guard. Her balance shifted and she nearly cried out -- she bit her lip just in time to keep the sound in.

...

Eventually, she was almost entirely boneless against him. Her cheeks deeply flushed, her hair at her temples slightly damp, a glimmer of tears at the corners of her eyes.

Qin Yuan set her down on the bed.

It was always the same -- whenever it reached this point and he saw her in that small, limp, helpless state, some fraction of his irritation always dissolved. And in its place, another kind of restless feeling stirred, one that required considerable effort to keep in check.

Lying on the soft bed, Jiyao came back to herself fully. Her body still ached pleasantly, and she knew better than to continue.

She glanced at him standing beside the bed and, to prevent anything else from happening, let her thoughts shift -- in an instant, they were both fully dressed again.

She had not seen her husband in over half a month. To simply end the dream here felt abrupt.

She thought for a moment and suggested brightly, "Shall I teach you chess?"

Her voice still carried a faint, drowsy softness from before.

Qin Yuan glanced at her. "I can play chess."

"Then even better. Let's play." Jiyao clapped her hands together, and with a thought, they were seated at the board.

She had been nursing a quiet hope of recreating that sudden flash of skill from that one dream.

Qin Yuan gave a faint, dry laugh.

He was not in the mood to try to pull information from her. Zhang Zan's search was already underway.

So: chess.

He had nothing better to do while he was here. And she was, he would admit, the only person in recent years who had ever played against him with full sincerity.

Jiyao had spent the past while absorbed in the Tuichuang Manual, and felt her game had sharpened. What delighted her even more was that her husband's moves were once again surprising her, with something of that earlier inspired quality.

At first, Qin Yuan played distractedly. But before long he noticed: she had improved since last time. He had underestimated her.

He was genuinely startled, though his face showed little. "Your game has gotten better."

Jiyao's face lit up. She thought: this must be her own deeper mind acknowledging her own progress through him.

She said nothing and focused on the board.

In the end, Jiyao won by a narrow margin, mostly by luck. She sprang up and went to him at once, kissing his cheek, barely able to contain herself. "I like you so much."

Playing against someone with a completely different approach was clearly useful.

Qin Yuan's brow twitched. She liked him because he lost?

He had studied under a master in his youth, and his chess had once been exceptional. Years of being consumed by affairs of state had let it slip. And now he had lost to someone whose face he could not even recall. That stung more than he cared to admit.

He said, quietly, "Again."

"Yes, let's!" Jiyao could not have wanted anything more.

She was already worried this state of his would not last -- what if he became hopeless again? Better to make the most of it while it held.

So they played another game.

This time, Qin Yuan gave his full attention. The match was long and hard-fought, and he took it back.

Losing by one game was not enough to discourage Jiyao. If anything, she was more determined. "Again! Again!"

They played several rounds, the wins split between them.

Jiyao felt a particular and distinct pleasure in it -- chess was not as visceral as certain other things she enjoyed in her dreams, but it had its own kind of joy.

She could not stay in the dream too long, though -- she had the academy in the morning. After a few more rounds, she ended it.

This had been a good night. A genuinely good night.

The second evening, she went back to the chess in her dream.

That kind of excitement was not something she could have every night. Chess, on the other hand, she could have as often as she liked.

She had once played against Grandmother. Since Grandmother's passing, she had almost never played another person -- almost always studying alone, or deconstructing positions on her own, or imagining different identities for herself to explore different approaches. Now that the dream had given her an unexpected partner, she was not about to let it go.

And so for several nights in a row, she played chess with him in the dream.

Qin Yuan was growing impatient.

So she was absorbed in chess now, after that other thing?

No -- she had always loved chess. That had been true from the beginning.

He thought about being deliberately careless again, throwing the game, ending it early. Then he remembered the look in her eyes that one time. He found he did not want to do it.

He was the emperor, and he had always been proud. He did not want to lose -- even in a dream. Exchanging wins and losses was not the outcome he wanted. He wanted to win consistently.

And so, strangely, Qin Yuan found himself using his free time during the day to think through chess.

Among the court officials, several were skilled players. Fang Jun, the Minister of Rites, was one of them.

This man, a former third-place graduate in the imperial examinations, had once had a reputation as the finest chess player in the capital in his earlier years, and had often played with the previous emperor.

One day, after morning court, Qin Yuan held Minister Fang behind.

Fang Jun was mildly alarmed. He was a clean official -- no factions, no corruption. He had remained at court through the previous reign, the regency, and this reign without anyone finding cause to fault him. He could not imagine what he had done wrong.

"Sit. Play a game with me." The young emperor's expression was reasonably mild.

Fang Jun quietly exhaled. Chess. Just chess.

He had not played in some time, but the emperor was asking and he could not refuse.

He collected himself and sat down.

Years in officialdom had taught him a thing or two. Playing chess with the emperor meant: do not lose in a way that offends him, but also do not win in a way that embarrasses him.

Fang Jun played with care, watching for every shift, and eventually maneuvered the game to an even draw.

The emperor was clearly not pleased with this result.

Qin Yuan's gaze went cool. "Minister Fang has gotten old."

He remembered, from childhood, watching this man play with the previous emperor -- that Fang Jun had dared to win.

Fang Jun only smiled. "Not so young anymore."

He was sixty-two. He had already become a great-grandfather. Several of his less robust colleagues had already submitted their resignations at this age. He himself would likely step down within three to five years.

Qin Yuan lost interest in continuing. He was about to dismiss him when a thought surfaced. "Minister Fang. We should hold a chess tournament in the capital. Have the Ministry of Rites arrange it."

Fang Jun blinked. "Does Your Majesty wish to follow the example of Emperor Liang?"

The Liang emperor of the previous dynasty had been obsessed with chess, frequently calling players to the palace for matches and holding grand tournaments to identify the finest players in the land.

"No. I'm not that devoted to chess." Qin Yuan's tone was light, almost casual. "The Grand Empress's birthday is approaching. I thought it would be a lively way to celebrate. Something to please her."

An imperial birthday was a perfectly reasonable occasion for a public event, and Fang Jun had no argument against it. "If I recall correctly, the Grand Empress's birthday falls next month."

"It does. So the arrangements need to begin at once. Hold it within the capital, no restrictions on origin, status, age, or sex. Outstanding performance will be rewarded handsomely -- from my private treasury."

That thought had been taking shape in Qin Yuan's mind for some time. She loved chess. Might she be drawn out by this?

The investigation could continue on one track. This would be another.

"This subject obeys your command." Fang Jun bowed.

Qin Yuan added a deliberate emphasis: "In honor of the Grand Empress's birthday, women may also participate in this tournament."

An entirely reasonable condition. Fang Jun saw nothing suspicious in it and agreed at once.

In principle, the Ministry of Rites managed ceremonial matters, sacrifices, and civil examinations. Hosting a chess tournament was not strictly within their purview. But the emperor had asked, the ministry was not heavily burdened at present, and Fang Jun applied himself to the task without complaint.

He had a draft of the rules drawn up and presented it to the emperor for review.

Qin Yuan looked it over and frowned slightly. "The prizes are not generous enough. Anyone who passes the first round should receive a reward. The funds will come from my private treasury. Don't be stingy, Minister Fang."

Fang Jun could only agree, and revised accordingly. When the emperor approved, he had announcements posted throughout the capital and the surrounding areas.

...

Word of the capital chess tournament spread quickly, even reaching the Grand Empress in Shoukang Palace.

A sharp-eyed palace maid hurried to say what a filial gesture it was.

"Very filial," the Grand Empress agreed, nodding -- while privately baffled. She did not play chess. Why a chess tournament? A dance performance, a poetry contest, an embroidery competition -- any of those would have suited her better.

But she kept these thoughts entirely to herself, and smiled pleasantly while her attendants praised the emperor's devotion.

...

Jiyao heard about it too.

Second Cousin Fang Lin told her.

He had heard the news and come specifically to Haitang Courtyard to share it, then asked, "Second Sister, are you going to enter?"

"Me?" Jiyao was caught off guard.

Participate in a chess tournament? The idea had never once occurred to her.

"It's being held right here in the capital. The Ministry of Rites is running it -- open to men and women alike, they say. I'd enter myself if I were any good." Fang Lin grinned. "You have no idea how much I wish I were you right now."

Jiyao hesitated. "I genuinely don't know how strong my chess is."

She had spent years working through manuals, but had played against very few real opponents. She had no way to gauge where she stood.

And she was, by nature, careful and quiet. She rarely left the house. The idea of going to some large public competition, mixing with men and women she did not know, organized by a government ministry --

Even imagining it made her anxious.

Fang Lin pushed back. "What's there to be afraid of? Your chess is something even Grandfather praises. How many others has he ever given one of his personal chess manuals to? You're the only one in this whole household."

Jiyao thought: that's only because everyone else finds chess dull. Of course Grandfather gave it to me -- I was the only one who wanted it.

Still, his words had planted something in her.

"How often does a competition like this come along -- one that accepts both men and women? Only because of the Grand Empress's birthday. An opportunity this rare, if you miss it, who knows when the next one will come?" He was getting genuinely worked up on her behalf. "And competing against strong players sharpens your own game. That's obvious."

"I know," Jiyao said quietly.

After he left, Third Cousin Zhiyao came by to talk, and brought up the same topic.

Jiyao was surprised. "You heard about it too?"

"Mm." Zhiyao nodded. "Fourth Sister and Fifth Sister mentioned it. Their maternal cousin is planning to enter -- they said it's a rare chance, and if he impresses the right people, he might end up with a court position, like the chess officials from the old dynasty."

Jiyao said nothing. Something in her was genuinely wavering.

Third Sister was not trying to persuade her -- she was just sharing the news. She moved on to other things soon enough.

But Jiyao's mind stayed on it.

She had learned chess since she was small. She had absorbed every manual she could find. And all of it had been done alone, shut inside the house, with almost no opportunity to test herself against anyone.

She had studied for years, and she had no real idea how she measured up.

Did she want to try?

Playing against true masters, encountering approaches she had never seen before -- yes, she was deeply, genuinely drawn to the idea.

But she thought of what it would actually mean -- being seen in public, standing out, the potential for things to be said about her.

She had always been the quiet, unremarkable Second Miss Fang. She had never wanted to be the center of attention, had never sought it.

When Third Sister left, she was still thinking.

Go? Don't go? Two voices going back and forth in her head, and neither one winning.

She had always slept easily. That night, for the first time she could remember, she lay awake.

It was the small hours before she finally fell into a restless half-sleep.

The following evening, she lay down early.

She had decided: she would ask herself in the dream. Let her truest voice answer.

chapters.title: Her Heart's Answer
chapters.content:
The night was quiet.

Perhaps because she had not slept well the night before and was genuinely exhausted, Jiyao lay down, closed her eyes, and drifted into the dream almost immediately.

In the dream, the peach trees at Haitang Courtyard had lost their fruit and burst again into blossom. The air was soft with the faint scent of peach flowers.

Her parents sat together in the courtyard, talking.

Jiyao told them about the chess tournament and asked what they thought.

Exactly as she had suspected, they disagreed.

Her mother said gently, "You should try. Opportunities like this are rare. You love chess more than anything, don't you?"

Her father was not convinced. "This needs careful thought. Let's not rush into anything."

"Careful thought about what? Take too long thinking and the opportunity is gone."

"Even so, you can't just leap in without considering--"

...

Jiyao breathed out quietly. She knew perfectly well: this was not really her parents arguing. It was her own uncertainty, playing itself out.

She thought of the other person in this dream. The husband she had imagined.

"Father, Mother, I'll be back in a moment."

"Go ahead."

She went inside and pushed open the door. There was her husband, standing by the window with a scroll in hand, just as she had imagined.

The same familiar face -- sixteen or seventeen, tall and well-built, with clear, refined features.

Jiyao walked quickly across the room and wrapped her arms around his waist from behind, murmuring against his back, "I've missed you."

...

For the past several nights, Qin Yuan had been playing chess in his sleep.

So when the strange dream arrived without warning, he felt no particular surprise.

What he did not expect was what greeted him as soon as he got there: a soft, warm body pressing itself against his back, arms wrapping around him, and then that voice, low and a little wistful. "I've missed you."

He felt the familiar shape of her against him through his robe -- every curve of her -- and could fill in the rest from memory.

His body went rigid. Inwardly, he laughed at himself. Here we go again.

He had thought, given her recent preoccupation with chess, that perhaps she had set that other thing aside for now.

But the woman stepped around him and they sat down together at the table.

"Husband, I want to ask your opinion about something." Jiyao took hold of his hand and turned it over idly, running her thumb along his fingers without really paying attention. Her mind was elsewhere.

Qin Yuan felt a small, sharp internal movement. He thought he already had a sense of what this was. He suppressed the urge to pull his hand back, kept his tone easy, and said, "Of course. Tell me."

She said slowly, "The Emperor has issued an order for a chess tournament to be held in the capital. Open to everyone, men and women alike. Should I go?"

When she had said that, she emptied her mind, stopped directing the dream, and simply waited to hear what came back.

Qin Yuan thought: she really does love chess. And she truly is in the capital.

His earlier guesses had been correct. She did not know who he was. What was strange was -- if she did not know, how had she ended up sharing his dreams in the first place?

A question for later. When he found her, he would have plenty of time to demand an explanation.

Jiyao was still waiting. She nudged him gently. "Husband?"

Qin Yuan's gaze was steady. "Go, of course. Why would you not?"

"Should I really?"

"Yes." No hesitation. Absolute certainty.

Jiyao was quiet. So her deeper self did want to go. But there was still a flicker of doubt. "But what if my results are poor? What if it's embarrassing? What if people laugh at me?"

She had always tended to imagine the failures before the successes.

Qin Yuan held his patience. "It won't be embarrassing. Your chess is good. Your results will be fine. No one will laugh at you."

This was not flattery for the sake of drawing her out. He genuinely meant it. They had played many times. He knew: she had broad knowledge of openings, she improved fast, and she thought clearly under pressure.

"But what if I do too well?"

Qin Yuan breathed in. "...That seems unlikely."

There were extraordinary players everywhere in the country, and the capital drew the finest of them. Just within the Ministry of Rites, Fang Jun's game alone was formidable.

After several more exchanges like this, Jiyao had mostly made up her mind -- but one last sliver of uncertainty remained. She said softly, "Let me think a little more."

"What is there to think about? The opportunity is rare and the prizes are generous. You love chess and you have the ability. Go and show what you're made of." He pushed a little harder, wanting to give her the final nudge.

Jiyao was quiet.

"Do you want to play against the finest players in the country or not? Do you want to refine your game, or do you want to keep sitting at home theorizing from manuals forever?"

Jiyao did not like that tone at all. "Stop talking."

She was trying to think, and he was hovering at the edge of her thoughts like a bad omen.

She sent the thought: be quiet, don't say another word, don't disturb me.

With that, Qin Yuan found he could not speak.

His mouth opened and closed. No sound.

He had endured a great deal in this strange dream, but abruptly finding himself unable to speak still sparked a flash of genuine fury. The urge to do something about it was sharp and immediate.

He reached out and caught her wrist with one hand, and pointed at his own throat with the other.

He was demanding to know what she had done to him.

But Jiyao only sighed, shifted herself into his lap, and kissed his throat in a gesture of vague appeasement.

In Qin Yuan's mind, a bright, wordless noise went off. Every drop of blood lurched upward.

This again. She was doing this again.

That was not what he had wanted at all.

And Jiyao, entirely oblivious to his mental state, had already noticed the change in him while adjusting her position.

They looked at each other.

Jiyao thought for a moment, and made her decision -- about both the chess and what was happening right now.

With a small thought, the barrier between them dissolved.

A breath of cool air, and Qin Yuan felt a start of surprise.

He could still move at this point -- his voice was gone, but his body was not restricted.

And now, with things as they were, with her sitting where she was -- he drew a sharp breath, gripped her waist, and tried to lift her out of his lap.

His hands closed on warm, smooth skin.

He hesitated.

In the space of that hesitation, Jiyao kissed his lips.

Something like a flame caught from that single point of contact and spread through him in an instant.

Lips met lips, skin met skin. The two of them pressed close in the most intimate way imaginable.

Qin Yuan closed his eyes. Let it be. She was going to enter the tournament, which meant he would find her soon. He would repay all of it in full when that day came.

As for right now -- this was simply one more entry on the ledger.

...

They sat in the same chair, face to face, arms around each other.

Jiyao thought: this was a little like the eleventh page of the manual.

The one disadvantage was that her husband had his hands locked around her waist and she could not set her own pace.

So she thought: stay completely still, let me be in charge.

With that thought, Qin Yuan could not move.

He drew a slow breath, fury rising in the stillness. And could do absolutely nothing about it.

The woman above him was unhurried, taking her time, drawing things out deliberately -- which for Qin Yuan was nothing short of exquisite torment.

He even found himself imagining pulling her hands behind her back and pressing her flat against the table...

But there was nothing he could do. He could not speak, he could not move, he could only sit in the quiet of his own mind and hope, with some urgency, that she would pick up the pace.

...

In less than a quarter of an hour, Jiyao collapsed forward against him, trembling.

After a moment, she summoned enough energy to press a small kiss to the corner of his mouth. "I know what I want to do," she murmured.

She was going to follow her heart.

Qin Yuan's jaw was clenched. His body was in a significantly worse state than before.

What -- what did she know?

The dream ended before he could form another thought, and he was suddenly awake.

In the inner chambers of Zichen Palace.

The young emperor lay still in the darkness, expression grim, eyes unreadable.

He glanced at the state of things, got up, and went directly to the bathing room.

Then called for water.

From the way she had spoken, she had clearly been leaning toward entering the tournament all along -- but hesitating. And he had not quite managed to push her over the edge tonight.

He had no way to know what she had ultimately decided.

chapters.title: The Tournament
chapters.content:
That night, Jiyao shaped her dream once more.

In the dream, she and her husband played chess.

Having learned his lesson from the last dream -- when she had suddenly silenced him -- Qin Yuan did not push her this time. He simply played alongside her and waited quietly for his moment.

When two games were done, Jiyao asked softly, "I should go and participate in the tournament, shouldn't I?"

She had already made up her mind. She only wanted to hear the truest voice from the deepest part of herself, to give herself a little more encouragement.

Qin Yuan answered simply, "Yes. You should."

"All right, then I'll go." Jiyao drew a slow breath, said nothing more, and ended the dream.

...

Qin Yuan snapped awake.

He had entered the strange dream many times by now. But this was the first time he had woken without irritation, without displeasure -- without even going straight to the bathing room. Only a quiet, tightly contained anticipation.

As long as she entered the tournament, he would find her.

And when he did -- how exactly would he repay her?

The night was long, and the young emperor could not sleep.

...

The next day, Jiyao went to find her second cousin Fang Lin and told him with quiet seriousness, "Second Brother, I want to enter the tournament. The way you suggested."

"Then I'll help you." He answered without a moment's hesitation.

When he said he would help, he meant it. He not only found Jiyao an excuse to take leave from the women's tutor, he also made plans to accompany her to the registration.

"We need to be clear about one thing first," he said, brow furrowed. "If you're going to compete, you absolutely cannot use the name Fang Jiyao. Grandfather is right there in the Ministry of Rites -- the list of participants will definitely pass through his hands."

Even if registration succeeded, one word from Grandfather could undo everything.

"I know," Jiyao said, perfectly composed. "Call me Lin Yao. The yao of the six lines."

Fang Lin looked at her oddly. "Lin Yao? That sounds like a man's name."

"Yes. Lin Yao. That's the one."

Female names from good families were rarely circulated publicly, so it hardly mattered what she called herself as long as it was her. Lin was her mother's family name; "Yao" was a near-homophone of her own name; and perhaps it would borrow a little of the legendary master player Gu Songyao's chess fortune.

But that offhand remark about it sounding like a man's name had planted something in Jiyao's mind. She asked, a little slowly, "Second Brother -- when I compete, could I wear men's clothing?"

"What?" Fang Lin stared.

The cousin who was generally the most timid and well-behaved in the entire household was looking at him now with those clear, bright eyes of hers.

Jiyao explained quietly, "The tournament does say women may participate, but when we went to look yesterday, almost no women had registered. Even if my name gets past Grandfather, sooner or later he'll recognize my face..."

The Ministry of Rites was running this event. Of course Grandfather would be present. And of course a grandfather would recognize his own granddaughter.

She had originally planned to slightly disguise her appearance. But now a different idea had taken shape: if she was going to use a false name and hide herself anyway, why not do it properly and dress as a man entirely?

"I think it could work." Fang Lin thought it over briefly. "The competition is open to both sexes. What difference does it make whether you're a man or a woman? They won't be checking identities at registration."

The more he thought about it, the better it seemed. And there was a certain thrill to doing something right under Grandfather's nose -- his pulse quickened slightly just imagining it.

Fang Lin was decisive and thorough once he had made up his mind. He sorted out the identity documentation first, then lent Jiyao some of his old clothes sized to her frame. He also obtained some dark powders so she could darken her complexion a little.

With everything in place, he accompanied Jiyao to the new official school to register.

There were less than two hours left before the registration closed.

The whole way there, Jiyao was a tangle of nerves. She thought: if today's registration fails, then it is heaven's will. She would accept it and give up.

But the registration turned out to be surprisingly, almost unbelievably smooth.

By the time they arrived, only a handful of people remained.

The registrar gave her documents a cursory glance, asked a few questions about the rules of the game, heard her answer correctly and without hesitation, and wrote the name "Lin Yao" in the ledger. He handed her a small, specially made wooden token.

"First round begins at the hour of Chen on the day after tomorrow, right here. Failure to appear will be counted as forfeit."

"Understood." Jiyao accepted the token and left with her cousin.

Sitting in the carriage on the way home, Jiyao turned the token over and over in her hands, feeling faintly dazed.

Was that really it?

She could hardly believe it.

But the cool weight of the token in her palm confirmed it: this was real. She had registered. She was going to compete in a chess tournament.

She closed her eyes and breathed slowly, telling herself: stop overthinking. Heaven's will. Go.

Not just go -- give it everything. She would not waste a chance this rare.

She said nothing about the tournament when she got home, removed her disguise, and went to bed early. The next day she went to the academy as usual.

Shuangxi watched her young mistress carefully, opening her mouth several times and closing it again without saying anything.

Of all the Fang cousins and siblings, not one -- except for Second Cousin Fang Lin -- knew that the quiet, obedient Second Miss of the Fang family had done something so breathtakingly out of character.

...

Minister Fang presented the final list of participants to the emperor.

"Your Majesty, a total of three hundred and thirty-two people have registered. Of these, two hundred and sixty are from the capital..."

"Mm." Qin Yuan skimmed it briefly with no particular interest in what the Minister was saying, and asked directly, "Of these three hundred or so, how many are women? How many men?"

Looking at names alone could not tell him which one she was. But one thing was certain: she was somewhere in this list.

Minister Fang blinked slightly. "Your Majesty, two hundred and eighty-three of the registrants are male. Forty-nine are female."

Even though the competition was open to all, the actual number of women who had registered was less than half of the men.

Qin Yuan's gaze dropped, and he asked as though it were an idle thought, "When does the competition begin?"

"Your Majesty, the first round takes place tomorrow morning at the hour of Chen."

"Mm." The emperor gave a small nod. Then tomorrow.

He would go and see for himself.

The day arrived slowly, stretched long by Jiyao's anxiety and anticipation.

She was up before dawn. She applied the darkening powder carefully, adjusted every detail of her disguise, pulled on her cousin's borrowed clothes, and slipped away under Fang Lin's cover, arriving at the new official school in time.

At the stroke of the hour, the grounds were full of people.

Jiyao stood among them, her pulse racing, her face perfectly still.

For sixteen years she had lived within every proper boundary. Aside from her dreams, she had been the most ordinary of well-bred young ladies -- she barely left the house. This was the first genuinely transgressive thing she had ever done in real life.

Standing in the morning light, with a gentle breeze against her face, she could scarcely believe she was not dreaming.

An official was calling out names and having participants draw lots.

The rules for the first round were simple: two players, one game, winner advances. The winner received ten taels of silver and entry into the second round. The loser was eliminated.

Of the three hundred and thirty-two who had registered, three hundred and eleven had shown up. Twenty-one had forfeited.

That was none of Jiyao's concern.

What mattered was her first-round opponent.

Nerves made her body tremble faintly. She forced herself to close her eyes and draw a slow, steadying breath.

As it turned out, she knew her opponent: it was her Fourth Aunt's nephew, Chen Qingyun.

Chen Qingyun had dressed with particular care today -- a fine brocade robe, his dark hair neatly bound under a formal cap. He looked more put-together than usual.
