He had clearly not recognized the disguised Jiyao.

He only raised his chin slightly in acknowledgment.

Jiyao kept her head low and said nothing. Chen Qingyun had seen her before; caution was best.

They drew lots to determine who played first.

Jiyao's luck was poor -- she did not draw the first move. But the moment they began to play, she realized something: her opponent was not particularly strong.

She gave a small internal sound of surprise. Her Fourth Aunt had said he could play. Was his level really this poor? Or was he hiding his ability, lulling her into complacency before striking at a critical moment?

That possibility deserved some caution.

What Jiyao did not know was that while she had played very few real opponents, her foundations were extremely solid. The people she had played -- her grandmother, and her husband in the dreams -- had both been genuinely skilled. Chen Qingyun knew how to play chess, but he was nowhere near her level.

Jiyao had no real sense of her own strength. This was her first competition, and she was giving it her full focus. She leaned over the board and applied herself with complete concentration.

She barely noticed when officials passed nearby to observe.

...

Qin Yuan arrived half a quarter-hour after the competition began.

He had dismissed morning court and gone straight from the palace to the new official school without stopping to eat, moving as quickly as protocol allowed.

The Ministry of Rites officials who saw the emperor hurried over with their bows.

"No ceremony, and no announcement. Don't disturb the competition." Qin Yuan waved them off. "I'm going to look."

"Yes, Your Majesty."

There were a great many competitors today. The venue had been divided into eight separate halls.

Qin Yuan moved through them one by one. In each hall, his gaze went immediately to the women in the room.

With so few women among so many men, they stood out easily.

But strangely, in all eight halls, not a single one of the female competitors looked like the person he was looking for.

Qin Yuan's brow drew together slightly.

The officials accompanying him felt cold sweat forming. They could not imagine what they had done wrong to produce that expression on the emperor's face.

"When does today's competition end?" the emperor asked suddenly.

Minister Fang answered promptly. "Your Majesty, the full schedule runs for five days. The first three days have two rounds each, with elimination by single game, working down to the top five. The final two days will then--"

"I am asking when today's competition ends." Qin Yuan cut him off, his patience thin.

"Within two hours of a game starting, a winner must be determined. If two hours pass without resolution, the appointed judges will make a ruling."

Chess was famously time-consuming. Some scholars could spend an entire day on a single game. But since this tournament was being held to celebrate the Grand Empress's birthday, it could not drag on indefinitely. The Ministry had accordingly capped each game at two hours, with a brief extension of one incense stick at the judges' discretion.

The emperor made a quiet sound. "When the first round ends, keep all female participants here. The Grand Empress has gifts for them."

Minister Fang and the others were somewhat puzzled but answered, "Yes, Your Majesty."

Qin Yuan closed his eyes briefly. Perhaps with so many people it was hard to see clearly. He would take a closer look once they were gathered.

...

Jiyao had satisfied herself: Chen Qingyun was not hiding anything. His level was simply what it appeared to be.

Within an hour, she could see the path to victory clearly ahead of her.

But at that point Chen Qingyun became more cautious by the minute. Every move he made was preceded by long deliberation, the stone hovering in his hand for what felt like a quarter-hour at a stretch.

Jiyao sometimes suspected he was stalling deliberately. She could not say a word to hurry him, only endured it patiently.

Two hours passed. The game was still unfinished.

This was precisely what the judges had been assigned to handle. The examiner -- a man of about forty -- studied the board and followed procedure, lighting another stick of incense.

"A winner must be determined within one incense stick. No further delay."

Jiyao was untroubled by this. Chen Qingyun, however, could no longer afford his earlier slowness. Just a few moves in, beads of sweat broke out on his brow. He had no choice but to concede.

"Thank you for the game." Jiyao offered a small smile.

A good start. She was pleased.

The judge announced without expression, "This game goes to Lin Yao. Please proceed to Minglun Hall to collect your prize and prepare for this afternoon's round."

"Thank you." Jiyao bowed to the judge, then gave Chen Qingyun a polite nod.

Chen Qingyun gave a short huff and did not respond.

He was privately furious at his misfortune. First round, and he had been matched against this dark-complexioned short fellow with deceptively strong play. Against anyone else, he might at least have won one game.

The more he thought about it, the more it stung. He shot Jiyao a hard look before leaving.

Jiyao paid his attitude no mind. The one who had won was her, and that was what counted.

She followed the other winners to Minglun Hall to collect her prize.

Ten taels was not a great sum. But she had won it.

...

By midday, the first round was almost entirely concluded.

At the emperor's word, thirty-nine female competitors were brought before him.

The women had no idea what was happening and were all quietly frightened.

Qin Yuan scanned the group. "Ten women forfeited?"

"Your Majesty, yes -- twenty-one people forfeited today in total, ten of them women." Minister Fang replied with a sigh.

Female participants were already few. For so many to drop out was regrettable.

Qin Yuan gave a quiet hum and studied the thirty-nine women before him with a cold, unhurried gaze.

The oldest among them was past forty. The youngest was a girl of eleven or twelve.

But none of them were right. Not in form, not in coloring, not in bearing.

She could not be among these thirty-nine.

Had she not come after all?

Impossible. She loved chess this much. She had asked him about it twice, and said she would come. She would not have simply not shown up.

Had he missed something?

chapters.title: An Auditory Illusion
chapters.content:
"Your Majesty, everyone is present." Minister Fang stepped forward and broke Qin Yuan's train of thought.

Qin Yuan's eyes narrowed slightly. He addressed the assembled women in a cold, flat voice. "All of you. One by one, from first to last, speak."

His voice was not raised, but there was no warmth in it whatsoever. The cold emanating from him in that moment was unmistakable.

Every woman in the room was visibly frightened.

It was Minister Fang who gathered his nerve and asked, "Your Majesty, what would you like them to say?"

"Say: 'I thank the Grand Empress for her grace.'" Qin Yuan pressed his fingers to his aching brow, gave the instruction offhandedly, then waved a hand to signal the attendants to distribute the "gifts" -- which were, in fact, each worth a considerable sum.

It was a fabricated excuse, but the rewards he gave were genuine and generous.

The women exchanged glances, baffled but obedient. One by one, they stepped forward in order and said the words with whatever feeling they could summon, "I thank the Grand Empress for her grace."

Qin Yuan listened with his eyes half-closed, comparing each voice against the one in his memory.

No. None of them.

Her voice was light and soft. At times it carried a faint, subtle warmth; when moved it would take on a slight trembling quality.

He believed that the moment he heard it, he would know.

But of the thirty-nine women before him, the voices ranged from clear and bright to sweet to gentle to low and husky -- and not one was the voice he held in his memory.

He also had someone check, discreetly, as they spoke.

Not one of the thirty-nine had a red mole behind her ear.

She was clearly not here.

The emperor's face went very still. He said nothing.

The women standing there were terrified. A few of the younger and more timid ones had gone pale and were close to tears.

Minister Fang steeled himself once more and carefully reminded, "Your Majesty, several of these women have another round to compete in shortly, if there are no further instructions..."

"Mm." Qin Yuan's eyes lifted slightly, and he dismissed them.

Everyone breathed out quietly and bowed their way out.

To their surprise, Qin Yuan then turned to Minister Fang and said, "Arrange for all of them to be placed in the same hall for the afternoon round."

Minister Fang paused, then answered respectfully, "Yes, Your Majesty."

A thought had just occurred to Qin Yuan. In the strange dream, his own appearance was not quite as it was now -- he had looked more as he had three years ago, slightly younger.

So could the same be true of her? Could she appear different from what he expected? Her voice, her features, her figure -- perhaps they had changed?

The probability was small. But he needed to verify before he could put it to rest entirely.

He had played chess with her many times in the dream. He knew her style intimately. He ought to be able to recognize it.

The emperor's thinking was opaque to Minister Fang, but placing all these women in the same hall was no great difficulty.

He looked over the list. Thirty-one of the thirty-nine had won their first-round games.

He found himself quietly impressed. The female participants were few in number, but they were not weak.

If Jiyao were among them...

Minister Fang caught the thought and pushed it down hard, then hurried to give the appropriate instructions.

As the emperor had commanded, all thirty-one women were assigned to the same hall for the second round that afternoon.

While they played with their full concentration, Qin Yuan moved through the hall periodically, standing behind each of them in turn, watching their chess.

There were players of varied and impressive styles. But Qin Yuan knew with complete certainty: none of them were her.

So she truly had not come today.

She had deceived him again.

Qin Yuan stood with his hands clasped behind his back, and a slow fury rose from somewhere in his chest -- tangled with something that was not quite disappointment, and something else he could not name at all.

The young emperor lowered his lashes, hiding whatever was churning in his eyes.

After a moment, he opened them and turned to Minister Fang. "The ten women who forfeited -- do you have their information?"

"Yes." Minister Fang replied at once and had someone fetch it.

Qin Yuan's face showed nothing. He wanted to see whether she had intended to come but been forced to withdraw for some particular reason.

If that was the case, even if she had not made it to the venue, he could still find her from the records.

...

Jiyao knew nothing of any of this.

She had won the first round and was ten taels of silver richer -- carefully tucked into her sleeve pocket. The moment she stepped outside, she spotted her cousin waiting at the gate.

"Well? Well?" Fang Lin's expression was even more tense than hers had been.

"Won one game. I'm in the second round. There's another match this afternoon." She answered truthfully, then showed him what she had collected.

Fang Lin laughed and clapped his hands. "I knew you could do it."

It had not been for nothing -- all the schemes he had devised, the cover he had run, slipping her out past their elders to give her this chance.

Jiyao said modestly, "Just luck. I think I happened to draw a weak opponent."

She thought: perhaps her fortune had been good. Chen Qingyun's chess had been rather poor.

"Are you hungry? Have something to eat." Fang Lin was not interested in her modesty and changed the subject smoothly. He opened a food box he had bought from a nearby restaurant while she was inside.

Jiyao was hungry. She thanked him without ceremony and ate quickly before going to prepare for the next round.

Like the first, the second round was also decided by lot -- two players, one game.

This time, Jiyao's opponent was an elderly man with white hair and a long white beard.

Before they had even begun, Jiyao felt her caution deepen. A man his age, she thought, would surely be like her grandparents -- experienced, seasoned, someone to be extremely careful with.

They drew lots for the first move again.

This time, Jiyao played first.

Contrary to her expectations, the old man's style was sharp and expansive, bold in both attack and retreat -- nothing like the steady, patient approach she had imagined.

But this was familiar ground. In her dreams, her husband played with something of the same incisive spirit, though with considerably greater skill.

Facing this old man, Jiyao settled into her natural rhythm and found she had room to breathe.

Still, she did not let down her guard.

A little over an hour later, Jiyao won the game.

"Thank you for the game." She smiled sincerely and bowed.

The old man was gracious in defeat and laughed. "A fine game, young friend. Who taught you?"

Jiyao thought for a moment and gave a vague answer. "No formal teacher. I only picked up a little from my grandparents."

The old man looked faintly surprised, then smiled. "Ah, a natural talent nurtured at home. That explains it."

Jiyao only smiled in return.

Her luck today had really been something. First round she drew Chen Qingyun, whose chess was not particularly strong. Second round she drew this old man whose style, while different from what she expected, was not unfamiliar.

This competition had generous prizes. The first-round winner received ten taels. The second round: twenty.

Walking out of the hall, Jiyao still felt a little dazed.

She spotted Fang Lin waiting at a distance and hurried toward him. "Second Brother!"

The words were barely out before she realized her mistake.

How had she forgotten? She was playing a man right now. She could not use her natural voice.

She cleared her throat hastily and roughened her tone. "Second Brother, you've been waiting long?"

Fang Lin laughed. "Not very. Come on, let's go."

Looking at his cousin's disguise, he thought it was holding up remarkably well. She had added height in her boots, bound her hair high, and evenly darkened her complexion to a yellowish-brown. She had even padded her clothes with something underneath until she looked at least two sizes broader than usual.

Even if Grandfather were standing right in front of her, Fang Lin doubted he could tell.

...

After collecting the ten forfeiting women's information, Qin Yuan set off immediately to return to the palace.

He left the new official school while the competition was still going on.

He had barely settled into the carriage when a swell of voices rose outside -- a large wave of competitors leaving the venue all at once.

Qin Yuan was already in a poor mood. The noise only made it worse.

An irritating coincidence, choosing exactly this moment.

And then, in the middle of all that noise, Qin Yuan thought he heard, very faintly, the words -- "Second Brother."

Two simple words. But they stopped him cold.

The timbre was too familiar.

Qin Yuan's eyes flew open. He lifted the curtain and looked out.

A large number of competitors were streaming out of the venue at that moment -- nearly a hundred people at once. At a glance, they were all male. Not a young woman in sight.

There was one man near the gate who had a small girl waiting for him -- but she was clearly only six or seven years old. That was not who he was looking for.

Had he imagined it?

No. He had heard something. He was certain.

Qin Yuan steadied himself and asked the guard riding alongside, "Did you just hear someone call out 'Second Brother'?"

"I think so, yes." The guard answered carefully.

Then, right as the words left his mouth, the little girl nearby went running toward a young man, calling out excitedly, "Second Brother, Second Brother! Did you win?"

The young man caught her, laughing. "Of course I won."

A warm and ordinary scene. And yet Qin Yuan's expression darkened.

That was not right. The girl's voice was clear and high with a child's lilt. It was not the voice he had just heard.

But there were no other women nearby.

Had he genuinely experienced an auditory illusion?

Qin Yuan's face was difficult to look at. He closed his eyes. After several long breaths, he opened them again and searched the surroundings carefully for a long time.

Nothing.

Finally, he let the curtain fall.

Two words, low and quiet: "Return to the palace."

"Yes, Your Majesty."

The ten women who had forfeited -- he had not yet reviewed their information. Before he was back inside the palace walls, he had already given a command: "Have them brought to the palace tomorrow. Tell them the Grand Empress wishes to see them."

He wanted to see for himself whether she was among the forfeits.

...

Jiyao loved chess, and she would be the first to admit that chess was mentally taxing.

Two consecutive wins today had tired her out.

The moment she came out of the venue, she and her cousin got into the carriage.

She let herself relax slightly for the first time.

"Won again?" Fang Lin asked, watching her expression.

"Yes. Just barely."

"Still ten taels?"

Jiyao smiled and held up two fingers.

Fang Lin let out a low sound. "Twenty taels?"

"Mm."

He clicked his tongue admiringly. "Ten for the first round, twenty for the second. What will the third round pay? Thirty taels? Forty?"

"Thirty."

"That's quite something. No wonder so many people registered."

"It wasn't really the money that brought me here," Jiyao said. She hesitated, then moved to hand the thirty taels to her cousin. Her expression was entirely sincere. "Thank you so much for your help, Second Brother. I truly don't know how to repay you. Please take this as a first installment, and if I'm lucky enough to win a few more rounds, those prizes too--"

Fang Lin waved her off, cutting her short. "No, no. Keep it and keep competing. We're cousins -- don't be so formal with me."

"Second Brother..." Jiyao felt a sting behind her eyes.

She had thought they were not particularly close. She had not expected him to go to all this trouble for her.

Fang Lin smiled lazily. "If you really want to thank me, then go and win it all."

"All right." Jiyao nodded firmly. "I'll do my best. I promise."

The carriage sped on, and they reached the Minister's residence by dusk.

Fang Lin covered for Jiyao as she slipped back into Haitang Courtyard.

"Miss, you're back." Shuangxi looked as though she might cry. "Third Miss came looking for you today. I had no idea what to say, so I told her your face had broken out in a rash and you couldn't see visitors..."

Before Jiyao could respond, Fang Lin burst out laughing. "That's brilliant. Excellent cover."

"How is it excellent? Our Miss never gets rashes!" Shuangxi pressed her foot to the ground in exasperation.

Fang Lin looked momentarily abashed.

Jiyao said gently, "It's all right, Shuangxi. Since you've already said it, we'll keep the story for now. It's at most four more days, and then I'll be back."

The competition only ran five days. She would not be absent for long.

After a moment, she added, "If it comes to it, you can tell Third Sister the truth. She can be trusted."

Jiyao was closer to Third Cousin Zhiyao than to any of the others.

Shuangxi gave a helpless sigh, said nothing further, and quietly began wiping the disguise from her young mistress's face.

...

That night.

Jiyao lay in bed quietly replaying the two games she had played. The second had been interesting; the first had been rather dull.

Without noticing, she fell asleep.

In that blurry, half-dreaming space, she caught a glimpse of her husband.

The two of them were lying in bed together.

He was wearing a white sleeping robe, the collar slightly open, a small patch of skin visible at his chest. He had apparently just bathed -- his hair was faintly damp. A droplet of water traced its way slowly down the line of his jaw, gathering at his chin...

Their eyes met. Jiyao was caught off guard and reached out instinctively to touch his face.

And then she came to herself.

No. She still had competition tomorrow. This was not the time to dream of him.

Not just tonight -- these next few days were not the time. She needed to stay focused.

Jiyao's thoughts shifted with quiet deliberateness. In moments, the dream that should not have come was over.

She drew a slow breath, closed her eyes again, and was soon in a deep and dreamless sleep.

chapters.title: Suspicion
chapters.content:
That night, in the inner chambers of Zichen Palace.

Qin Yuan's eyes flew open.

The palace lamps were dim. The young emperor's expression was something beyond dark.

Just now, Qin Yuan had unmistakably felt himself slipping into the strange dream. And then, in the span of an instant, it had ended.

He had not even managed to say a single word.

A furious wave rose and crested in him, threatening to sweep him entirely under.

Qin Yuan closed his eyes and wrestled his emotions into something approaching steadiness. He called for the calming incense to be relit and tried to sleep again.

He managed to fall asleep several more times. But he did not re-enter the strange dream.

He drew a long breath and turned the situation over in his mind. Had she sensed his intentions? Did she know he was looking for her, and was she toying with him deliberately?

No. If that were the case, she could have made the dream far more tormenting before ending it.

Qin Yuan narrowed his eyes and went carefully back over what he remembered of the dream. Almost immediately, another possibility surfaced: perhaps, in the strange dream, she had been actively avoiding him.

The dream had lasted a very short time. And from his appearance within it -- his clothing, his state -- it had clearly been headed somewhere she did not intend to go.

Ending it so abruptly looked less like provocation and more like avoidance.

So. Why was she avoiding him?

Could it really be that she had withdrawn from the competition and was now too ashamed to face him, even in a dream?

Qin Yuan pressed his fingers to his brow. He had the distinct sense that the old headache was beginning to return.

...

Jiyao was up before dawn, going through the same careful steps as the day before.

At the venue, Fang Lin stopped at the gate with a simple instruction: "Go in and compete without worrying. I'll be here."

"Thank you, Second Brother." Jiyao bowed with genuine feeling, then joined the stream of competitors entering the hall.

After two rounds of elimination, fewer than eighty participants remained.

As before, lots determined the matchups.

This time, Jiyao's opponent was a woman.

She was approximately twenty years old, dressed in a pale blue-green robe. Her complexion was fair and her manner cool and contained, with a faint scholarly quality to the way she carried herself.

When she drew her lot, Jiyao caught her name: Zhang Lingyue.

A lovely name, Jiyao thought. It suited her.

They began. Zhang Lingyue played first.

Her style matched her appearance -- spare and precise, her moves clean and economical. She gave up material without hesitation or regret whenever the position called for it.

Jiyao had never encountered this type of opponent in real life, but she had studied too many manuals to be caught off-guard. After a few exchanges, she had a reasonable sense of the shape of things.

The early game was close to even. After more than an hour, the direction of the game began to emerge.

Jiyao won.

"Thank you for the game."

Zhang Lingyue was quiet for a moment. Then she said, without expression, "Congratulations." And then, with a rare trace of feeling, she added, "Your chess is very good. I thought I was--"

Jiyao had always been well-mannered. Without thinking, she responded, "Yours is not bad either, Elder Sister."

The words left her mouth before she realized her mistake. She had been so caught up in the moment she had forgotten she was dressed as a man. The casual address of "Elder Sister" had been entirely wrong for the performance.

She forced a quick cough and roughened her voice. "I mean -- your chess is strong, Miss."

Then she produced an awkward smile and added, "I grew up with sisters. It just slipped out. No offense intended."

Zhang Lingyue did not respond to this. She gave Jiyao a small nod and rose to leave without indicating whether she believed the explanation.

Jiyao collected her thirty taels with the other winners and went to Minglun Hall.

By the afternoon, fewer than forty competitors remained.

Jiyao was managing, but Fang Lin was getting visibly anxious on her behalf.

"Don't worry. Three consecutive wins is already remarkable," he said, though it was not clear whether he was reassuring her or himself.

Jiyao smiled. "I'm not worried."

And she wasn't -- not really. She had stumbled into this chance by accident. Whatever placement she managed was more than she had any right to expect. She would simply keep moving forward as far as she could.

Her composure now was entirely different from what it had been before she had decided to come.

While the competition continued in full force, the six forfeiting women had been quietly summoned to the palace.

They had expected to meet the reclusive Grand Empress. Instead, they found themselves facing the emperor, whose reputation for harshness was known to everyone.

When the announcement came -- "His Majesty the Emperor approaches" -- all of them went rigid with shock. Several could not move until someone near them gave a quiet nudge, and they stumbled into their bows.

"We pay our respects to Your Majesty."

The voices were unsteady. A few were clearly frightened.

The emperor glanced at them, and his expression tightened. "Why are there only six?"

"Your Majesty, only these six could enter the palace. Of the remaining four -- two are ill and convalescing at home. One left the capital two days ago. And the last..."

The attendant trailed off.

Qin Yuan's patience shortened. "The last?"

The attendant kept his eyes carefully down. "The last -- the registration information was incorrect, and we have not been able to locate that person."

"Extraordinary." Qin Yuan produced something that might have been a laugh, his eyes lifting slightly, the cool light in them anything but amused. "Incorrect information? Unable to locate?"

"...Yes. Not yet found." The attendant's voice had a faint tremor.

Qin Yuan's smile didn't reach his eyes. "Keep looking. That person will be found."

He filed away the Ministry of Rites' incompetence for later. For now, he turned his attention to the six women standing before him.

All six were within the right age range -- each past fifteen, none yet twenty, all unmarried. Two of them were sisters.

All six came from official families, their fathers' ranks varying from high to low. Two were daughters of Hanlin scholars, two came from declining noble houses, one was the daughter of a vice minister in the Ministry of Revenue, and one was the daughter of a sixth-rank military official.

None of them were right.

The women stood there in varying degrees of apprehension.

The emperor spoke. "Why did each of you withdraw from the competition?"

Dead silence. A silence that verged on painful.

When no one answered, Qin Yuan raised an eyebrow. "Well?"

His voice was not particularly loud. But one of the young ladies still gave a small involuntary flinch.

It was the military official's daughter who spoke first. "Your Majesty, I had intended to participate. But my parents forbade it and I had no choice but to withdraw."

Once the first had spoken, the rest became easier.

One by one, the others offered much the same story. Most had been stopped by a parent or grandparent. Only one had simply arrived too late to the venue and been marked as a forfeit. The others -- prevented by a father, or a mother, or parents who agreed but grandparents who did not.

"Your Majesty, please forgive this subject's daughter -- she never intended to withdraw, but a parent's word cannot be defied."

Qin Yuan's brow drew together slightly. He pressed his fingers to his temple.

These six were all wrong. None of them were her.

He had no clear image of the face from his dreams, but he knew with certainty that the woman he was looking for was not in this room.

A wave of heavy disappointment moved through him.

He did not make things difficult for them. He waved a hand, let them kowtow at the gates of Shoukang Palace as a gesture of respect to the Grand Empress, and sent them home.

The six young women had not even left the palace before tears were streaming down more than one face -- relief, emotion, the release of prolonged fear all arriving at once.

The two daughters of Academician Cao clutched each other's hands and repeated the same words over and over: "It's all right. We're all right."

They had assumed they were being summoned to account for their forfeit.

Even after they were home, they could not quite work out why the palace had reacted so dramatically to a simple forfeit, or why they had been called before the emperor instead of the Grand Empress.

...

The Grand Empress herself did not know the reason either.

She knew only that her birthday was approaching and a chess tournament had been held in her honor. A few young women who had forfeited had been called to the palace, but they had not been presented to her -- just asked to kowtow outside Shoukang Palace and sent away.

She turned to her attendants. "What was that about?"

No one knew. A palace maid offered vaguely, "Perhaps it was His Majesty showing his filial devotion, having them pay their respects to Your Highness in advance of the celebration?"

"Is that so?" The Grand Empress's brow creased slightly.

"Yes, possibly he did not wish to trouble Your Highness," another maid added helpfully.

The Grand Empress smiled and let it rest. If everyone said it was filial devotion, then filial devotion it was.

...

Of the forty-nine women who had registered, forty-five had now been accounted for. Only four remained.

"Send a palace physician to the homes of the two women who forfeited due to illness. If they are well enough to leave their beds, bring them here -- tell them the Grand Empress has invited them."

Qin Yuan gave the next instruction with a flat expression.

He did not trust secondhand reports. He needed to see for himself.

"Yes, Your Majesty." The attendant hurried off.

The woman who had already left the capital, Qin Yuan dismissed without further inquiry. The registration record showed she was sixty-two years old -- the oldest person in the entire participant pool -- and had been traveling with her son. She was not going to be the person he was looking for.

As for the one with incorrect registration information, Qin Yuan continued pressing the Ministry of Rites and his intelligence network to investigate until that person could be produced before him.

...

Jiyao knew none of this and stayed focused on her competition.

The further she advanced, the stronger her opponents became.

Her fourth-round opponent was someone named Li Cai.

The game went the full two hours without resolution. The extension incense was lit. Only at the very end did Jiyao emerge victorious by the slimmest possible margin -- one stone.

By the time she walked out of the hall, she was so drained she could barely form words.

On the way home, Fang Lin asked, "Tough opponent?"

Jiyao rallied herself and leaned against the carriage wall. "Very. His name is Li Cai. Very unusual style."

If she had not had such thorough grounding in the manuals and played with extra careful steadiness throughout, she would likely have lost.

"Who?" Fang Lin exclaimed, sitting up straight. "Li Cai?"

"Yes. Do you know him, Second Brother?"

"Know him?" Fang Lin made a rueful sound. "He's from Bingzhou too, same as our ancestral home. In the county examination, I came second. Do you know who came first?"

"...Li Cai?"

"Exactly. I have been waiting for a chance to beat him in the autumn examinations. And here you go and do it ahead of me." Fang Lin's excitement was unmistakable. "Good little sister -- you've avenged me before I even had the chance. It wasn't for nothing that I went to all this trouble for you."

Jiyao didn't quite know what to say to that. She just smiled.

Seeing how exhausted she was, Fang Lin left her to rest and did not talk further. The moment they arrived home, he covered her return to Haitang Courtyard.

Jiyao wasted no time. She removed her disguise, ate a little, bathed, and went to bed.

That night, she slept deeply and did not shape her dreams.

She woke at full daylight, feeling like herself again. She got ready early, left the house, and went back to the venue -- where, with great difficulty, she won the fifth and sixth rounds.

Every game over these past days had taught her something.

Each round eliminated roughly half the remaining competitors, and others continued to drop out voluntarily. By the end of the third day of competition, only four people remained who had not yet lost -- and Jiyao was one of them.

She felt faintly disoriented. She had actually won six consecutive games and made it this far?

She was apparently considerably stronger than she had imagined herself to be.

No wonder Second Brother had kept pushing her to enter.

"Congratulations." The judge smiled. "Another win. Go to Minglun Hall to collect your prize -- sixty taels this time."

"Thank you." Jiyao bowed, nodded to her most recent opponent, and walked briskly toward Minglun Hall.

She had been there to collect prizes five times now. She was beginning to feel rather fond of the place.

But today, the moment Jiyao stepped through the door of Minglun Hall, she spotted a familiar figure. Her heart lurched straight up into her throat.

Why was Grandfather here?

She blinked.

She had not imagined it. It was definitely Grandfather.

Minister Fang sat in his official robes at a table inside the hall, going over the registration records of the participants.

He had received a directive from the emperor the day before: the registration information was inconsistent, and the Ministry of Rites was tasked with investigating the discrepancy and locating the forfeiting participant. Minister Fang had found this particular headache deeply unwelcome -- a forfeiting participant who had vanished into thin air was not something the Ministry of Rites could simply produce out of nowhere.

Then one of the registrars nearby called out, "Lin Yao, is it?" and Minister Fang's brow jumped. Without quite meaning to, he looked up.

He saw the young person standing in the doorway of Minglun Hall and went very still for a moment.

Jiyao understood clearly: the Ministry of Rites was running this competition, and Grandfather as its head would naturally be present. That was entirely ordinary.

But that did not stop her heart from hammering. She had gone to considerable lengths to disguise herself. At this level of concealment, surely even Grandfather could not recognize her?

She was about to turn and quietly slip away, come back after he had left.

But the sharp-eyed registrar had already spotted her the moment she appeared in the doorway, and called out before she could move. "Lin Yao, is that you?"

Jiyao had no choice. She set her jaw and walked forward, pitching her voice lower and rougher. "That's me."

"What are you standing around for? Come on, you're the last one -- sixty taels, don't you want them?"

Jiyao gave an awkward twitch of the lips.

And then Grandfather's voice broke in: "Lin Yao? Your name is Lin Yao?"

"Yes." Jiyao had no choice. She kept her head lowered, avoiding his gaze. "Lin Yao greets the Minister."

Her heart was hammering so loudly she was half-convinced the whole room could hear it. She was praying silently with everything she had: don't recognize me, don't recognize me...

Perhaps heaven heard her. At that exact moment, someone came to the door with a message.

"Minister Fang, His Majesty requests your presence at once."

"Noted." Minister Fang rose to his feet. His gaze rested on Jiyao for just a moment -- one long, considering moment -- before he turned and walked away.

Jiyao exhaled slowly.

That had been very, very close.

...

Qin Yuan was in a poor mood that day.

He had given the orders; others had not dared to be slow about it.

On the third day of the tournament, Qin Yuan met the two women who had forfeited due to illness.

One look was enough. Neither of them was her.

And the participant with incorrect registration information still had not been found.

Since removing the regent, Qin Yuan had held absolute power. Whatever he set out to accomplish, he had always succeeded.

Yet this woman in the dream had defeated him, again and again, in a way nothing else had.

Had she not even entered the competition at all?

Impossible.

She loved chess that much. She had asked him about it twice, and said she was going. She would not have simply failed to register.

Qin Yuan closed his eyes. Image after image moved through his mind: her firm declaration in the dream that she would compete; the voice near the venue gate calling out "Second Brother"; the report that registration information had been found incorrect...

In a flash of sudden clarity, Qin Yuan went cold.

The registration information was incorrect for the forfeiting participant. But what about the others?

The Ministry of Rites had clearly been less than thorough in its review. If one false entry could slip through, there could be a second, a third...

For the past few days, Qin Yuan had been searching exclusively among the female competitors. Only now did he realize with sharp, startling clarity that he had made a serious error.

He had overlooked one possibility entirely.

What if she had concealed the fact that she was a woman?

The competition was open to both sexes. But what if she had chosen to disguise herself as a man regardless?

chapters.title: Resolved
chapters.content:
Sixty taels of silver was rather heavy.

Jiyao tucked the prize money into her sleeve pocket and walked out of the venue quickly.

She was still shaken.

The moment she spotted her cousin, she said, "That was close. I ran into Grandfather today."

"He recognized you?" Fang Lin's expression immediately went taut.

"I'm not sure." Jiyao hesitated.

Once they were in the carriage, she described the encounter in detail and asked him to help her think it through.

"This one..." Fang Lin rubbed his jaw. "I genuinely can't say for certain. But don't panic. Wait and see what happens tonight. Don't fall apart just yet."

"Right." Jiyao nodded. There was nothing else to do.

The carriage stopped at the back gate of the Fang residence.

They had done it this way every day. Fang Lin was bold, and he had a ready excuse prepared -- visiting friends -- but even he did not dare to march his cross-dressed cousin straight through the main halls in broad daylight.

It was dusk.

The moment the two of them stepped out of the carriage, they ran into two people coming out of the back gate.

It was cousin Zhao Jinde and his elder cousin Lu Ming.

At the sight of a familiar face, Fang Lin stepped instinctively in front of Jiyao.

The movement was quick enough to draw Zhao Jinde's attention. "Second Cousin, what are you doing?"

"Nothing. My friend here is a little shy." Fang Lin replied without missing a beat, expression natural.

"All right, you two have fun. My cousin and I are heading home." Zhao Jinde didn't think twice, gave Fang Lin a friendly nod, and left with Lu Ming.

Fang Lin waved them off expansively. "Go ahead, be careful on the road, and say hello to Aunt for me."

Jiyao stayed quietly behind her cousin, not saying a word.

Once the two had walked far enough away, she followed Fang Lin back into the residence.

They turned a corner. Zhao Jinde was still chatting with Lu Ming about something he'd seen at the Fang family school today, when he noticed his cousin had gone rather quiet.

"What's wrong?" Zhao Jinde asked, puzzled.

"Nothing." Lu Ming shook his head. After a moment, he started to ask something, then stopped. "Actually, never mind."

What he'd almost asked -- he'd overheard people mention that the Second Miss of the Fang family had been unwell for three days. He had wanted to ask how she was. But somehow the words wouldn't come.

He wasn't sure what it was that suddenly made him feel so self-conscious. He was usually direct and at ease with people.

At that moment, the Second Miss Fang had just arrived back at Haitang Courtyard.

With Shuangxi's help, she removed her disguise and changed quickly, then handed over the day's earnings. "Keep this for now."

"Of course." Shuangxi took it carefully.

She had never wanted her young mistress to go running around in disguise competing in chess tournaments. But in just three days, her young mistress had won two hundred and ten taels.

That was a sum Shuangxi had never even dared to imagine.

And not just Shuangxi -- Jiyao herself was surprised.

But right now Jiyao had no time to dwell on it. She was still anxious about having run into Grandfather. That quiet unease hadn't left her.

She hoped he hadn't recognized her.

...

By the time Minister Fang arrived at the palace, the sun was nearly down. The sky was stained deep red and orange.

The young emperor stood with his hands clasped behind his back, expression mild. When he spoke, it was this: "Someone entered this competition using a false identity. That is a failure of oversight by the Ministry of Rites."

The words "false identity" hit Minister Fang like a blow. Against his will, a face rose before his eyes.

He had seen that person barely half an hour ago, in Minglun Hall. Slightly dark complexion. A respectful, careful demeanor.

But one look had been enough to make him think of his granddaughter, Fang Jiyao.

In almost every way, the two were different -- build, coloring, voice. They weren't even the same gender. And yet the moment he had seen those eyes, something had moved in him.

Unfortunately, before he could find an opportunity to speak with the person alone, the summons to the palace had arrived. He could not delay.

He had departed immediately. But as he was leaving the venue and preparing to enter his palanquin, he had glanced back -- and noticed a familiar figure. His grandson Fang Lin.

Fang Lin was not home studying. He was standing at the venue gate. Doing what?

The way Fang Lin kept glancing around, it was obvious he was waiting for someone. But by that point in the day, almost no competitors remained inside.

A terrible suspicion had taken shape in Minister Fang's mind at that moment, growing clearer by the second. But with the imperial summons pressing, he had no choice but to push it down and leave.

And now the emperor had opened with those words -- false identity.

Minister Fang thought it might refer to the missing forfeiting participant. But he found his thoughts going immediately to his granddaughter.

He did not offer excuses. He simply said with honest sincerity, "This subject has been derelict in his duties. I ask for Your Majesty's forgiveness."

Qin Yuan had no interest in prolonging this. He said directly, "This concerns the Grand Empress's celebration. It must be handled with the utmost care. Minister Fang, please gather all competition participants. I have my own thinking on this."

Minister Fang paused internally. Was that really necessary? The competition had progressed to this point; there were only four competitors left. The eliminated and forfeited participants could not approach the Grand Empress...

But this was not the sort of thought he could speak aloud. When the emperor gave instructions, a minister obeyed.

"Yes, Your Majesty. This subject complies."

After taking his leave and bowing out, Minister Fang returned briefly to the Ministry of Rites to relay the emperor's command, then headed home.

The moment he stepped through the door, he asked, "What has Second Miss been doing lately? Is she still attending the women's academy?"

"No. Second Miss has been feeling unwell these past days and has been resting quietly in Haitang Courtyard."

Minister Fang's expression shifted. "Unwell? How many days?"

"Three days."

Three days...

With all these details adding up, what was left to misunderstand?

Minister Fang lowered his eyes and breathed carefully, doing his best to keep his composure. "Have her come to my study immediately." He thought for a moment and added, "And Fang Lin. Bring Fang Lin as well."

"Yes, Minister."

...

Jiyao had finished dinner and was feeling a little more like herself. She was sitting quietly reviewing the day's games in her mind and had just reached a crucial position when someone arrived from the front courtyard with word that the Minister wished to see her.

"Now?" Her heart gave a jump. A sense of foreboding settled over her immediately.

But this was not something she could avoid. There was nothing for it. Jiyao steeled herself and went.

She had not gone far before she encountered Second Cousin Fang Lin on the path.

They looked at each other. Neither needed to say anything. They both understood: they had probably been found out.

And indeed, the moment they stepped into the study, they were met with Grandfather's voice, visibly restrained but unmistakably furious. "Outrageous. Absolutely outrageous. Who gave the two of you the nerve to falsify an identity and enter a competition?"

Fang Lin immediately stepped forward and took it all on himself. "This has nothing to do with Second Sister. It was my idea. I forged the identity. I was the one who pressured her into it. If you're going to blame anyone, Grandfather, blame me."

Jiyao startled and responded at once. "No -- this had nothing to do with Second Brother. It was because I wanted to play chess, so I asked him. Please don't blame Second Brother."

She had been about to try playing innocent, hoping that since Grandfather hadn't confronted her directly, there might be room to negotiate. But now that Second Brother had confessed outright, she could not let him take all the blame alone.

The sight of the two of them defending each other gave Minister Fang a headache, despite himself.

If he was honest, he was dissatisfied with what they had done. But when faced with his anger, the two of them hadn't turned on each other -- they had both immediately rushed to take the blame for the other. That part, he was satisfied with.

He drew a slow breath and tried to settle his temper. "I know exactly how this happened. It was obviously Fang Lin's idea."

"You're right, Grandfather, it was my idea. I couldn't bear to see Second Sister's talent go to waste, so I took a risk to give her one chance." Fang Lin's face showed more excitement than fear. "And Second Sister didn't disappoint. She won every single round, six games straight. Who's to say that in the remaining games, she couldn't have--"

"There will be no remaining games. You are not going back." Minister Fang cut him off, his voice cold.

"Grandfather..." Jiyao looked up, her voice small, her heart quietly protesting.

If she had never gone at all, she probably could have accepted it. But she had dared to enter, had won six consecutive games, had faced all kinds of opponents. She had wanted to know how far she could go.

Minister Fang met those bright black eyes of hers and fell silent for a moment. His expression eased by a fraction, but his stance did not waver. "You truly cannot go."

"Why?"

"Because His Majesty has become aware that someone in this competition entered under a false identity, and he is taking it very seriously."

Jiyao blinked. "His Majesty?"

Fang Lin was also surprised.

A chess tournament. How had the emperor become involved?

Minister Fang sighed. "His Majesty commissioned this competition. The prize money even comes from his private treasury. To enter under a false identity is, if one wanted to be strict about it, a form of deceiving the emperor. If His Majesty chooses to pursue it, both of you would be in serious trouble. And the Ministry officials who processed the registration would also face punishment."

If it had not come to the emperor's attention, it might have been handled quietly. But now that the emperor had personally involved himself, it was no small matter.

At the phrase "deceiving the emperor," Jiyao felt the color leave her face. "Deceiving the emperor?"

Was it really that serious?

Fang Lin asked quickly, "Grandfather, is there a way to fix this?"

Minister Fang shot his grandson a withering look. "Fix it? Now you think about fixing it? You were so bold before. And now you're afraid?"

Both of them hung their heads and said nothing.

In the end, Minister Fang was too fond of these two to stay completely unmoved. He exhaled. "You are not to go back for the remaining rounds. And for the time being, neither of you is to leave the house. As for the matter of the false identity -- I will handle it."

He had intended to let them suffer a little more. But the matter had too many tendrils reaching in dangerous directions, and Fang Lin still had the imperial examinations ahead of him. He could not let a foolish mistake destroy the boy's future.

Grandfather's "I will handle it" was as good as a promise, and Fang Lin felt the knot in his chest loosen entirely.

"Thank you, Grandfather." He bowed deeply, sincere gratitude in every line of him.

Jiyao breathed out quietly too.

She was disappointed not to continue. But she knew what mattered more.

Minister Fang shot his grandson another look. "That false identity -- who made it? Can it be traced?"

"No one can trace it. I made it myself. No one else's hands were on it." Fang Lin answered immediately.

Minister Fang's eye twitched. "Three months confined to the house, no going out. Your allowance is suspended. Now go."

Fang Lin did not dare argue. He bowed and withdrew.

Jiyao moved to follow, but Grandfather called her back. "Jiyao, stay a moment."

"Yes." She stopped.

Minister Fang's gaze rested on her for a long moment before he spoke. "I used to think your temperament was nothing like your father's. Now I see it is, after all."

He had not known until today that this outwardly obedient child had such stubbornness running through her bones.

Jiyao was not sure how to respond. She managed a small smile.

Minister Fang let out a quiet sigh. "To win six games in a row -- your chess is good."

He did not regret preventing her from continuing, even so.

He had seen with his own eyes how the emperor behaved toward the female competitors. In his view, Jiyao not competing as a woman had been the right thing. And if she had simply not competed at all, that would have been better still.

But the past could not be changed. There was no point dwelling on it.

He waved his hand to dismiss her, then turned his mind to managing the matter of the false identity.

On his way home, he reviewed the details of the false identity Fang Lin had arranged: Lin Yao, a visitor to the capital from Jincheng.

An outsider. Good -- that made it easier to obscure. Someone passing through who had entered the competition and then left on family business would be difficult to trace once they had supposedly departed the city.

...

Jiyao left Grandfather's study and had barely taken a few steps before she found Second Cousin Fang Lin waiting for her.

They looked at each other. She felt a rush of guilt.

"I'm sorry, Second Brother, I--"

"Don't apologize to me. I was the one who pushed you into it. If anyone is more at fault, it's me." He was completely unbothered.

After a moment, he added, "Though, if you really do feel sorry. You could share some of your prize money with me. You know my allowance is now..."

"Done." Jiyao agreed before he even finished.

She had always planned to give him a share.

It was unfortunate that the competition had ended early because the emperor was involved. But what she had accomplished was more than she had dared to hope for. She was not dissatisfied with it.

The only thing that still worried her was whether the matter of the false identity could truly be resolved without consequences.

...

Back at Haitang Courtyard, she tidied up briefly and went to rest.

She could not compete anymore, but she could replay the games in her mind.

The more she thought about them, the more alert she felt. She was exhausted, and yet it was a long time before sleep finally came.

Perhaps because she had been thinking about chess just before falling asleep, she was playing chess with someone in the dream too.

When she became aware she was dreaming, she thought for a moment, then formed the image: come out, husband.

With that single thought, she was suddenly in a space with a chessboard before her, and her husband was seated across from her.

...

Qin Yuan did not put much faith in the Ministry of Rites' capabilities.

He had instructed Minister Fang to gather all competition participants, while simultaneously deploying his most trusted intelligence operatives to verify the registration records one by one.

It was not until the hour of Hai that he finally went to bed.

He was not sure how much time had passed when he found himself in the strange dream again.

He pressed down every emotion rising in him, glanced at the board in front of them, and asked with an air of detachment, "Not competing anymore?"

Jiyao did not think twice. She assumed this was some dissatisfied, unresolved part of herself surfacing through her husband's voice.

She sighed. "I'd like to keep competing. But I can't."

Those simple words landed differently for Qin Yuan.

She had said "keep" competing. Not simply "compete." Which meant she had entered.

He pressed carefully. "Not even in disguise?"

Jiyao felt a flash of irritation. It was exactly the kind of thing her deepest, most stubborn self would say -- prodding the sore spot.

Had she not already come to terms with not continuing? Why did her dreams keep bringing it back? Was some part of her still not at peace with it?

Her interest in replaying games evaporated. She let her thoughts drift: be quiet, say nothing at all.

In the next instant, Qin Yuan found he could not speak.

Jiyao glanced down at the board, then up at her husband -- whose lips were moving silently with nothing coming out -- and with a thought, rose and kissed him.

Forget the chess. Her mind wasn't settled enough for it tonight. Better to do something else.

When the young woman's soft lips came to him without warning, Qin Yuan's first instinct was to pull back. But in the next moment, he changed his mind.

Let it be. He was going to catch her very soon. No point making unnecessary complications now.

chapters.title: Confirmed
chapters.content:
And so Qin Yuan stayed still, and let her kiss him.

The consequence of staying still was that before long, his body in the dream had made itself unmistakably known.

She still hadn't noticed. She kept kissing him, slowly, softly.

Qin Yuan's body went taut. And she kept going, her faint, delicate scent filling his senses. He turned the thought over and simply decided: he folded both arms around her waist and pulled her close.

Their bodies pressed together with only thin layers of fabric between them, and Jiyao felt the change in him at once.

She glanced down, then bit his lip -- not hard, not gently. With a small shift of thought, they were on the bed.

She adjusted things in her mind: her husband was exactly as he had been in a previous dream -- white sleeping robe half-dry, hair slightly damp. A drop of water tracing down his jaw to his collarbone.

She liked this version of him. She reached out and touched the collarbone lightly, then let her fingers drift.

Her fingers were slender and faintly cool, but wherever they moved, the sensation was anything but -- warmth flared up immediately in their wake.

Qin Yuan's body gave an involuntary shiver. His throat moved, and he caught her wandering hand.

"Hm?" Jiyao blinked, and then a mischievous idea crossed her mind. She said, slowly, "Husband, shall we play chess on you?"

Qin Yuan's brow jumped. Surely he had misheard.

Play chess. On him.

Jiyao thought: he's not saying anything, which means he agrees. And while she was at it, best if he didn't move either -- pieces wouldn't stay put if he kept shifting around.

With that thought, Qin Yuan found he could not move at all.

Unable to speak, unable to move. No different from a puppet. And yet every sensation in the dream was crystalline and vivid, amplified far beyond anything ordinary.

Jiyao's game was more playful than serious.

With each piece she placed, her soft hand brushed lightly across his chest. His lashes trembled; his cheeks had gone red. He was clearly enduring something with tremendous effort.

Time seemed to stretch out and slow.

Qin Yuan could do nothing at all. He could only keep telling himself, over and over: endure it. It will be soon. He would have her.

There was even a moment when he found himself genuinely hoping she would develop less interest in chess and more interest in other things.

Perhaps heaven heard him.

Jiyao played for a while, found it wasn't as interesting as she'd expected. The games she'd already won didn't really need replaying.

She glanced at her husband -- and at what was quite visible beneath his robes -- and made a small sound of surprise. Something stirred in her.

She gathered the pieces and carefully settled herself over him.

Qin Yuan felt a bright, tingling rush move over his scalp and drew a sharp breath.

Only when she was trembling and slumped against his chest, barely conscious, did Qin Yuan finally regain control.

Almost without hesitation, he pressed her beneath him and kissed her.

Jiyao, still hazy, thought hazily that this was probably just her frustration over the competition coming out -- she was indulging herself because of it.

And so she did not resist.

After some time, Jiyao felt the edge approaching and quickly gathered herself, ending the dream abruptly.

...

In the inner chambers of Zichen Palace.

Qin Yuan opened his eyes. Went to the bathing room first. Then called for water.

It was still early. He rested a little longer before going to morning court.

The Ministry of Rites, as it turned out, could not do even simple things properly. They reported that they were unable to gather all participants, because several were no longer in the capital.

"No longer in the capital?"

"Yes, Your Majesty." Minister Fang's manner was respectful. "This competition was open to all regardless of origin. Several participants came from outside the capital. Some left after being eliminated."

"Is that so? Unfortunate timing, then." Qin Yuan's expression was unreadable, his voice slightly odd.

"Indeed. Rather unfortunate."

Minister Fang had arranged for "Lin Yao" to be recorded as a visitor who had suddenly left the capital on family matters. An outsider passing through, mixing in with others who had already departed -- that would be very difficult to verify.

Qin Yuan gave a thin smile. He had known better than to rely entirely on the Ministry.

Fortunately, the operatives he had deployed were somewhat more capable. And tracking men was considerably easier than tracking women. Going through the registration information person by person, within two days they had identified several individuals whose details didn't add up.

Eliminating them one by one, a single suspect remained: Lin Yao.

Lin Yao, from Jincheng, eighteen years old. Exceptional chess ability. Won six consecutive games over three days, then forfeited without a trace on the fourth day.

And upon investigation: in all the vast capital, not a single person who knew a "Lin Yao." It was as though he had materialized from thin air.

Too many coincidences. Something was wrong.

Qin Yuan then had someone question the officials, referees, and all six opponents who had faced "Lin Yao" in the competition.

Chen Qingyun, when suddenly summoned and asked about "Lin Yao," looked baffled. "I don't know anything. During the game he barely spoke, kept his head down the whole time. I only remember he was quite dark, I don't remember what he looked like."

He was still privately furious about losing in the first round to a dark-skinned nobody. He had been hoping to impress the right people in this competition.

The old man from the second round recalled, after some thought, offering this vaguely: "Lin Yao? Quiet. Steady style. Impressive for someone so young."

He had appreciated "Lin Yao's" chess, but they had only played one game against each other with no other interaction. He had nothing more to offer.

Zhang Lingyue, Lin Yao's third opponent and the only female one, looked somewhat uneasy when questioned. "I don't know. I don't remember. I only remember that I lost, and it hurt."

What she did not say was that she remembered quite clearly. "Lin Yao" had slightly dark, yellowish skin, but unusually beautiful eyes. When "Lin Yao" had apologized and bowed to her after the slip in form of address, they had been standing close enough for her to catch a faint, pleasant scent from the person.

She had also had a small private suspicion about "Lin Yao" after their brief exchange. But getting involved in other people's business had no appeal. She said she didn't remember, and left it at that.

Of the six opponents, the one who provided the most was Li Cai -- the fourth-round opponent.

Li Cai had an exceptional memory, something close to total recall. He gave a clear and accurate description of "Lin Yao's" height, the length of his hands, the shape of his face and eyes, and even produced a sketch from memory. Unfortunately, he was not skilled at drawing, and the result was only about sixty or seventy percent accurate.

Combining all the information gathered, the consensus portrait of "Lin Yao" was: dark complexion, few words, slightly husky voice, extremely steady chess style, neither arrogant nor anxious.

This was the unanimous impression.

When asked to reconstruct game positions, some opponents could do so calmly from memory; others said they had forgotten.

For Qin Yuan, it was more than enough. He examined two reconstructed game records and concluded without hesitation: Lin Yao was the person he was looking for.

He knew her chess too well. He had played with her countless times in the dream. She had even replayed half a game on his body in the dream, and that he could not mistake.

The memories of the dream rose sharp and clear. Just thinking about it made the fury in him surge back up.

Qin Yuan looked at the sketch that had been submitted to him and frowned slightly.

She had been disguised as a man. Of course her appearance had been changed. This drawing could not show her actual face. Even her height and complexion would have been different from what he remembered.

Finding her from a drawing of her male disguise would be unreliable.

The frustrating reality was that even though Qin Yuan had confirmed "Lin Yao" was the person he wanted, actually locating her was not straightforward.

"Lin Yao" had appeared for only three days. On the fourth day, she simply stopped coming, and no trace remained.

No one knew where she had come from or where she had gone.

Throughout the competition, she had interacted with no one beyond what was necessary. She had been accompanied by someone -- but that person's appearance had gone completely unnoticed.

Qin Yuan ordered a thorough investigation, sparing no resources.

After a moment's thought, he added one more instruction: "Focus particularly on the families and households of Ministry of Rites officials, including minor clerks."

Something about this struck him as too convenient. "Lin Yao" had competed for three days, and the very moment Qin Yuan began to suspect someone had entered under a false identity and ordered an investigation, "Lin Yao" forfeited and vanished.

It was possible she had always intended to leave after three days. The competition's final rounds required the top three to be presented to the emperor and the Grand Empress -- she might have feared things going too far.

But there was another possibility: someone had tipped her off and told her to leave while she could.

He remembered her mentioning in the dream that her father was on duty at his office one night. Qin Yuan had always assumed she meant the Ministry of Rites. If she was a family member of a Ministry of Rites official, it would explain perfectly why she had disappeared the very moment he began pressing the matter.

"This subject obeys." Zhang Zan bowed with proper gravity and took his leave.

...

Minister Fang had not anticipated that the emperor would take the false identity matter this seriously -- deploying his intelligence network over it.

Once suspicion had focused on "Lin Yao," it had not stopped there. The investigation was being pressed further, clearly determined to dig all the way down and produce the person.

Minister Fang found himself with a headache.

Jiyao, he thought, was relatively protected. She had disguised her appearance and had spent her whole life largely confined to the inner quarters. Aside from the name, very few people would connect a young lady from the Fang household with "Lin Yao."

The real vulnerability was Fang Lin.

He had accompanied Jiyao to register and waited outside the venue for three consecutive days. Whether anyone had noticed him was uncertain.

That evening, Minister Fang summoned Fang Lin to the study again and asked him directly, "Who knows about Jiyao's participation in the competition?"

"Almost no one." Fang Lin answered quickly. "Besides me and Grandfather, only Shuangxi in Haitang Courtyard and my personal attendant Laibao. No one else. Both Shuangxi and Laibao have been with the family for years -- they won't talk."

"While you were accompanying your cousin to the competition, did anyone recognize you?"

Fang Lin shook his head. "No."

He thought for a moment and added, "Except Grandfather."

He had taken care of this kind of thing too many times to be careless. At the venue, when the crowd was large, he'd shown himself briefly near the carriage so Jiyao could find him easily. After that, he'd stayed inside the carriage the whole time.

Not even his personal rival Li Cai had spotted him.

It was only on the third evening, when Fang Lin judged the crowd had thinned enough that he could step out for air, that Grandfather happened to see him. If not for that, Minister Fang might still have known nothing.

"You are certain no one else knows?" Minister Fang pressed again, brow slightly drawn.

"Absolutely certain," Fang Lin said.

Minister Fang gave a quiet hum and waved him out.

If no one else knew, there was more room to work with.

After leaving Grandfather's study, Fang Lin didn't go straight to his own room. He went to find Jiyao.

After three days of "convalescing," Jiyao had made a full recovery and resumed her classes at the women's academy.

She went through each day quietly, looking entirely the same as before.

Only when she saw Second Cousin Fang Lin did her mind go immediately to their shared secret.

"Don't worry." Fang Lin reassured her. "Nothing is going to happen. Grandfather is handling it."

He trusted himself. He trusted Grandfather. Grandfather had been at court for years, had outlasted three different powers in turn, had never once been swept away no matter how much the political winds shifted. If Grandfather said he would resolve it, it would be resolved.

"Right." Jiyao nodded. She hoped so.

Perhaps because she had something weighing on her mind, Jiyao had a rare nightmare that night.

She was running through a forest, something pursuing her from behind, terrifyingly close.

The moment she realized it was a dream, she immediately took control -- escaped the threat first, then formed the thought: change, change, not this, home, husband come out.

With a shift of thought, the forest dissolved, replaced by the familiar peach grove.

Jiyao let out a breath. There, that was better.

Her husband stood beneath a peach tree not far away.

A pale blue robe. Tall and upright. Hands clasped lightly behind his back, expression elsewhere, lost in some private thought.

"Husband!" Jiyao's eyes brightened. She crossed the distance and buried herself against his chest, her voice soft and slightly plaintive. "I've missed you so much."

Her tone was warm and completely unguarded.

After all the tension of the past few days, being with him in the dream was so much better than being chased through the forest.

Qin Yuan blinked.

He had barely fallen asleep when he found himself in the strange dream again.

The young woman's soft body came to him carrying that familiar scent. Qin Yuan put his arms around her instinctively and answered, "Mm. I have too."

His voice, unusually, was gentle.

What he was thinking was: no need to imagine. They would be meeting very soon.

chapters.title: Ripples
chapters.content:
Jiyao was satisfied with his answer. She stepped back from his arms and reached instead for his hand.

His hand was nothing like her own soft, delicate one -- broad and warm, the knuckles defined, the fingers long.

Qin Yuan did not pull away. He let her hold it.

She would be caught very soon. He would have all the time in the world to repay everything then. There was no point getting worked up over something so small.

Jiyao described what had happened in the nightmare she had just escaped. "Husband, just now there was a wolf chasing me, trying to bite me. Luckily I managed to fly up in time before it caught me."

Qin Yuan's brow creased.

A wolf? Flying?

He had witnessed too many strange things in this dream to question the contents of what she said. He offered an adequately bland response. "Mm. That does sound frightening."

Jiyao tilted her head. That felt a little flat.

If it were Second Brother or Third Sister who had heard this, she was sure they would have been immediately curious: "What kind of wolf? How did you fly?"

Her husband's response had no curiosity in it at all.

She thought about it and concluded: that made sense. Somewhere in her own mind, she knew perfectly well that the nightmare was already over, so there was no real emotion attached to it.

Not that she would tell Second Brother or Third Sister about her nightmares in real life anyway.

Dreams were her own private world, belonging to no one else.

Lately she had been meeting her husband in the dream to play chess. But with the matter of her false-identity competition still unresolved, she had no heart for chess tonight.

Something else, then.

What?

She didn't feel like the other kind of thing right now. She thought for a moment, then her eyes brightened. "Husband, dance with your sword for me. Would you?"

The idea had come to her suddenly. She remembered -- when her husband had first appeared in the dreams, he had danced with a sword under the peach trees, robes flowing, the blade catching the light. It had been beautiful to watch.

Now they were in the peach grove again. The memory surfaced and the wish came with it.

"What?" Qin Yuan's brow drew together.

Dance with the sword?

This was Jiyao's dream, and she was its master. If she wanted to see it, she would.

And so, in the next instant, a sword appeared in Qin Yuan's hand.

He moved without intending to -- stepping back, moving through the peach grove in long, fluid strides, the blade sweeping arcs through the air, and the cold of it travelling with him.

With every motion, petals shook loose from the trees and drifted down, arranging themselves across the ground in patterns.

Jiyao watched from the side with a warm smile, clapping at intervals. "Beautiful. That's really beautiful."

He was exactly the husband she had imagined.

Watching him with the sword was so much more enjoyable than anything in real life right now.

Playing in the dream for a while had quietly eased the tension that had been sitting in Jiyao's chest without her quite noticing.

Qin Yuan, still performing his unwilling sword display, silently seethed: missed him? She had missed watching him perform tricks, more like.

He was the emperor. Even the filial gesture of dressing gaily to amuse one's parents had never been asked of him. And here he was, supplying entertainment in a dream -- and not for the first time.

He would make note of this. When he found her, he would not let it go easily.

Jiyao, completely unaware of his feelings, watched the sword dance until her interest gradually faded. With a thought she dismissed him, and went to spend the rest of the dream with her parents.

In the presence of her parents, Jiyao was always simply a child with someone to lean on.

She loved spending time with them, even in dreams.

...

One moment Qin Yuan was dancing with the sword; the next, he was jolted out of the dream.

The young emperor lay staring up at the canopy of the bed, his gaze dark and still.

How many more days until he found her?

He was running out of patience.

The Grand Empress's birthday was drawing closer, and the chess tournament had concluded.

And "Lin Yao" had still not been found.

Qin Yuan pressed his fingers to his brow and summoned his intelligence chief, Zhang Zan.

Faced with the emperor's inquiry, Zhang Zan stood with his hands at his sides, his expression apologetic. "Your Majesty, this subject has been incompetent. We have found no trace of Lin Yao thus far."

He and his operatives had located and detained four individuals in the capital who specialized in producing false identities and travel documents. None of them had ever made anything for "Lin Yao," and none of them recognized the name.

The word "incompetent" made Qin Yuan's expression shift.

Incompetent, again. He was thoroughly tired of hearing it lately.

The Ministry of Rites had been incompetent, failing to screen registrants properly and letting her in under a false name.

The intelligence operatives were incompetent, unable to find her after all this time.

Was he incapable of cultivating people who were worth something?

He closed his eyes and asked with strained patience, "Any progress at all?"

Zhang Zan steeled himself and answered truthfully. "Not yet, Your Majesty."

He called himself incompetent, but inwardly he felt the injustice keenly -- both for himself and for his people.

"Lin Yao" had appeared from nowhere. No background, no trail, present for only three days, gone without trace. Aside from a drawing the emperor himself had rejected, they had nothing to go on.

Where were they supposed to start?

They knew "Lin Yao" was a strong chess player. But strong chess players were everywhere, and every notable one came with a name and a reputation -- no one had sprung up from nowhere like "Lin Yao."

A few days prior, they had received word from the city gate guards that someone by the name of "Lin Yao" had left the capital. But the emperor had stated with complete confidence that "Lin Yao" was a woman in disguise, and directed them to focus on the household of Ministry of Rites officials.

Which made everything harder. In this day and age, investigating women was far more difficult than investigating men. Official households kept their female members behind closed doors. Getting close to them, let alone looking into their affairs, was not easy for outsiders. And the emperor expected results in two days.

That was asking rather a lot.

Unless the emperor issued a formal order allowing his people to search private households one by one. But that was something Zhang Zan knew better than to suggest.

Qin Yuan's cold gaze rested on Zhang Zan for a long, uncomfortable moment.

Beneath the invisible weight of it, Zhang Zan's head dropped lower. A thin film of cold sweat had formed on his back.

Finally -- whether it had been a short time or a long one, Zhang Zan could not say -- the emperor's voice came. "Keep looking. Spare no expense. Find her."

"Yes, Your Majesty." Zhang Zan felt a rush of relief. He bowed and retreated quickly.

But privately, he thought: spare no expense.

...

Jiyao and her cousin had arrived at a silent mutual understanding not to mention the chess competition again, as though it had simply never happened.

Fang Lin went home and stayed there, reading diligently.

Jiyao was equally careful.

In practice, "careful" looked almost identical to her ordinary life. She attended the women's academy each day. After class, she returned to Haitang Courtyard and read or worked through chess manuals quietly.

The Second Miss Fang was famously well-behaved and timid -- everyone in the household knew it.

Even the few days she had taken leave, her tutor and cousins had assumed she was genuinely unwell. In changing seasons, a minor illness was nothing unusual.

Who would ever suspect the gentle, quiet, careful Second Miss Fang?

Certainly no one in the Fang household.

The eighth month had arrived. Osmanthus flowers were blooming.

Third Cousin Zhiyao had recently taken a sudden interest in making osmanthus cakes.

One afternoon she arrived at Haitang Courtyard carrying a small plate of her latest attempt.

"Second Sister, try one and tell me what you think."

Jiyao smiled before tasting, offering a compliment first. "They look lovely."

The Fang kitchen had plenty of molds, and Third Sister's osmanthus cakes were neat and pretty.

The taste, however, was quite sweet -- rather more than Jiyao preferred. But she couldn't say so bluntly. She thought for a moment and said, with full diplomacy, "Very sweet. Sixth Sister will love them."

Third Sister laughed. "Exactly."

If Sixth Sister -- who had an almost legendary sweet tooth -- would love them, that meant they were a touch too sweet.

"I'll use less sugar next time." Third Sister shifted to another topic. "...I heard the top three finishers from the chess tournament get to enter the palace and meet the emperor and the Grand Empress. What a shame you didn't go, Second Sister."

"I like chess well enough, but my level is only passable for my own amusement. I'm not cut out for competitions." Jiyao said it quietly.

She had initially considered telling Third Sister the truth about her participation, since they were close. But once the words "false identity" had become part of the story, she had decided to say nothing. Let the secret stay a secret.

"It's probably for the best that you didn't go," Third Sister said, consolingly. "I heard from Fourth and Fifth Sister that someone apparently snuck into the competition, and the court is searching for them -- no one knows when they'll be found..."

Said without any particular intention. Heard with great attention.

Jiyao's eyelid twitched. She kept her responses casual, and the moment Third Sister left, she composed herself and went to find Grandfather at the front study.

Minister Fang happened to be home. Hearing that Jiyao was asking to see him, he set aside what he was doing and had her shown in.

"Something on your mind?" he asked the moment she arrived.

Jiyao gathered her nerve. "Grandfather, is my situation very serious?"

In the lamplight, the young woman's eyes were wide and luminous, bright with nerves and quiet worry.

Jiyao had always followed the rules in real life. In sixteen years she had done one thing outside of them. She kept telling herself it was fine, that Grandfather was handling it, that there was nothing to fear. But occasionally the anxiety surfaced anyway.

She was afraid of creating trouble for others. She was afraid of disappointing Grandfather.
