When he met those eyes, something in Minister Fang softened without warning. He said quietly, "It is a little complicated. But don't worry. It can be resolved."

He had been careful. The day after she withdrew from the competition, he had arranged for a short, dark-complexioned "Lin Yao" to leave the capital through the north gate with travel documents in hand. To make sure the guards at the gate remembered the departure, he had orchestrated a small, memorable bit of friction -- nothing alarming, just enough to leave an impression.

He had thought that would be sufficient to establish that "Lin Yao" had forfeited and left. But then the emperor had deployed intelligence operatives to continue the investigation, which was rather more than he had expected.

Still -- Minister Fang ran a careful household, and Fang Lin had been thorough. The operatives might not be able to trace anything back to Jiyao.

Given a little more time, this would most likely fade and be forgotten.

"Really?" Jiyao's expression brightened.

The specifics were not something he could explain to a granddaughter. He only said, "Really. Go home and rest."

"Yes." Jiyao nodded, and felt considerably more at ease.

She should trust Grandfather. She should not let herself worry about things that hadn't happened yet.

She went back to Haitang Courtyard, practiced her calligraphy, and let her mind gradually settle.

...

At that same moment, in the palace, Zhang Zan requested an urgent audience with the emperor and said he had something of extreme importance to report in person.

Qin Yuan was preparing for dinner. He heard this, and his brow lifted slightly. He ordered at once, "Send him in."

As for dinner, he waved a hand at the eunuchs. It could wait.

The palace lamps burned bright, illuminating the inner chambers of Zichen Palace like daylight.

Zhang Zan entered with measured haste and bowed deeply. "This subject Zhang Zan pays his respects to Your Majesty."

Qin Yuan's gaze fell on him with a look of idle assessment. "You found something?"

From Zhang Zan's manner, it was obvious he had.

But then Zhang Zan drew a breath, and his expression was strange. "Your Majesty, this subject has found evidence of treasonous conduct by the Ministry of Rites Vice Minister Pei Chong'an."

The mild look on Qin Yuan's face vanished in an instant. He blinked once. "What did you just say you found?"

He had told Zhang Zan to find "Lin Yao." How had the Ministry of Rites Vice Minister ended up involved?

"This subject has discovered evidence that Vice Minister Pei Chong'an has been plotting treason. I respectfully submit it for Your Majesty's inspection." Zhang Zan held out a sheaf of letters.

Qin Yuan's eyes narrowed. He signaled to the attendant beside him, who delivered the letters.

The handwriting on the topmost letter was immediately familiar. So familiar, in fact, that Qin Yuan's breath caught, and his eyelid gave a single sharp twitch.

The letter was in his mother's hand. Queen Consort Wang's hand.

He had not thought of his mother in some time.

The last time they had seen each other was three years ago.

The contents of the letters were not complex. They were all from Queen Consort Wang to Pei Chong'an, instructing him to produce a blood-written document at the Grand Empress's birthday banquet -- a public declaration exposing the emperor's crimes of poisoning his own brother and imprisoning his mother, calling for his removal from the throne and the installation of a new ruler.

Zhang Zan watched the emperor's face from beneath carefully lowered lids.

The emperor was too still. Not a flicker of expression. Even after years at his side, Zhang Zan could not guess what was moving through his mind right now.

He pressed on steadily. "This subject and his people were pursuing Your Majesty's orders to investigate Ministry of Rites official households when we noticed the Vice Minister's behavior was unusual. We eventually found this correspondence with the detached palace in his study. This subject did not dare conceal it and could only bring it to Your Majesty at once."

Zhang Zan was privately conscious of being on shaky ground. The emperor's assigned task had been to find "Lin Yao." Instead, in the course of that search, they had stumbled across something else entirely. In Zhang Zan's assessment, this was considerably more significant than finding "Lin Yao" -- and might buy him some extra time before being pressed about the search again.

Qin Yuan said nothing. He looked at the letters for a long time.

The silence in the chamber became heavy.

Zhang Zan's anxiety grew until he could almost hear his own heartbeat. "Your Majesty?"

Qin Yuan closed his eyes. When he opened them again, they were still and deep as a well -- no surface disturbance, no visible movement.

His voice was cold and quiet. "Send a contingent of palace guards. Seal every exit from the Pei household. No one in or out. You go personally and search the premises. See if there are any other letters."

These letters could not be made public yet. Zhang Zan was the right person to handle them.

As for finding "Lin Yao" -- he would assign someone else to continue. Zhang Zan had proven he was not suited for finding people.

"This subject obeys." Zhang Zan answered at full volume, bowed, and withdrew.

Qin Yuan lowered his eyes and looked at the letters again. His mother's face, full of resentment, rose in his mind unbidden.

The scheme described in these letters was almost laughable. But seeing it laid out in her handwriting still produced a small, involuntary sting somewhere in his chest.

He thought: perhaps it was time to go and visit his mother at the Western Hills detached palace.

chapters.title: Comfort
chapters.content:
Three years ago, Queen Consort Wang had been relocated to the Western Hills Detached Palace. Since then, mother and son had not seen each other once.

And yet the detached palace was only a few dozen li from the imperial palace.

In terms of formal rank, a detached palace was less than the main imperial residence. In terms of comfort, the Western Hills Palace was lacking in nothing. The landscape was beautiful, natural hot springs were available, and all provisions were supplied at the full standards appropriate to a queen consort. It was, by any reasonable measure, a fine place to live out one's days in ease.

And yet Queen Consort Wang spent her days there in low spirits. The beauty that had once made her famous throughout the capital had been giving way, gradually, to the lines of age.

One afternoon, a disturbance broke the quiet of the detached palace.

Queen Consort Wang was in the prayer hall, leafing through a Buddhist sutra. She heard the noise and frowned immediately. "What is that?"

She had not believed in Buddhism once. But in recent years, as the emperor suppressed the faith across the empire, Wang had found herself drawn to it in spite of everything.

"Your Highness..." The palace maid beside her was visibly frightened. "It's His Majesty. He has arrived."

Wang's hand went still. Something complicated moved across her face. "Oh? He has come."

Even as she spoke, footsteps approached from outside -- many of them -- and then a group of people entered, the one at the head wearing dark robes and a gold crown.

Every attendant in the room dropped to the floor in prostration.

Wang simply narrowed her eyes. "A rare guest. What has brought Your Majesty to my poor residence?"

Qin Yuan said nothing. He removed one of the letters from his sleeve and let it fall at his mother's feet.

Wang saw the letter and her expression changed completely. She threw the sutra aside and gave two short, sharp laughs. "So you found out. And now what? Are you going to kill me? The way you killed your brother?"

Qin Yuan's eyes were lowered. He spoke each word with deliberate slowness. "I said I would not kill you. You may go on living here."

Until the end of your days.

There was nothing more between them. After those words, Qin Yuan left the prayer hall and ordered his guards to take away Wang's most trusted attendants for questioning.

Every person who had been involved in carrying those letters was to be removed. Every single one.

Wang remained in the prayer hall, eyes closed, her lips moving over sutras in a low murmur.

But as screams and pleas rose and fell outside, her chest heaved, and she could no longer contain it. The words that came out of her were sharp as a blade. "You miserable wretch. Why couldn't it have been you? Why was it the other one who died and not you?"

These were the last few people she had left, and he was taking them all.

He claimed he would not kill her. But what he was doing -- cutting out her heart, breaking off her hands and feet -- was nothing short of killing her slowly.

Wang's voice was high and carrying, and it traveled far.

Outside the prayer hall, the emperor's attendants heard every word and did not dare move, wishing they could stop their own ears. At that distance, the emperor would have heard it too.

But the emperor's face showed nothing. He watched the interrogations proceed as though he had not heard a sound.

One by one, the attendants broke under pressure and gave up every detail -- how the correspondence had been conducted, how letters had been passed, who had been involved.

Qin Yuan gave the order to deal with them and walked on.

After this, the staff surrounding Wang was replaced entirely, again.

The emperor left specific instructions: those assigned to wait on the queen consort were to be loyal to the emperor and sparing with words. The queen consort's health was fragile, and she was prone to episodes. He did not wish to hear anything further of the queen consort from the palace.

As he left the Western Hills Detached Palace, he could still faintly hear her cursing behind him.

This was the most exalted pair of mother and son in the world, and they were enemies.

Back in the palace, Qin Yuan did not touch affairs of state. Instead he went to the practice grounds and ran through mounted archery until the sun went down.

He rode hard, loosed arrow after arrow. He let every other thought leave his mind. Arrow after arrow to the target, each one precise. Gradually, the edge inside him eased.

Only when the light was fading did he return to the inner chambers.

That night, Qin Yuan dreamed.

In the dream he was very small -- perhaps four or five years old -- reciting his lessons for his parents. Warm sunlight fell on both of them, a pale golden light on their faces.

The scene shifted. His mother's voice, cracking at the edges: "He forced me. I had no choice."

Then his younger brother -- two years younger -- who had conspired with palace attendants to poison him. Qin Yuan, vomiting blood, had gathered what remained of the poisoned wine and with the last of his strength had it poured down his brother's throat. He had stood there and watched as the poison worked.

...

Qin Yuan rarely dreamed of these things. After the palace coup three years ago, he had developed insomnia. The palace physicians had eventually formulated the calming incense, which addressed the worst of it. But then had come the strange dream, and the loss of control that went with it.

Tonight, perhaps because of visiting his mother, the incense had carried him into these old memories instead.

He had been the late emperor's eldest son. In his earliest memories, his parents seemed reasonably loving toward each other. But the late emperor had died suddenly before he was yet thirty.

Qin Yuan had been young when he took the throne. The regent -- the Prince of Jing -- and his mother had governed together during the interim. The prince had been ambitious: in those years he had suppressed the senior ministers, destabilized the inner court, and made several attempts on Qin Yuan's life.

Qin Yuan had once believed that he and his mother were natural and unbreakable allies. He had learned eventually that she and the regent had been lovers. His younger brother was not the late emperor's son -- he was the regent's. Even the late emperor's sudden death had had more to it than was known at the time.

And his beloved younger brother, once he had learned the truth of his parentage, had feared that Qin Yuan would move to eliminate him and had chosen to strike first -- to kill Qin Yuan and take the throne for himself.

...

That night, Qin Yuan dreamed of the time after the palace coup: his mother, cradling his brother's body, tears streaming down her face as she cursed him. "You killed your own kin. You deserve a miserable death. If I had known how ruthless you were, I would have let him kill you when he had the chance."

There was nothing but regret in her.

After the late emperor's death, her son had taken the throne. The regent had originally intended to quietly remove Qin Yuan and place her own son instead. But at the time, she had still felt something for the bond of mother and son, and she had not agreed. Then Qin Yuan had grown into himself, had removed the regent, and had killed the only child she and the regent had shared.

Wang knew that it had been her younger son who had struck first. But what did that matter? Her elder son was still alive.

In the dream, Qin Yuan simply looked at his mother. The feeling of the poison seemed to return -- something shifting and displaced in his organs, a sharp pain in his chest.

He had spent more than half a year recovering from that poisoning.

He did not like remembering these things. He hated this dream.

The pain in his chest made him want to kill something, the urge rising fast.

In a flash, Qin Yuan remembered: he had studied dream control. He could end this.

He steadied his breathing, gathered his concentration, and began to direct his thoughts toward leaving the dream. Then, in an instant, a brightness crossed his vision -- and he found himself standing in a peach grove.

His imperial robes were gone. The pain in his chest had also vanished, completely.

The young woman before him was smiling, her eyes warm and bright. She reached out and took his hand. "Husband!"

Qin Yuan went still for a moment. He understood. He had slipped into the strange dream.

...

Jiyao had gone to bed late that night.

She had barely finished dinner when Third Cousin Zhiyao appeared at her door with reddened eyes.

One look at her cousin's face was enough. Jiyao sent someone to bring tea at once, then sat with her and listened, offering quiet sounds of sympathy.

It was some time before the full story came out: Third Aunt had scolded Zhiyao.

Third Aunt had been spending more time at home lately, with less to manage since the household duties had been partly redistributed. Idle time had led her to be increasingly critical of her daughter -- Zhiyao was too slow, too careless, hadn't developed the proper demeanor of a young lady soon to be married.

Third Miss Fang had been raised with great care and tenderness. Being criticized by her mother felt deeply unfair.

Jiyao didn't need to say much. She listened attentively, nodded at the right moments, offered a few words of understanding, and kept her cousin's tea cup full.

After getting it all out, Zhiyao felt considerably better. She washed her face, drank a fresh cup of tea, ate a few pieces of cake.

Then a maid arrived from Third Aunt's side, calling her back for a late evening snack. Third Miss straightened slightly, collected herself, said her goodbyes, and went home.

Jiyao shook her head with a small smile.

The sand clock showed it was late. Time to sleep.

She washed up and went to bed.

She was asleep quickly, and the dream began at once.

Third Sister was in the middle of pouring her heart out to her again.

Jiyao blinked. She recognized that she was dreaming. With a thought, her cousin vanished, replaced by a stand of peach trees.

Her parents sat in the courtyard -- one of them playing the qin, the other drinking tea.

When the piece finished, Jiyao went to them, settled close, and talked about the things that had been weighing on her lately. She was playful and affectionate, taking her place as the child of the family.

The three of them were easy and warm together.

After a while, Jiyao thought of her husband in the dream.

She thought: Mother and Father have gone back inside. Husband, come out from among the peach trees.

And everything unfolded exactly as she had imagined.

Her parents smiled and said, "Our Little Darling, we're heading inside. Stay and play a while."

"All right." Jiyao watched them go. A few breaths later, she saw her husband appear from behind a peach tree.

...

Qin Yuan had always resented the strange dream.

But in this moment, seeing the young woman in front of him, something unfamiliar moved through him -- a brief, ridiculous thought: compared to dreaming about the past, he would almost rather be here, tangled up with her, even like this.

But the thought was barely formed before he caught himself. He pushed it away sharply.

Had he forgotten the last time she made him dance with a sword?

Two types of dreams, both not what he wanted. Was he really comparing them?

Of course, in this dream, Jiyao had no intention of making him do anything of the sort.

She glanced at the qin resting not far away and said with a warm smile, "Husband, shall I play the qin for you?"

In truth, she had simply felt the impulse and wanted to play.

Without waiting for an answer, she let go of his hand, walked to the instrument, and settled herself.

"Listen."

In a dream, the strings required no tuning. They were already in perfect harmony.

Jiyao's qin skill in real life was unremarkable. But in the dream, whatever her fingers produced was something else entirely -- a sound like water over stones, like light moving through leaves.

She played Flowing Water, the piece she knew best. It moved through its variations smoothly, like a stream washing the mind clean.

The piece was not unfamiliar to Qin Yuan. But listening to it now, he found himself drifting unexpectedly back to that time in the strange dream on Qiyun Mountain -- the bamboo raft on the stream, the walk through the mountain paths, the moment when he had genuinely felt, just for a second, that he had left everything behind.

When the song ended, Jiyao turned her head and asked, smiling, "What did you think?"

Qin Yuan was quiet for a moment. Then: "Good."

Jiyao's smile brightened. Satisfied with that. She launched immediately into another piece.

Qin Yuan's eyes drifted half-closed. He did not interrupt, did not speak. He simply listened.

One piece followed another, and something inside him grew quiet.

But Jiyao did not play forever. After a few songs, her energy shifted. She set the qin aside, went to sit beside her husband, and began to study his hand -- examining the lines of his palm with great pretend-seriousness, telling his fortune.

She had noticed it before -- her husband's hand was nothing like her own. Wide across the palm with narrow fingers, spare in structure, the bones visible. She found it interesting.

She studied every line carefully, filling the air with conventional blessings. "Great prosperity, a long life to a hundred years..."

At the most satisfying part, she kissed his palm, then held his hand up next to her own to compare.

"Can you?" her husband said, out of nowhere.

Jiyao blinked. "What do you mean, can I?"

Qin Yuan repeated her words back to her. "Great prosperity, a long life to a hundred years..."

"Of course!" Jiyao answered with absolute certainty. She thought: obviously -- he was someone she had imagined, so naturally she could arrange for him to live as long as she chose. But she didn't say any of that aloud, only pointed seriously at the lines of his palm and made things up with great conviction. "Look, this line is so long -- that clearly means a long life. And here, where it branches slightly -- that must mean there was a crisis in the fate, but it was survived, disaster turned to fortune..."

Petals drifted down now and then, turning lazily in the air.

Perhaps it was the contrast with the nightmare that had come before. Perhaps it was that Qin Yuan had been able to maintain his own control throughout this dream. Perhaps it was simply that her qin playing was not unpleasant to listen to.

For whatever reason, Qin Yuan found that he did not hate this particular strange dream. He did not pull away. He simply let her ramble.

The clear, unhurried sound of her voice reached him, and a thought crossed his mind -- formless, barely there: if this was all she did in the strange dream, he might be willing to forgive her several entries in his account.

This time, Jiyao did not move toward anything more intimate. She played for a while, sat with him, and then ended the dream.

...

In the inner chambers of Zichen Palace.

Qin Yuan opened his eyes.

The light was dim. He glanced at his own palm.

A long life to a hundred years.

The night was still early. He went back to sleep.

This time, no nightmares came.

...

Zhang Zan was not good at finding people. But when it came to gathering evidence, he was genuinely skilled.

At daybreak, he came to present the letters and blood-written document retrieved from the Pei household.

Qin Yuan glanced at them briefly. "Is that everything?"

"Yes, Your Majesty. That's all of it."

"Mm." A cold edge entered his voice. "By imperial edict: the Pei household is to be imprisoned in full. Await sentencing."

"Yes, Your Majesty."

He paused. "The person I asked you to find -- any progress?"

Zhang Zan's face immediately fell. He hedged. "Your Majesty, these past two days this subject has been entirely occupied with the Pei Chong'an treason investigation, so the matter of finding the person..."

"Then set it aside for now," Qin Yuan said directly.

He had given up on Zhang Zan for that particular task.

Hearing this, Zhang Zan quietly exhaled. Then the emperor spoke again. "The Ministry of Rites performed considerable service in organizing the chess tournament. The Grand Empress, in her benevolence, has granted special permission for all Ministry of Rites personnel to bring their families into the palace to offer birthday wishes to the Grand Empress."

Even now, Qin Yuan believed she was most likely a family member of a Ministry of Rites official.

Since the intelligence operatives couldn't find her quickly, he would create an opportunity to look for himself.

chapters.title: An End
chapters.content:
After the chess tournament concluded, two significant events struck the Ministry of Rites in quick succession.

The first: the entire family of Vice Minister Pei Chong'an was suddenly imprisoned. According to what circulated afterward, the intelligence operatives had found evidence of treason in his household.

The second: the emperor had issued an order for Ministry of Rites officials to bring their families into the palace to pay birthday respects to the Grand Empress.

Either of these alone would have been enough to set the whole Ministry buzzing. Together, they produced a level of whispered discussion that was difficult to ignore.

Minister Fang had served long enough to have seen many things. He took one look at the quiet conversations spreading among his staff and immediately put a stop to it. "Everyone is to attend to their duties and carry out what is asked of them. What should not be said should not be said."

He was the head of the Ministry of Rites, and his authority there was considerable. One word from him, and the whispers stopped.

But Minister Fang himself was uneasy.

Pei Chong'an was his subordinate. If the man truly had been plotting something, then as head of the ministry, Minister Fang bore some responsibility for failing to notice. The charge of "dereliction in supervision" would have to be answered for eventually.

At the moment, however, the emperor seemed more focused on the Grand Empress's upcoming birthday banquet than on pressing the Pei Chong'an matter further.

And the birthday banquet itself gave Minister Fang its own concerns: the entire Ministry of Rites, families included, was to enter the palace for the celebration?

This was without precedent.

The emperor had just taken him to task for allowing someone to enter the competition under a false identity. And now, suddenly, a personal invitation to bring family members into the palace?

Minister Fang had spent many years at court. But this time, he found he could not read the emperor's thinking at all. Something felt strange about it.

There was one piece of good news, however. That same day, he happened to cross paths with Zhang Zan, the intelligence chief, and learned that the search for the missing person had been called off.

That was clearly the emperor's doing.

Minister Fang breathed a quiet sigh of relief. Perhaps, he thought, the real purpose of sending the operatives after the false-identity competitor had simply been to flush out whoever was plotting treason. "Lin Yao" had been incidental.

Of course, that was only a guess.

In any case, there was now a more pressing matter that required his attention.

...

That afternoon, Jiyao came to Grandfather's study and greeted him with a respectful bow.

Minister Fang set aside what he was doing and looked up, his expression mild. "Jiyao. I called you here to tell you two things. The first: the intelligence operatives have stopped searching for 'Lin Yao.'"

Jiyao's eyes lit up. "Grandfather means I'm out of trouble?"

Minister Fang gave a small smile. "You could say that. But don't let your guard down."

He had been thinking of adding that she shouldn't leave the house for the next few months. But the complication of the Grand Empress's birthday banquet made that awkward.

"I understand." Jiyao was quick to reassure him.

A genuine wave of relief moved through her. These past few days, even with Grandfather's reassurances, she had occasionally found herself worrying -- mostly that she might cause trouble for her cousin, or for Grandfather himself.

Minister Fang smiled and continued more slowly, "The second matter is your marriage."

"My marriage?" Jiyao blinked, her lashes trembling faintly.

Was it time for another round of candidate selection behind a screen?

In truth, she had not felt particularly urgent about marriage. She was satisfied with her life as it was. Grandfather's protection, days filled with reading and chess. In the dreams, her parents, and her husband. She was not in a hurry to change any of it.

Minister Fang went on, "I had planned to wait another year or two, perhaps after the spring examinations, and select someone carefully. But with recent affairs in the Ministry keeping me busy, I thought it better to settle your engagement now."

He was sixty-two. He might retire at any time. While he still held his position, Jiyao's marriage prospects would benefit from his standing. Once he stepped down, that was less certain.

And there was another reason, one he did not say aloud.

He had recently heard, by chance, that the Grand Empress was considering selecting a few daughters of officials for the emperor's inner court. The upcoming birthday banquet had also specifically called for Ministry of Rites families. And before that, the chess tournament had singled out female competitors for special recognition.

Minister Fang had concerns he preferred not to voice.

In his heart -- not to flatter himself -- his granddaughters were all fine young women who deserved peaceful lives and happiness, not years spent within the depths of the palace.

Better to settle the marriage and set his mind at rest.

"Grandfather..." Jiyao said hesitantly, "With so much happening in the Ministry, Grandfather should focus on that first. My situation is not urgent."

Minister Fang sighed, a slow sound. "It cannot wait. I am old. I am afraid that if I do not settle this now, I will not be able to watch over you."

One thing after another lately had unsettled him.

At the words "I am old," something tightened in Jiyao's chest. Grandfather was past sixty. His hair at the temples was white. His spirit was still sharp, but he was not young.

They said that seventy was rare in a lifetime. She did not know how long Grandfather could still be there to shelter her.

Her throat ached. She said quietly, "Grandfather is not old. Grandfather will never grow old."

She had lost her father when she was small. Her mother had vanished. Even her grandmother, the one who had played chess with her, was gone now. Grandfather was all she had left.

The thought of a future without him left her briefly unmoored, and tears pressed dangerously close.

Minister Fang shook his head with a gentle laugh. "Foolish child. Who does not grow old? While I am still capable of it, I want to see your affairs settled."

He had many grandchildren. She was the only one who had nothing but him.

"Yes." Jiyao fought back the tears, keeping her voice low. "I will do as Grandfather says."

Minister Fang waited a moment, then continued. "You once said that in a husband, you would like someone good-looking. What do you think of Lu Ming? Does his appearance meet your standard?"

Jiyao blinked. Who? Lu Ming? The Lu Ming she knew? Cousin Zhao Jinde's elder cousin?

"Your Aunt came today to say that the Lu family's elder matriarch has been sounding out my thoughts on a possible match." He smiled slightly.

Jiyao's heart gave a small, uncertain beat.

"My feeling is this," Minister Fang said. "Lu Ming is easygoing and steady -- not proud, not rash. He has real aptitude for scholarship and he works hard. He will certainly pass next year's examinations; you need not worry about his future. And the Lu household is simple in structure, with clean family values. They do not permit concubines or additional women. The Lu family has promised that if they are fortunate enough to have a young lady from the Fang family, their son will remain faithful."

He watched his granddaughter's expression carefully as he spoke.

He had thought long about this particular granddaughter, and after quiet observation and comparison across many possibilities, his inclination had settled on Lu Ming. The timing was fortunate: the Lu family had expressed interest at the same moment.

He could not imagine a more suitable arrangement.

"Can I ask..." Jiyao hesitated. "What does Lu Ming himself think?"

Marriage was ultimately an elder's decision. But at least it was worth asking what the other person felt.

Minister Fang smiled. "He is willing, of course. Who do you think gave the promise of faithfulness?"

Jiyao turned it over in her mind, then nodded. "All right. I will trust Grandfather's judgment."

Her parents were gone. Her marriage had always been Grandfather's decision to make, and by every measure it sounded like a good one.

"Good. I'll let the Lu family know. Now go -- I have some matters to attend to."

"Yes, Grandfather. Your granddaughter takes her leave." Jiyao curtsied and withdrew.

Walking away from the study, she was still thinking about what had just happened.

Grandfather had considered everything carefully for her. And yet -- the thought of stepping into an entirely different life -- she felt a small, vague, nameless flutter of unease.

Was this really how one's whole future was decided?

She found herself, unexpectedly, thinking of the conversation she had once had with her cousin Zhao Jinyun just before Jinyun's wedding -- the things a girl kept close to her heart.

Then she remembered: it had been that same day, at the Zhao household, that she had first seen Lu Ming.

They had crossed paths a few times since then. Perhaps that was a kind of fate?

She was still loosely following this thread of thought when she turned a corner and walked straight into the path of her cousin Zhao Jinde -- and Lu Ming beside him.

"Second Cousin!" Zhao Jinde called out cheerfully.

Jiyao smiled. "Cousin."

She looked, almost without meaning to, toward the young man beside him.

She had seen the two of them together before, but she had always mostly talked to Zhao Jinde and barely noticed Lu Ming. Now, glancing over, she found that he was looking at her.

Their eyes met. Lu Ming startled slightly, then gave her a quiet smile.

Jiyao felt abruptly self-conscious and looked away.

But she was sharp-eyed, and even in that brief glance she noticed that his ears had gone red -- entirely unlike the easy confidence he had shown when they first met.

Jiyao stared for a moment, and then something loosened unexpectedly in her chest. So it wasn't only her. He was uncomfortable too.

They nodded to each other as a greeting.

Jiyao did not linger, and she turned to go.

Long after she had left, Lu Ming still felt faintly distracted.

He remembered: the day they had gone to Ziyun Temple, he had accompanied his mother, and they had run into Third Aunt from the Fang family and two of the Fang daughters. His mother had noticed, and afterward had asked for his opinion. When he had agreed, she had asked his maternal aunt to sound out the Fang family's position.

He wasn't sure whether the Second Miss Fang knew any of this.

Part of him wanted to tell her -- that this was not just the Lu family's wish, but his own. But he worried that saying so outright would startle her.

He still remembered the second time they had met, and how badly frightened she had been by a reckless young man.

He had also been meaning to ask whether she had fully recovered from her recent illness.

He thought about it and decided not to ask. He had already seen the answer for himself just now. She was clearly well.

...

Jiyao returned to Haitang Courtyard.

She sat down at the table, her thoughts still unsettled.

Shuangxi, sensing that her mistress was in the middle of something, did not interrupt -- only brought a cup of tea and set it quietly on the table.

Jiyao did not drink. She went on sitting, lost in thought. She thought of the eldest cousin who had already married, of Third Sister who was already engaged, of the young man she had met a handful of times who might now become her husband.

And then, all at once, something else struck her.

She had always kept dreams and reality neatly separate. But if she was truly engaged -- and if she continued to meet her husband in the dream at night, doing what she did there -- that would not be right.

She was reluctant to give up the husband of her dreams. He was, after all, her own imagining, and he suited her so perfectly. But thinking about it from the other side: she would not want a future husband, in his own dreams, to have someone else.

If the Lu family had promised faithfulness, then she should offer the same.

...

That night, Jiyao shaped her dream deliberately.

At first she was in the courtyard, telling her parents about the engagement.

Her parents disagreed with each other, as they sometimes did.

Father said warmly, "Trust your grandfather. He must have your best interests at heart."

But Mother said, "What about the husband you have now -- in the dream?"

Yes. What about her husband in the dream? Jiyao wasn't quite sure how to answer that either.

She let the thought settle. When choices had to be made, choices had to be made.

Perhaps she could listen to what the deepest part of herself had to say.

With that, she thought: husband, come out.

With a shift of thought, a familiar figure stepped from behind a peach tree.

...

Qin Yuan had not been asleep long when he found himself unexpectedly in the strange dream again.

Because the last dream had not been altogether unpleasant, he was not particularly resistant -- only mildly surprised.

What surprised him far more was seeing her parents in the courtyard.

He had tried so many times to reach them -- to memorize her father's face, to draw a portrait and have someone search for him. She had deflected every attempt with excuses, or simply looked him in the eye and told him things that were not true.

He had eventually given up on that route and found other ways forward. He had already made some progress. And now, here were her parents again, entirely unannounced.

Exactly as he had guessed: he could not hold onto her face in memory, but he could hold onto her parents'.

This was an important thread. Qin Yuan gave no outward sign of anything, only observed their faces quietly and committed them to memory.

Looking carefully now, he found that her father had a faint quality of familiarity -- as though he had seen the man somewhere before, without it leaving a deep impression.

It was possible that her father really was an official in the capital whom he had encountered once or twice in passing. If he now knew the face, finding her would be considerably easier.

"Ahem..." Her father gave a mild cough. "Little Darling, speak with your husband."

Jiyao considered and agreed. This was different from the original dream-marriage -- a simpler setting was better.

She took her husband's hand, smiled at her parents, and said, "Father, Mother, we're going inside."

At the words "going inside," Qin Yuan's eyelid twitched.

He knew perfectly well what they had done most often in that room.

He was still in control of the dream, but he did not pull away from her hand.

Why resist, he thought. There were not many more times left in any case.

And the last dream had been reasonably agreeable.

And if she truly wanted to, he would not be able to refuse.

The door swung shut behind them.

Jiyao wrapped her arms around his lean waist and pressed her face against his chest, saying softly, "Husband, I like you so much."

Qin Yuan said nothing.

Jiyao rubbed her face against him for a moment, then tilted her head back to look at him. She kissed him once. Then stepped back and looked at him carefully.

What a perfect face. Every feature exactly as she could have wished.

What a shame.

The dream was wonderful. But reality had to come first.

Qin Yuan could not hold onto her face in memory, but he could feel her gaze -- direct and unguarded, resting on him without any effort to conceal itself.

He thought: what comes next is probably that.

Jiyao took his hand and drew him to sit beside her on the edge of the bed.

Before she had even spoken, she already knew her own answer.

Jiyao was a person who tried to be fair. She had always given back in kind what others gave her. If she was truly getting engaged, and if her future husband kept his word and remained faithful, then she would not keep a husband in her dreams.

She had tried the intimate things in her dreams many times now. At first it had been curiosity, something thrilling and new. But with time -- it was what it was. Not as fresh as it had been.

Seeing that she sat there without moving, Qin Yuan felt a flicker of puzzlement.

Was she trying some new game?

Jiyao steadied herself. "Husband, I don't think I'll be seeing you anymore."

Her husband was her own imagining -- she could simply let him fade out of her dreams and never appear again. But they had exchanged vows in this dream, in a way. She wanted to do this properly. A real goodbye.

"What?" Qin Yuan's brow furrowed.

Jiyao said quietly, "My family is arranging a marriage for me. It isn't right for me to keep meeting with you."

A bright ringing sound went through Qin Yuan's head. His temple throbbed.

What?

He heard himself ask, "Who is getting married?"

In this dream, she had already taken a husband who had married into her family. Was she planning to find another one in the dream?

"Me. I'm the one. They're arranging a match for me." Jiyao sighed, sincere and serious. "Husband, I will truly miss you. But a person has to act with some fairness. I cannot be negotiating a marriage with someone on one side while meeting with you in dreams on the other. That wouldn't be right to him."

Qin Yuan almost laughed.

Not right to whom, exactly? After all of this, she had found fairness?

Wait. She had said "while meeting with you in dreams on the other" -- she was being arranged into a real-world marriage?

Qin Yuan went cold and sharp inside. He reached out and caught her wrist, pulling her toward him with enough force to make her stumble forward. "Who are you being matched with?"

He had thought he would be relieved to hear she intended to stop entering the strange dream. What he actually felt, in this moment, was a tide of fury.

He had almost found her. He hadn't had the chance to repay any of it yet. And she was ending things and getting engaged? Just like that?

The force of his grip was enough to hurt. Jiyao didn't like it.

She hadn't come to this dream for a confrontation. She had come to end things properly, to say a real goodbye.

This reaction from her husband was wrong.

She sent the thought -- and Qin Yuan found he had lost control again.

Against his will, his grip loosened. His voice came out gentle and not his own: "Little Darling, I don't want to be parted from you. Will we see each other again?"

Jiyao nodded inwardly, satisfied. Yes. That was more like it.

That was how her imagined husband should sound.

"Probably not." She thought for a moment, then added, "Although -- if the match falls through, or if my future husband turns out to be unkind to me, I will come back to find you."

She leaned over and kissed his cheek.

Her familiar, delicate scent drifted close. Qin Yuan could not move, could not speak. His mouth shaped words that were not his: "Good. I'll wait."

Inside, fury churned.

Good. Very good. He had been used as a convenience -- summoned and dismissed at will. And now he was expected to be a backup, brought back out if the real husband proved inadequate?

Infuriating. And absurd.

But not everything in this world would go as she decided.

This had already begun. When and how it ended was no longer entirely up to her.

chapters.title: The Palace Banquet
chapters.content:
When she had said everything she wanted to say, Jiyao looked up at her husband.

His eyes were dark as ink, and cold, and steady -- fixed on her without moving.

Memory after memory from their time together rose in her mind, and the reluctance in her grew heavier.

But she had always tried to be a person who was fair. She had agreed to the match with Lu Ming. She could not keep a husband in her dreams as well.

It was not right.

Jiyao leaned in and kissed his lips once more, very softly, and said, "Goodbye."

Goodbye, the husband she had imagined into being.

Goodbye, the dream she had carried through her girlhood.

Before her husband could respond, she ended the dream.

The night was perfectly still. Jiyao opened her eyes.

Moonlight filtered through the gauze curtain, casting a dim, soft light inside the bed hangings. She stared at the canopy overhead for a long time.

...

In the inner chambers of Zichen Palace.

The young emperor jolted awake.

His expression was darker than it had ever been.

What had happened in the dream was a humiliation beyond what he could simply endure. He wanted to put her in front of him right now.

The eunuch keeping watch that night had been half-dozing. The faint sounds from the imperial bed brought him sharply awake.

Based on experience, he was about to reach for the water preparations.

But tonight, for the first time, the emperor simply pushed back the covers and got up. He called for lamps.

The small eunuch was startled but dared not ask questions. He moved quickly.

In moments, several palace lamps blazed to life, and the inner chambers of Zichen Palace were as bright as day.

The emperor called for brush, ink, and paper. Then he bent over the table and began to draw.

The eunuch stood at a respectful distance, quietly puzzled. The emperor had a sudden interest in art? At this hour of the night, instead of sleeping?

What Qin Yuan was drawing was the face of the young woman's father in the dream.

His own skill with the brush was limited, but his memory was strong, and he had made a deliberate effort to study and retain the details during the dream itself. Reproducing what he remembered was not especially difficult.

After about half a quarter-hour, the portrait was done.

Without waiting for dawn, Qin Yuan gave an order. "Summon Zhang Zan to attend at once."

"Yes, Your Majesty."

Zhang Zan arrived before the fifth watch, the shadows under his eyes just visible.

The emperor's gaze held a quiet, controlled intensity. "Zhang Zan. Look at this portrait. Find me the man in it."

At the word "find," Zhang Zan's eye gave a hard twitch. Every last trace of sleep left him. Only one thought remained: another search.

He had just been told the last search was suspended.

Finding people was exactly like searching for a needle in the sea. He would rather track down evidence any day.

But this was not something he could say. He composed his expression and leaned in to examine the portrait. The ink was barely dry, the smell of it still fresh.

The drawing showed a middle-aged man. A refined, pleasant face. The features tugged at something -- familiar, as though seen somewhere before.

"Your Majesty, is this man a wanted criminal?" Zhang Zan asked carefully.

The emperor's gaze was flat. "He is very likely a court official. Find out where he serves."

Qin Yuan believed her father was probably in the Ministry of Rites, which was why he had invited all Ministry families to the palace birthday celebration.

But other possibilities existed.

Now that he had another lead, he would use it.

Zhang Zan told himself he had no choice, accepted the order, and quietly despaired. The capital had so many officials. And there was no guarantee the portrait was even a good likeness.

He had his artists make several copies from the original and sent his operatives to inquire across the capital's various ministries.

The following day, Zhang Zan came to the palace to report.

"You've found him?" Qin Yuan was mildly surprised. Zhang Zan had moved quickly for once.

"Your Majesty, this subject must confess to incompetence -- the person in the portrait has not been found..."

Qin Yuan's brow creased almost imperceptibly. That word again.

"...but someone with a marked resemblance to the portrait has been identified."

"Oh?" Qin Yuan's expression shifted. "A resemblance?"

Zhang Zan, careful not to cast any doubt on the quality of the emperor's drawing, said diplomatically, "Yes. The person bears approximately sixty to seventy percent resemblance to the portrait. He is a Fang official serving in the Ministry of Works. His name is Fang Jing. This subject is not certain whether Fang Jing is the person Your Majesty is looking for."

Qin Yuan frowned, caught off guard. "Not the Ministry of Rites?"

"No, Your Majesty. The Ministry of Works." Zhang Zan thought for a moment and added, "This Fang official is the fourth son of Minister of Rites Fang Jun."

Imperial regulations required family members to avoid serving in the same department. Fang Jing had been able to remain in the capital largely because of his low rank, and because he and his father served in different ministries.

Something moved in Qin Yuan's mind. A shape, half-formed.

He had been too narrow in his thinking. He had only considered that her father might be a Ministry of Rites official. He had forgotten there was also the possibility of a grandfather.

If she was truly a member of Minister Fang's household, it would explain perfectly why she had disappeared from the competition the very day he had begun pressing the investigation.

Qin Yuan closed his eyes briefly. "By my word: summon Fang Jing to present himself at once."

...

Like his father and elder brothers, Fang Jing had entered official service through the imperial examinations. Unfortunately, his ambitions were modest and his career had not flourished. He spent his days in the Ministry of Works in a comfortable enough existence, and had been a seventh-rank official in the same position for several years.

That day, he had just lifted his teacup when a palace messenger arrived with a personal summons from the emperor.

Fang Jing's hand shook. Tea sloshed dangerously close to the rim.

A summons to the palace? What had he done? Had someone reported him for being too idle?

No, surely not.

He could not keep the emperor waiting. He gathered himself, put on a composed face, and entered the palace.

The emperor received him in a side hall.

Fang Jing bowed deeply, profoundly nervous, barely daring to breathe.

Qin Yuan studied him for a moment and felt a quiet settling of his expectations.

The man before him was not the father from the strange dream. But the resemblance to the portrait was there, as Zhang Zan had said -- in the region of the brows and eyes. Clearly the same bloodline.

Minister Fang had more than one son.

Qin Yuan kept his expression still.

The emperor's silence was making Fang Jing genuinely anxious when, abruptly, the emperor asked: "How many brothers do you have? Where are they posted?"

"Your Majesty, there are four of us brothers in total. My eldest brother Fang Chang currently serves as prefect of Quanzhou. My youngest brother Fang Xu is now in the south as an educational commissioner." He answered carefully and with full attention.

"And your second brother?"

Fang Jing paused briefly. "Your Majesty, my second brother passed away ten years ago."

Qin Yuan remembered, with that, that Minister Fang had indeed lost a son some years ago. The story of "two third-place examination graduates from the same family" had been spoken of as something remarkable for a time.

But the details were slightly at odds with the information from the dream. In the dream, her father had still been alive and serving in the capital.

Then again -- it was a dream. Small inconsistencies were not surprising. The peach trees in the dream had blossomed in midsummer.

Qin Yuan asked nothing further. He offered a few words of general encouragement and dismissed Fang Jing.

Fang Jing was still puzzled when he walked out of the palace.

The emperor had summoned him personally just to ask how many brothers he had?

Could it be some kind of consideration for a promotion?

...

After Fang Jing withdrew, Qin Yuan summoned Zhang Zan again. "How many granddaughters does Minister Fang have?"

The Grand Empress's birthday banquet was imminent, and he did not want to question Fang Jing further and risk arousing suspicion. But the desire to confirm the identity of the person in his dreams was pressing enough to keep his focus sharp.

"Six." This was something Zhang Zan could answer directly. He had investigated Ministry of Rites household members not long ago. He could even be more specific: "The eldest and youngest sons each have two daughters; the second and third sons each have one daughter."

"Are any of them skilled at chess?"

Zhang Zan looked somewhat uncomfortable. As inner-household women, he had little direct knowledge of them -- everything he knew came through intermediaries.

After a moment, he offered his best estimate. "The Fang family maintains a women's academy. In addition to academic subjects, it teaches music, chess, calligraphy, and painting. Whether any of the young ladies in particular are skilled at chess, this subject cannot say."

Qin Yuan gave a quiet sound. If the academy covered chess, then all six granddaughters would have been taught it.

"Do you know their ages?"

Zhang Zan thought carefully. "The eldest daughter is approximately eighteen or nineteen and was married off last year. The sixth daughter is under ten. The other four are between fifteen and seventeen."

Qin Yuan's gaze went still with a cool, quiet certainty.

One of those four, then.

As for which one specifically -- the birthday banquet would tell him tomorrow.

...

That evening when Fang Jing came home, he described the imperial summons to his father in full detail, leaving nothing out.

Minister Fang listened, and his expression became measured. "The emperor asked nothing else?"

"Nothing."

Minister Fang found it difficult to interpret. The emperor had been increasingly opaque in his behavior lately.

But there was no time to linger on it. Tomorrow was the Grand Empress's birthday banquet, and there was still a great deal to manage on the Ministry side. And the palace had made a point of specifying that all of the Fang granddaughters were to attend -- including nine-year-old Mengyao.

Concerned, Minister Fang called all five granddaughters before him and gave them careful instructions. "The Grand Empress has graciously invited you to the palace. You must conduct yourselves with discretion and perfect propriety. Do not be careless."

"Yes, Grandfather," all five answered together.

He paused, then added, "In terms of dress -- nothing that calls attention to itself. Neat and appropriate is sufficient."

All five young ladies agreed again.

After a few more instructions, he sent them on their way.

Jiyao had already been a little nervous. Grandfather's tone made it worse.

She had never set foot inside the palace before.

Back in Haitang Courtyard, Shuangxi laid out several sets of clothing for her consideration. "Miss, which one for tomorrow?"

Jiyao pointed to one without much deliberation. "That one -- the lotus pink."

Pale and refined, it was neither conspicuous nor overly plain. Perfectly suited to Grandfather's "neat and appropriate."

His intention was clear: he did not need them to stand out or charm the Grand Empress. He only needed them to be unobtrusive and make no mistakes.

That was something Jiyao was very good at. She had always been quiet and inconspicuous.

Since she was entering the palace the next day, she went to bed early. No dream-shaping -- she slept straight through until morning.

The next day, with Shuangxi's help, she pinned her hair in a low, half-up style with a single pearl and jade hairpin, and nothing more.

Jiyao had good features -- a straight, fine nose, a delicate mouth, eyes and brows that were easy and pleasant to look at. Even without cosmetics, even with simple clothing, nothing could quite conceal how she looked.

"Miss is so lovely," Shuangxi said softly.

Jiyao said nothing. She did not often look closely at herself. Now, gazing at her reflection, she could see that it was true.

She thought: she probably takes after her mother.

Minister Fang was extremely occupied that day and could not accompany them. The Fang granddaughters went with Third Aunt and Fourth Aunt in a carriage to the palace.

The carriage stopped at the palace gate, and they proceeded on foot.

Jiyao had never entered the palace before. Now, walking through it, she felt a faint, odd sense of recognition.

Red walls, dark-tiled roofs. Solemn and magnificent. As though she had seen it somewhere.

In a dream, perhaps?

She did not dwell on it. This was the palace -- she could not afford to be distracted. She pushed the thought away and kept her attention fixed, following close behind the elders.

The nineteenth day of the eighth month. The weather was gentle, a fine autumn wind, neither warm nor cold. The Grand Empress's birthday banquet was being held within the palace.

This year was different from previous years. In addition to the titled ladies of the inner and outer court, the families of Ministry of Rites officials had also been invited -- reportedly at the Grand Empress's specific request.

The banquet had a great many guests. Considerable thought had gone into the seating.

Jiyao and her cousins were seated in an unobtrusive spot, with titled ladies ahead of them and the other Ministry of Rites families behind.

The banquet had not yet formally begun. Occasional murmurs of conversation drifted through the hall.

But mindful of Grandfather's instructions, all five Fang girls were well-behaved and composed. Even the youngest, Mengyao, did not take an extra step or say an extra word.

Then the music stopped. A eunuch's sharp voice rang through the hall: "The Grand Empress approaches!"

A palanquin surrounded by attendants was carried to the front of the hall. The curtain lifted, and the Grand Empress descended with the help of her attendants and walked slowly forward.

The hall went utterly quiet. Every person bowed their head, and the unified sound of their greeting rose: "We pay our respects to the Grand Empress. May she live ten thousand years, ten thousand times ten thousand years."

Jiyao made herself small in the crowd and bowed with the rest.

Third Cousin Zhiyao stole a bold glance at the Grand Empress. Jiyao kept her eyes firmly on the floor.

The Grand Empress settled into her seat, her expression warm but naturally authoritative. She raised a hand, smiling. "No need for ceremony. Please be seated."

"We thank the Grand Empress." Everyone settled in turn, orderly and composed.

The Grand Empress swept her gaze across the assembled guests, privately puzzled as ever -- she still did not understand why the emperor had organized a chess tournament, and then invited Ministry of Rites families to her birthday celebration.

But she had long understood: to live well in the deep palace, one did not ask too many questions. One simply cooperated.

Then came another sharp announcement: "His Majesty the Emperor approaches!"

Everyone rose again, heads bowed, voices raised: "Long live the Emperor, long live, long live forever."

Jiyao was perfectly correct and quiet, her voice pitched neither too loud nor too soft.

And then from above came a voice -- cold, and strangely familiar.

"Rise."

Jiyao froze for an instant.

As she was sitting back down, she looked up instinctively.

And what she saw nearly stopped her in place.

The emperor seated above -- how did he look exactly like the husband in her dreams?

chapters.title: Confirmed
chapters.content:
Third Cousin Zhiyao noticed her elder sister had gone oddly still, and reached over to give her sleeve a quiet tug.

Jiyao snapped back to herself, lowered her head quickly, and sat down.

Seated, her heart was still hammering, and her mind felt as though it had gone white. There was a faint ringing in her ears that would not stop.

How was it possible? How could the person she had imagined -- how could he simply exist in the real world?

If she had known her husband was a real person, she would never have deliberately shaped those dreams, never have done any of those things with him.

The color came and went in Jiyao's face. Her long lashes trembled and trembled again. She found herself wondering, desperately: could she have been mistaken? She had been so nervous, and the emperor was so far away. She could easily have seen wrong in a moment of distraction.

Reassuring herself with that thought, Jiyao found a small moment of cover, lifted her tea cup, and used the motion to steal another careful look at the person seated above.

And then she felt cold right down to her center.

Upswept phoenix eyes, dark lashes like raven feathers, strong brow bones, a straight high-bridged nose, complexion like polished jade, beautiful in a way that was almost intimidating.

It was definitely him. The husband from her dreams.

What was she supposed to do now?

Her mind flooded all at once with everything she had ever heard about the current emperor: decisive and effective in affairs of state, significant achievements to his name, but also a reputation for cruelty, for ruthlessness. Those close to him, who served him -- his own full-blooded brother, his own birth mother -- anyone who had offended him had suffered the consequences without exception.

If he ever found out what she had done in those dreams...

Jiyao's thoughts tangled into a knot, her heart almost in her throat, a panic rising in her unlike anything she had ever felt before.

She squeezed her hands tight against her palms.

And then, in a flash: wait. The things that happened in a dream -- if she never said a word, how would anyone know?

Could anyone else read what another person had dreamed?

Secrets could be leaked from almost anywhere. But her dreams belonged entirely to her alone. They were her private world, and no one else could enter.

There could never be a second person who knew.

If that was true, then why was she frightening herself?

At that thought, the tightness in Jiyao's chest began, slowly, to ease. The white drained from her cheeks, and warmth crept back in.

The banquet had officially begun. Ladies from titled households were coming forward one by one to present their congratulations to the Grand Empress.

Jiyao stole one more careful look at the emperor.

On closer examination, there were slight differences.

The emperor looked three or four years older than her husband in the dreams -- no longer what one could properly call a young man. He was not only more mature in appearance, but the air he carried was colder, more formidable.

He could not be the same person who had danced with a sword for her and brought her flowers, who had called her Little Darling and held her close.

Taking it all together, Jiyao reached a conclusion: her husband in the dreams was not the emperor. He was simply someone she had imagined who happened to look like the emperor. Two people with similar faces -- that happened in the world, and it meant nothing.

Besides, she had already said her goodbyes to her husband in the dream. She had answered the call of the match with Lu Ming. That chapter was closed.

With that thought, Jiyao felt considerably steadier.

She did not realize that at this very moment, the emperor seated above was letting his gaze move through the hall.

In the strange dream, as though under some strange enchantment, Qin Yuan had always been unable to retain her face. But now -- he needed no mark behind the ear to confirm it. His gaze traveled over the assembled guests and landed, with complete precision, on the person he was looking for.

There were five Fang granddaughters seated together. The youngest was eight or nine -- irrelevant. Of the remaining four, two were twins who looked exactly alike. Of the other two: one was lively, her eyes moving around the hall with open curiosity even as she sat still. The other was quiet and composed, every bit the picture of a well-bred young lady from a good family.

Based on his impression from the dreams, she should be someone with boldness in her nature. But some instinct told him: no. The lively one was not her. Nor were the twins.

It was the quiet, composed one who gave him the overwhelming sense of familiarity.

Yes. Familiarity.

The moment he saw her, every scene from the dream came back into clarity.

But he needed to be careful. He needed to verify.

Qin Yuan turned to the Grand Empress at his side and offered a mild smile. "Grandmother, all five of Minister Fang's granddaughters have come today. Shall we have them come forward for a moment?"

The Grand Empress paused briefly, then smiled and went along with it. "Yes, the Emperor is quite right. We should meet them."

She still had no idea what the emperor was trying to accomplish. But he had made his meaning plain enough, and she would cooperate.

And so, after the titled ladies had finished their greetings, the Grand Empress made a point of calling for the five Fang daughters to come forward.

Jiyao's heart lurched. She looked instinctively toward Third Aunt, not far away.

Second Miss Fang was famously timid and well-behaved, and she had Grandfather's instructions to stay quietly in the background. She had come to this banquet wanting nothing more than to sit through it uneventfully and go home without incident.

But the Grand Empress had called for them, and Third Aunt smiled and nodded, indicating they should comply.

Jiyao steadied herself as best she could and walked forward with her four cousins.

The five sisters curtsied in unison. "We wish the Grand Empress boundless grace and long life."

All five of the Fang daughters were pretty, and they all had pleasant voices. The Grand Empress had been cooperating with the emperor's unexplained wishes, but finding five girls as lovely as flowers standing before her, hearing their sweet wishes delivered with charming sincerity, she found a genuine smile forming on her face. She beckoned them closer, her manner warm. "No need to stand on ceremony. Come, let me have a look at you."

"Yes, Your Highness."

The five girls took a few steps forward.

"Lovely, all of you." The Grand Empress surveyed them with evident pleasure. "Minister Fang is truly fortunate to have so many fine granddaughters."

Each one well-behaved and bright -- rather more appealing to look at than a certain nominal grandson of hers.

The Fang daughters smiled with modest warmth in response.

With her eldest cousin absent, Jiyao was the oldest among her sisters and stood at the front of the group. She was not very practiced at managing situations like this, and made herself focus.

She could not shake the feeling that a burning gaze had settled on her somewhere. Was it the Grand Empress?

Or someone else in the hall?

The Grand Empress glanced at the emperor beside her, wondering what he was actually trying to do.

But he gave no signal, and she could not simply dismiss several daughters of a Minister without some cause, so she patiently continued making conversation -- asking their ages, asking who was the elder and who the younger, asking what they liked to do at home.

The Fang sisters answered each question in turn.

"Lovely," the Grand Empress said, again and again, looking from one to the next with genuine appreciation. If the emperor had any interest in bringing a Fang daughter into the inner court, she would not object to any of the older ones. Even the sixth sister, who was still very young, was a sweet child.

...

Qin Yuan's attention had not left the Second Miss Fang from the moment she came forward.

No wonder she felt familiar. Her silhouette, her movements, her voice -- all of it identical to the woman in the dream.

He had spent enough time in that dream to know her in ways that went far beyond faces. He knew her exact height. He knew what lay beneath those robes. He knew the small habitual gestures she made when she moved.

He could not remember her face -- had never been able to. He had never seen this particular robe on her before. And yet Qin Yuan knew, with absolute certainty, that it was her.

He knew especially when she dipped into a bow of respect and, from his angle, he could see the smooth pale curve of her ear and the small mark behind it.

Small, deep red, against snow-white skin. Like a red plum on a field of new snow.

He had kissed that spot more times than he could count in the dream. He could not possibly mistake it.

The young emperor's gaze moved across her, slow and complete, his dark eyes deep and still, a trace of something moving within them like a flame.

He closed his eyes briefly, and hid whatever was surging behind them.

Good. He had finally found her.

His mouth curved, almost without his awareness. His hand tightened on the silver cup he was holding, and the elegant vessel crumpled in his grip like paper.

The amber wine flooded over his fingers and ran.

Qin Yuan set the ruined cup down quietly and glanced at the attendant at his side.

The attendant understood at once and produced a clean cloth.

Qin Yuan accepted it and wiped his hand with unhurried attention, and then asked, as though it were a passing thought, "Minister Fang was once known as the finest chess player in the capital. Do his granddaughters play chess?"

The Grand Empress was mildly surprised, but she smiled and turned to the Fang daughters. "Yes -- do any of you play? The tournament not long ago -- did any of you enter?"

The Fang sisters exchanged a brief glance. Jiyao answered, "Your Majesty, Your Highness -- your humble servants have only a passing acquaintance with chess. Our skill is quite ordinary, and so we did not participate."

"What a shame," the Grand Empress said with a note of gentle regret.

Qin Yuan smiled, thin and private.

Did not participate. And yet a certain half-game of chess had been played directly on his body in a dream, using the same style that one of "Lin Yao's" opponents had perfectly reconstructed.

He found himself comparing the image of "Lin Yao" in his mind with the Second Miss Fang before him. There were two or three points of resemblance -- but only two or three.

Because the woman in front of him was something else entirely. Skin like snow, dark luminous eyes, features serene and refined. Even in plain clothes, there was no hiding what she was. Nothing at all like the unremarkable dark-skinned young man of the "Lin Yao" portrait.

What struck him as strange, though, was this: standing before him now, the Second Miss Fang seemed entirely like any other well-bred young lady making her first visit to the palace. Careful, composed, respectful -- nothing more. Not the faintest trace of anything unusual.

Had she not recognized him?

A quiet, slight displeasure settled in Qin Yuan.

The Grand Empress, unable to read the emperor's layered intentions, and unwilling to keep several daughters of a Minister standing indefinitely for no apparent reason, smiled and let them return to their seats once it seemed the emperor had no further instructions.

Jiyao turned back, and let out a very quiet, very private breath of relief.

The emperor looked far too much like her husband. Even just that brief proximity had made her nervous.

At least it had only been a short while. She could disappear back into the crowd again now.

...

The birthday banquet continued.

The Grand Empress occasionally called other guests forward, chatting and receiving well-wishes.

But the emperor did not ask any more questions. He beckoned a eunuch close and murmured something privately.

The eunuch looked faintly puzzled, then nodded with careful deference.

Qin Yuan did not stay long. He offered a word to the Grand Empress, rose, and left.

When he had gone, Jiyao felt the tension ease from her shoulders. The hall felt lighter without him in it.

Without the emperor present, the Grand Empress herself relaxed a little as well. She spoke warmly with the titled ladies she was acquainted with, and then smiled as she received congratulations from the top three finishers of the chess tournament, presenting them with generous rewards and offering a few words of gracious encouragement.

The tournament had been baffling to her from the start, but the Grand Empress was always dignified, and she was happy to play her part. If the emperor had said it was in her honor, then in her honor it was -- as though she had always been passionately fond of chess.

Down below, Jiyao found herself looking at the three tournament finalists.

Seeing them, she felt a quiet pang of what might have been regret. If Grandfather had agreed from the beginning, if she had entered under her real name instead of a false one -- she would never know how far she might have gone.

But there were no second chances for what had already happened. There was no point dwelling.

Jiyao breathed in slowly, adjusted her thoughts, and looked down at the food in front of her.

The palace banquet had no shortage of fine dishes. But she was not particularly hungry and had barely tasted anything.

The palace was grand and imposing, and the banquet was -- truthfully -- rather dull. She was not sure when it would end.

Then a eunuch came to announce that the emperor had arranged fireworks for the Grand Empress, and that she was invited to step outside to watch.

"Fireworks?" The Grand Empress's eyes brightened slightly. She turned to her guests with a warm smile. "The Emperor has been thoughtful. Come outside with me, all of you."

"By your gracious command." The assembled guests answered in unison and filed toward the doors in an orderly stream.

The youngest Fang daughter, Mengyao, had stars in her eyes already. She murmured under her breath, "Fireworks in the palace..."

They must be spectacular.

Jiyao thought so too -- she always had loved fireworks. But after seeing the emperor and his unsettling resemblance to her husband, she had no real feeling for watching fireworks. She just wanted the banquet to be over so she could go home to Haitang Courtyard.

She could not say any of that, of course.

In situations like this, Jiyao had always followed the crowd without fuss. She cleared her mind, tucked away whatever was bothering her, and joined the flow of people moving toward the door with her cousins.

But she had barely stepped outside the Hanzhang Hall when a group of palace maids came sweeping through directly in front of her, cutting between her and her cousins.

By the time the maids had passed, her cousins were nowhere to be seen.

Jiyao felt a spike of anxiety. She started to step quickly forward to catch up -- and a eunuch appeared directly in her path, blocking the way.

He kept his eyes carefully lowered, his manner perfectly respectful. "Second Miss Fang. His Majesty requests an audience."

chapters.title: Good Girl
chapters.content:
Jiyao's heart gave a violent lurch. A premonition of disaster rose in her chest.

The Emperor wished to see her? See her for what?

Surely not because of...

No. No, that was impossible.

Nothing that had happened in the dreams could be known by anyone else. She must not panic and give herself away.

Jiyao steadied herself, let a look of polite difficulty show on her face, and spoke: "The Emperor has summoned me, and I would not dare refuse. But, eunuch — my younger sisters..."

"They are watching the fireworks. You can rejoin them shortly, Second Miss Fang." The eunuch smiled. "For now, please come with me. We mustn't keep His Majesty waiting."

Jiyao had no choice but to steel herself, pull the corners of her mouth into something resembling composure, and follow. "Of course. Please lead the way."

Her heart, however, was racing — her mind turning over one possibility after another, dismissing each in turn.

The eunuch led her through a long, dim corridor, then west for several paces, before coming to a stop.

"Your Majesty, Second Miss Fang has arrived."

His voice, slightly shrill, cut through the noise in Jiyao's head.

She raised her eyes — and saw the Emperor standing beside a column, head bent, polishing a sword.

Tall and upright. Elegant and commanding.

The palace lanterns hanging from the eaves cast a warm, amber glow. In that hazy light — the glinting sword blade, the familiar profile — for just a moment, Jiyao thought she was looking at her husband from the dreams.

But the thought vanished as quickly as it came. She lowered her head and made her obeisance. "Your subject greets Your Majesty. Long live the Emperor, ten thousand years."

A soft scrape of metal — the Emperor sheathed the sword.

Jiyao's heart gave a small, involuntary shudder.

He set the sword aside and stepped toward her, eyes fixed on her, his tone carrying a strange note: "Second Miss Fang. We meet again."

Jiyao's heart gave another startled tremor. The phrasing struck her as odd. He had specifically summoned her himself — and yet he said "we meet again."

But there was no time to parse it. She stepped back and kept her manner carefully deferential. "I do not know what instructions Your Majesty has for me."

"Instructions?" Qin Yuan gave a soft, sharp laugh, his gaze keen as a blade. "Do you truly not know why I have summoned you specifically?"

Jiyao's breath caught for a moment.

She genuinely did not know. She could not tell whether it was because someone had discovered her use of a false identity in the chess tournament, or whether the Emperor meant to use her to pressure her grandfather, or whether it was something else entirely.

She kept herself composed, gave a slight shake of her head. "Your subject truly does not know. Will Your Majesty please instruct me."

The Emperor let out a quiet laugh, and said something that made the world tilt: "How should I address you, I wonder? Second Miss Fang? Or... Good Girl? Or perhaps... my wife?"

At the words "Good Girl," something inside Jiyao snapped taut — a silent, resonant vibration that traveled through her whole body. She went rigid, feeling for a moment as though her soul had left her.

"Good Girl" was the pet name her parents had called her since childhood. Between the waking world and the dream, only three people had ever called her that: her father, her mother, and her husband in the dream.

Not even her grandparents used it, calling her simply "Jiyao."

How did the Emperor know?

He looked so much like the husband from her dreams — were they truly the same person? But that was impossible. Their rank, their age, their temperament — everything was different. And even if he were the same man, he should not have been able to know what she had dreamed, nor what had taken place inside those dreams.

Dreams were her own private secret. That had always been Jiyao's understanding — so long as she never spoke of them, no one could know their contents.

So how had this happened?

Was it a coincidence? Or —

Jiyao's thoughts were tangled. But she knew, above all else, that the more dangerous the moment, the more essential it was to keep her head.

She made herself be firm: she would not betray herself. She would not fall apart. What had happened in the dreams, she would never reveal to anyone.

No matter what anyone else did, she would remain exactly who she had always appeared to be — the quiet, gentle, slightly timid Second Miss Fang.

With that resolve fixed in her mind, Jiyao stumbled back two steps. She let the panic show on her face, because it was entirely real. "Your Majesty, please conduct yourself with propriety."

The Emperor's expression darkened. His cold eyes narrowed. "Propriety? You don't recognize me?"

Jiyao shook her head. "Your Majesty is the Son of Heaven. Of course your subject recognizes you. But even the Emperor cannot speak to a woman in such a manner..."

Her voice faded as she spoke, growing quieter, though her bearing held a quiet, genuine firmness.

She knew the words were bold. But she was the granddaughter of a Minister, raised with strict propriety. For a man — any man, including a notoriously ruthless emperor — to address her as "Good Girl" or "my wife" with such easy familiarity was not something she could let pass without protest.

The moment the words left her, she felt a small stab of misgiving.

Perhaps she should have been less direct. If she had truly offended him...

Qin Yuan found himself half-amused, half-vexed. The two of them had been tangled together in those dreams for so long — had done everything that could be done, and then some. And now she was talking to him about "improper speech"?

Had she not called herself "Good Girl" first, in the dream? Why hadn't she raised the issue of impropriety then?

"This counts as improper speech?" He stepped forward, reaching out to pinch her earlobe lightly, his tone carrying a note of deliberate provocation. "I had the impression this was more the sort of thing that qualified..."

Without waiting for an answer, his fingers moved to brush the red mole behind her ear. "...or perhaps this."

They were standing very close. Qin Yuan caught the same faint, familiar scent from the dreams — delicate, not quite jasmine, not quite musk, drifting from her and settling at the edge of his awareness.

The moment his fingers touched behind her ear, Jiyao's body gave an involuntary shiver. Her eyes went wide, and the dark premonition in her chest deepened.

She was sensitive there. She had always been sensitive there.

Could it be that the Emperor truly knew the contents of her dreams?

The thought hardened her resolve. Whatever he knew or did not know — she would act as though she knew nothing. She would not waver.

She was the Second Miss Fang, law-abiding and proper, who had just been subjected to the Emperor's unwanted advances. That was all she was.

So what should she do?
