Jiyao stepped back instinctively, and felt the sting of tears rise in her eyes. "Your subject spoke out of turn, and begs Your Majesty's forgiveness. But there is a proper distinction between ruler and subject, between the inner and outer court. Your Majesty is the sovereign of this nation, a model for all people — you set the example for the realm..."

The light shifted. Qin Yuan's expression went flat and still.

He withdrew his hand and clasped it behind his back, a visible chill settling into his eyes.

The girl dried her tears. Then, with courage that surprised him, she continued: "Your subject is a person of no consequence, but even so, I know enough to conduct myself with propriety. I beg Your Majesty not to make things difficult for me..."

Qin Yuan's expression soured.

Not because of her words. But because the woman standing before him bore almost no resemblance to the one from the dream.

She looked at him with composed, wary, unfamiliar eyes — as though she had never known him at all. Qin Yuan suddenly recalled that before the banquet, he had asked Zhang Zan about the temperaments of the Fang daughters. When he had come to the Second Miss, Zhang Zan had said: "timid, well-behaved, quiet, and proper."

At the time, Qin Yuan had dismissed the description as unhelpful. Now he thought of it again.

Timid. Well-behaved. Quiet. Proper.

From the banquet to this very moment, she had been all four.

A sudden, unsettling thought: had he found the wrong person? A girl like this — could she really be responsible for what had happened in those dreams?

But he dismissed it the next moment. It was impossible. Her build, her voice, the red mole behind her ear, even the scent that clung to her — all of it matched precisely. He could not have been wrong.

Then — was it possible she did not remember the dreams?

He had heard Cloud Crane say once that there were people who forgot their dreams entirely upon waking, as though they had never dreamed at all.

But no, that didn't fit either. Those dreams had continued in a connected sequence, and the woman in them had clearly retained memory from one to the next.

So what, then?

In the span of a few breaths, he had turned the question over a dozen times.

At that moment, with a loud crack, fireworks burst open in the sky — an enormous character for "longevity" blooming overhead, brilliant enough to light the whole world.

In that flash of light, Qin Yuan saw clearly: a pale face, dark luminous eyes.

Something moved in him.

She was probably pretending.

A girl who had dressed as a man and entered the chess tournament under a false name was no timid little creature. He had been mistaken to expect otherwise.

Besides, he had found her now. His revenge could wait. Frightening her too thoroughly would only take the sport out of it.

They had all the time in the world.

He could take his time deciding exactly how to make her pay.

With that decided, Qin Yuan gave a mild sound and gestured offhandedly at the sky. "Fireworks."

Then, after a pause, he spoke again, his tone deliberately measured: "I had too much to drink tonight. I may have spoken to the wrong person. My apologies, Second Miss Fang."

The words were almost gentle — not at all the manner of the tyrant people spoke of.

"Not at all." Jiyao should have felt relief. Instead, inexplicably, her unease only deepened. She steadied herself and spoke with careful courtesy. "If Your Majesty has no further instructions, your subject will withdraw."

"You may go." Qin Yuan raised a hand. The eunuch waiting at a respectful distance hurried forward. "See her back."

"Yes." The eunuch bowed and turned to Jiyao with a gesture of invitation. "Second Miss Fang, this way."

"Your subject withdraws." Jiyao gave the Emperor one last bow and left at a pace that could only be described as a controlled flight.

She moved fast, as though afraid of being called back.

Overhead, the fireworks went on cracking and blooming.

Not unlike the state of Jiyao's heart just then.

She did not know whether she had managed to deceive him. She only knew that the evening had been a disaster from beginning to end.

The eunuch escorted her to the terrace below the viewing platform, where her cousins stood among the other guests, watching the fireworks.

Seeing her, Third Cousin Zhiyao looked over curiously. "Second Sister, what took you so long?"

"I went to get some air." Jiyao answered without thinking.

The fireworks that night were spectacular — golden chrysanthemums, fluttering butterflies, cascades of starlight, characters of good fortune blazing against the dark sky for the Grand Empress's birthday, one after another...

A rare and stunning display. All around her, guests watched in rapt delight.

Only Jiyao stood among them with her mind elsewhere, quietly retracing every word of her exchange with the Emperor, her palms slowly growing cold.

...

The fireworks ran for the better part of half an hour, never repeating the same pattern twice.

When it was over, everyone returned to Hanzhang Hall.

The Grand Empress was in excellent spirits, but age told in the end — she grew tired, lingered a little while longer, then rose and withdrew.

The Emperor did not return.

Without either of them present, the banquet dispersed quickly.

On the ride home, Jiyao sat inside the carriage and said nothing.

The others assumed she was tired. They left her in peace and chatted quietly among themselves about the splendors of the evening.

Back at Haitang Courtyard, Jiyao felt exhausted in body and mind. She washed up as quickly as she could and lay down.

But though she was tired, she could not sleep. Every time she closed her eyes, she heard the Emperor's voice, with its strange inflection: "How should I address you? Second Miss Fang? Or... Good Girl? Or perhaps... my wife?"

Turning everything over, Jiyao came to one conclusion: the Emperor knew about her dreams. How much he knew, she was not certain.

What he made of it — that, she could not begin to guess.

The uncertainty was maddening. It left her suspended, her heart neither rising nor settling.

Then, all at once, a memory surfaced.

She had been able to control her dreams since childhood. As she grew older, she had searched through various books trying to understand her ability — and in one of them, she had come across the concept of shared dreaming. A shared dream, as the book described it, was when two people dreamed the same dream at the same time.

But that didn't quite fit either. Shared dreams were said to occur between people who knew each other. She had never known the Emperor before. How could something like this have happened between them?

She could not make sense of it.

Jiyao tossed and turned for a long time. It was nearly midnight by the time she finally drifted off to sleep.

But the mind carries what the day has stirred.

She dreamed of her husband standing before her, and in the dream he was suddenly older by several years — and looked exactly like the Emperor she had seen that day.

Jiyao instinctively tried to make him vanish from the dream. But before she could, he opened his mouth and said: "Second Miss Fang. We meet again."

She startled awake.

She lay in the dark, breathing unsteadily. Outside, the sound of rain had begun — a soft, unhurried pattering.

Jiyao let out a long, quiet sigh.

The night was still long. She did not sleep again.

The next day, Jiyao was in the girls' school for morning lessons. After a poor night's sleep, she could not quite keep her mind on the work.

Suddenly, there was a commotion outside. Word came that visitors had arrived from the palace.

These days, the mere mention of "palace" made Jiyao's eye twitch.

The visitor was a eunuch.

He was all smiles, directing attendants to carry in several elegantly lacquered boxes. "These are gifts from the Grand Empress, bestowed upon the young ladies of the Fang household."

"Gifts from the Grand Empress?" The girls all startled, and went forward one by one to accept their boxes with both hands.

Jiyao set aside her thoughts and accepted her gift with the rest.

After the palace party had gone, the sisters lost all interest in lessons and opened their boxes on the spot.

All five boxes looked identical on the outside, but the contents varied. There were longevity locks, peace pendants, hanging ornaments, prayer beads...

Inside Second Miss Fang's box lay a hairpin: a gold cicada on a jade leaf.

Jiyao's face went white.

That hairpin. It was identical to the one her husband had bought for her in the dream, at a street stall.

chapters.title: Summoned to the Palace
chapters.content:
Palace gifts were always fine and costly, and gifts from the Grand Empress in particular carried a significance beyond ordinary measure.

Third Cousin Zhiyao turned her gold-inlaid jade peace pendant over and over, unable to put it down. Then, curious, she glanced at her second cousin, with whom she had always been close. "Second Sister, what did you get?"

Jiyao met her gaze without a word. She simply opened her box and slid it quietly across toward her.

Against the red velvet lining, the glint of gold and jade was unmistakable.

Third Sister leaned in for a closer look, and let out a soft sound of surprise. "A gold cicada and jade leaf hairpin? Isn't this the one we saw at Liuyun Pavilion that time..."

"Yes," Jiyao said.

Zhiyao's eyes widened further.

She remembered it clearly. The previous year, before their eldest sister's wedding, the six of them had gone to Liuyun Pavilion together. Second Sister had seemed quite taken with that hairpin — but the price was steep, and she had set it back down without buying it.

Zhiyao had asked her then: "If you like it, why not buy it?"

The Fang family was not nobility, but with several members in office and their combined salaries, the hairpin was hardly beyond their means.

Second Sister had replied: "It's too expensive. I have nowhere to wear something like that, and I don't want to spend so much on ornaments."

That small exchange had stayed with Zhiyao, along with the distinctive design of the pin. She had even thought privately that when Second Sister married, she would spend lavishly to buy it as a wedding gift.

And yet now, here it was — given by the Grand Empress herself.

The hairpin was barely an inch long, its wings thin as paper, lifelike in every detail. Gold and jade caught the light together, brilliant and understated at once.

Zhiyao marveled aloud: "The Grand Empress is remarkable — she chose exactly what Second Sister likes."

Sixth Cousin Mengyao chimed in: "What a coincidence!"

Jiyao forced a faint smile, thinking: a coincidence?

She had the distinct feeling this hairpin had not come from the Grand Empress at all. The true giver was someone else — and this was not a gift so much as a test, or a provocation.

She remembered clearly: in one of the dreams, she and her husband had gone out together to a street market. He had behaved oddly and left without warning. She had exerted her dream-control and made him come back — and return with the gold cicada hairpin. At the time, she had not thought much of it. The hairpin was expensive; she had no need for it in waking life, but it was pleasant enough to have in a dream. As for his odd behavior, she had not dwelt on it either — small complications in dreams were perfectly normal.

He had come back with the hairpin, just as she had intended.

But now, holding the real thing in her hands, Jiyao's unease returned.

She hoped she was imagining things.

Taking a slow, quiet breath, she steadied herself, and carefully put the hairpin away.

...

Meanwhile, in the imperial palace.

The young eunuch Chang Fu had returned from the Fang household and gone immediately to report to the Emperor.

This was Chang Fu's first errand outside the palace since taking up his post in the imperial presence. He was deeply honored by it — even if it was only something as minor as delivering gifts, most eunuchs would never be given such an opportunity in their lifetime.

He dared not be anything less than meticulous.

The Emperor was reviewing memorials when Chang Fu finished his report. His gaze barely lifted. "She received the gift — what was her reaction?"

Chang Fu was confused for a moment, uncertain which "she" the Emperor meant. He answered carefully: "Your Majesty, all five young ladies of the Fang household were very pleased, and very grateful."

"That's all?"

"That's all." Chang Fu felt faintly apprehensive, wondering if he had somehow erred.

But the Emperor only gave a quiet sound of acknowledgment and said nothing further.

The moment the words had left his own mouth, Qin Yuan had already recognized the question as unnecessary.

She would not have opened the box in front of a eunuch. Which meant she would not have discovered the "surprise" inside it yet.

A pity. He could not see her face when she found the gold cicada hairpin.

But that was all right. The Second Miss Fang wished to play ignorant. He could remove her pretenses one layer at a time.

...

Jiyao spent the whole day unable to focus. The image of the gold cicada hairpin kept surfacing in her mind, glinting, impossible to ignore.

After the girls' lessons ended, she went straight to her father's study.

From the back of a shelf, Jiyao found the book on dreams she had consulted years before.

It described prophetic dreams, spirit-contact dreams, illusory dreams, heart-born dreams — a whole taxonomy. Among them, shared dreaming.

She read the entry on shared dreams again and again. Her situation resembled it, and yet did not quite match.

After turning the matter over many times, she came to the same decision as before: she would continue to pretend she knew nothing.

Even if she had somehow been unlucky enough to share a dream with the Emperor, there was no proof that everything that had happened in those dreams had been her doing. Her ability to control dreams — she could deny it entirely, and would. She had never told anyone, and she had always appeared to be nothing more than the quiet, law-abiding Second Miss Fang.

With her mind made up, she returned the book to its place on the shelf.

She went on as before — attending the girls' school, reading chess manuals in her free time, practicing her calligraphy.

Perhaps because of the previous sleepless night, she went to bed early. She fell asleep quickly.

And dreamed.

She dreamed of being with her parents, sitting together and talking quietly about nothing in particular. Some things she could not say to anyone in the waking world, so she had always found it easier, in dreams, to speak them to her parents.

Her mother stroked her hair gently and said: "It's all right, Good Girl. If you don't say a word, no one will know."

Her father added: "And besides — you only had a dream. You didn't actually do anything. There has never been a law in this world that punishes people for their dreams."

"That's true." Jiyao nodded. She knew, clearly, that these were her own thoughts — a reassurance she was giving to herself, a reminder not to worry over what had not yet happened.

After talking with her parents for a while, Jiyao felt much lighter.

She said her goodbyes to them, as she always did, and turned to go back to her room.

But when she pushed open the door, she found a familiar figure standing at the window.

A young man of sixteen or seventeen, polishing a sword with unhurried calm. At the sound of her entrance, he looked up immediately.

Their eyes met, and Jiyao felt a sudden jolt of alarm.

Why was she dreaming of him again?

Had she thought of him, without meaning to, just moments before?

But this was not the time to examine the cause. She made a quick decision and ended the dream outright.

The night was dark and deep. Jiyao's eyes opened.

She lay still for a moment, her heart still pounding. She could not quite shake the feeling that, in that brief glimpse before she ended the dream, his eyes had been looking at her strangely.

Jiyao sighed.

It was no use dwelling on it. She should rest.

She settled herself, and let herself fall back to sleep.

...

In the inner chambers of Zichen Palace.

The young Emperor's eyes opened suddenly.

The night lamp burned low. Qin Yuan's phoenix eyes were unnervingly bright in the dimness.

He had slipped into the dream only briefly — a matter of seconds.

But for the first time since the strange dreams had begun, he had managed to hold onto her face afterward.

He had always thought it must be because he had not yet seen her in waking life. But the face that had appeared in the dream just now — clear and precise, unmistakable — was the face of the Second Miss Fang.

She had pushed open the door and looked at him. Mountains in her brows, an autumn river in her eyes. Surprise and unease, plainly visible.

He lay back and closed his eyes briefly.

He had already been certain of her identity before this. But having it confirmed in the dream itself, in the space of a real moment — the certainty settled into him differently.

Yes. He had not been mistaken.

The only regret was that the dream had been so short. He had not even had the chance to speak her name out loud and see what expression she would make.

He found himself wanting to. The thought produced an odd, restless feeling he could not quite name.

But it didn't matter. She was here now, in the waking world. He had found her.

He was the Emperor. He had every means at his disposal for revenge, and all the time in the world to use them.

"Someone come!" he called suddenly.

The eunuch on night duty jolted awake and approached with deference. "Your Majesty, what is your command?"

"After daybreak, go to the household of Minister Fang and relay — not my word, the Grand Empress's command. Summon the Second Miss Fang to the palace for a conversation."

"Yes." The eunuch bowed, though inwardly he found it strange. When had the Grand Empress issued such a command? Why was His Majesty only mentioning it in the middle of the night? And if it was the Grand Empress's command, why not send someone from Shoukang Palace to deliver it?

But these were not his questions to ask. He simply obeyed.

...

The next morning, as usual, Jiyao attended the girls' school after washing and dressing.

But it was barely past nine when another visitor arrived from the palace.

The same eunuch as before, in his red uniform. He had a cheerful look about him, and introduced himself as surnamed Chang. "By command of the Grand Empress, Second Miss Fang is invited to the palace for a conversation."

Jiyao's eye twitched. "Me?"

Fourth Cousin Pinyao asked: "Only Second Sister? No one else?"

"That is correct." Eunuch Chang Fu smiled pleasantly. "Those are the Grand Empress's exact words. Second Miss Fang, if you would please come with me."

Jiyao hesitated. "Is it absolutely necessary?"

Protocol-wise, she ought to go to the palace to give thanks for the Grand Empress's gifts. But something in her deeper instincts kept insisting the situation was not as simple as it appeared.

Chang Fu let his smile fade somewhat, his voice pitching up just slightly: "This is the Grand Empress's personal command. Does Second Miss Fang mean to refuse a royal decree?"

— He had learned the art of borrowing his superior's authority quite thoroughly in his months at court.

Zhiyao quickly stepped in: "Please don't be offended, eunuch. My second sister is simply nervous about conducting herself properly in the palace. She means no disrespect at all."

She shot Jiyao a meaningful look.

Jiyao nodded along. "Please lead the way."

She told herself she was probably worrying for nothing. It could be a genuine coincidence — a real summons from the Grand Empress. After all, the Emperor, the other night, had not made any particular effort to conceal his identity.

But then — what would the Grand Empress want with her?

Jiyao could not work it out.

The carriage set her down at the palace gates.

Jiyao descended, fell in behind Eunuch Chang Fu, and walked in silence, eyes careful, steps precise. She did not look around, did not stray an inch from the path.

After about a quarter of an hour, another eunuch in red came toward them from the opposite direction. He drew Chang Fu aside and murmured something in his ear.

"Really?" Chang Fu looked faintly surprised.

The other eunuch nodded with certainty. "Absolutely."

"I see." Chang Fu turned back to Jiyao and made his polite gesture. "Second Miss Fang, if you will."

Jiyao inclined her head slightly, her unease sharpening.

This path. It seemed longer than it should have been.

She kept her voice low. "Eunuch, is the Grand Empress's residence at Shoukang Palace?"

"Yes," said Chang Fu, and then after a brief pause, added, "Though the Grand Empress is not there at the moment."

Jiyao's lashes dipped. She said nothing more, only followed.

They walked another quarter of an hour before stopping.

The space that opened before her was vast and exposed.

It was a training ground.

Jiyao's eye began to twitch: the Grand Empress would never receive a guest in a training ground.

Her apprehension had been right.

"Eunuch, the Grand Empress..."

She had barely managed three words before Chang Fu said, cheerfully: "The Grand Empress is resting at present. We'll wait here for a moment."

His manner was perfectly pleasant. But Jiyao believed not a single word of it.

Presently, she noticed there was someone already in the training ground, going through forms with a longsword. The blade rose and fell, cutting the air in clean, powerful arcs.

Jiyao's face went pale even from a distance.

She recognized him at once.

It was the Emperor.

His swordsmanship bore no resemblance to her husband's elegant forms in the dream. Every movement was heavy and decisive, with no ornamentation whatsoever — less a display than a method of killing.

Jiyao saw it very clearly: he and the young man from her dreams were not the same.

The husband of her dreams had bent to her wishes. The man before her was the opposite.

While she stood turning this over in her mind, Qin Yuan had already stopped, tossed the sword to a waiting guard, and walked directly toward her.

Jiyao quickly put her thoughts away and bowed.

"No need for ceremony." He raised a hand to halt the gesture, and his gaze did not linger on her.

It was early enough in August to be cool. There was a faint sheen of perspiration at Qin Yuan's temple and nose.

An attentive young eunuch immediately brought forward a basin and towels.

Qin Yuan washed his hands and face unhurriedly, dried them, then said: "Second Miss Fang, the Grand Empress has just retired to rest and cannot be disturbed at present."

Jiyao lowered her eyes, her manner composed. "Then your subject will withdraw and call upon the Grand Empress another day."

"No need to go to such trouble." The Emperor paused. "The Grand Empress summoned you to play chess. Why not keep me company for a game first."

chapters.title: A Marriage Proposal
chapters.content:
Zichen Palace.

Jiyao had never in her life imagined she would set foot in this place.

About a quarter of an hour ago, faced with the Emperor's "why not keep me company for a game first," Jiyao had instinctively tried to demur: "Your subject's skill is quite ordinary, and would not dare to presume —"

She got no further. The Emperor said "It's fine," and that was that.

She had no choice but to accept.

And then, somehow, she had found herself being led directly to one of Zichen Palace's side chambers.

The Emperor said he was going to change clothes and asked her to wait.

Jiyao had said yes — what else could she say — and waited.

And waited.

The side chamber was very quiet, suffused with some faint, unidentifiable fragrance: clean, cool, slightly austere.

Jiyao sat at the table with nothing to do but stare at the tea bowl in front of her, her mind churning. She still could not fathom what the Emperor was really after.

Should she hide her ability at chess? How much?

Why was changing clothes taking this long?

...

Perhaps half an hour had passed before she finally heard footsteps approaching.

She looked up instinctively — and caught herself blinking.

The Emperor had said he was going to change, and he had. He now wore a dark everyday robe, standing with the natural, unhurried authority that seemed to accompany him everywhere.

But what Jiyao had not anticipated was that he appeared to have done more than change clothes. His hair carried the faint dampness of a recent bath.

Her heart gave an odd, quiet lurch — and against her will, her mind skipped to certain scenes from the dreams.

But it wasn't the same, she told herself. In the dreams, her husband would come to her after bathing in a white sleeping robe, half-dry and casual. The man before her wore heavy dark silk with subtle embroidery — every inch of it reminding her that this was the Emperor, elevated beyond anything the dream had ever shown her.

There was no time to dwell on it. She inclined her head and greeted him.

"Sit," he said, his expression neutral. He had a chess board and pieces brought in. "Do you want to go first, or shall I?"

"Please, Your Majesty," she said.

She had already decided privately: not only would she cede the first move, she would deliberately underplay her ability.

She had told the Grand Empress she barely knew the rules of chess. And the Emperor was almost certainly testing her — she had to be careful.

Qin Yuan gave her a brief glance and opened with a stone.

Jiyao gathered her attention and followed.

She had been playing long enough to recognize a person's style within a few moves. It took no time at all before she felt it with complete clarity: this style, these lines — they were identical to her husband's in the dream.

If she had held on to any lingering doubt before, it was gone now. The man sitting across from her was the same person who had played chess with her, game after game, in those dreams.

She had thought she was the one who had pulled him into those games. It turned out to be...

She did not let herself finish the thought. Now was not the time.

Jiyao pushed everything aside and focused on the board.

It was not easy. She had to suppress her ability, and consciously alter her style at the same time. Dividing her concentration this way, she fell behind before long.

She made a show of struggling a little longer, then conceded with due humility: "Your subject has lost."

"Again," Qin Yuan said.

"Yes." She agreed, and they played another round.

The second time was smoother — she had calibrated her disguise more precisely.

But the Emperor's expression had been growing steadily colder, and now he spoke, his tone carrying a peculiar edge: "You reached the top four in the tournament. This is your game?"

He had not yet even begun to retaliate in earnest, and she was already playing tricks in front of him. Again.

Did she think he was still the same person she could manipulate at will from the dream?

Jiyao felt a jolt of alarm, though she kept her face carefully neutral. "Your subject doesn't understand what Your Majesty means."

"You don't understand?" He gave her a brief, blade-sharp look and a thin smile. "Perhaps you would understand better if I used your alias."

He paused, then said it quietly, with absolute certainty: "Lin Yao."

At the sound of those two syllables, Jiyao's hand went still. The stone she had been holding slipped from her fingers with a sharp clatter against the board.

So this too.

She was generally quiet and law-abiding, and she had managed to get herself entangled in an impossible amount of trouble.

Her grandfather had said the court was no longer pursuing those who had competed under false names.

Terror gripped her chest — not the dread of the unknown, but something worse: the sudden realization that things had gone even further off course than she had feared. She had come prepared to face questions about the dreams. She had not been prepared for this.

Her lashes trembled fractionally. Her decision came almost at once: deny it. Deny everything. There was still room to maneuver as long as she did not confess. If she confessed, it was over — not just for her, but for her second cousin and her grandfather, both of whom were implicated.

Nothing would be admitted until proof was placed in front of her face.

With the composure of someone who had spent a lifetime playing the obedient girl, Jiyao shook her head, quietly and steadily: "Your subject does not understand. Who is Lin Yao?"

Her eyes were clear and still, like shallow water. You could see straight to the bottom.

Qin Yuan raised an eyebrow. He thought: the entire Fang household must take her for a simpleton, if they all believed her to be an honest, timid creature.

He studied her. His dark eyes were deep and still. "Who helped you with the false identity? Minister Fang? Or Fang... Lin?"

He had not been able to trace anything back to her while she remained a private girl in an inner courtyard, unknown and untraced. But once her identity was confirmed, a slow and careful investigation had turned up certain suggestive details.

Such as: her second male cousin had been leaving the house very early every morning for several days, claiming to be visiting friends, and returning only at dusk.

Such as: the Second Miss Fang had happened to be unwell on those same days.

"Your subject does not understand," Jiyao said again.

Qin Yuan let out a quiet laugh. There was an unmistakable quality of warning in it. "Second Miss Fang. This matter can be handled as something small, or as something quite grave. If you come clean now, I am in a generous mood today, and out of consideration for Minister Fang, I am prepared to overlook the matter. If you continue to conceal it..."

He left the sentence unfinished. He simply extended his index finger and tapped the chess board, twice.

Two quiet taps. Each one landed somewhere inside her chest.

Jiyao's thoughts warred with themselves.

She had come in determined to deny everything. But "can be handled as something small" and "overlook the matter" kept ringing in her ears. And he had specifically named her grandfather and second cousin.

The incident with the tournament was different from the dreams. It had happened in the waking world. In the waking world, things left traces. And the Emperor had said he would overlook it...

Jiyao bit down on her resolve, rose, and gave a measured half-confession: "Your Majesty, your subject was not trying to deceive you. When Your Majesty organized the chess tournament in honor of the Grand Empress, your subject wished to participate, but Grandfather did not approve. I did indeed attend in disguise for a time. But I quickly realized that what I was doing was wrong, and withdrew."

She paused, then added quickly: "This matter has nothing to do with my second cousin or my grandfather. It was entirely my own idea. I beg Your Majesty's forgiveness."

Qin Yuan studied her.

Dark, liquid eyes, and behind them — a faint mist, and unmistakable anxiety.

He had been so intent on finding her and making her pay. Now that she was actually sitting in front of him, he found the question of how to do it less simple than he had imagined.

Have her killed? It didn't warrant that.

Have her beaten? Looking at her now, she didn't look as though she could survive it.

Thinking it over, the most satisfying approach seemed to be this: keep her unsettled, keep her in his grip, until he decided on the appropriate form of retribution.

The long silence was making Jiyao anxious. She was beginning to wonder whether her partial confession had been too impulsive — when the Emperor said simply: "Sit down."

Two words, without inflection.

Jiyao blinked, startled — then felt a surge of quiet relief. She thanked him and sat.

"Play me another game," said the Emperor. "With your real ability this time."

"Yes."

She had not entirely believed it until now — that he truly intended to let the matter go. But the fact seemed to be presenting itself, and a small, involuntary warmth crept into her expression before she could stop it.

This time she played as herself — no more altered style, no more hidden moves. She gave her full attention to the game.

They had played against each other so many times in the dreams that each knew the other's strategies well.

They fought each other to a standstill for over an hour without a clear winner.

Then a eunuch hurried forward: "Your Majesty, shall I have the midday meal set?"

Qin Yuan's brow creased slightly. He glanced at the eunuch with mild displeasure.

Jiyao was already on her feet. "Your Majesty, please take your meal. Your subject will withdraw."

"This game isn't finished." The Emperor said flatly. He looked at the hourglass at the side of the table, and acknowledged that the hour was late, though he did not ask her to continue playing. Instead, he simply said, quietly: "Tonight, we continue."

Jiyao's heart lurched.

Tonight? Continue?

Not what she thought he meant. Surely not.

She did not understand, and could not act on something she did not understand.

Qin Yuan glanced at her, then rose and gave instructions to have the meal set. He turned to another attendant. "Escort Second Miss Fang to Shoukang Palace to pay her respects to the Grand Empress."

"Yes."

Given permission to leave, Jiyao quietly exhaled with relief, and withdrew with appropriate courtesy.

...

The Grand Empress kept strict meal hours, as elderly people often do.

She was just about to have luncheon set when a palace attendant reported: "The Second Miss Fang of the Fang household is here to pay her respects."

"Who?" The Grand Empress blinked.

"Second Miss from Minister Fang's family," the attendant clarified helpfully. "His Majesty said it was by Your Highness's command. A eunuch from Zichen Palace accompanied her here."

The Grand Empress blinked again, and quietly tried to remember when she had said any such thing.

Had she mentioned, in passing, during the banquet, that Second Miss Fang ought to come visit her? The Grand Empress searched her memory. She genuinely could not recall.

But the girl was already at the door, and a eunuch from Zichen Palace had come with her. There was no time to puzzle it out — the Grand Empress had the girl brought in.

Well. If the Emperor said it was her command, then it was her command.

This was Jiyao's second meeting with the Grand Empress.

The Grand Empress was as warm and kind as before, smiling and beckoning her close. "No need for formalities. Come, sit near me."

"Thank you, Your Highness." Jiyao thought for a moment, then expressed gratitude again on behalf of her sisters for the gracious gifts.

The Grand Empress's brow knitted faintly: gifts? What gifts?

But as she looked at the girl before her — sixteen or seventeen years old, skin like white jade, lips like a brushstroke of red, her features quietly lovely — an idea took shape in the Grand Empress's mind, growing clearer by the moment.

In this palace, no one would presume to act in her name. Except the Emperor.

Could it be that the Emperor...

"Oh," said the Grand Empress, and her smile widened into something more genuine. "Don't even mention gifts. As long as you like it, that's all that matters."

Jiyao was surprised.

She had already suspected the gold cicada hairpin was the Emperor's doing. But looking at the Grand Empress's reaction — had she been wrong? Was it a genuine coincidence after all?

Then what had the Emperor meant by "tonight, we continue"?

Surely she hadn't misheard. Or perhaps he intended to summon her to the palace again in the evening?

Jiyao's heart beat anxiously, and she could not make sense of any of it.

The Grand Empress was remarkably attentive to her — she held Jiyao's hand and looked her over carefully, and then, in her warm manner, insisted she stay for luncheon.

Jiyao accepted.

The palace kitchens were talented, but Jiyao's appetite was not cooperating. She managed a few bites and put down her chopsticks.

"Is it not to your taste?" the Grand Empress asked with concern. "You're so young — why do you eat so little?"

"It is very much to my taste," Jiyao said, and took a few more bites to demonstrate.

The Grand Empress looked more pleased than ever. She would have liked to keep the girl talking, but almost without noticing, it had grown to the hour of her daily rest.

"Good child, go on home for now. I'll call you back again soon." The Grand Empress held Jiyao's hand with obvious reluctance, and then personally instructed a trusted attendant to see Second Miss Fang out of the palace.

"Your subject withdraws."

Leaving Shoukang Palace, Jiyao felt slightly dazed.

The Grand Empress really did seem to genuinely like her.

That was unexpected. She had always heard that older people tended to favor lively, clever children — not a quiet, reserved, not-very-talkative sort like her.

She could not work it out.

...

Back in her chambers, the Grand Empress found herself strangely restless. She lay down to nap, and after nearly half an hour, still had not slept.

She gave up, rose, and sent someone to invite the Emperor.

This was unusual for her. But today, she felt she had ample justification.

The Emperor arrived quickly, his manner respectful. "Grandmother."

"Emperor — that Second Miss Fang..." The Grand Empress had a great deal to say, but now that the Emperor was actually in the room, found it oddly difficult to begin. She hesitated, then asked: "Are you thinking of bringing her into the inner court?"

"What?" Qin Yuan frowned.

The Grand Empress elaborated carefully: "She is, after all, the granddaughter of the Minister of Rites. The position would need to be considered..."

But the Emperor said: "I have no such intention."

"She's not engaged yet, is she? Her younger sister seems to be..." The Grand Empress caught up a moment later. "Wait — you're not bringing her into the palace?"

"No." Qin Yuan's answer was immediate and definitive.

He found her because he intended to make her pay for what she had done. Not to make her the mother of the nation.

If he elevated her to Empress and let her sit in glory — that would hardly be revenge.

As for her engagement, she had mentioned in the dream that a match was being discussed. But his people had looked into it and found nothing. In all likelihood, the talks had fallen through.

"I see..." The Grand Empress smiled a little self-consciously. "I must have misunderstood."

She had thought the Emperor had taken an interest in the Fang girl.

"Mm." Qin Yuan offered nothing further, found a pretext, and took his leave shortly after.

The Grand Empress sighed quietly once he was gone.

...

The Fang family's residence was about a quarter-hour's carriage ride from the palace.

Jiyao sat in the carriage on the way home, turning over in her mind how she might explain the day's events to her family.

She had barely set foot in Haitang Courtyard before her maid Shuangxi ran up to her with a beaming smile. "Congratulations, Miss!"

"What are we celebrating?"

"The Lu family came to propose today."

chapters.title: News
chapters.content:
Jiyao blinked. "The Lu family? A marriage proposal?"

It was true — between everything involving the Emperor, she had nearly forgotten that she had nodded in agreement to the match with Lu Ming.

"Yes, and the Old Master has accepted," Shuangxi said happily, pressing her palms together. "How wonderful — the Old Master loves you so dearly, he'd only choose a good husband for you."

"So soon?" Jiyao managed a faint smile, feeling somehow dazed, and unaccountably uneasy.

"What did you say, Miss?" Shuangxi had not quite caught it.

Jiyao only shook her head and said nothing more.

It seemed that when the Fang family had indicated their willingness to consider a match, the Lu family had been overjoyed and had taken it very seriously. Seeing the day was auspicious for the first of the six engagement rites, they had sent a go-between with gifts that very day to formally present their proposal.

Grandfather had already discussed the matter with his granddaughter beforehand. Finding the Lu family's sincerity apparent, he had agreed.

The news spread quickly through the household.

Not only was Shuangxi offering her congratulations — Third Cousin Zhiyao and Sixth Cousin Mengyao came together to wish Jiyao well.

Third Sister Zhiyao in particular meant it from the heart. She had long worried that her own early betrothal might somehow overshadow her second cousin's marriage prospects. Now that Jiyao's match was settled, the knot of anxiety in her chest finally unraveled.

Jiyao herself was oddly calm about it — distracted, even, as though the person being matched were someone else entirely.

"What is it?" Third Sister noticed her expression and found it lacking in either excitement or shyness. She waited until Sixth Sister had gone, then doubled back and lowered her voice: "Second Sister, is there something about this match you don't like?"

"Hmm?" Jiyao came back to herself with a start.

Zhiyao racked her brain for something encouraging: "Well, Lu Gongzi only has a xiucai degree at the moment, but you should trust Grandfather's judgment. He's a very good judge of character..."

"That's not what I meant," Jiyao said quickly, seeing the misunderstanding. "Third Sister, Grandfather mentioned this match to me a few days ago, and I agreed to it."

"Then why do you look so unhappy?"

Jiyao's thoughts were too complicated to share, and the real reasons were not ones she could voice to her cousin. She found a vague excuse: "I'm not unhappy. I'm just... it happened so fast, that's all. I didn't expect to be entering the formal rites so quickly."

Zhiyao relaxed visibly. "Oh, if that's all."

Jiyao nodded. "Yes, just that."

"Second Sister, formal betrothal is quite involved," Zhiyao explained, patient as always. "Think of the three letters and six rites. The first four of the six rites all belong to the engagement process. Today's visit was only the first — the presentation of the proposal. After this comes the inquiry of name, the declaration of affinity, and the gift of betrothal. Each step must be done properly. Only after the horoscopes match and the betrothal gifts are sent is the engagement truly sealed."

Jiyao murmured something in acknowledgment.

Her mind was elsewhere entirely.

"Of course, our family keeps to the order of seniority," Zhiyao went on with a smile. "Second Sister will marry before me, naturally." She then turned to asking about Jiyao's visit to the palace.

This topic made everything even more muddled. Jiyao couldn't tell Zhiyao the truth, so she composed herself and described in simple terms the Grand Empress's warmth and the kind gesture of being invited to stay for a meal.

"How lovely," Zhiyao said admiringly.

After a while, she seemed to sense her cousin's low spirits and put it down to fatigue from the day's palace visit. She did not stay much longer, and took her leave.

As for the Fourth House twins, they had not come to offer congratulations today. This was not because their relationship with Jiyao was strained — it had long since healed — but because they were occupied at home.

The Fourth Aunt, Madam Chen Wenjun, was confronting her daughters with thinly veiled exasperation: "How is it that you're both daughters of this family and yet the Grand Empress shows no interest in either of you?"

The palace had sent for Jiyao alone. The Fourth Aunt found this hard to swallow. At the banquet, the Grand Empress had seemed to regard all five girls equally. The gifts afterward had also been distributed to everyone. Why, then, had only Jiyao been singled out for a private visit?

Of course, the Fourth Aunt's real grievance had nothing to do with the Grand Empress. She was still nursing her pride over the matter of her nephew Chen Qingyun being turned down by Jiyao's family — and she had been hoping her own daughters might make up for it.

The twins said nothing, keeping their heads down.

Their father, Fourth Uncle Fang Jing, urged restraint: "As long as our own girls are happy, what does it matter what anyone else does? Besides, the most important thing for a young woman is a good match, and Jiyao is betrothed now — whether the Grand Empress notices her or not hardly changes anything."

Madam Chen gave a dismissive sound.

Old Master Fang's favoritism was plain to see. He had refused to let her nephew Chen Qingyun join the Fang family school, yet had turned around and admitted Lu Ming. And now with marriage matters, he was marrying his granddaughter off to Lu Ming — what exactly did Lu Ming have over Chen Qingyun, beyond a xiucai degree?

Fourth Uncle Fang spoke soothingly for a long while before his wife's expression softened. "Then at least make yourself useful," she told him. "Find a good match for our daughters."

"Yes, yes, of course," Fang Jing agreed readily. "Don't worry."

The Fourth House gradually fell quiet.

Meanwhile, Jiyao had finished her evening meal in Haitang Courtyard.

Shuangxi was in high spirits, recounting Lu Ming's many fine qualities.

She had been by Jiyao's side for years. Nothing in the world could have made her happier than seeing her young lady's future settled. She was more excited than she would have been about a raise in her own wages.

"Does Miss remember? That time we went to the bookshop, and someone blocked the path — it was Lu Gongzi and the young master who helped us drive him off."

"Mm, I remember."

"And I've heard Lu Gongzi is very diligent in his studies..."

Jiyao's mind was too occupied for this. She finally said, quietly: "Shuangxi, I'm a little tired. Can we talk about this tomorrow?"

"Oh — of course." Shuangxi caught herself. "Then Miss should rest."

"Mm."

After Shuangxi withdrew, Jiyao washed up quickly, did not pick up a chess manual, and went straight to bed.

She drew the curtains, closed her eyes. But sleep was a long time coming.

Too much had happened today. The Emperor's strange behavior. The discovery that her tournament deception was known. The Lu family coming to make a formal proposal.

One thing after another, all crowded into a single day. Her thoughts were unusually tangled.

There was also something she had almost forgotten.

When she had been leaving the side chamber of Zichen Palace, the Emperor had said, quietly: "Tonight, we continue."

How would they continue?

Continue what?

Did he mean for them to play chess in the dream? Was this a test?

Jiyao weighed it back and forth. In the end, she decided to ignore it.

If she were to enter the dream and seek him out to play chess, that would be as good as admitting she knew what had happened in those dreams — and that she had been the one directing them. That was the one thing she absolutely could not do.

The tournament matter was different. That had happened in the real world. Things done in the real world leave traces, and she had not been able to deny it away entirely.

But the dreams were different.

What happened in dreams left no trace whatsoever. She could not go out of her way to confirm any of it.

Better to stay safe. Continue playing ignorant.

With that decided, Jiyao drew a long breath and let her mind go quiet.

A long while later, she finally slept.

...

In the inner chambers of Zichen Palace.

That night, Qin Yuan had incense lit — the soothing kind that eased sleep. He had grown used to its scent over the months. He closed his eyes, cleared his mind, and drifted off without effort.

He was quite certain that Second Miss Fang had heard his parting words. He had watched her face carefully.

But the night passed. He slept deeply, and the strange dream did not come.

Qin Yuan was displeased. He tried consciously to steer himself toward it.

It was no use. He could dream — he could even shape the contents of ordinary dreams — but the particular quality of that other dream, the full-bodied, vividly present quality, simply was not there.

After several failed attempts, Qin Yuan was forced to acknowledge the truth: he could not enter that dream by his own will. Every time he had been there before, it had happened without any intention on his part.

Which meant it depended on her. What was happening on her end?

Had she not understood? Or had she simply chosen to treat his words as nothing?

The hour before dawn. The lamps burned low. The young Emperor's expression was dark.

The eunuch on duty had stopped yawning entirely, standing rigidly at the edge of the room, awaiting instruction.

None came. The Emperor's gaze was distant and still, and he said nothing for a long while.

Eventually the hour arrived for morning court. Qin Yuan allowed his attendants to dress him.

A row of young eunuchs brought forward basins of water, cloths, and washing implements. He washed his face and hands, dried them, set down the cloth, and said: "Summon Zhang Zan. I want him here after morning court."

"Yes."

...

When Zhang Zan heard the Emperor wished to see him, he felt a quiet headache coming on.

Gathering intelligence, running investigations — that was the work he and his operatives excelled at. But ever since His Majesty had started directing him to look into matters involving women of the inner court, things had grown considerably more difficult.

First the owner of a bracelet. Then a person entering a tournament in disguise. Then tracking someone down from a portrait.

Before entering the imperial presence, Zhang Zan said a private prayer: please let this not be another search for a person.

But the Emperor opened with: "Zhang Zan. I need you to look into someone."

Zhang Zan's eye twitched. "Who does Your Majesty wish to inquire about?"

"The Second Miss Fang, granddaughter of Minister Fang." Qin Yuan's voice was neutral. "Find out if she is ill."

He supposed he ought to give her some margin. If she was genuinely unwell, he could afford to be magnanimous about the previous night.

Zhang Zan wondered if he had misheard. That was it?

He, the head of the imperial intelligence network, was being sent to find out whether a sheltered young lady from a good family had a cold?

And how was it Fang's Second Miss again?

But one does not express such thoughts before the Emperor. Zhang Zan bowed dutifully. "Yes, Your Majesty. I accept the commission."

He withdrew.

Zhang Zan had been making inquiries at the Fang household frequently enough to have developed useful channels by now. Where inner-court women were concerned, his people could not go directly in to observe whether a young lady was unwell, but they could gather information from the outside and piece it together.

The next day, Zhang Zan returned to report.

The Emperor was reviewing memorials. He did not look up. "Well?"

"Your Majesty, it appears the Second Miss Fang is not unwell." Zhang Zan chose his words carefully.

Qin Yuan disliked the phrasing. "Appears?"

Zhang Zan hastened to clarify: "Your subject did not observe the Second Miss Fang directly. However, inquiries reveal that no physician has been called to the Fang household in the past three days, and the Second Miss Fang attended her lessons as usual today."

"Mm." Qin Yuan set down his brush, and let his eyes narrow slightly. If she was well enough to attend lessons, she was in all likelihood not ill.

He need not go on finding excuses on her behalf.

Zhang Zan hesitated, then added: "As it happens, there was a joyful occasion for the Second Miss Fang two days ago."

Qin Yuan frowned. "A joyful occasion?"

"Yes — two days ago, a family sent a go-between to the Fang household to make a formal marriage proposal. Minister Fang accepted."

Zhang Zan had weighed whether to mention this at all.

He remembered the Emperor asking him a few days ago to investigate the Second Miss's matrimonial situation. At that time, there had been nothing to report. But circumstances had since changed, and it seemed right to inform him.

He kept his voice low, and stole a look at the Emperor's expression as he finished speaking.

Qin Yuan raised his head sharply. His eyes were knife-edged. His voice, without quite meaning to, rose a fraction. "Say that again. A marriage proposal?"

"Yes. Two days ago, a family sent a go-between to formally present a marriage proposal." Zhang Zan had not anticipated this reaction, and felt a sudden alertness. He answered directly: "It was the first rite — the presentation of the proposal."

Qin Yuan's expression closed like a shutter. His face was markedly unpleasant.

He knew the first rite. In the six formal rites of marriage, the first step — the presentation of the proposal — indicated that both families had expressed willingness to form an alliance. Unless something went wrong, the steps of inquiry, declaration, betrothal gifts, setting the date, and finally marriage would follow in sequence.

He had been wondering whether she was ill. In fact, she had been attending to a marriage negotiation.

Which made the absence from the dream quite easy to understand.

He remembered it clearly. In the last of those strange dreams, Second Miss Fang had said it herself, without hesitation: "One should behave with principle. I cannot be conducting a marriage negotiation on one side and conducting myself with you in dreams on the other. That would be unfair to the other person."

And then she had walked away from him without a backward glance, to conduct exactly that negotiation.

Excellent. How very thorough of her.

A wave of fury rose in Qin Yuan's chest, nearly swallowing him whole. He drew a slow breath and held it, bearing down on the unfamiliar emotion until it subsided.

He closed his eyes, then asked in a measured voice: "Who came to propose?"

"His name is Lu Ming," Zhang Zan reported. "He is the younger brother of General Lu Xiao. He does not follow a military path but has pursued a scholarly one since childhood, and has already passed the xiucai examination. He currently studies at the Fang family school."

Qin Yuan let out a short, cold laugh. At the Fang family school, of all places.

Zhang Zan really was useless, not to have uncovered this earlier.

Not that Lu Ming's path or his degree interested Qin Yuan in the slightest. What mattered was the thought that had been crystallizing in him, sharp and clear: he did not want Second Miss Fang's marriage negotiations to proceed.

He had spent a long time unable to think of the right form of revenge. Now, perhaps, he had found it.
